Using S3 Vectors requires running your own OpenSearch cluster

explanation: S3 Vectors is a supported KB vector store; Bedrock ingests and writes embeddings into the S3 Vectors index. Not "S3 Vectors cannot be used with Bedrock Knowledge Bases": It is supported as a KB vector store. Not "S3 Vectors only stores text, not embeddings": S3 Vectors is purpose-built to store and query embeddings. Not "Using S3 Vectors requires running your own OpenSearch clu…": S3 Vectors is independent of OpenSearch. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A near-real-time, resilient ingestion pipeline must add newly uploaded S3 documents to a Knowledge Base ASAP and remove deleted ones ASAP, tolerating spikes. Which architecture is best?

options.text: Manual re-ingestion through the console
EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes to scan S3 and re-sync
S3 Event Notifications → Amazon SQS → Lambda that calls IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments / DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments
S3 → Lambda directly with no queue

explanation: An SQS queue holds the S3 events during spikes until the Lambda function has processed them, delivers them in batches, and makes a failed batch visible again for retry, so ingestion is resilient and event-driven. The function calls the direct-ingestion APIs, which are supported for S3 and custom data sources. Not "Manual re-ingestion through the console": Manual steps do not meet the automated, near-real-time requirement. Not "EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes to scan S3 and re-sync": Polling on a schedule is time-based, not near-real-time, and is inefficient. Not "S3 → Lambda directly with no queue": S3 invokes Lambda asynchronously, and Lambda does queue and retry those events (a function error is retried two more times, throttling for up to 6 hours). But when the function cannot keep up, events can expire or be deleted from that internal queue without being processed, which an SQS queue in front of the function avoids. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async-error-handling.html

prompt: A team needs to monitor Knowledge Base data ingestion to troubleshoot why some documents fail to process (e.g., ignored, embedding failed, indexing failed). Which solution is correct?

options.text: Use AWS CloudTrail to see document-level processing details
Use Bedrock model invocation logging
Enable Knowledge Base logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and query statuses with Logs Insights
Enable CloudWatch Application Signals

explanation: KB logging records per-file ingestion status (e.g., RESOURCE_IGNORED, EMBEDDING_FAILED, INDEXING_FAILED) to CloudWatch. Not "Use AWS CloudTrail to see document-level processing details": CloudTrail logs API calls, not per-document ingestion status. Not "Use Bedrock model invocation logging": That logs inference calls, not KB ingestion. Not "Enable CloudWatch Application Signals": Application Signals monitors app performance, not KB ingestion. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: An Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base must pull content from a managed SaaS source. Which TWO are native data-source connectors it supports? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Amazon Lightsail
Amazon Inspector
Confluence
Microsoft SharePoint
AWS Step Functions

explanation: Confluence is a native connector of a Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. Microsoft SharePoint is a native connector of a Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. Status note: starting September 30, 2026, new Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Salesforce and Web Crawler connectors can no longer be created on customer-managed knowledge bases (existing ones keep working); AWS points applications that need these connectors to a Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, whose native connectors are S3, SharePoint, Confluence, Web Crawler, Google Drive, OneDrive and Custom. Salesforce is not in the Managed Knowledge Base list, although older material names it as a Knowledge Bases connector. Not "Amazon Lightsail": Lightsail is simplified compute hosting, not a data source connector. Not "Amazon Inspector": Inspector is vulnerability scanning, not a data source. Not "AWS Step Functions": Step Functions orchestrates workflows; it is not a KB data source. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-build-managed.html

prompt: Which statement about the Retrieve vs RetrieveAndGenerate APIs is correct?

options.text: Both always call a foundation model
Retrieve returns chunks only; RetrieveAndGenerate returns chunks plus an FM-generated answer
Neither can be used for RAG
RetrieveAndGenerate returns only raw chunks

explanation: Retrieve = retrieval only; RetrieveAndGenerate = retrieval + generation. Not "Both always call a foundation model": Retrieve does not call an FM. Not "Neither can be used for RAG": Both are core RAG APIs for Knowledge Bases. Not "RetrieveAndGenerate returns only raw chunks": It also generates an answer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team must store binary (quantized) vectors to save memory in their vector store for a Knowledge Base. Which store supports binary vectors?

options.text: Amazon S3 Vectors
Amazon OpenSearch (Serverless or managed cluster)
Amazon Timestream
Amazon DynamoDB

explanation: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and Amazon OpenSearch Managed clusters are the only Knowledge Bases vector stores that support storing binary vectors. Not "Amazon S3 Vectors": S3 Vectors supports only floating-point embeddings; binary embeddings are not supported. Not "Amazon Timestream": Timestream is time-series, not a vector store. Not "Amazon DynamoDB": DynamoDB is not one of the vector stores Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: An OpenSearch Serverless workload ingests new data rarely but serves a very high volume of vector queries. How should capacity be approached?

options.text: Scale search OCUs up for query volume while keeping indexing OCUs low, since they scale independently
Add a NAT gateway to improve query speed
Increase indexing OCUs to speed up queries
Switch to Provisioned Throughput model units

explanation: Because search and indexing scale separately, you can right-size each to the workload. Not "Add a NAT gateway to improve query speed": Networking does not change OCU-based search capacity. Not "Increase indexing OCUs to speed up queries": Indexing OCUs do not serve query throughput; search OCUs do. Not "Switch to Provisioned Throughput model units": Model Units are a Bedrock model-capacity concept, not OpenSearch query capacity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A team with an existing Amazon Kendra index wants to combine it with a Bedrock FM for grounded answers. What is the typical role split?

options.text: Kendra generates the final answer and the FM indexes data
Kendra retrieves relevant passages from indexed enterprise content; the Bedrock FM generates the answer from those passages
Kendra reserves model capacity for the FM
Both train a new model on each query

explanation: Kendra supplies retrieval/grounding (its Retrieve API returns relevant passages) and has no native answer generation, so the FM composes the final response from those passages. Status note: Kendra entered maintenance mode on June 30, 2026 and has been closed to new customers since July 30, 2026; existing customers stay fully supported, and AWS recommends Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base for new search and RAG applications. A Managed Knowledge Base does both steps natively through its RetrieveAndGenerate API. Not "Kendra generates the final answer and the FM indexes data": This reverses their roles. Not "Kendra reserves model capacity for the FM": Capacity reservation is Provisioned Throughput, unrelated to Kendra. Not "Both train a new model on each query": Neither trains a model per query. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kendra/latest/dg/kendra-availability-change.html

prompt: Which statement about IVFFlat vs HNSW indexes (as used in stores like DocumentDB) is most accurate?

options.text: They only apply to relational joins
Both are approximate-nearest-neighbor index types for vector search, trading off build time, memory, and recall differently
They are encryption algorithms for vectors
They are foundation models

explanation: HNSW (graph-based) and IVFFlat (inverted-file) are both ANN index types with different performance/recall trade-offs. Not "They only apply to relational joins": They are for vector similarity search, not relational joins. Not "They are encryption algorithms for vectors": They are index structures, not encryption. Not "They are foundation models": They are vector index types, not models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: A retrieval system over highly connected/graph-structured knowledge wants vector search integrated with graph relationships in a managed store usable by a Knowledge Base. Which option fits?

options.text: Amazon S3 (general-purpose bucket)
Amazon Neptune Analytics
Amazon CloudSearch
Amazon DynamoDB

explanation: Neptune Analytics combines graph analytics with vector search and is a supported KB vector store (GraphRAG). Not "Amazon S3 (general-purpose bucket)": A standard bucket is object storage, not a graph+vector store. Not "Amazon CloudSearch": CloudSearch is legacy text search, not a graph+vector KB store. Not "Amazon DynamoDB": DynamoDB is a key-value and document database; it has vector search since August 2026 but is not a graph store and is not a Bedrock Knowledge Bases vector store. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: In a Bedrock Knowledge Base, why is the source content split into "chunks" before embedding?

options.text: To reserve model capacity
To encrypt the documents
To convert audio to text
So each piece fits embedding/context limits and retrieval returns focused, relevant passages

explanation: Chunking keeps units small enough to embed and retrieve precisely, improving relevance and fitting context windows. Not "To reserve model capacity": That is Provisioned Throughput, not chunking. Not "To encrypt the documents": Chunking is about segmentation for retrieval, not encryption. Not "To convert audio to text": That is transcription, unrelated to chunking. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Which TWO chunking strategies are offered by Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: OCU chunking
Fixed-size chunking
Semantic chunking
Temperature chunking
Shard chunking

explanation: Fixed-size splits text into uniform token/character windows. Semantic chunking splits on meaning boundaries to keep coherent ideas together. Not "OCU chunking": OCUs are OpenSearch capacity units, not a chunking strategy. Not "Temperature chunking": There is no "temperature chunking"; temperature is an inference parameter. Not "Shard chunking": Sharding is a vector-index concept, not a KB chunking strategy. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A document set has nested structure (sections, subsections) and the team wants retrieval to use both fine-grained child chunks and broader parent context. Which chunking strategy fits best?

options.text: No chunking (one big document)
Fixed-size only
Hierarchical chunking
Custom chunking with random splits

explanation: Hierarchical chunking creates parent/child chunks so retrieval can use granular matches with broader context. Not "No chunking (one big document)": A single large chunk loses granularity and hurts retrieval precision. Not "Fixed-size only": Fixed-size ignores the document's nested structure. Not "Custom chunking with random splits": Random splits do not capture hierarchy and degrade relevance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team has small, self-contained records where each document is already a single coherent unit. Which Knowledge Base chunking option may be appropriate?

options.text: Semantic chunking with tiny windows
Fixed-size chunking at 10 tokens
Hierarchical chunking with many levels
No chunking — treat each document as one chunk

explanation: When documents are short and self-contained, the "no chunking" option indexes each as a single chunk. Not "Semantic chunking with tiny windows": Over-splitting atomic records can fragment meaning. Not "Fixed-size chunking at 10 tokens": Extremely small fixed chunks destroy context for whole-record content. Not "Hierarchical chunking with many levels": Hierarchy adds needless complexity for already-atomic records. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team needs full control over how content is split (e.g., by their own delimiters or a Lambda transformation) in a Bedrock Knowledge Base. Which option supports this?

options.text: Sharding
Fixed-size chunking only
Custom chunking (e.g., via a Lambda transformation)
No chunking

explanation: Custom chunking lets you define your own splitting logic, including a Lambda-based transformation. Not "Sharding": Sharding is a storage-layer concept, not content splitting. Not "Fixed-size chunking only": Fixed-size cannot express custom delimiter logic. Not "No chunking": No chunking is the opposite of fine-grained custom control. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports configurable output dimensions. Which set of dimensions is supported?

options.text: 256, 512, or 1024 dimensions
16, 32, or 64 dimensions
Exactly 1 dimension
Unlimited arbitrary dimensions

explanation: Titan Text Embeddings V2 can output 256, 512, or 1024 dimensions, trading storage/speed against fidelity. The older Titan Embeddings G1 - Text model is fixed at 1,536 dimensions. Not "16, 32, or 64 dimensions": These are not the supported Titan embedding sizes. Not "Exactly 1 dimension": Embeddings are high-dimensional vectors, not scalars. Not "Unlimited arbitrary dimensions": Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports specific sizes (256/512/1024), not arbitrary values. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: What is a practical trade-off of choosing a smaller embedding dimension (e.g., 256 vs 1024) with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2?

options.text: Smaller dimensions always improve accuracy
Smaller dimensions require Provisioned Throughput
Smaller dimensions reduce storage and can speed search, potentially at some loss of representational fidelity
Dimension size has no effect on storage

explanation: Lower-dimensional vectors cost less to store/search but may capture slightly less nuance; higher values improve accuracy but increase cost and latency. Only Titan Text Embeddings V2 offers the choice (1,024, 512 or 256); Titan Embeddings G1 - Text is fixed at 1,536. Not "Smaller dimensions always improve accuracy": Fewer dimensions can reduce fidelity; it is a trade-off, not a pure win. Not "Smaller dimensions require Provisioned Throughput": Dimension choice is unrelated to capacity reservation. Not "Dimension size has no effect on storage": Dimension directly affects vector storage size. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-create.html

prompt: A search experience must match both exact keywords (like product codes) and semantic meaning. Which retrieval approach combines both?

options.text: Pure keyword search only
Pure vector search only
Random retrieval
Hybrid search — combining keyword (BM25) and semantic vector search

explanation: Hybrid search blends lexical BM25 matching with vector semantic matching for better coverage. Not "Pure keyword search only": Keyword-only misses semantic matches and paraphrases. Not "Pure vector search only": Vector-only can miss exact tokens like codes/IDs. Not "Random retrieval": Randomness is not a retrieval strategy. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: In hybrid search, what does the "BM25" component contribute?

options.text: Neural embedding generation
Vector dimensionality reduction
Lexical/keyword relevance scoring based on term frequency
Document chunking

explanation: BM25 is a classic keyword ranking function; it provides the lexical half of hybrid search. Not "Neural embedding generation": Embeddings power the vector half, not BM25. Not "Vector dimensionality reduction": BM25 is a ranking function, not a dimensionality technique. Not "Document chunking": BM25 ranks, it does not chunk. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: After initial retrieval, the most relevant passages sometimes rank below less relevant ones. The team wants a managed way to reorder results by query relevance with minimal custom code. Which Bedrock capability fits?

options.text: The Amazon Bedrock Rerank API with a reranker model
Switching to no chunking
Increasing model temperature
Sharding the vector index

explanation: The Rerank API uses a cross-encoder reranker to reorder retrieved passages by relevance to the query. Not "Switching to no chunking": Chunking strategy does not reorder results by relevance. Not "Increasing model temperature": Temperature affects generation randomness, not retrieval ordering. Not "Sharding the vector index": Sharding affects capacity/latency, not relevance ranking. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Which TWO reranker models are available through the Amazon Bedrock Rerank API? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Cohere Rerank 3.5
Claude Rerank 2
Titan Image Generator
Stable Diffusion
Amazon Rerank 1.0

explanation: Cohere Rerank 3.5 is available via the Bedrock Rerank API. Amazon Rerank 1.0 is offered through the Rerank API. Not "Claude Rerank 2": No such Bedrock reranker model; rerankers are Amazon Rerank and Cohere Rerank. Not "Titan Image Generator": That is an image model, not a reranker. Not "Stable Diffusion": Stable Diffusion is an image model, not a reranker. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: How can reranking be applied to a Bedrock Knowledge Base query?

options.text: Reranking requires Provisioned Throughput on the embeddings model
Reranking is only available outside AWS
Enable the reranker as a setting in the Retrieve / RetrieveAndGenerate request
It can only be used by training a custom model

explanation: KB users turn on reranking through the Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate APIs. Not "Reranking requires Provisioned Throughput on the embeddin…": Reranking is invoked via the API; it does not mandate provisioned embeddings capacity. Not "Reranking is only available outside AWS": It is available in Amazon Bedrock. Not "It can only be used by training a custom model": Reranking is a managed feature, no custom training needed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Why does a reranker (cross-encoder) often improve RAG relevance compared to vector similarity alone?

options.text: It guarantees deterministic generation
It jointly examines the query and each candidate passage to score true relevance, refining the first-stage results
It increases the embedding dimension automatically
It removes the need for any retrieval step

explanation: Cross-encoders consider query+passage together, capturing relevance signals a single-vector similarity may miss. Not "It guarantees deterministic generation": Reranking orders passages; it does not control generation determinism. Not "It increases the embedding dimension automatically": Reranking does not change embedding dimensions. Not "It removes the need for any retrieval step": Reranking refines retrieved candidates; retrieval still happens first. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A RAG app starts returning "no relevant information found" after a deploy. The FM invokes fine, OpenSearch is healthy, latency is normal, and there are no errors. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The temperature parameter was increased
The query embeddings are now generated by a different embedding model/version than the one used to index the documents
The IAM role lost bedrock:InvokeModel
The vector index was sharded

explanation: Embedding drift creates a vector-space mismatch between queries and stored vectors, silently breaking retrieval. Not "The temperature parameter was increased": Temperature affects generation, not retrieval matching. Not "The IAM role lost bedrock:InvokeModel": The FM invokes successfully, so the permission is present. Not "The vector index was sharded": Sharding affects capacity/latency, not vector-space alignment. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Which rule must hold for vector retrieval to work correctly?

options.text: Embeddings must be regenerated for every query at index time
Any embedding model can be mixed freely
Queries must always use a larger embedding model than indexing
Query embeddings must be produced by the same embedding model used to index the documents

explanation: Matching the embedding model/version keeps queries and documents in the same vector space. Not "Embeddings must be regenerated for every query at index time": Document embeddings are created at ingestion; queries are embedded at query time with the same model. Not "Any embedding model can be mixed freely": Mixing models causes a vector-space mismatch and poor retrieval. Not "Queries must always use a larger embedding model than ind…": They must match, not differ by size. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team is deciding chunk size. What is the typical trade-off between very large and very small chunks?

options.text: Smaller chunks always retrieve better in every case
Large chunks preserve context but can dilute relevance and exceed limits; small chunks are precise but may lose surrounding context
Larger chunks always reduce cost
Chunk size has no effect on retrieval quality

explanation: Chunk size trades context retention against retrieval precision and token limits. Not "Smaller chunks always retrieve better in every case": Too-small chunks can lose needed context. Not "Larger chunks always reduce cost": Larger chunks can increase tokens per retrieval and cost. Not "Chunk size has no effect on retrieval quality": Chunk size materially affects relevance and context. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team wants chunk boundaries that follow the meaning of the text (paragraph/topic shifts) rather than arbitrary token counts. Which strategy should they pick?

options.text: Semantic chunking
Sharding
Fixed-size chunking
No chunking

explanation: Semantic chunking places boundaries at meaning shifts to keep coherent ideas intact. Not "Sharding": Sharding is storage distribution, not semantic splitting. Not "Fixed-size chunking": Fixed-size splits by counts regardless of meaning. Not "No chunking": No chunking keeps the whole document as one unit. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A developer is exposing tools to an LLM-based application using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). For a lightweight, event-driven MCP server, which AWS compute pattern is recommended?

options.text: Store it as an S3 object
Run it only on a developer laptop in production
Run it on a dedicated mainframe
Run the MCP server on AWS Lambda

explanation: A common AWS pattern is hosting a lightweight MCP server on Lambda for serverless, event-driven tool exposure. Not "Store it as an S3 object": An MCP server is a running service, not a static object. Not "Run it only on a developer laptop in production": Local laptops are not a production hosting pattern. Not "Run it on a dedicated mainframe": Mainframes are not an AWS MCP hosting pattern. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A complex, long-running MCP server needs more control over runtime, networking, and resources than a function provides. Which AWS pattern fits best?

options.text: Host it as a static website on S3
Use Amazon SES
Convert it to a CloudFront function
Run the MCP server on Amazon ECS (containers)

explanation: For complex/long-running MCP servers, containers on ECS give more control than Lambda. Not "Host it as a static website on S3": Static hosting cannot run a stateful MCP server. Not "Use Amazon SES": SES is email, not compute for an MCP server. Not "Convert it to a CloudFront function": CloudFront functions are tiny edge scripts, unsuitable for a complex MCP server. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: What does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardize?

options.text: How S3 buckets replicate
How vectors are quantized for storage
How AI applications/agents connect to external tools and data sources through a common protocol
How IAM roles are rotated

explanation: MCP is an open protocol for connecting models/agents to tools and context sources uniformly. Not "How S3 buckets replicate": Bucket replication is unrelated to MCP. Not "How vectors are quantized for storage": That is a vector-storage concern, not MCP. Not "How IAM roles are rotated": Credential rotation is unrelated to MCP. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Which TWO statements about combining hybrid search and reranking in a RAG pipeline are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Hybrid search only works without embeddings
Reranking improves precision by reordering the retrieved candidates by relevance
Both require fine-tuning the base model
Reranking replaces the need to retrieve any candidates
Hybrid search broadens recall by mixing keyword and semantic matches

explanation: A reranker refines ordering so the best passages surface first. Hybrid search improves the set of candidate passages retrieved. Not "Hybrid search only works without embeddings": Hybrid search specifically uses embeddings plus keywords. Not "Both require fine-tuning the base model": Neither requires fine-tuning the generation model. Not "Reranking replaces the need to retrieve any candidates": Reranking operates on already-retrieved candidates. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team's retrieval returns many candidates but the final answer quality is limited by irrelevant top results. With minimal overhead, what is the best next step?

options.text: Disable chunking entirely
Add a Bedrock reranker (Rerank API) to reorder candidates before generation
Switch the vector store to DynamoDB
Increase max tokens on the FM

explanation: A reranker model scores the retrieved chunks against the query and reorders them, a low-overhead, managed way to push the most relevant passages to the top. Not "Disable chunking entirely": Removing chunking typically hurts retrieval precision. Not "Switch the vector store to DynamoDB": Changing the vector store does not reorder the retrieved candidates, and DynamoDB is not a vector store that Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports. Not "Increase max tokens on the FM": More tokens do not improve which passages are most relevant. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/rerank.html

prompt: A team wants a managed library to create, parameterize, test, and version prompt templates that multiple applications reuse. Which Amazon Bedrock feature provides this?

options.text: AWS CodeCommit
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

explanation: Prompt Management lets you create and save reusable prompts with variables, compare variants while testing, and save versions to use in applications. Not "AWS CodeCommit": CodeCommit is a Git repo, not a Bedrock prompt template service. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails enforce content policies; they do not version prompts. Not "Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases": Knowledge Bases handle RAG, not prompt versioning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A company must govern prompt templates used across business units: versioned templates, controlled access, and an approval step before a new version is used in production, with minimal operational overhead. Which solution fits best?

options.text: Store prompts in DynamoDB and build a custom approval app
Keep prompts only in application source code
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management for versioned templates, with IAM policies limiting who can create versions and a manual approval action in the release pipeline
Email prompt diffs for manual sign-off

explanation: Prompt Management supplies the managed, versioned prompt library, and IAM policies scope who may perform its actions. It has no built-in approval workflow, so the approval gate comes from the release process, for example a manual approval action in AWS CodePipeline before the application is pointed at a new prompt version. Not "Store prompts in DynamoDB and build a custom approval app": Custom storage and approval logic adds significant development and maintenance overhead. Not "Keep prompts only in application source code": Embedding prompts in code lacks a governed, reusable prompt library. Not "Email prompt diffs for manual sign-off": Manual email review is not scalable or auditable. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-deploy.html

prompt: A no-code builder is needed to visually chain prompts, models, and logic into a generative AI workflow without writing orchestration code. Which Bedrock feature is this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
AWS Step Functions Workflow Studio
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows)

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows) provides a visual builder for linking prompts, foundation models and other AWS services into an end-to-end workflow. Not "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management": Prompt Management creates and versions reusable prompts; Flows orchestrates them into workflows. Not "AWS Step Functions Workflow Studio": Step Functions is general orchestration; the Bedrock-native visual generative AI workflow builder is Flows. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails are safety policies, not a workflow builder. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows.html

prompt: A developer wants the model to stop generating as soon as it produces a specific phrase or delimiter. Which inference parameter should they use?

options.text: temperature
max_tokens only
stop_sequences
top_k

explanation: Stop sequences deterministically halt generation when a specified string is produced. Not "temperature": Temperature controls randomness, not where generation stops. Not "max_tokens only": max_tokens caps length but cannot stop precisely at a chosen phrase. Not "top_k": top_k limits candidate tokens; it does not stop on a phrase. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Which statement best contrasts stop_sequences, temperature, and top_k?

options.text: stop_sequences control WHERE generation ends; temperature controls HOW random it is; top_k controls HOW MANY candidate tokens are considered
They are all storage settings
All three control where generation stops
temperature controls stopping and top_k controls randomness

explanation: Each parameter governs a different aspect: stopping, randomness, and candidate breadth. Not "They are all storage settings": They are inference parameters, not storage settings. Not "All three control where generation stops": Only stop_sequences controls stopping. Not "temperature controls stopping and top_k controls randomness": These roles are swapped/incorrect. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A team wants more deterministic, focused output from a model for a compliance-sensitive summarization task. Which parameter change is most appropriate?

options.text: Lower the temperature toward 0
Raise the temperature near maximum
Add more stop sequences to increase creativity
Increase max_tokens to reduce randomness

explanation: Lower temperature reduces randomness, producing more deterministic, focused output. Not "Raise the temperature near maximum": High temperature increases randomness, the opposite of deterministic. Not "Add more stop sequences to increase creativity": Stop sequences end generation; they do not control creativity. Not "Increase max_tokens to reduce randomness": max_tokens affects length, not determinism. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Which inference parameter limits sampling to the top K most probable next tokens?

options.text: presence_penalty
top_k
stop_sequences
temperature

explanation: top_k restricts sampling to the K highest-probability tokens. Not "presence_penalty": Presence penalty discourages repetition; it is not a top-K cap. Not "stop_sequences": Stop sequences end generation; they do not limit token candidates. Not "temperature": Temperature scales the probability distribution; it does not cap the candidate count. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Which inference parameter uses cumulative probability (nucleus sampling) to choose the candidate token set?

options.text: max_tokens
top_p
stop_sequences
top_k

explanation: top_p (nucleus sampling) selects the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p. Not "max_tokens": max_tokens caps output length, not sampling. Not "stop_sequences": Stop sequences end generation, not select candidates. Not "top_k": top_k uses a fixed count, not cumulative probability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A team needs an audit trail of who used which prompt and runtime logs for a governed prompt library. Which TWO AWS services support observability for Bedrock Prompt Management? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Amazon Macie
Amazon CloudWatch Logs for runtime logging
Amazon Polly
AWS Shield
AWS CloudTrail for API usage/auditing

explanation: CloudWatch Logs captures runtime logs for monitoring prompt activity. CloudTrail records Bedrock API calls, providing an audit trail of prompt usage. Not "Amazon Macie": Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it is not a Prompt Management observability tool. Not "Amazon Polly": Polly is text-to-speech, unrelated to observability. Not "AWS Shield": Shield is DDoS protection, unrelated to prompt observability. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management from Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows)?

options.text: Both are vector stores
They are the same feature with different names
Flows stores versioned prompts and Prompt Management builds workflows
Prompt Management is a versioned library of reusable prompt templates; Flows is a visual builder for linking prompts, models and other services into workflows

explanation: Prompt Management = create, test and version reusable prompts; Flows = link prompts, models and other AWS services into a workflow in a visual builder. Not "Both are vector stores": Neither is a vector store. Not "They are the same feature with different names": They are distinct: one stores prompts, the other orchestrates workflows. Not "Flows stores versioned prompts and Prompt Management buil…": This reverses their roles. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows.html

prompt: A prompt asks the model to finish its answer with a closing delimiter such as `</answer>`, but the model keeps generating extra text after the delimiter. Which parameter cleanly ends generation at that boundary?

options.text: Increasing top_k
stop_sequences set to the expected end delimiter
Lowering max_tokens to 1
Increasing temperature

explanation: Stop sequences are character sequences that stop the model from generating further tokens: once the model generates the delimiter, it stops. Not "Increasing top_k": top_k changes candidate breadth, not stopping behavior. Not "Lowering max_tokens to 1": Truncating to one token breaks the output rather than stopping at the right boundary. Not "Increasing temperature": Higher temperature adds randomness; it does not control termination. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-parameters.html

prompt: A team wants reusable prompts with input variables that applications fill at runtime (e.g., {{customer_name}}). Which capability supports parameterized prompt templates?

options.text: AWS AppConfig feature flags
Amazon SQS
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management (parameterized prompt templates with versions)

explanation: Prompt Management prompts can include variables in double curly braces that are filled in when the prompt is called, and the prompt can be saved as versions for reuse. Not "AWS AppConfig feature flags": AppConfig manages application configuration, not parameterized prompt templates. Not "Amazon SQS": SQS is messaging, not prompt templating. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails filter content; they do not template prompts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-create.html

prompt: Which scenario is the best use case for Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows)?

options.text: Detecting PII in documents
Reserving model capacity
Storing 7 years of model invocation logs
Visually orchestrating a multi-step GenAI process (e.g., classify → retrieve → summarize) without writing orchestration code

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Flows links prompts, foundation models and other AWS services in a visual builder to create multi-step generative AI workflows. Not "Detecting PII in documents": That is Comprehend, not Flows. Not "Reserving model capacity": That is Provisioned Throughput. Not "Storing 7 years of model invocation logs": That is invocation logging to S3, not Flows. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows.html

prompt: A team wants to compare two versions of a prompt template and roll back if the new one performs worse. Which feature supports this?

options.text: HNSW index tuning
Cross-Region inference profiles
Stop sequences
Prompt versioning in Bedrock Prompt Management

explanation: Prompt Management versions templates so you can compare and revert. Not "HNSW index tuning": That is vector index tuning, unrelated to prompts. Not "Cross-Region inference profiles": Profiles route traffic; they do not version prompts. Not "Stop sequences": Stop sequences end generation; they do not version prompts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: What does raising the temperature parameter generally do to model output?

options.text: Reduces the vocabulary to one token
Guarantees factual accuracy
Increases randomness/creativity and diversity of responses
Forces the model to stop sooner

explanation: Higher temperature flattens the distribution, yielding more varied output. Not "Reduces the vocabulary to one token": It does not collapse the vocabulary to a single token. Not "Guarantees factual accuracy": Temperature does not control factual correctness. Not "Forces the model to stop sooner": Stopping is controlled by stop_sequences/max_tokens, not temperature. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A regulated workload requires capturing full prompt content and model responses for 7 years with immutable retention and minimal overhead. Which combination is best?

options.text: CloudTrail data events only
Storing logs in an ephemeral cache
Prompt Flows execution history only
Bedrock model invocation logging to Amazon S3 with S3 Object Lock (compliance mode) for 7-year retention

explanation: Invocation logging captures prompts/responses; S3 Object Lock enforces immutable retention. Not "CloudTrail data events only": CloudTrail logs API metadata, not full prompt/response content. Not "Storing logs in an ephemeral cache": Ephemeral storage cannot meet immutable long-term retention. Not "Prompt Flows execution history only": Flow history is not a compliant 7-year immutable record of all invocations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer relies on a prompt instruction ("please stop after the summary") to halt generation, but the model sometimes ignores it. What is the more reliable mechanism?

options.text: Increase temperature
Repeat the instruction three times in the prompt
Lower top_p to 0
Use the stop_sequences inference parameter

explanation: Stop sequences are enforced by the API and reliably terminate generation, unlike prompt-only instructions. Not "Increase temperature": That adds randomness and makes behavior less controlled. Not "Repeat the instruction three times in the prompt": Restating instructions does not reliably enforce stopping. Not "Lower top_p to 0": top_p shapes candidate selection, not stopping. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A team wants consistent, governed prompts injected into a real-time application that routes by request type, with the ability to update prompts without redeploying code. Which approach is most aligned?

options.text: Store prompts only in client-side JavaScript
Manage prompts centrally in Bedrock Prompt Management and reference versioned templates at runtime
Use Provisioned Throughput to manage prompts
Hard-code each prompt variant in the Lambda source

explanation: Central versioned templates let you update governed prompts without code redeploys. Not "Store prompts only in client-side JavaScript": Client-side prompts are ungoverned and insecure. Not "Use Provisioned Throughput to manage prompts": Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity; it does not manage prompts. Not "Hard-code each prompt variant in the Lambda source": Hard-coding requires redeploying to change prompts and lacks governance. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A team wants a managed agent on Amazon Bedrock that can reason over a task, call APIs/tools, and consult a knowledge base, without building the orchestration loop themselves. Which feature fits?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Amazon SageMaker Processing
Amazon Bedrock Agents
Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows)

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Agents orchestrates interactions between the foundation model, data sources, software applications and the user conversation, automatically calling APIs and invoking knowledge bases, so the team does not write the orchestration loop. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is the managed agent harness, where you declare the model, tools and instructions and AgentCore runs the loop. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails enforce content safety; they are not an agent runtime. Not "Amazon SageMaker Processing": Processing runs data jobs, not agents. Not "Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows)": Flows links prompts, models and other services into a workflow that you lay out in a visual builder; it is not the managed agent feature. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: How can tools (actions) be defined for an Amazon Bedrock Agents agent? (Select TWO.)

options.text: By setting the temperature parameter
By creating an S3 lifecycle policy
With an OpenAPI schema describing the API actions
With function definitions (function details) for the actions
By uploading a vector index

explanation: An action group in Amazon Bedrock Agents is defined either with an OpenAPI schema that describes each action as an API operation, or with function details that list the parameters the agent must elicit. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is tools exposed through AgentCore Gateway as MCP tools that wrap REST APIs and Lambda functions. Not "By setting the temperature parameter": Temperature is an inference setting, not a tool definition. Not "By creating an S3 lifecycle policy": Lifecycle policies manage object storage, not agent tools. Not "By uploading a vector index": A vector index is for retrieval, not tool definitions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/action-define.html

prompt: A developer is debugging why an Amazon Bedrock Agents agent chose certain steps. Which capability lets them inspect the agent's reasoning/decision steps?

options.text: Agent tracing
S3 access logs
VPC Flow Logs
AWS Config timeline

explanation: Each agent response can be accompanied by a trace that details the steps the agent orchestrated, including its reasoning and the inputs and outputs of the action groups and knowledge bases it used. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is AgentCore Observability, which gives persistent end-to-end tracing of agent actions. Not "S3 access logs": S3 access logs track object requests, not agent reasoning. Not "VPC Flow Logs": Flow Logs capture network traffic, not agent decisions. Not "AWS Config timeline": Config tracks resource changes, not agent reasoning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/trace-events.html

prompt: A company needs to deploy and operate AI agents at scale in production, with managed serverless runtime, identity, tool gateway, memory, and observability — usable with multiple agent frameworks. Which AWS offering targets this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store

explanation: AgentCore provides production-grade, framework-agnostic services (Runtime, Identity, Gateway, Memory, Observability, etc.) to deploy and scale agents. Not "Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases": Knowledge Bases provide RAG, not agent runtime/identity/observability. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails are safety policies, not an agent operations platform. Not "Amazon SageMaker Feature Store": Feature Store manages ML features, not agents. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Which AgentCore component provides a secure, serverless runtime that can host agents built with various frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, Strands, etc.) and protocols (MCP, A2A)?

options.text: AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Runtime
AgentCore Memory
AgentCore Identity

explanation: AgentCore Runtime is the secure serverless runtime for deploying/scaling agents across frameworks, protocols, and models. Not "AgentCore Gateway": Gateway turns APIs/Lambda into tools; it is not the runtime. Not "AgentCore Memory": Memory manages context retention, not the runtime host. Not "AgentCore Identity": Identity handles access control, not hosting. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Which AgentCore component turns existing REST APIs and AWS Lambda functions into agent-ready tools (including via MCP) with tool discovery?

options.text: AgentCore Code Interpreter
AgentCore Observability
AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Browser

explanation: Gateway converts APIs and Lambda functions into agent tools and supports tool discovery over protocols like MCP. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter": Code Interpreter runs code; it does not expose APIs as tools. Not "AgentCore Observability": Observability monitors agents; it does not create tools. Not "AgentCore Browser": Browser provides managed web browsing, not API-to-tool conversion. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Which AgentCore component manages both short-term (session) and long-term memory so agents can retain context and learn from past interactions?

options.text: AgentCore Runtime
AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Identity
AgentCore Memory

explanation: Memory provides session and long-term memory for context retention across interactions. Not "AgentCore Runtime": Runtime hosts/scales agents; memory is a separate component. Not "AgentCore Gateway": Gateway exposes tools, not memory. Not "AgentCore Identity": Identity handles secure access, not memory. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent must securely access third-party services like GitHub, Salesforce, and Slack on behalf of a user, with pre-authorized consent. Which AgentCore component handles this?

options.text: AgentCore Code Interpreter
AgentCore Browser
AgentCore Identity
AgentCore Memory

explanation: Identity lets agents securely access AWS and third-party services on behalf of users or with pre-authorized consent. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter": Code Interpreter runs code, not identity brokering. Not "AgentCore Browser": Browser automates web sessions; access/consent is Identity's role. Not "AgentCore Memory": Memory stores context; it does not broker third-party access. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent needs to run code it generates in a secure, isolated sandbox (e.g., for data analysis). Which AgentCore component provides this?

options.text: AgentCore Identity
AgentCore Code Interpreter
AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Memory

explanation: Code Interpreter offers an isolated environment to execute agent-generated code. Not "AgentCore Identity": Identity manages access, not code execution. Not "AgentCore Gateway": Gateway exposes tools; it does not run arbitrary generated code in a sandbox. Not "AgentCore Memory": Memory stores context, not a code sandbox. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent must perform web automation (navigating sites, filling forms) at scale using managed browser instances. Which AgentCore component fits?

options.text: AgentCore Runtime
AgentCore Browser
AgentCore Observability
AgentCore Memory

explanation: Browser provides managed web browser instances for agent web-automation workflows. Not "AgentCore Runtime": Runtime hosts agents; managed browsing is the Browser component. Not "AgentCore Observability": Observability monitors agents; it does not browse the web. Not "AgentCore Memory": Memory is context retention, not browsing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A team needs step-by-step visualization of an agent's execution, trajectory inspection, and troubleshooting filters in production. Which AgentCore component provides this?

options.text: AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Identity
AgentCore Observability
AgentCore Code Interpreter

explanation: Observability gives step-by-step execution visibility, trajectory inspection, and debugging filters. Not "AgentCore Gateway": Gateway exposes tools, not observability. Not "AgentCore Identity": Identity manages access, not monitoring. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter": Code Interpreter runs code; it is not the monitoring component. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Which statement about how AgentCore's services are consumed is correct?

options.text: Its services (for example Runtime, Gateway, Identity, Memory, Observability, Browser and Code Interpreter) are modular: use them together or independently, with consumption-based pricing
AgentCore only supports one agent framework
AgentCore only works with Amazon Nova models
You must adopt all AgentCore services as a single bundle

prompt: How does AgentCore relate to Amazon Bedrock Agents?

options.text: AgentCore is an older, deprecated version of Bedrock Agents
AgentCore is a vector database
AgentCore only stores prompts

AgentCore is the newer agentic platform (managed harness, serverless runtime, gateway, identity, memory, observability) that works with any framework and foundation model, and is where AWS recommends moving Amazon Bedrock Agents workloads

explanation: AgentCore is an agentic platform for building, deploying and operating agents at scale using any framework and foundation model; its modular services can be used together or independently. AWS recommends it as the migration target for Amazon Bedrock Agents (now documented as Agents Classic, in maintenance mode), with the managed harness as the closest equivalent of the managed agent. Not "AgentCore is an older, deprecated version of Bedrock Agents": AgentCore is the newer offering, not deprecated. Not "AgentCore is a vector database": AgentCore is an agent platform, not a vector store. Not "AgentCore only stores prompts": That describes Prompt Management, not AgentCore. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-classic-maintenance-mode.html

prompt: A team must deploy existing Python agent code to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with minimal overhead. It must auto-handle the HTTP server, /invocations and /ping endpoints, and support both sub-second and streaming responses. Which TWO approaches fit best? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Hand-build a FastAPI server with custom /invocations and /ping and your own container orchestration
Deploy on a SageMaker real-time endpoint with a custom inference container
Deploy on Amazon ECS Fargate with a fully custom container image and task definitions
Use the AgentCore CLI (`agentcore create`, `agentcore deploy`) to package the code (CodeZip by default, or a container build) and deploy it to AgentCore Runtime
Use the AgentCore Python SDK (`BedrockAgentCoreApp` with the @app.entrypoint decorator) so the required endpoints are handled for you

explanation: `agentcore deploy` packages the code into a zip artifact uploaded to Amazon S3 (the default CodeZip build type, which needs no Docker) or builds a container, then creates the AgentCore Runtime endpoint. Wrapping the agent with the AgentCore Python SDK satisfies the Runtime HTTP contract: port 8080, POST `/invocations` returning JSON or SSE streaming responses, and GET `/ping`. Not "Hand-build a FastAPI server with custom /invocations and …": Manual server and orchestration work is the overhead AgentCore is meant to remove. Not "Deploy on a SageMaker real-time endpoint with a custom in…": A custom inference container adds infrastructure work AgentCore avoids. Not "Deploy on Amazon ECS Fargate with a fully custom containe…": Custom ECS deployment increases operational overhead versus AgentCore's managed flow. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-get-started-cli.html

prompt: What does the AgentCore SDK's @app.entrypoint decorator automatically provide?

options.text: A managed vector database
A no-code visual workflow builder
An HTTP server (port 8080) with the required /invocations and /ping endpoints and content/streaming handling
Automatic 7-year log retention

explanation: The decorator wires up the server, endpoints, content types, and JSON/streaming responses automatically. Not "A managed vector database": It does not provision a vector store. Not "A no-code visual workflow builder": That is Prompt Flows, not the AgentCore SDK. Not "Automatic 7-year log retention": Retention is configured via logging/S3 Object Lock, not this decorator. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A developer wants an open-source SDK that builds agents with a "model-driven" approach — defining just a model, a system prompt, and a set of tools, and letting the model plan and call tools. Which is this?

options.text: Strands Agents
Amazon Macie
AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon Polly

explanation: Strands takes a model-driven approach centered on a model, a system prompt, and tools, letting the model direct its own steps. Not "Amazon Macie": Macie is data discovery, not an agent SDK. Not "AWS Glue Data Quality": That scores datasets; it is not an agent SDK. Not "Amazon Polly": Polly is text-to-speech, not an agent SDK. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: What are the three core components of the Strands Agents model-driven approach?

options.text: A vector store, a reranker, and a chunker
A language model, a system prompt, and a set of tools
A VPC, a subnet, and a route table
A bucket, an index, and a metric

explanation: Strands centers on model + system prompt + tools, relying on the model to plan and call tools. Not "A vector store, a reranker, and a chunker": Those are RAG components, not the Strands agent triad. Not "A VPC, a subnet, and a route table": Those are networking constructs, unrelated to Strands. Not "A bucket, an index, and a metric": Those describe S3 Vectors, not Strands. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Which statement about Strands Agents tool integration is correct?

options.text: Strands requires Provisioned Throughput to define tools
Strands cannot call any external tools
Strands only works with a single proprietary tool format
Strands can use thousands of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as tools

explanation: Strands integrates with MCP, letting agents use a large ecosystem of MCP tool servers. Not "Strands requires Provisioned Throughput to define tools": Tool definitions are code; they do not require provisioned capacity. Not "Strands cannot call any external tools": Calling tools is central to its model-driven design. Not "Strands only works with a single proprietary tool format": It supports MCP and flexible tool definitions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Which model providers can Strands Agents work with?

options.text: Only models hosted on-premises
Any Amazon Bedrock model supporting tool use and streaming, plus Anthropic, Llama, Ollama, and others via LiteLLM
Only Amazon Titan models
Only image-generation models

explanation: Strands is model-flexible across Bedrock and many external providers. Not "Only models hosted on-premises": It supports cloud and local models, not on-prem only. Not "Only Amazon Titan models": It is not limited to Titan. Not "Only image-generation models": It targets tool-using LLMs, not just image models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: How does Strands Agents typically deploy in AWS for serverless or orchestrated workflows?

options.text: It must run inside Amazon QuickSight
It can only run on bare-metal servers
It runs exclusively in the browser
It works with AWS Lambda for serverless deployments and AWS Step Functions to embed an agent call in a larger workflow

explanation: Strands Agents is an open-source SDK (Python and TypeScript) that integrates with AWS Lambda and AWS Step Functions; an agent built with it can also be hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Not "It must run inside Amazon QuickSight": QuickSight is BI; it does not host agents. Not "It can only run on bare-metal servers": It runs on serverless and managed compute, not bare metal only. Not "It runs exclusively in the browser": It is a server-side SDK, not browser-only. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/agentic-ai-frameworks/strands-agents.html

prompt: A "model-driven" agent framework differs from a workflow-heavy framework in what key way?

options.text: The model dynamically plans steps and decides tool use, instead of developers hand-coding complex fixed workflows
It removes the need for any model
It forbids using tools
It only supports deterministic if/else graphs

explanation: Model-driven agents let the model reason and orchestrate, reducing hand-built workflow logic. Not "It removes the need for any model": The model is central to a model-driven approach. Not "It forbids using tools": Tool use is a core capability. Not "It only supports deterministic if/else graphs": That describes the workflow-heavy approach it contrasts with. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A team wants to run a Strands-built agent in a managed, secure, serverless environment at production scale without managing servers. Which is a natural fit?

options.text: Run it only on a developer's laptop
Deploy it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
Store the code in S3 and never run it
Embed it in a CloudFront cache

explanation: AgentCore Runtime hosts agents from frameworks like Strands in a managed serverless runtime. Not "Run it only on a developer's laptop": A laptop is not production-scale managed hosting. Not "Store the code in S3 and never run it": Storing code does not run the agent. Not "Embed it in a CloudFront cache": CloudFront is a CDN, not an agent runtime. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A production agent platform must provide identity/access to tools, persistent memory, tool gateways, and end-to-end observability across agents built in different frameworks. Which single AWS offering is designed to deliver all of these?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Amazon Kendra

explanation: AgentCore bundles Runtime, Identity, Gateway, Memory, and Observability for production agents across frameworks. Not "Amazon SageMaker Model Registry": The registry versions models; it is not an agent operations platform. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails are safety policies only. Not "Amazon Kendra": Kendra is enterprise search, not an agent platform. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A customer-support solution needs to route each user query to one of several specialized agents (billing, technical, account) and keep a coherent conversation across them. Which open-source framework is purpose-built for this kind of multi-agent orchestration and routing?

options.text: AWS Agent Squad (multi-agent orchestrator)
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows)
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

explanation: Agent Squad routes each user query to the most suitable of several specialized agents and maintains conversation context across them. The exam guide calls it AWS Agent Squad; the project (formerly multi-agent-orchestrator) was hosted at `awslabs/agent-squad` and is now maintained at `2fastlabs/agent-squad`. Not "Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases": Knowledge Bases provide RAG retrieval, not multi-agent routing. Not "Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows)": Flows is a managed Bedrock workflow builder, not an open-source framework that classifies each query to an agent. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails": Guardrails enforce content safety; they do not orchestrate multiple agents. Read more: https://github.com/2fastlabs/agent-squad

prompt: In AWS Agent Squad, how is each incoming user request assigned to the right specialized agent?

options.text: Requests are assigned round-robin regardless of content
The user must manually pick an agent each turn
An LLM-powered classifier analyzes the input, agent descriptions, and conversation history to select the best-suited agent
Agents are chosen by alphabetical order of their names

explanation: The classifier uses an LLM to analyze the user's request, the agent descriptions and the conversation history, then returns the name of the selected agent. The framework ships built-in classifiers and accepts a custom one. Not "Requests are assigned round-robin regardless of content": Routing is intent-based via the classifier, not blind round-robin. Not "The user must manually pick an agent each turn": Routing is automatic; users do not hand-pick agents per turn. Not "Agents are chosen by alphabetical order of their names": Selection is based on classification of intent/context, not naming order. Read more: https://github.com/2fastlabs/agent-squad

prompt: Which TWO are accurate about AWS Agent Squad? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can only run a single agent at a time and has no routing
It is a vector database
Member agents can be different types, such as Amazon Bedrock model agents, Amazon Lex bots, or AWS Lambda functions
It requires Provisioned Throughput to classify requests
It maintains unified conversation context across agents for coherent multi-turn interactions

explanation: Agent Squad provides pre-built agents including Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Lex and AWS Lambda agents. The orchestrator maintains conversation context across agents so conversations stay coherent as routing changes. Not "It can only run a single agent at a time and has no routing": Its entire purpose is routing across multiple agents. Not "It is a vector database": Agent Squad is an orchestration framework, not a vector store. Not "It requires Provisioned Throughput to classify requests": Classification uses a model/classifier; it does not mandate provisioned capacity. Read more: https://github.com/2fastlabs/agent-squad

prompt: In Agent Squad, what is the difference between the classifier's view and an individual agent's view of conversation history?

options.text: The classifier has a global view across agents, while each agent sees only its own conversation history
History is never retained anywhere
Every agent always sees the full global history
The classifier sees nothing and routes blindly

explanation: The classifier sees the conversation history from all agents for the current user and session, while each agent retrieves only its own conversation history. This lets the classifier route with full context while keeping each agent focused on its domain. Not "History is never retained anywhere": Agent Squad maintains conversation context. Not "Every agent always sees the full global history": Agents see only their own history; the global view belongs to the classifier. Not "The classifier sees nothing and routes blindly": The classifier specifically uses global context to route. Read more: https://github.com/2fastlabs/agent-squad

prompt: How do Strands Agents and AWS Agent Squad differ in purpose?

options.text: Both are vector stores

Strands is a model-driven SDK for building agents (including its own multi-agent patterns); Agent Squad is an orchestrator that classifies each user query and routes it to one of several specialized agents
They are identical products
Strands classifies and routes user queries across agents, and Agent Squad is the SDK for building the agents themselves

explanation: Strands Agents is an open-source SDK with a model-first design for building autonomous agents, and it includes multi-agent patterns such as Swarm, Graph and Workflow. Agent Squad is narrower: a classifier picks the best-suited specialized agent for each user query and the orchestrator keeps the conversation context across them. Not "Both are vector stores": Neither is a vector store. Not "They are identical products": They serve different roles: an agent-building SDK versus a query-routing orchestrator. Not "Strands classifies and routes user queries across agents,…": This reverses their roles. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/agentic-ai-frameworks/strands-agents.html

prompt: A team wants an agent to interleave reasoning with tool actions (think, act, observe, repeat) using structured steps orchestrated on AWS. Which pattern/approach matches?

options.text: Sharding the vector index
A single one-shot prompt with no tools
The ReAct pattern, which can be implemented with AWS Step Functions to structure reasoning and tool-use steps
Provisioned Throughput scaling

explanation: ReAct (Reason + Act) interleaves reasoning and actions; Step Functions can structure these steps. Not "Sharding the vector index": Sharding is storage tuning, unrelated to agent reasoning. Not "A single one-shot prompt with no tools": One-shot prompting does not interleave reasoning and tool actions. Not "Provisioned Throughput scaling": That reserves capacity; it is not a reasoning pattern. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A complex task benefits from breaking the problem into intermediate reasoning steps before producing a final answer. Which prompting technique is this?

options.text: Top-k sampling
Chain-of-thought reasoning
Hybrid search
Stop sequences

explanation: Chain-of-thought prompts the model to reason through intermediate steps, improving complex task performance. Not "Top-k sampling": top-k controls candidate tokens, not reasoning structure. Not "Hybrid search": Hybrid search is a retrieval technique, not a reasoning method. Not "Stop sequences": Stop sequences end generation; they do not elicit step-by-step reasoning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agentic workflow must pause for a human to review and approve high-impact actions before continuing. Which approach implements this human-in-the-loop control on AWS?

options.text: Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate a review/approval step (e.g., with a callback) before the agent proceeds
Remove all guardrails to speed approvals
Store the action in S3 and hope a human notices
Increase the model temperature so it self-approves

explanation: Step Functions can pause for human approval (task tokens/callbacks) to gate sensitive actions. Not "Remove all guardrails to speed approvals": Removing safeguards is the opposite of controlled human review. Not "Store the action in S3 and hope a human notices": Passive storage is not an orchestrated approval mechanism. Not "Increase the model temperature so it self-approves": Temperature affects randomness, not human approval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A developer calls Amazon Bedrock with the InvokeModel API across several providers and finds each model expects a different request body. What is the most accurate statement?

options.text: InvokeModel cannot be used for text models
InvokeModel uses one identical body for every model
InvokeModel request/response bodies are model-specific, so the JSON payload must match each model's schema
InvokeModel only accepts CSV

explanation: With InvokeModel you format the body to the chosen model's native request schema. Not "InvokeModel cannot be used for text models": InvokeModel is a primary API for text models. Not "InvokeModel uses one identical body for every model": Native InvokeModel bodies differ per provider/model. Not "InvokeModel only accepts CSV": Bedrock requests are JSON, and the schema is model-specific. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team wants a single, consistent request/response format for multi-turn chat that works across multiple Bedrock models without hand-coding each model's native schema. Which API should they use?

options.text: The Rerank API
StartIngestionJob
InvokeModel with a model-specific body for each model
The Amazon Bedrock Converse API, which provides a unified messages interface across supported models

explanation: Converse abstracts model-specific formats into a consistent messages structure with roles, simplifying portability. Not "The Rerank API": Rerank reorders retrieved documents; it is not a chat interface. Not "StartIngestionJob": That ingests data into a Knowledge Base; it is not a chat inference API. Not "InvokeModel with a model-specific body for each model": InvokeModel requires per-model formatting, which is what they want to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: When formatting input for a dialog-based application using the Bedrock Converse API, how is the conversation typically structured?

options.text: As a CSV of tokens
As a sequence of messages with roles (e.g., user and assistant), plus an optional system instruction
As a vector embedding only
As a single concatenated string with no roles

explanation: Conversation formatting uses role-tagged messages (user/assistant) and an optional system prompt. Not "As a CSV of tokens": Conversations are structured messages, not token CSVs. Not "As a vector embedding only": Embeddings are for retrieval, not the chat message structure. Not "As a single concatenated string with no roles": Dialog formatting uses structured role-tagged turns, not one undifferentiated string. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A pipeline sends requests to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. What determines the required input data format?

options.text: All SageMaker endpoints require the Bedrock Converse schema
The endpoint/container's expected content type and serializer (e.g., application/json or text/csv) per the model's contract
SageMaker endpoints accept any format without serialization
SageMaker endpoints only accept audio

explanation: SageMaker endpoints expect input matching the container's content type and the model's input contract. Not "All SageMaker endpoints require the Bedrock Converse schema": SageMaker input depends on the container, not the Bedrock Converse format. Not "SageMaker endpoints accept any format without serialization": Input must match the endpoint's expected content type/serializer. Not "SageMaker endpoints only accept audio": Format depends on the model; it is not audio-only. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Inconsistent, messy text is degrading FM response quality. A team wants to normalize and reformat inputs before inference with minimal custom infrastructure. Which approach fits?

options.text: Send raw messy text directly and raise temperature
Disable all preprocessing to save cost
Use AWS Lambda functions to normalize/reformat the data (and optionally Amazon Comprehend to extract entities) before calling the FM
Provision a large GPU cluster to compensate

explanation: Lambda is a low-overhead way to clean and reformat inputs; Comprehend can enrich them prior to inference. Not "Send raw messy text directly and raise temperature": Higher temperature adds randomness and does not fix input quality. Not "Disable all preprocessing to save cost": Skipping preprocessing worsens response quality. Not "Provision a large GPU cluster to compensate": Hardware does not fix input formatting/quality issues. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: Why is correct input formatting important when integrating foundation models?

options.text: Models have model-specific input requirements; malformed or mismatched formatting causes errors or poor responses
All models accept identical raw input, so formatting never matters
Formatting is only relevant for image models
Formatting only affects billing, not behavior

explanation: Matching each model's expected request/message format is necessary for valid calls and good output quality. Not "All models accept identical raw input, so formatting neve…": Input requirements vary by model/API; formatting matters. Not "Formatting is only relevant for image models": It applies to text, chat, and other modalities, not just images. Not "Formatting only affects billing, not behavior": Formatting affects whether the call succeeds and the quality of the response. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A regulated company is applying the security and responsible-AI guidance of the Generative AI Lens to a Bedrock assistant. It needs a managed, configurable control plane to block denied topics, filter harmful content, and redact PII consistently across multiple foundation models. Which AWS capability best meets this need with the LEAST custom code?

options.text: CloudWatch alarms on invocation metrics.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
A set of IAM identity-based policies on the model.
Lowering the model temperature parameter.

explanation: Guardrails provide configurable, model-agnostic policies for denied topics, content filters, word filters, and PII redaction that apply consistently across FMs. Not "CloudWatch alarms on invocation metrics.": Alarms detect operational anomalies after the fact; they do not filter or redact content. Not "A set of IAM identity-based policies on the model.": IAM controls who can call the model, not what content the model may produce or must redact. Not "Lowering the model temperature parameter.": Temperature affects randomness, not topic blocking, content filtering, or PII redaction. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: An interactive customer assistant must minimize the latency end users perceive while keeping output quality acceptable for routine questions. Which combination best reflects the Performance Efficiency pillar for a Bedrock workload?

options.text: Always use the largest available model for every request.
Increase max tokens to ensure complete answers.
Route all interactive traffic through batch inference.
Select a smaller, latency-optimized (or distilled) model and stream tokens to the client.

explanation: Right-sizing to a smaller/distilled model reduces inference time, and response streaming lowers perceived latency by showing tokens as they are generated. Not "Always use the largest available model for every request.": The largest model maximizes capability but adds latency and cost that routine questions do not require. Not "Increase max tokens to ensure complete answers.": Larger outputs increase generation time, worsening perceived latency. Not "Route all interactive traffic through batch inference.": Batch inference is asynchronous and offline; it is unsuitable for interactive latency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A platform team wants to operationalize quality assurance for a deployed generative AI feature so regressions are caught automatically as models and prompts change. Which practice best reflects the Operational Excellence pillar?

options.text: Establish automated evaluation pipelines with continuous monitoring of output quality and drift, feeding results back into release decisions.
Monitor only infrastructure metrics such as CPU and memory.
Run a single manual quality check before the initial launch.
Rely on end-user complaints to surface quality problems.

explanation: Operational Excellence emphasizes automating evaluation and observability so quality is measured continuously and improvements are driven by data. Not "Monitor only infrastructure metrics such as CPU and memory.": Infrastructure health says nothing about generation quality or drift.
