Not "Instruct the model in the system prompt to stay within th…": Prompt instructions do not control retrieval and can be bypassed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Relevant passages ARE being retrieved but appear LOW in the result list, so answers miss them. The team wants to fix the ordering with the least overhead. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Increase the number of results returned.
Re-ingest with semantic chunking.
Switch to hybrid search.
Add a Bedrock reranker model to reorder the retrieved candidates by query relevance.

explanation: A reranker reorders already-retrieved candidates so the most relevant passages move to the top. Not "Increase the number of results returned.": Returning more results does not move the relevant ones to the top. Not "Re-ingest with semantic chunking.": Re-chunking is a heavier ingestion change and does not directly reorder results. Not "Switch to hybrid search.": Hybrid search improves whether relevant items are retrieved (recall); the problem here is ordering of items already retrieved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Queries that contain exact product codes and acronyms are frequently MISSED by pure semantic search. Which change BEST fixes retrieval?

options.text: Enable hybrid search that combines semantic vectors with keyword matching.
Raise the generation temperature.
Add a reranker model.
Increase the embedding dimensions.

explanation: Hybrid search adds keyword matching so exact tokens like product codes are found alongside semantic matches. Not "Raise the generation temperature.": Temperature affects generation, not retrieval of exact terms. Not "Add a reranker model.": A reranker reorders retrieved items but cannot surface an exact-keyword match that the vector search failed to retrieve. Not "Increase the embedding dimensions.": Higher dimensions do not reliably solve exact-token matching. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Content must be ingested into one Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base from Amazon S3, Confluence, and SharePoint with the LEAST custom code. What should the team do?

options.text: Fine-tune the model on each source instead of ingesting.
Use the knowledge base's native data source connectors for each source.
Write custom crawlers that copy everything to S3 first.
Manually export each source to S3 on a schedule.

explanation: Native connectors for S3, Confluence and SharePoint ingest the content without custom code. Status note: starting September 30, 2026, new Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Salesforce and Web Crawler connectors can no longer be created on customer-managed knowledge bases (existing ones keep working); AWS points applications that need these connectors to a Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, whose native connectors are S3, SharePoint, Confluence, Web Crawler, Google Drive, OneDrive and Custom. Not "Fine-tune the model on each source instead of ingesting.": Fine-tuning is not ingestion and does not keep content current. Not "Write custom crawlers that copy everything to S3 first.": Custom crawlers add development and maintenance the connectors remove. Not "Manually export each source to S3 on a schedule.": Manual exports are brittle and lag behind source changes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/data-source-connectors.html

prompt: A RetrieveAndGenerate chat must keep context across follow-up questions with the LEAST custom state management. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Use a model with a larger context window.
Store every message in DynamoDB and rebuild the prompt each turn.
Pass a session identifier to RetrieveAndGenerate so Bedrock maintains the conversation context.
Re-embed the chat history into the vector store each turn.

explanation: The session ID preserves multi-turn context without the developer building custom conversation state. Not "Use a model with a larger context window.": A larger window does not automatically carry prior turns into each call. Not "Store every message in DynamoDB and rebuild the prompt ea…": Manual state assembly is more work than the built-in session support. Not "Re-embed the chat history into the vector store each turn.": Re-embedding history is costly and is not how session context is maintained. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Complex, multi-part questions retrieve passages for only ONE part, yielding incomplete answers. Which built-in capability BEST addresses this?

options.text: Enable query decomposition (reformulation) so the knowledge base splits the question into sub-queries.
Increase the number of results returned.
Add a reranker model.
Switch to a larger generation model.

explanation: Decomposition retrieves passages for each sub-question, improving coverage and completeness. Not "Increase the number of results returned.": More results add noise but do not ensure each sub-question is covered. Not "Add a reranker model.": Reranking reorders retrieved items but cannot fetch passages for an unaddressed sub-question. Not "Switch to a larger generation model.": A larger model cannot use passages that were never retrieved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: New and deleted documents in Amazon S3 must be reflected in a Bedrock knowledge base quickly, WITHOUT re-scanning the entire source each time, in a scalable and resilient way. Which design is BEST?

options.text: Run an EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes to diff the bucket.
Send S3 object-created/deleted events to an SQS queue, and have a Lambda call the incremental IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments / DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments APIs.
On every change, call StartIngestionJob to sync the whole data source.
Invoke a Lambda directly from S3 events with no queue.

explanation: Event-driven SQS buffering with the direct-ingestion APIs indexes or removes only the documents named in each event, and the queue holds events during spikes and retries failed batches. Not "Run an EventBridge Scheduler every 5 minutes to diff the …": Polling on a timer is not near-real-time and is less efficient than event-driven updates. Not "On every change, call StartIngestionJob to sync the whole…": A sync is incremental in what it processes (only added, modified or deleted documents), but StartIngestionJob scans each document in the data source to find them, which is exactly the re-scan the requirement rules out. Not "Invoke a Lambda directly from S3 events with no queue.": S3 invokes Lambda asynchronously, and Lambda does queue and retry those events (a function error is retried two more times, throttling for up to 6 hours). But when the function cannot keep up, events can expire or be deleted from that internal queue without being processed, which an SQS queue in front of the function avoids. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-direct-ingestion.html

prompt: A team wants grounded answers WITH citations over their documents, with the least operational overhead and no retrieval pipeline to build. Which option is BEST?

options.text: A custom pipeline with Lambda and a self-managed vector database.
Amazon Kendra by itself.
Fine-tune a model on the documents.
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (managed RAG).

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases are managed RAG: Bedrock runs ingestion, embedding and retrieval, and the RetrieveAndGenerate API returns a generated answer with citations to the source documents. With a Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, the type AWS now recommends, Bedrock also owns the datastore, so there is no vector store to provision. Not "A custom pipeline with Lambda and a self-managed vector d…": A hand-built pipeline maximizes operational overhead. Not "Amazon Kendra by itself.": Kendra is enterprise search with no native answer generation; RAG with it requires an external LLM integration. It has also been in maintenance mode since June 30, 2026 and is closed to new customers. Not "Fine-tune a model on the documents.": Fine-tuning is not RAG and does not provide citations or freshness. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-build-managed.html

prompt: A RAG assistant returns confident answers that the retrieved passages do not actually support. The team wants a MANAGED, tunable way to block ungrounded responses. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Switch to a larger model.
Enable the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding check with a tuned threshold.
Lower the temperature.
Add a reranker model.

explanation: The contextual grounding check scores whether a response is supported by the source and can block low-scoring answers. Not "Switch to a larger model.": A larger model can still produce ungrounded answers without a grounding control. Not "Lower the temperature.": Lower randomness does not guarantee grounding in the retrieved context. Not "Add a reranker model.": A reranker improves ordering of retrieved passages but does not verify or block ungrounded generation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base.html

prompt: Retrieval must MATCH on small, precise text units but then give the language model the BROADER surrounding context for those matches. Which chunking strategy is BEST?

options.text: Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking.
Large fixed-size chunking.
Semantic chunking.
No chunking.

explanation: Hierarchical chunking matches on small child chunks for precision and supplies the larger parent chunk as context for generation. Not "Large fixed-size chunking.": Large fixed chunks sacrifice precise matching on small units. Not "Semantic chunking.": Semantic chunking yields coherent chunks but does not provide the parent-context-on-child-match behavior required here. Not "No chunking.": Treating each document as one chunk loses the precise small-unit matching. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Long documents mix several topics. Each chunk must hold ONE coherent topic for precise matching; there is no need to also pass a larger parent context. Which strategy is BEST?

options.text: Only increasing chunk overlap.
Semantic chunking.
Fixed-size chunking.
Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking.

explanation: Semantic chunking splits on meaning so each chunk is one coherent topic, which fixes topic bleed without an extra parent layer. Not "Only increasing chunk overlap.": Overlap helps boundary continuity but does not make each chunk a single coherent topic. Not "Fixed-size chunking.": Fixed sizes cut across topic boundaries, the root problem. Not "Hierarchical (parent-child) chunking.": Hierarchical adds a parent-context layer that is unnecessary here and does not specifically fix topic boundaries. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Answers are frequently cut off because relevant sentences fall right at the boundary between two chunks. Which adjustment most directly fixes this?

options.text: Reduce the chunk size.
Increase the number of results returned.
Switch to hierarchical chunking.
Add chunk overlap so adjacent chunks share boundary text.

explanation: Overlap repeats boundary text so information spanning a boundary is captured in at least one chunk. Not "Reduce the chunk size.": Smaller chunks create MORE boundaries and can make boundary loss worse. Not "Increase the number of results returned.": Returning more chunks does not fix content split across a boundary. Not "Switch to hierarchical chunking.": Hierarchical chunking is heavier than needed and does not specifically target boundary cut-offs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: After upgrading to a newer embedding model, retrieval quality collapsed even though documents are present. What must the team do?

options.text: Clear the application cache.
Lower the generation temperature.
Re-embed only the queries with the new model.
Re-embed (re-index) the entire corpus with the new model so document and query vectors share the same space.

explanation: Query and document embeddings must come from the same model; switching models requires re-embedding the whole corpus. Not "Clear the application cache.": Caching is unrelated to embedding-space mismatch. Not "Lower the generation temperature.": Temperature does not affect embedding compatibility. Not "Re-embed only the queries with the new model.": Mismatched query and document spaces still produce poor retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A growing vector index is too expensive. The team wants to cut storage and query cost while keeping acceptable recall. Which change helps MOST?

options.text: Switch to a multimodal embedding model.
Use an embedding model with smaller output dimensions (for example, Titan Text Embeddings V2) and pick a smaller dimension.
Store each chunk twice for redundancy.
Use the maximum embedding dimension available.

explanation: Smaller-dimension embeddings shrink the index and query cost while keeping acceptable recall. Not "Switch to a multimodal embedding model.": Multimodal embeddings are for image+text retrieval and do not reduce text storage cost. Not "Store each chunk twice for redundancy.": Duplication increases cost without improving accuracy. Not "Use the maximum embedding dimension available.": Maximum dimensions increase storage and cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Evaluation shows the correct passage EXISTS in the store but is sometimes NOT returned, so the model lacks the facts to answer. Which change should the team try FIRST?

options.text: Reduce the chunk overlap.
Add a reranker model.
Increase the number of results (top-k) returned per query.
Lower the temperature.

explanation: Returning more candidates raises recall so the correct passage is more likely included. Not "Reduce the chunk overlap.": Less overlap does not improve whether the missing passage is retrieved. Not "Add a reranker model.": A reranker reorders retrieved results but cannot rank a passage that was never retrieved. Not "Lower the temperature.": Temperature affects generation, not retrieval recall. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: Chunks were configured very large, so retrieval returns passages where the relevant sentence is buried among unrelated text and match quality is weak. Which change is BEST?

options.text: Increase the embedding dimensions.
Add more chunk overlap.
Reduce the chunk size to more focused units of meaning.
Increase the chunk size further.

explanation: Smaller, focused chunks produce embeddings that better represent specific content, improving match precision. Not "Increase the embedding dimensions.": Dimension size does not fix oversized, diluted chunks. Not "Add more chunk overlap.": Overlap addresses boundaries, not the dilution caused by oversized chunks. Not "Increase the chunk size further.": Larger chunks dilute the embedding more and worsen precision. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A knowledge base ingests many short, self-contained FAQ entries, where each file is already one complete question-and-answer. Which chunking choice is BEST?

options.text: Apply small fixed-size chunking to every file.
Use hierarchical chunking.
Merge all FAQ files into one chunk.
Use a no-chunking strategy so each short file is one chunk.

explanation: When each file is already atomic, no chunking preserves the complete meaning per entry. Not "Apply small fixed-size chunking to every file.": Splitting atomic FAQ entries fragments coherent answers. Not "Use hierarchical chunking.": Hierarchical structure is unnecessary for already-atomic entries. Not "Merge all FAQ files into one chunk.": Merging unrelated entries dilutes each entry's embedding. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A catalog must be searchable by EITHER a text query or an image query against the same items. Which embedding approach supports this?

options.text: Use a multimodal embedding model (such as Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings) so images and text share one vector space.
Index Amazon Rekognition labels only.
Use a text-only embedding model for everything.
Embed base64 image strings as text.

explanation: Multimodal embeddings place images and text in a shared space, enabling cross-modal similarity search. Not "Index Amazon Rekognition labels only.": Label detection is not a shared semantic embedding space for text-and-image retrieval. Not "Use a text-only embedding model for everything.": A text-only model cannot embed images for similarity search. Not "Embed base64 image strings as text.": Embedding base64 as text does not capture visual semantics. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team wants to raise the overall quality of what their RAG system retrieves and answers. Which TWO techniques are most effective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Choose a chunking strategy (semantic or hierarchical) aligned to the documents' structure.
Raise the generation temperature for variety.
Add a reranking step to reorder retrieved candidates by relevance.
Increase maxTokens on the response.
Always return only the single top result.

explanation: Structure-aligned chunking produces more coherent, relevant chunks and better retrieval. A reranker moves the most relevant passages to the top for generation. Not "Raise the generation temperature for variety.": Higher temperature increases randomness and does not improve retrieval quality. Not "Increase maxTokens on the response.": Output length does not change which passages are retrieved. Not "Always return only the single top result.": Returning just one result can drop relevant passages and reduce answer quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team must A/B test two wordings of a production prompt and revert instantly if one underperforms, WITHOUT redeploying application code. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Hard-code both prompts behind an application feature flag.
Deploy two Lambda functions, each hard-coding one prompt.
Adjust the temperature to switch behavior.
Save each wording as an Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management version, and keep the version to invoke (and the traffic split) in AWS AppConfig, which the application reads at runtime.

explanation: A Prompt Management version is a snapshot of the prompt, and the application chooses which one runs by passing the prompt ARN with its version as the `modelId`. Prompt Management itself has no alias or traffic split, so the pointer lives in runtime configuration: AWS AppConfig changes application behavior without redeploying code and can roll a change back. Variants are a prompt-builder aid for comparing up to three alternatives while testing, not a production routing mechanism. Not "Hard-code both prompts behind an application feature flag.": Shipping or changing the hard-coded prompts still requires a code deploy, and there is no managed prompt versioning. Not "Deploy two Lambda functions, each hard-coding one prompt.": This is custom, requires code deploys, and has no managed prompt versioning. Not "Adjust the temperature to switch behavior.": Temperature does not select between prompt wordings. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-deploy.html

prompt: A developer must cap response length to control cost and avoid overly long chat outputs. Which inference setting is correct?

options.text: Increase top-k.
Set the maxTokens (maximum output tokens) parameter.
Raise the temperature.
Add unrelated stop sequences.

explanation: maxTokens directly bounds output length and cost. Not "Increase top-k.": Top-k changes token diversity, not length. Not "Raise the temperature.": Temperature changes randomness, not maximum length. Not "Add unrelated stop sequences.": Unrelated stop sequences do not reliably cap general length. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Durable behavior rules (role, tone, safety constraints) must govern EVERY turn of a conversation, separate from each user question. Where should they go?

options.text: Appended by the user to each message.
In the system prompt.
In the stop sequences list.
In the temperature setting.

explanation: The system prompt sets persistent instructions that apply across the conversation, separate from per-turn user messages. Not "Appended by the user to each message.": Relying on users to repeat rules is inconsistent and unreliable. Not "In the stop sequences list.": Stop sequences end generation; they do not encode behavior rules. Not "In the temperature setting.": Temperature is a sampling parameter, not a place for rules. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Outputs must follow a precise structured format, instructions alone have not worked, and the team needs a fix QUICKLY without a training step. Which technique is BEST?

options.text: Increase the temperature.
Fine-tune the model on formatting examples.
Shorten the prompt to one sentence.
Add a few worked examples (few-shot exemplars) of the exact format to the prompt.

explanation: Few-shot examples show the model the precise structure to imitate and require no training. Not "Increase the temperature.": Higher temperature increases variability and undermines format consistency. Not "Fine-tune the model on formatting examples.": Fine-tuning is heavier and slower than needed when few-shot prompting can fix formatting quickly. Not "Shorten the prompt to one sentence.": Over-shortening removes the structure cues the model needs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Several applications reuse the same prompt with only a few values changing per request, and the team wants central management with runtime value injection. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Copy the prompt into each application and edit by hand.
Concatenate strings ad hoc in each service.
Raise the temperature to make the prompt flexible.
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management templates with input variables.

explanation: Parameterized managed templates are reused centrally and take values at invocation time. Not "Copy the prompt into each application and edit by hand.": Duplicated prompts drift and are hard to govern centrally. Not "Concatenate strings ad hoc in each service.": Ad hoc concatenation has no central governance or versioning. Not "Raise the temperature to make the prompt flexible.": Temperature does not parameterize or manage prompts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer needs a MANAGED, low-code way to build and version a multi-step generative workflow with branching (classify, then retrieve, then generate). Which Amazon Bedrock feature is BEST?

options.text: Hand-built AWS Step Functions wiring each step.
Amazon Bedrock Agents.
A single InvokeModel call.
Amazon Bedrock Flows (prompt flows).

explanation: Bedrock Flows visually build and version multi-step, branching workflows chaining prompts, knowledge bases, and other components with little code. Not "Hand-built AWS Step Functions wiring each step.": Step Functions can orchestrate but require more custom build than a managed flow builder. Not "Amazon Bedrock Agents.": Agents provide autonomous tool-using reasoning, which is heavier and different from a defined, branching prompt-chain workflow. Not "A single InvokeModel call.": One call cannot orchestrate a multi-step, branching workflow. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A regression suite needs the same prompt to produce as close to identical output as possible on each run. Which SINGLE parameter change most increases determinism?

options.text: Set a very high top-k.
Increase maxTokens.
Set the temperature to 0.
Raise the temperature to 1.

explanation: A temperature of 0 makes decoding effectively greedy, maximizing run-to-run consistency. Not "Set a very high top-k.": A high top-k widens sampling and increases variability. Not "Increase maxTokens.": Output length does not control determinism. Not "Raise the temperature to 1.": A high temperature maximizes randomness. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: In a RAG assistant, the team wants to reduce fabricated answers by making the model rely only on the supplied context and admit when the answer is absent. Which prompt technique helps MOST?

options.text: Instruct the model to always produce an answer.
Raise the temperature for more creative answers.
Remove the retrieved context to shorten prompts.
Instruct the model to answer only from the provided context and to say it does not know when the context lacks the answer.

explanation: Explicit grounding plus an allowed abstention reduces fabrication when the context does not contain the answer. Not "Instruct the model to always produce an answer.": Forcing an answer encourages fabrication when information is missing. Not "Raise the temperature for more creative answers.": More creativity increases fabrication. Not "Remove the retrieved context to shorten prompts.": Without context the model must guess, increasing hallucination. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A developer must prevent unbounded, runaway generations that drive up cost and ramble past the answer. Which TWO controls directly help? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set a sensible maxTokens limit.
Enlarge the context window.
Define stop sequences that end generation at a known marker.
Increase the temperature.
Increase top-k substantially.

explanation: maxTokens caps how many tokens can be generated, bounding cost and runaway length. Stop sequences halt generation at a defined boundary so the model does not ramble on. Not "Enlarge the context window.": The context window governs input size, not output length. Not "Increase the temperature.": Higher temperature does not limit length and can make output more verbose. Not "Increase top-k substantially.": Top-k affects diversity, not length. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A model's outputs occasionally include bizarre, very low-probability words. The team wants to remove that long tail of unlikely tokens while keeping SOME variety. Which single adjustment is BEST?

options.text: Lower top-p (nucleus sampling) so only the most probable tokens are eligible.
Increase top-k substantially.
Add stop sequences.
Set temperature to 0.

explanation: A lower top-p trims the low-probability tail while still allowing variety among the top tokens, directly removing bizarre word choices. Not "Increase top-k substantially.": A larger top-k widens the candidate pool, making rare tokens more likely, not less. Not "Add stop sequences.": Stop sequences end generation; they do not filter the token probability distribution. Not "Set temperature to 0.": Temperature 0 removes the tail but also eliminates the variety the team wants to keep. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: An Amazon Bedrock Agents agent must call an internal order-management API to look up and update orders. What is the standard way to give it that capability?

options.text: Put the API documentation in the agent's instructions.
Associate a knowledge base with the agent.
Define an action group backed by a Lambda function, described with an API or function schema.
Raise the agent model's temperature.

explanation: Action groups define the actions the agent can perform, described with an OpenAPI schema or function details, and a Lambda function can carry out the action when the agent decides to act. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is tools exposed through AgentCore Gateway as MCP tools that wrap REST APIs and Lambda functions. Not "Put the API documentation in the agent's instructions.": Instructions describe behavior but provide no executable tool to call the API. Not "Associate a knowledge base with the agent.": A knowledge base grounds answers in documents; it does not execute API actions. Not "Raise the agent model's temperature.": Temperature has nothing to do with tool or API access. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-action-create.html

prompt: For compliance, the company's OWN application must execute the tool calls of an Amazon Bedrock Agents agent, while the agent still decides which action to take. Which capability supports this?

options.text: Configure the action group to return control to the caller, which executes the action and returns the result.
Use an action group with a Lambda the agent invokes directly.
Disable the agent's reasoning.
Associate a knowledge base.

explanation: With return of control configured on an action group, the agent does not send the action to a Lambda function; it returns the chosen action and its parameters in the InvokeAgent response (`invocationInputs` with an `invocationId`), and the application executes it and sends the result back in `sessionState`. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is inline function tools in the AgentCore harness, where the agent pauses and returns `tool_use` to the client. Not "Use an action group with a Lambda the agent invokes direc…": With a Lambda action group the agent executes the action, which is exactly what the compliance rule forbids. Not "Disable the agent's reasoning.": That would remove the agent's ability to decide which action to take. Not "Associate a knowledge base.": A knowledge base is for retrieval, not for delegating execution to the caller. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-returncontrol.html

prompt: An Amazon Bedrock Agents agent must ground its answers in company policy documents, with the least custom code. What should the developer do?

options.text: Add an action group to fetch documents from S3.
Fine-tune the agent's model weekly on the policies.
Paste the entire policy library into the agent instructions.
Associate an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the agent.

explanation: Associating a knowledge base lets the agent query it to augment its responses, without custom retrieval code. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is a knowledge base fronted by AgentCore Gateway, or a code-level retrieval tool. Not "Add an action group to fetch documents from S3.": Action groups execute operations; grounding from a corpus is what a knowledge base provides. Not "Fine-tune the agent's model weekly on the policies.": Repeated fine-tuning is heavy and unnecessary versus a knowledge base. Not "Paste the entire policy library into the agent instructions.": Instructions cannot scale to a full library or stay current. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-kb-add.html

prompt: Each user's agent must remember preferences and prior context ACROSS separate sessions, as a managed AgentCore capability. Which component is correct?

options.text: AgentCore Gateway.
A custom DynamoDB table you build and maintain.
AgentCore Memory.
Per-invocation session state only.

explanation: AgentCore Memory provides managed short-term and long-term memory that persists across sessions. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes APIs as tools; it is not a memory store. Not "A custom DynamoDB table you build and maintain.": That works but is not the managed AgentCore capability the scenario asks for. Not "Per-invocation session state only.": Session state lasts within a single session; it does not persist across sessions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A company wants to expose its MANY existing internal REST APIs and Lambda functions to agents as secure, governed tools without writing per-API integration code. Which AgentCore capability fits?

options.text: AgentCore Identity.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.
AgentCore Gateway.
Defining a separate action group for each API in every agent.

explanation: Gateway turns existing APIs/Lambdas into agent-ready tools (for example via MCP) with built-in authentication and governance. Not "AgentCore Identity.": Identity manages access/credentials, not exposure of APIs as tools. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter.": Code Interpreter executes code; it is not an API-to-tool exposure layer. Not "Defining a separate action group for each API in every ag…": Per-agent action groups require wiring each API repeatedly; Gateway centralizes existing APIs as managed tools. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An analytics agent must safely execute Python to perform calculations and data transformations, isolated from other workloads, as a managed capability. Which AgentCore component is correct?

options.text: AgentCore Browser.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.
A self-built Lambda action group for code execution.
AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: Code Interpreter gives the agent a managed, isolated sandbox to run code. Not "AgentCore Browser.": Browser automates web pages, not arbitrary code execution. Not "A self-built Lambda action group for code execution.": You would have to build and secure the sandbox yourself; Code Interpreter is the managed option. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes external tools; it is not a code-execution sandbox. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: An agent must NAVIGATE websites and interact with web pages to complete tasks, in a managed, secure environment. Which AgentCore capability fits?

options.text: AgentCore Gateway.
AgentCore Memory.
AgentCore Browser.
AgentCore Code Interpreter.

explanation: The Browser tool provides a managed, secure cloud browser the agent uses to navigate and interact with pages. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes APIs as tools; it does not provide interactive web browsing. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory persists context, not web interaction. Not "AgentCore Code Interpreter.": Code Interpreter runs code; it is not a browser. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: Agents must securely access third-party SaaS services ON BEHALF OF users, handling tokens and consent, without a custom credential broker. Which AgentCore capability addresses this?

options.text: Amazon Cognito user pools alone.
AgentCore Identity.
AWS Secrets Manager.
AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: AgentCore Identity manages secure identity and access for agents, including authenticating to and accessing third-party services on a user's behalf. Not "Amazon Cognito user pools alone.": Cognito authenticates end users to your app; it is not the agent's outbound identity to third-party services. Not "AWS Secrets Manager.": Secrets Manager stores secrets but is not the agent identity/consent broker for acting on a user's behalf. Not "AgentCore Gateway.": Gateway exposes tools; it is not the identity/consent layer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A research agent has sessions that can run for several hours and must be deployed serverlessly with per-session isolation, regardless of the framework it was built in. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime.
A self-managed Amazon ECS on Fargate service.
A SageMaker real-time endpoint.
AWS Lambda.

explanation: AgentCore Runtime is a serverless hosting environment that is framework agnostic, runs each user session in a dedicated microVM with isolated CPU, memory and filesystem, and supports sessions of up to 8 hours on microVMs. Not "A self-managed Amazon ECS on Fargate service.": ECS works but requires building and operating the serving infrastructure and the session isolation yourself. Not "A SageMaker real-time endpoint.": SageMaker endpoints serve models, not framework-agnostic agent runtimes. Not "AWS Lambda.": A Lambda function invocation can run for at most 15 minutes, far short of a multi-hour session. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agents-tools-runtime.html

prompt: An operations team must trace WHY an agent chose a tool and inspect each reasoning step, tool call, and latency in production. Which AgentCore capability provides this?

options.text: AgentCore Memory.
AWS CloudTrail.
AgentCore Observability.
Bedrock model invocation logging.

explanation: Observability captures detailed traces of the agent's reasoning steps and tool invocations for debugging and monitoring. Not "AgentCore Memory.": Memory persists context; it is not a tracing tool. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API calls, not the agent's internal reasoning steps and tool decisions. Not "Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures model prompts/responses, not the agent's step-by-step tool orchestration. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A workflow needs ONE coordinating agent to dynamically delegate subtasks to several specialized agents (billing, shipping, returns) and combine results. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Run independent agents with no coordination.
Put every capability in one agent's prompt.
Use Amazon Bedrock Agents multi-agent collaboration, with a supervisor agent coordinating specialized collaborator agents.
Build the workflow in Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prompt Flows).

explanation: With multi-agent collaboration you designate one agent as the supervisor and associate collaborator agents with it; the supervisor creates a plan, routes tasks to the appropriate collaborator and returns the combined result. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is limited: the harness supports a supervisor through the agent-as-tool pattern, and fuller multi-agent collaboration is written in framework code (for example Strands) deployed on AgentCore Runtime. Not "Run independent agents with no coordination.": Without a supervisor there is no way to combine sub-agent results. Not "Put every capability in one agent's prompt.": A single monolithic agent provides no structured delegation or specialization. Not "Build the workflow in Amazon Bedrock Flows (formerly Prom…": A flow links prompts, models and services in a workflow you lay out in advance; it is not dynamic agent-to-agent delegation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-multi-agent-collaboration.html

prompt: An Amazon Bedrock Agents agent can issue refunds, and the user must explicitly approve before any refund executes. Which agent feature enforces this directly?

options.text: Use return of control for the action.
Enable user confirmation (require confirmation) on the sensitive action.
Set temperature to 0.
Add a note in the system prompt to confirm first.

explanation: When user confirmation is enabled for an action, the agent responds with a confirmation question and the action is carried out only if the user answers CONFIRM; on DENY it is not. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is inline function tools in the AgentCore harness, where the agent pauses and returns `tool_use` so the client can handle the human-in-the-loop step. Not "Use return of control for the action.": Return of control changes WHERE execution happens (the caller), but it is not itself a built-in confirm-or-deny gate. Not "Set temperature to 0.": Temperature does not create an approval step. Not "Add a note in the system prompt to confirm first.": Prompt instructions do not enforce a hard approval gate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-userconfirmation.html

prompt: A developer wants an OPEN-SOURCE, code-first, model-driven framework to build tool-using agents in a few lines of Python and then deploy them to AgentCore Runtime. Which option fits?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Agents configured in the console.
AWS Glue.
The Strands Agents SDK.
Amazon Q Developer.

explanation: Strands Agents is AWS's open-source, model-driven SDK for building agents in code and deploying them to AgentCore Runtime. Not "Amazon Bedrock Agents configured in the console.": Bedrock Agents is a managed, configuration-driven service, not the open-source code-first SDK described. Not "AWS Glue.": Glue is an ETL service, unrelated to building agents. Not "Amazon Q Developer.": Q Developer is a coding assistant, not an agent-building runtime SDK. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: The responses of an Amazon Bedrock Agents agent must be filtered for harmful content and PII regardless of which tools or knowledge bases it uses. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Lower the agent's temperature.
Write the safety rules into the agent's instructions.
Filter content inside each action group Lambda.
Attach an Amazon Bedrock Guardrail to the agent.

explanation: Associating a guardrail with the agent (a `GuardrailConfiguration` on CreateAgent or UpdateAgent) applies the safeguards to user messages and model responses for that agent. Amazon Bedrock Agents is now documented as Amazon Bedrock Agents Classic, in maintenance mode; the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore equivalent is a Bedrock guardrail configured on the model, plus policy enforcement on AgentCore Gateway. Not "Lower the agent's temperature.": Temperature does not filter harmful content or PII. Not "Write the safety rules into the agent's instructions.": Instructions are not a reliable, enforced safety control and can be bypassed. Not "Filter content inside each action group Lambda.": Per-tool custom filtering is inconsistent and misses responses that do not go through that Lambda. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-guardrail.html

prompt: An application needs synchronous, low-latency predictions for SMALL payloads with steady, predictable traffic. Which SageMaker AI option is BEST?

options.text: A real-time inference endpoint.
Batch transform.
Serverless Inference.
Asynchronous Inference.

explanation: Real-time endpoints give persistent, low-latency synchronous inference, ideal for steady small-payload traffic. Not "Batch transform.": Batch transform is offline; it cannot serve synchronous requests. Not "Serverless Inference.": Serverless can cold-start and does not support GPUs, adding latency variability not wanted for steady low-latency traffic. Not "Asynchronous Inference.": Async adds queueing latency meant for long-running or large requests, not small fast ones. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A CPU model serves intermittent traffic with long idle gaps, can tolerate occasional cold starts, and must not incur idle cost. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: An always-on real-time endpoint.
Asynchronous Inference sized for peak.
SageMaker Serverless Inference.
Provisioned, always-on GPU instance.

explanation: Serverless scales (including to zero) for intermittent CPU workloads, billing only while serving. Not "An always-on real-time endpoint.": An always-on endpoint pays for the long idle periods. Not "Asynchronous Inference sized for peak.": Provisioning for peak wastes capacity for intermittent traffic. Not "Provisioned, always-on GPU instance.": A continuously running GPU is the most expensive and unnecessary for a CPU workload. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Requests carry payloads up to ~1 GB and take several minutes on a GPU; responses can be delivered asynchronously. Which SageMaker option is BEST?

options.text: Asynchronous Inference.
Serverless Inference.
Batch transform.
Real-time Inference.

explanation: Async supports large payloads (up to ~1 GB), long processing, and GPU instances with queued, asynchronous responses. Not "Serverless Inference.": Serverless does not support GPUs and has small payload limits. Not "Batch transform.": Batch transform is for bulk offline scoring, not on-demand per-request handling. Not "Real-time Inference.": Real-time endpoints cap payloads near 25 MB and target short synchronous calls, so large/long requests fail. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A team deploys several large language models to GPU instances and wants to pack multiple models/copies onto shared accelerators, scale each independently, and scale unused ones to ZERO. Which capability fits?

options.text: SageMaker inference components.
Serverless Inference.
One real-time endpoint per model.
A multi-model endpoint (MME).

explanation: Inference components place multiple models/copies on shared instances, allocate resources per component, scale independently, and can scale to zero. Not "Serverless Inference.": Serverless does not support the GPUs these LLMs need. Not "One real-time endpoint per model.": Separate endpoints cannot pack models onto shared accelerators with independent scaling. Not "A multi-model endpoint (MME).": MME loads many (typically smaller) models on demand behind one endpoint but is not designed for GPU-packing LLMs with independent per-model scaling and scale-to-zero. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A company must host HUNDREDS of small, similar models (one per customer) behind as few endpoints as possible, loading each on demand to save cost. Which option is BEST?

options.text: A multi-model endpoint (MME).
SageMaker inference components.
One dedicated endpoint per model.
Batch transform per model.

explanation: MME hosts many models behind one endpoint, loading them on demand and sharing resources to cut cost. Not "SageMaker inference components.": Inference components target packing and independently scaling (often larger) models, not the classic many-small-models-on-demand pattern. Not "One dedicated endpoint per model.": Hundreds of endpoints multiply cost and management. Not "Batch transform per model.": Batch transform is offline scoring, not on-demand hosting. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Real-time endpoint traffic swings widely between day and night, and the team wants instances added and removed automatically based on load. What should they configure?

options.text: Switch to batch transform during the day.
A fixed instance count sized for peak.
Use a larger instance type only.
Automatic scaling (for example, target tracking on invocations per instance).

explanation: Endpoint auto scaling adjusts instance count against a target metric, matching capacity to demand. Not "Switch to batch transform during the day.": Batch transform is offline and cannot serve real-time daytime traffic. Not "A fixed instance count sized for peak.": A fixed peak size wastes money at night and cannot adapt automatically. Not "Use a larger instance type only.": A bigger instance does not automatically scale with demand. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Before promoting a new model version, the team wants to send a COPY of live production traffic to it and compare results WITHOUT affecting any users. Which capability is correct?

options.text: A blue/green switch all at once.
Shadow testing (shadow variants).
Batch transform on yesterday's data.
A canary deployment with deployment guardrails.

explanation: Shadow testing mirrors live traffic to a shadow variant so you validate against real requests with no impact on user-facing responses. Not "A blue/green switch all at once.": An all-at-once cutover exposes all users immediately and is not a no-impact comparison. Not "Batch transform on yesterday's data.": Offline scoring does not exercise the new version against live traffic. Not "A canary deployment with deployment guardrails.": Canary routes a slice of REAL user traffic to the new version, so some users are affected, unlike shadow testing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: When updating a production endpoint, the team wants to shift a small percentage of REAL traffic first and automatically roll back if errors spike. Which capability is correct?

options.text: Shadow testing.
Deployment guardrails with a canary (or linear) traffic-shifting strategy and automatic rollback.
Recreate the endpoint in place.
Increase the instance count during the switch.

explanation: Deployment guardrails gradually shift live traffic, watch alarms, and roll back automatically if the new version misbehaves. Not "Shadow testing.": Shadow testing mirrors traffic without serving users, so it does not perform a controlled production rollout. Not "Recreate the endpoint in place.": An in-place replace has no gradual shift or automatic rollback and risks downtime. Not "Increase the instance count during the switch.": More instances does not provide controlled traffic shifting or rollback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A developer wants to deploy a popular open foundation model fast, with a tested container and example notebooks. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Deploy the model from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart.
Use batch transform to expose an endpoint.
Build a custom serving container from scratch.
Use AWS Glue to host the model.

explanation: JumpStart provides prebuilt, deployable models with curated containers and notebooks for fast deployment. Not "Use batch transform to expose an endpoint.": Batch transform does not create an online endpoint. Not "Build a custom serving container from scratch.": Building everything yourself is the slowest path. Not "Use AWS Glue to host the model.": Glue is an ETL service and cannot host a model endpoint. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A fixed dataset already in Amazon S3 must be scored in a SINGLE offline run with no persistent endpoint, at the lowest cost. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Asynchronous Inference per record.
A batch transform job.
Serverless Inference.
A real-time endpoint invoked in a loop.

explanation: Batch transform scores a whole S3 dataset in one offline run and releases compute afterward, with no endpoint to pay for. Not "Asynchronous Inference per record.": Per-record async adds overhead versus a single batch over the dataset. Not "Serverless Inference.": Serverless targets intermittent online requests, not bulk offline scoring. Not "A real-time endpoint invoked in a loop.": Looping over a persistent endpoint is more expensive and complex than one batch job. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Profiling a model served with DJL on an 8-GPU instance shows the model fits entirely within 4 GPUs and per-instance concurrency is low. Which change BEST improves GPU utilization?

options.text: Enable speculative decoding.
Use a tensor parallelism degree of 8.
Add more instances and spread requests.
Use a tensor parallelism degree of 4 so two model replicas run on each 8-GPU instance.

explanation: Since the model fits in 4 GPUs, a tensor-parallel degree of 4 places two replicas per instance, using all 8 GPUs. Not "Enable speculative decoding.": Speculative decoding reduces latency, not GPU utilization. Not "Use a tensor parallelism degree of 8.": Degree 8 serves a single replica across all GPUs, leaving half the capacity idle since the model fits in 4. Not "Add more instances and spread requests.": More instances does not raise per-instance utilization or concurrency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: Logs show the real maximum sequence length is about 10x smaller than the configured value and concurrency per GPU is low on a DJL-served model. Which change BEST increases throughput per GPU?

options.text: Increase the maximum sequence length.
Enable speculative decoding.
Lower the rolling batch size.
Reduce the configured maximum sequence length to allow a larger rolling batch size.

explanation: Lowering the max sequence length frees memory so more requests fit in each rolling batch, increasing throughput and concurrency. Not "Increase the maximum sequence length.": A larger max sequence length reserves more memory per request and reduces batch size. Not "Enable speculative decoding.": Speculative decoding targets latency, not batch-size-driven throughput. Not "Lower the rolling batch size.": A smaller batch reduces throughput. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model.html

prompt: A development team must upgrade its Java 8 applications to Java 17, working project by project in the IDE and automating the repetitive code changes. Which Amazon Q Developer capability is BEST?

options.text: Amazon Q Developer code transformation.
Amazon Macie.
Manually editing each project.
Amazon Q Developer inline code suggestions.

explanation: Amazon Q Developer code transformation upgrades Java applications to newer language versions in the IDE (for example Java 8 or 11 to Java 17 or 21), updating deprecated APIs and libraries. For organization-wide upgrades across hundreds of applications, AWS now positions AWS Transform custom, which automates Java, Node.js and Python version upgrades at scale. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies sensitive data and is unrelated to code upgrades. Not "Manually editing each project.": Manual edits are slow and error-prone, which automation avoids. Not "Amazon Q Developer inline code suggestions.": Inline suggestions speed typing in the editor but do not perform an automated, project-wide upgrade. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/code-transformation.html

prompt: A team wants an assistant that takes a natural-language feature request, plans it, and implements the change across MULTIPLE files. Which Amazon Q Developer capability fits?

options.text: Amazon Comprehend.
Single-line inline completion.
Amazon QuickSight Q.
Amazon Q Developer agentic coding in the IDE chat (formerly the /dev feature-development agent).

explanation: With agentic coding, Amazon Q Developer helps develop code features and makes the code changes to the project files directly; this capability used to be referred to as /dev. Not "Amazon Comprehend.": Comprehend is an NLP service, not a coding agent. Not "Single-line inline completion.": Inline completion helps at the cursor but cannot plan and implement a multi-file feature. Not "Amazon QuickSight Q.": QuickSight Q answers questions over BI data, not multi-file code changes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/q-in-IDE-chat.html

prompt: Developers want their assistant to scan SOURCE CODE for vulnerabilities and suggest fixes inside the IDE. Which option is correct?

options.text: Amazon Macie.
Amazon GuardDuty.
Amazon Inspector.
Amazon Q Developer code reviews (formerly /review).

explanation: Amazon Q Developer code reviews check a codebase from the IDE for security vulnerabilities (SAST scanning, secrets detection, IaC issues) and code quality issues, on a file, a project or as you write code. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies sensitive data, not code vulnerabilities. Not "Amazon GuardDuty.": GuardDuty detects account/workload threats, not source-code vulnerabilities. Not "Amazon Inspector.": Inspector Code Security does scan first-party source code, dependencies and infrastructure as code, but through scan configurations applied to code repositories, not as an assistant inside the IDE. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/code-reviews.html

prompt: To raise coverage quickly, a team wants to automatically GENERATE unit tests for existing functions. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Single-line inline completion only.
AWS CodeBuild.
Amazon Q Developer unit test generation.
Amazon QuickSight.

explanation: Q Developer generates unit tests for existing code with minimal manual effort. Not "Single-line inline completion only.": Inline completion does not systematically generate a test suite for existing functions. Not "AWS CodeBuild.": CodeBuild runs builds/tests but does not author tests. Not "Amazon QuickSight.": QuickSight is for dashboards, not test generation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A team wants automated test generation and quality checks to run CONTINUOUSLY as code is merged, not ad hoc. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Integrate Amazon Q Developer automated test generation into the CI/CD pipeline.
Run Amazon Q Developer only manually in the IDE when remembered.
Hold periodic manual review cycles instead.
Add Amazon Inspector to the pipeline for unit tests.

explanation: Embedding Q Developer test generation in CI/CD continuously validates changes and catches defects early. Not "Run Amazon Q Developer only manually in the IDE when reme…": Ad hoc IDE use is not continuous and misses merges. Not "Hold periodic manual review cycles instead.": Manual cycles are slow and not continuous. Not "Add Amazon Inspector to the pipeline for unit tests.": Inspector finds vulnerabilities; it does not generate unit tests. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/what-is.html

prompt: A team must retain the FULL prompt and response content of every Bedrock model call for troubleshooting and audit, with the least custom code. Which capability is correct?

options.text: AWS X-Ray.
AWS CloudTrail.
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.
Amazon CloudWatch metrics.

explanation: Invocation logging records full prompts, responses, and metadata to S3 and/or CloudWatch with no custom instrumentation. Not "AWS X-Ray.": X-Ray traces request flow and timing, not full model content. Not "AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API metadata, not the full prompt/response content. Not "Amazon CloudWatch metrics.": Metrics are numeric aggregates, not request/response content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: An auditor needs to know WHICH IAM principal called WHICH Bedrock API and WHEN, across the account. Which service provides this?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch dashboards.
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.
AWS CloudTrail.
AWS Config.

explanation: CloudTrail records API calls with principal, action, time, and source, the audit trail of who did what. Not "Amazon CloudWatch dashboards.": Dashboards visualize metrics, not per-call caller identity. Not "Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures model prompt/response content, not a full account-wide API caller audit trail. Not "AWS Config.": Config tracks resource configuration compliance, not API caller activity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A team must identify and troubleshoot per-DOCUMENT failures during knowledge base ingestion (ingested, ignored, or failed). Which solution is correct?

options.text: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging.
Enable CloudWatch Application Signals.
Use AWS CloudTrail.
Configure knowledge base logging to CloudWatch Logs and query with Logs Insights.

explanation: Knowledge base logging records per-file ingestion status, which Logs Insights can query for failures. Not "Enable Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures model calls, not the document ingestion process. Not "Enable CloudWatch Application Signals.": Application Signals monitors application performance, not knowledge base ingestion. Not "Use AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records API calls, not document-level ingestion status. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A request flows through API Gateway, several Lambdas, a knowledge base, and Bedrock, and the team must find WHICH component causes high end-to-end latency. Which service is BEST?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch alarms on total latency.
Amazon Macie.
Bedrock model invocation logging.
AWS X-Ray.

explanation: X-Ray traces requests across components and shows segment timings that pinpoint the bottleneck. Not "Amazon CloudWatch alarms on total latency.": Alarms detect that latency is high but do not localize which component is responsible. Not "Amazon Macie.": Macie classifies data and has no tracing capability. Not "Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures model content, not cross-service timing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: Invocation logs are stored in CloudWatch Logs, and an engineer must interactively query them to find and aggregate error patterns. Which tool is BEST?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail Lake.
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Amazon Athena with no setup.
Amazon QuickSight Q.

explanation: Logs Insights provides an interactive query language to search and aggregate the CloudWatch log data. Not "AWS CloudTrail Lake.": CloudTrail Lake queries CloudTrail API events, not arbitrary invocation logs already in CloudWatch Logs. Not "Amazon Athena with no setup.": Athena would require exporting and cataloging the data first; Logs Insights queries the logs directly. Not "Amazon QuickSight Q.": QuickSight Q answers over prepared BI datasets, not ad hoc CloudWatch log querying. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A model on a SageMaker real-time endpoint must be continuously monitored for DATA DRIFT against a baseline, with automated alerts. Which capability is correct?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.
CloudWatch alarms on CPU only.
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify run once at training time.

explanation: Model Monitor continuously checks a deployed endpoint for data quality and drift against a baseline and can alert. Not "Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.": Guardrails filter content; they do not monitor endpoint data drift. Not "CloudWatch alarms on CPU only.": Infrastructure metrics do not detect data drift. Not "Amazon SageMaker Clarify run once at training time.": A one-time Clarify analysis measures bias/explainability but is not continuous endpoint drift monitoring. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A finance team must ATTRIBUTE Bedrock usage and cost to specific applications and teams that SHARE the same models and call them through the same IAM role. Which approach is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Use AWS Cost Explorer without any tagging.
Use AWS CloudTrail.
Use Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles with cost allocation tags.
Use model invocation logging.

explanation: Application inference profiles are created to track costs and model usage: each application or team invokes through its own tagged profile, and the tags are used for cost allocation. Bedrock can also attribute cost by IAM principal, but that cannot separate applications that share one role. Not "Use AWS Cost Explorer without any tagging.": Cost Explorer alone cannot split a shared model's spend across applications that use the same role without attribution tags. Not "Use AWS CloudTrail.": CloudTrail records who called the API, not per-application cost attribution. Not "Use model invocation logging.": Invocation logging records requests and responses, not billing attribution. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles.html

prompt: After launch, a team wants ongoing assurance of a generative feature's quality, catching regressions as prompts and models change. Which practice is MOST effective?

options.text: Log responses and run periodic automated evaluations on sampled production traffic, alerting on regressions.
Run one pre-launch test and never re-check.
Monitor only CPU and memory.
Wait for user complaints.

explanation: Response logging plus scheduled automated evaluation on samples gives continuous, data-driven quality monitoring. Not "Run one pre-launch test and never re-check.": A one-time test misses regressions introduced by later changes. Not "Monitor only CPU and memory.": Infrastructure metrics do not reveal generation-quality regressions. Not "Wait for user complaints.": Relying on complaints is reactive and lets defects reach users. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A mobile app's end users sign in and must then receive scoped, TEMPORARY AWS credentials to call Bedrock, with no AWS keys embedded in the app. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Use an Amazon Cognito user pool by itself.
Embed a shared IAM access key in the app.
Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool to exchange the sign-in for temporary, scoped AWS credentials.
Create one IAM user per end user.

explanation: Identity pools federate authenticated users to temporary AWS credentials tied to an IAM role, with no embedded keys. Not "Use an Amazon Cognito user pool by itself.": A user pool authenticates users but does not itself vend AWS credentials; the identity pool provides AWS credentials. Not "Embed a shared IAM access key in the app.": Embedding long-lived keys in a distributed app is a serious security risk. Not "Create one IAM user per end user.": IAM users issue long-lived keys and do not scale or provide temporary access. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: INTERNAL employees must authenticate through the corporate SAML identity provider to access Bedrock with temporary credentials (workforce SSO). Which solution is BEST?

options.text: AWS IAM Identity Center with SAML federation to the corporate IdP.
Access keys distributed to employees.
An Amazon Cognito identity pool.
IAM users for each employee.

explanation: IAM Identity Center is the workforce SSO service that federates corporate identities to temporary AWS access. Not "Access keys distributed to employees.": Distributing long-lived keys is insecure and unmanageable. Not "An Amazon Cognito identity pool.": Cognito targets application/customer identities; workforce SSO via the corporate IdP is IAM Identity Center. Not "IAM users for each employee.": IAM users rely on long-lived keys and do not integrate with the corporate IdP. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A regulated company must call Bedrock from its VPC WITHOUT traffic traversing the public internet. Which solution is correct?

options.text: Set up VPC peering.
Route Bedrock calls through a NAT gateway.
Create VPC interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon Bedrock.
Use an internet gateway with TLS.

explanation: Interface endpoints via PrivateLink keep traffic to Bedrock on the AWS network. Not "Set up VPC peering.": VPC peering connects VPCs to each other, not your VPC privately to the Bedrock service. Not "Route Bedrock calls through a NAT gateway.": A NAT gateway still sends traffic over the public internet. Not "Use an internet gateway with TLS.": TLS encrypts traffic but it still traverses the public internet. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: An application in Account A must call Bedrock resources governed by Account B using temporary credentials and no shared long-lived keys. Which mechanism is correct?

options.text: Make the Bedrock resources public.
Use the same root user across both accounts.
Create an IAM role in Account B and have Account A assume it via AWS STS AssumeRole.
Share Account B's IAM access keys with Account A.

explanation: Cross-account role assumption provides scoped, temporary credentials without sharing long-lived keys. Not "Make the Bedrock resources public.": Public access removes the required access control. Not "Use the same root user across both accounts.": Sharing root credentials is a severe security violation. Not "Share Account B's IAM access keys with Account A.": Sharing long-lived keys is insecure and unmanageable. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: An agent's Lambda must use a third-party API key that has to be stored securely WITH automatic rotation and fine-grained access. Which service is BEST?

options.text: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString.
A hard-coded constant in the function.
A plaintext environment variable.
AWS Secrets Manager.

explanation: Secrets Manager stores credentials with IAM-controlled access and supports built-in automatic rotation. Not "AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString.": Parameter Store can hold encrypted values but does not provide built-in managed rotation for arbitrary third-party secrets the way Secrets Manager does. Not "A hard-coded constant in the function.": Hard-coded secrets cannot be rotated and risk exposure. Not "A plaintext environment variable.": Plaintext secrets are insecure and cannot be rotated safely. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: Security policy requires that a specific IAM role be able to invoke ONLY one approved foundation model in Bedrock. How is this BEST enforced?

options.text: Allow all models and tell developers to use only the approved one.
Choose the model only in application code.
Write a least-privilege IAM policy that allows invoke actions only on the approved model's resource ARN.
Apply the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key.

explanation: Scoping the policy to the specific model ARN technically restricts the role to that model. Not "Allow all models and tell developers to use only the appr…": A verbal rule is not a technical control. Not "Choose the model only in application code.": Application-side selection is not an access control and can be bypassed. Not "Apply the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key.": That condition enforces that a guardrail is applied; it does not restrict which model the role may invoke. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A company must encrypt Bedrock-related data at rest using keys it can CONTROL, ROTATE, and AUDIT. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Rely on the default AWS owned key.
Store the data unencrypted for simplicity.
Use a client-side passphrase hard-coded in the app.
Encrypt with an AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK).

explanation: A customer managed key gives control over key policy and rotation, and CloudTrail audits its use. Not "Rely on the default AWS owned key.": AWS owned keys encrypt data but give the customer no control, rotation policy, or usage auditing. Not "Store the data unencrypted for simplicity.": Unencrypted data fails the requirement. Not "Use a client-side passphrase hard-coded in the app.": A hard-coded passphrase is insecure and not an auditable managed key. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A compliance team must ensure customer prompts are processed only within an approved Region and are NOT used to train the base models. Which statement and action are correct?

options.text: Use a global cross-Region inference profile, since routing never affects where data is processed.
Self-host the model, since only that prevents base-model training on your data.
Invoke the model by its model ID in the approved Region rather than through a cross-Region inference profile; Bedrock does not use your prompts/outputs to train the base models.
File a support ticket to opt out, or your data trains the models by default.

explanation: With Amazon Bedrock, your content is not used to improve the base models and is not shared with model providers. Where a request is processed depends on how you invoke: a cross-Region inference profile lets Bedrock select another Region, so calling the model directly in the approved Region is what keeps processing there. Not "Use a global cross-Region inference profile, since routin…": A global profile can route the request to any supported commercial Region worldwide; a geographic profile stays within its geography (such as US or EU) but still leaves the calling Region. Not "Self-host the model, since only that prevents base-model …": Using Bedrock already prevents your data from training base models; self-hosting is unnecessary for that guarantee. Not "File a support ticket to opt out, or your data trains the…": No opt-out is required; Bedrock does not use your data to train base models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A team must filter harmful content (hate, insults, violence, sexual, misconduct) in BOTH prompts and responses, with adjustable strictness PER category. Which Guardrails feature is correct?

options.text: Word filters.
Stop sequences.
Content filters with configurable strength per harmful category.
Denied topics.

explanation: Content filters detect and block harmful categories in input and output with per-category strength settings. Not "Word filters.": Word filters block specific words/phrases, not graded harmful-content categories. Not "Stop sequences.": Stop sequences end generation; they do not classify harmful content. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics block specific subjects you define, not the built-in harmful-content categories. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A banking assistant must refuse a specific prohibited SUBJECT (individualized investment advice) even when users rephrase it in new ways. Which Guardrails feature is BEST?

options.text: Denied topics, defined with a description and examples.
Word filters listing banned terms.
Content filters.
The PII filter.

explanation: Denied topics block a subject by semantic description and examples, catching varied phrasings. Not "Word filters listing banned terms.": A keyword list misses rephrasings and is brittle for a whole subject. Not "Content filters.": Content filters target harmful categories, not an arbitrary business subject. Not "The PII filter.": The PII filter handles personal data, not topic restriction. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: An assistant must ensure PII in model RESPONSES is masked or blocked before reaching users, as a managed guardrail control. Which feature is correct?

options.text: Denied topics.
Content filters.
The Guardrails sensitive information (PII) filter.
Run Amazon Comprehend on each response in custom code.

explanation: The PII filter detects and masks or blocks personal information in inputs and outputs. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics block subjects, not PII entities. Not "Content filters.": Content filters handle harmful categories, not PII masking. Not "Run Amazon Comprehend on each response in custom code.": Comprehend can detect PII but is a separate custom step, not the managed in-guardrail control the scenario asks for. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A public chatbot faces users trying to override its instructions and jailbreak it. Which Guardrails capability specifically detects these attempts?

options.text: Content filters for hate/violence.
Lowering the temperature.
The prompt attack filter.
Denied topics.

explanation: The prompt attack filter flags prompt injection and jailbreak inputs so they can be blocked. Not "Content filters for hate/violence.": Those categories do not target instruction-override attacks. Not "Lowering the temperature.": Temperature does not detect prompt attacks. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics block subjects, not injection attempts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A brand must block an EXACT list of competitor names and specific profane terms from outputs. Which Guardrails feature is the BEST fit?

options.text: Content filters.
The PII filter.
Denied topics.
Word filters (a custom word/phrase list plus managed profanity).

explanation: Word filters block specific, exact terms such as competitor names and profanity. Not "Content filters.": Content filters address harmful categories, not a specific custom term list. Not "The PII filter.": The PII filter handles personal data, not competitor names. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics target whole semantic subjects, which is heavier than blocking an exact word list. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: In a RAG assistant, the guardrail itself should block responses NOT supported by the retrieved source or off-topic from the query, using a tunable threshold. Which capability fits?

options.text: Content filters.
The contextual grounding and relevance checks.
Word filters.
Denied topics.

explanation: These checks score grounding in the source and relevance to the query and can block low-scoring responses at a configured threshold. Not "Content filters.": Content filters target harmful content, not grounding. Not "Word filters.": Word filters block specific terms, not ungrounded responses. Not "Denied topics.": Denied topics block subjects, not ungrounded answers within an allowed subject. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A self-managed pipeline calls a model hosted OUTSIDE Bedrock but wants to apply the same Bedrock guardrail policy to arbitrary text at chosen points. Which capability enables this?

options.text: Defining denied topics in the guardrail.
Inline guardrails only on Bedrock InvokeModel.
The ApplyGuardrail API.
Provisioned Throughput.

explanation: ApplyGuardrail evaluates input/output text against a guardrail independently of a Bedrock model call, covering external models and arbitrary points. Not "Defining denied topics in the guardrail.": Denied topics is a policy type, not the independent evaluation API. Not "Inline guardrails only on Bedrock InvokeModel.": Inline-only guardrails cannot cover text from a non-Bedrock model or arbitrary pipeline steps. Not "Provisioned Throughput.": Provisioned Throughput is a capacity feature, unrelated to guardrail evaluation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: A regulated insurer needs strong assurance that policy answers conform to its written rules, with VERIFIABLE logical checks rather than only probabilistic filtering. Which newer Guardrails capability fits?

options.text: The contextual grounding check.
Content filters.
Lowering the temperature.
