Automated Reasoning checks.

explanation: Automated Reasoning checks use formal, logic-based verification against an encoded policy to validate responses. Not "The contextual grounding check.": Grounding checks whether a response is supported by provided source text, not formal verification against encoded policy rules. Not "Content filters.": Content filters handle harmful content, not policy conformance verification. Not "Lowering the temperature.": Temperature does not verify outputs against policy. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html

prompt: Governance requires that EVERY InvokeModel and Converse call made in an AWS account, from many IAM roles, apply a specific guardrail, enforced as efficiently as possible. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Configure account-level guardrail enforcement (PutEnforcedGuardrailConfiguration) with a numeric guardrail version in each Region the account uses.
Add an IAM policy with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key to all roles that access Bedrock.
Store the guardrail ID in Parameter Store and fetch it per call.
Route all calls through a Lambda proxy that injects the guardrail.

explanation: Account-level enforcement designates a guardrail version for all Amazon Bedrock model invocations from the account, with one configuration per Region and no per-role or per-application work. Not "Add an IAM policy with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier co…": The condition key does require the guardrail on a role's calls, but it must be maintained on every role, and AWS documents that a user can bypass the guardrail on the prompt by using guardrail input tags. Not "Store the guardrail ID in Parameter Store and fetch it pe…": This relies on every application choosing to pass the guardrail; nothing is enforced. Not "Route all calls through a Lambda proxy that injects the g…": A proxy is a bottleneck and custom code to maintain, and it does not stop roles from calling Bedrock directly. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-enforcements.html

prompt: Compliance records must be stored so they CANNOT be altered or deleted for a mandated period, even by administrators or the root user. Which configuration is correct?

options.text: S3 versioning alone.
A bucket policy that denies deletes.
Amazon S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for the retention period.
Amazon S3 Object Lock in governance mode.

explanation: Compliance mode enforces WORM immutability that no one, including root, can override until retention expires. Not "S3 versioning alone.": Versioning preserves versions but does not prevent deletion or enforce retention. Not "A bucket policy that denies deletes.": A bucket policy can be changed by administrators, so it is not immutable retention. Not "Amazon S3 Object Lock in governance mode.": Governance mode can be overridden by users with special permissions, so it does not guarantee immutability against administrators. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: An auditor must determine which IAM principals called which Bedrock APIs and when. Which service provides this trail?

options.text: AWS Config.
Bedrock model invocation logging.
AWS CloudTrail.
Amazon CloudWatch metrics.

explanation: CloudTrail records API calls with principal, action, and time. Not "AWS Config.": Config tracks resource configuration, not API caller activity. Not "Bedrock model invocation logging.": Invocation logging captures prompt/response content, not the account-wide API caller audit trail. Not "Amazon CloudWatch metrics.": Metrics are numeric aggregates, not caller identity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: For regulatory reconstruction, a company must retain the ACTUAL prompt and response content of every Bedrock call in immutable storage. Which combination is correct?

options.text: Rely on CloudWatch metrics.
Print prompts to the application console.
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to S3 and apply S3 Object Lock for the retention period.
Enable AWS CloudTrail only.

explanation: Invocation logging captures full content, and Object Lock makes the stored logs immutable for retention. Not "Rely on CloudWatch metrics.": Metrics do not store prompt or response text. Not "Print prompts to the application console.": Console output is not durable, complete, or immutable. Not "Enable AWS CloudTrail only.": CloudTrail captures API metadata, not the full prompt/response content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A company wants to keep chat transcripts for analytics but is prohibited from RETAINING PII. What is the BEST approach before storage?

options.text: Lower the model temperature.
Encrypt the bucket and keep all PII.
Redact PII with Amazon Comprehend, then store the sanitized transcripts.
Store the raw transcripts unchanged.

explanation: Detecting and redacting PII before storage keeps useful analytics data while complying with the no-PII rule. Not "Lower the model temperature.": Temperature does not remove PII from stored text. Not "Encrypt the bucket and keep all PII.": Encryption protects data at rest but does not satisfy a rule against retaining PII at all. Not "Store the raw transcripts unchanged.": Storing raw PII violates the requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: Stored embeddings and invocation logs contain sensitive data, and the security team must CONTROL and AUDIT the encryption keys. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Encrypt with AWS KMS customer managed keys and audit usage via key policies and CloudTrail.
Make the storage public so keys are unnecessary.
Use one shared password stored in code.
Leave the data unencrypted for easy access.

explanation: Customer managed keys give control and rotation, and CloudTrail records key usage for auditing. Not "Make the storage public so keys are unnecessary.": Public storage exposes the data and is the opposite of the requirement. Not "Use one shared password stored in code.": A hard-coded shared secret is insecure and not auditable. Not "Leave the data unencrypted for easy access.": Unencrypted sensitive data fails the requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A user invokes their right to erasure. Their documents were ingested into a knowledge base whose embeddings live in a vector store. What must you do to FULLY remove their data?

options.text: Delete only the source files from Amazon S3.
Delete only the CloudWatch logs.
Rely on S3 Object Lock to expire the data.
Delete the source documents AND remove/re-sync them from the knowledge base so the corresponding vector embeddings are deleted.

explanation: Embeddings persist in the vector store until the knowledge base is updated, so both the source and the ingested vectors must be removed. Not "Delete only the source files from Amazon S3.": Deleting the source leaves the already-ingested embeddings in the vector store, so the data is not fully removed. Not "Delete only the CloudWatch logs.": Logs are unrelated to the embeddings retained in the vector store. Not "Rely on S3 Object Lock to expire the data.": Object Lock prevents deletion during retention, which is the opposite of fulfilling an erasure request. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A support assistant sends the same 18,000-token product manual as a prefix on every turn of a conversation, followed by a short user question. Input token spend dominates the bill. Which change reduces input cost the most while leaving answer quality unchanged?

options.text: Lower the maxTokens value on each request so the model is forced to produce noticeably shorter completions, cutting the tokens billed per turn.
Move the conversation to batch inference so the whole workload is billed at the discounted asynchronous rate.
Reduce temperature to 0 so the model stops exploring and converges on a shorter, more direct answer.
Add an explicit cache checkpoint after the manual and before the user turn, so the prefix is billed at the cache-read rate.

explanation: The manual is a long, static prefix repeated across requests - exactly the shape prompt caching targets. Placing a cache checkpoint at the end of the static content lets later requests read that prefix at the cache-read rate instead of the full input rate. Not "Lower the maxTokens value...": maxTokens caps output tokens; the cost here is input tokens, and truncating answers degrades quality. Not "Reduce temperature to 0...": temperature changes sampling, not token accounting, and does not shorten the input at all. Not "Move the conversation to batch inference...": batch is asynchronous and cannot serve an interactive chat - and prompt caching is not supported with the batch inference API. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: A team caches a large system prompt with a cache checkpoint using the Converse API, but cacheReadInputTokens is almost always zero. Their agent regenerates the tools array on every call, reordering tool definitions each time. What explains the cache misses?

options.text: A request may contain only one cache checkpoint, so adding a tools array silently disables the system prompt checkpoint.
Tool definitions are excluded from the cached prefix, so a changing tools array can never affect system prompt cache hits.
Cache checkpoints placed in the system field are ignored by the Converse API; only checkpoints inside the messages field are ever honored.
Cache checkpoints are processed tools then system then messages, so changing tools invalidates the system and messages caches.

explanation: Cached sections are chained in the order tools, then system, then messages, and the minimum token count is evaluated across the cumulative prefix. Because the sections are chained, changing an earlier section invalidates the cache for every later section - so a churning tools array destroys the system prompt cache on every call. The fix is to emit tool definitions in a stable order. Not "Cache checkpoints placed in the system field are ignored...": Converse accepts cachePoint in tools, system and messages. Not "A request may contain only one cache checkpoint...": Claude models allow up to four checkpoints per request. Not "Tool definitions are excluded from the cached prefix...": tools are the first section of the cached prefix, which is precisely why they matter. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: An agentic workflow runs long side-tasks, so follow-up calls that reuse the same 30,000-token context typically arrive 10 to 40 minutes after the previous call. The team already uses explicit prompt caching but sees poor hit rates. What should they change?

options.text: Split the context across four checkpoints so that at least one of them survives past the default expiry.
Specify a 1-hour TTL on the cache checkpoint, so the cached prefix survives the gap between calls.
Issue a small keep-alive request against the same prefix every four minutes to refresh the default cache window.
Switch from explicit to implicit prompt caching, which holds eligible prefixes for substantially longer.

explanation: The default cache TTL on supported models is 5 minutes, refreshed on each hit. Gaps of 10-40 minutes blow past it. Supported Claude models accept a ttl field of "1h" on the cache checkpoint (cachePoint in Converse, cache_control in InvokeModel), which is designed for exactly this longer-running-session case. Not "Issue a small keep-alive request...": it works mechanically but wastes invocations and quota to emulate a TTL the API already exposes. Not "Split the context across four checkpoints...": adding checkpoints does not lengthen any TTL; each checkpoint has the TTL you set on it (1-hour and 5-minute entries can be mixed in one request, with the longer TTL first), so four default checkpoints all still expire after 5 minutes. Not "Switch from explicit to implicit prompt caching...": implicit caching is best-effort and does not grant a longer TTL. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: After enabling prompt caching, a FinOps dashboard that sums the inputTokens field from Converse responses shows a sudden 70% drop in input tokens, but the Bedrock bill falls by far less. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Cached tokens are billed at the full standard input rate, so a drop in the reported token count cannot translate into any reduction in spend.
With caching on, inputTokens counts only non-cached tokens; total input is inputTokens plus cacheReadInputTokens plus cacheWriteInputTokens.
The dashboard is double counting, because cacheReadInputTokens is already included inside the inputTokens value it sums.
Prompt caching bills per cache checkpoint rather than per token, so token counts no longer correlate with the invoice.

explanation: When prompt caching is enabled, inputTokens reports only the tokens that were neither read from nor written to cache. Total input tokens = inputTokens + cacheReadInputTokens + cacheWriteInputTokens. A dashboard summing inputTokens alone therefore appears to show a collapse in usage that the bill does not match - cache reads are cheaper, not free, and cache writes can cost more than standard input tokens. Not "Cached tokens are billed at the full standard input rate...": cache reads are billed at a reduced cache-read rate. Not "The dashboard is double counting...": the fields are disjoint, which is why they must be added. Not "Prompt caching bills per cache checkpoint...": billing remains token-based. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: A media company must classify and summarize a 4-million-document archive. The job can run overnight, results are consumed by a downstream ETL process, and cost per token is the dominant concern. Which Amazon Bedrock execution model fits best?

options.text: On-demand InvokeModel from a fleet of AWS Lambda functions fanned out by an Amazon SQS queue, to maximize parallel throughput.
Provisioned Throughput with enough model units purchased to hold the whole archive within the overnight window.
Cross-Region inference profiles so the archive is spread across Regions and served at the highest available capacity.
Batch inference: upload JSONL input to Amazon S3, submit one job, and collect the output files from S3 when it completes.

explanation: Batch inference is built for exactly this shape: large volumes, no latency requirement, asynchronous submission via S3, and a lower per-token price than on-demand. Not "On-demand InvokeModel from a fleet of AWS Lambda functions...": it works but pays full on-demand rates and fights account throttling quotas. Not "Provisioned Throughput with enough model units...": PT buys dedicated capacity at a commitment price - the wrong instrument for a one-off offline sweep, and batch is not supported for provisioned models. Not "Cross-Region inference profiles...": cross-Region inference raises available on-demand capacity; geographic profiles are charged at standard pricing and a global profile saves only about 10%, well short of the 50% lower price of batch on supported models, and the calls are still synchronous on-demand requests. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/batch-inference.html

prompt: A team plans to migrate an existing on-demand pipeline to Amazon Bedrock batch inference to cut cost. The pipeline relies on a multi-turn tool-calling loop (the application runs each requested tool and returns the result to the model), and currently runs against a Provisioned Throughput model. Which statement correctly describes the blocker?

options.text: Batch inference supports provisioned models, but every record must use the InvokeModel format rather than the Converse format.
Batch inference supports tool calling only when the input records are supplied in the Converse API request format.
Batch inference does not support tool calling, and it cannot be run against provisioned models.
Batch inference supports tool calling but caps each job at a single tool definition, and provisioned models are supported.

explanation: Two independent constraints bite here. Batch processes each JSONL record independently with no multi-turn interaction, so tool calling (function calling), which needs a back-and-forth exchange between model and client, is not available. Separately, batch inference is not supported for provisioned models. The tool-calling loop has to stay on on-demand inference. Not "...caps each job at a single tool definition...": tool calling is unsupported outright, not limited. Not "Batch inference supports provisioned models...": it does not; and batch accepts both InvokeModel and Converse input formats. Not "...tool calling only when...Converse API request format": the input format does not re-enable tool calling. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/batch-inference.html

prompt: A production workload has a steady, well-understood invocation rate and a contractual latency SLA. It intermittently receives ThrottlingException under on-demand inference, and the team needs guaranteed capacity with predictable monthly spend. Which option should they choose?

options.text: Move the workload to batch inference, which is not subject to the on-demand throttling quotas that cause the errors.
Implement exponential backoff with jitter in the SDK and retry throttled calls until they eventually succeed.
Adopt a cross-Region inference profile so requests overflow into additional Regions during demand peaks.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput model units with a commitment term for the model the workload depends on.

explanation: Provisioned Throughput buys dedicated model units, which is what turns a best-effort on-demand quota into guaranteed capacity with a predictable, committed price - the combination the question asks for. Bedrock also offers a Reserved service tier (reserved tokens-per-minute capacity for 1 or 3 months at a fixed price, arranged through the AWS account team), which serves the same goal but is not among the options. Not "Adopt a cross-Region inference profile...": it materially raises available on-demand capacity and is the right first move for bursty traffic, but it is still shared best-effort capacity, so it guarantees neither throughput nor a latency SLA; inference profiles also do not support Provisioned Throughput, so the two cannot be combined. Not "Implement exponential backoff with jitter...": retries are mandatory hygiene but add latency and do not create capacity. Not "Move the workload to batch inference...": batch is asynchronous and cannot meet an interactive latency SLA. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A platform team serves 30 internal applications from one shared AWS account and one Amazon Bedrock model. All applications call Bedrock through the same shared execution role, which the team will not change. Finance requires per-application cost attribution in AWS Cost Explorer without splitting the account or duplicating infrastructure. Which approach meets the requirement?

options.text: Have each application pass a distinct requestMetadata key on every InvokeModel call and group the resulting CloudTrail events.
Create one application inference profile per application, tag each profile, and have each application invoke its own profile.
Enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 and run an Athena query that attributes token counts by IAM principal.
Create one system-defined cross-Region inference profile per application and apply cost allocation tags to each of them.

explanation: Application inference profiles are user-created resources that wrap a model (or a cross-Region profile) and can carry cost allocation tags. Invoking through a tagged profile lets Bedrock on-demand spend be tracked per application by tag. Bedrock also attributes cost by IAM principal (and by principal or session tags) in Cost Explorer and CUR 2.0, but with one shared role and no session tags every application looks like the same caller, so that method cannot separate them here. Not "...pass a distinct requestMetadata key...": request metadata is recorded in model invocation logs; it does not flow into Cost Explorer as a cost allocation tag. Not "Enable model invocation logging...Athena query...": this yields a usage estimate you must price yourself, and every application shares one IAM principal. Not "...system-defined cross-Region inference profile per application...": system-defined profiles are created by AWS, not per application; only application inference profiles are user-created for cost tracking. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles.html

prompt: A voice assistant needs the lowest possible response time from a supported Amazon Bedrock model, and the team does not want to fine-tune or re-architect anything. Which change should they make to the runtime request?

options.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput model units, because dedicated capacity always lowers per-token generation latency.
Set performanceConfig.latency to "standard" on the runtime call, which is the faster of the two available modes.
Set performanceConfig.latency to "optimized" on the runtime call to route it through latency-optimized inference.
Raise the top-k and top-p values so the sampler evaluates fewer candidate tokens at each generation step.

explanation: Latency-optimized inference is opted into per request with "performanceConfig": {"latency": "optimized"}; supported models are served with reduced latency and no accuracy loss, with no setup or fine-tuning. Not "...which is the faster of the two available modes": standard is the default and in fact the slower of the two. Not "Purchase Provisioned Throughput model units...": PT guarantees throughput and removes throttling, but does not by itself make token generation faster. Not "Raise the top-k and top-p values...": higher values widen the candidate pool rather than narrowing it, and sampling parameters are not a meaningful latency lever. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/latency-optimized-inference.html

prompt: An application sets performanceConfig.latency to "optimized" on every call. During a traffic spike, operators notice that p50 latency rises to standard levels and the bill does not show optimized-rate charges for those requests. No errors were returned. What happened?

options.text: Optimized mode automatically disables itself whenever input plus output token counts fall below the model's minimum.
Optimized requests silently fail closed once quota is exhausted, so the observed calls were served from a cached prior response.
The account hit its latency-optimization quota, so Bedrock served the overflow with standard latency and billed standard rates.
The latency setting is per inference profile, not per request, so the request-level field was ignored throughout the spike.

explanation: Once the usage quota for latency optimization on a model is reached, Bedrock attempts to serve the request with standard latency and charges standard rates - it degrades gracefully rather than erroring. The latency configuration actually used is visible in the API response and in CloudTrail, and CloudWatch exposes metrics under "model-id+latency-optimized", which is how you confirm this. Not "Optimized requests silently fail closed...": there is no response cache involved and requests are still served. Not "The latency setting is per inference profile, not per request...": it is a runtime request field. Not "Optimized mode automatically disables itself...below the model's minimum": there is no such minimum; the documented fallback for Llama 3.1 405B is an upper token bound, not a lower one. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/latency-optimized-inference.html

prompt: Analysis of a customer-service assistant shows that 40% of questions are near-restatements of a small set of common questions, with different wording each time. The team wants to avoid paying for a foundation model call when an equivalent question was already answered. What should they build?

options.text: An Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base populated with previous answers, queried through RetrieveAndGenerate on every turn.
A deterministic cache keyed on the SHA-256 hash of the raw prompt string, backed by Amazon ElastiCache for low-latency lookups.
A semantic cache that embeds each incoming question and returns a stored answer when similarity exceeds a tuned threshold.
Explicit Amazon Bedrock prompt caching with a cache checkpoint placed at the end of each user question.

explanation: Different wording with the same meaning defeats exact-match keys. Embedding the question and doing a vector-similarity lookup against previously answered questions - a semantic cache - is what catches paraphrases, with a similarity threshold tuned against a labeled set to control false hits. Not "A deterministic cache keyed on the SHA-256 hash...": request fingerprinting is cheap and useful, but it only catches byte-identical prompts, which is precisely what this traffic is not. Not "Explicit Amazon Bedrock prompt caching...at the end of each user question": prompt caching discounts a repeated static prefix; it still invokes the model, and a checkpoint after variable content caches nothing reusable. Not "An Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base...RetrieveAndGenerate on every turn": that still calls the model every turn, adding retrieval cost rather than avoiding inference. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: A document-QA product finds that a small, cheap model answers about 70% of queries as well as the large model does, but fails on multi-hop reasoning. The team wants to cut cost without a measurable drop in answer quality. Which pattern best achieves this?

options.text: Fine-tune the small model on the large model's multi-hop answers and retire the large model from the serving path.
Send every query to both models in parallel and return whichever response is produced first, discarding the slower one.
Route every query to the small model and raise its temperature so it explores more reasoning paths before answering.
Cascade: answer with the small model, score the result against a quality check, and escalate only failures to the large model.

explanation: Model cascading (tiered FM usage by query complexity) keeps the cheap model on the easy majority and pays for the expensive model only on the residual, so cost falls while a quality gate protects the hard cases. Not "...raise its temperature so it explores more reasoning paths...": temperature does not add reasoning capability and makes failures less predictable. Not "Send every query to both models in parallel...": this increases cost rather than reducing it, and first-to-respond selects for speed, not correctness. Not "Fine-tune the small model...and retire the large model": distillation is a legitimate cost lever, but retiring the teacher removes the safety net on exactly the queries the small model was shown to fail. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-routing.html

prompt: A team wants a managed way to send each prompt to either a cheaper or a more capable model within the same model family, based on a prediction of the response quality each would produce, without writing and maintaining their own routing logic. Which Amazon Bedrock feature should they use?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows, which conditionally branches to different models based on the token count of the prompt.
Intelligent prompt routing, which forwards each request to the model in the family predicted to answer it adequately.
A cross-Region inference profile, which selects the Region and model tier offering the best current price to performance.
An application inference profile, which selects the cheapest available model at invocation time from the profile's members.

explanation: Intelligent prompt routing is the managed feature that predicts, per request, whether a smaller model in the family will do and routes accordingly, aiming to cut cost while holding quality. Not "An application inference profile...": it wraps a model for tracking and cost attribution; it performs no quality-based model selection. Not "Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows...branches...based on the token count": Flows can branch, but you author and maintain that logic, and token count is not a quality prediction. Not "A cross-Region inference profile...": it distributes requests across Regions for capacity and resilience; it never changes which model answers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-routing.html

prompt: A chat UI switched from Converse to ConverseStream. End-to-end generation time per response is unchanged, and total token cost is identical, yet user-reported satisfaction with responsiveness improved sharply. Which statement correctly explains the result?

options.text: Streaming charges only for tokens the client actually consumes, so abandoned responses cost less than buffered ones.
Streaming raises the effective throughput quota for the account, so requests spend less time queued before generation.
Streaming reduces time to first token, so perceived latency drops even though total generation time is unchanged.
Streaming lets the model emit tokens in parallel across several workers, which cuts the real end-to-end generation time.

explanation: ConverseStream delivers tokens incrementally. Total generation time and token billing are unchanged, but the user sees output almost immediately instead of waiting for the whole response - the time-to-first-token improvement is what users experience as responsiveness. Not "...emit tokens in parallel across several workers...": autoregressive decoding is sequential; streaming changes delivery, not generation. Not "Streaming charges only for tokens the client actually consumes...": you are billed for tokens the model generates, whether or not the client reads them. Not "Streaming raises the effective throughput quota...": quotas are unaffected by the choice of streaming API. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html

prompt: A long-running assistant appends every prior turn to the prompt. Sessions now routinely exceed 100 turns; input cost grows quadratically over a session and some requests fail once the context window is exceeded. Which change addresses both problems with the least quality loss?

options.text: Raise the model's maxTokens setting so that the longer accumulated conversation fits inside a single request.
Truncate the conversation to the most recent turn on every request, discarding all earlier context unconditionally.
Store the full transcript in an Amazon DynamoDB table and continue sending every stored turn on each subsequent request.
Keep the last N turns verbatim and replace older turns with a rolling model-generated summary of the conversation so far.

explanation: Rolling summarization with a verbatim recent window is the standard context-pruning pattern: it bounds prompt growth (fixing both cost and context-window overflow) while retaining the semantic content of older turns. Not "Truncate the conversation to the most recent turn...": it bounds cost but destroys the conversational context the assistant depends on. Not "Raise the model's maxTokens setting...": maxTokens governs output length and has no effect on how much input fits. Not "Store the full transcript in an Amazon DynamoDB table and continue sending every stored turn...": persisting history is good practice, but sending all of it is the behavior causing the problem. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html

prompt: An internal tool calls a small self-hosted classification model (about 2 GB, served on CPU, responding in under a second) on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Traffic is bursty and idle for most of the day, spikes for about an hour, and the team accepts occasional multi-second cold starts. They want to stop paying for idle instances. Which deployment option fits best?

options.text: A SageMaker real-time endpoint with a target-tracking scaling policy set to a minimum capacity of one instance.
SageMaker Serverless Inference, which provisions capacity on demand and scales to zero between traffic bursts.
A SageMaker multi-model endpoint, which loads and evicts models on shared instances as requests arrive.
SageMaker Asynchronous Inference, which queues requests to Amazon S3 and returns results through a notification.

explanation: Serverless Inference scales to zero when idle and bills per invocation, which is what removes the idle instance cost. Accepting cold starts is precisely the trade-off it asks for. It fits only because the model is small and CPU-served: Serverless Inference does not support GPUs and allows at most 6 GB of memory. Not "SageMaker Asynchronous Inference...": async also scales to zero, but it is for large payloads and long processing times (up to one hour) and returns results out of band - the wrong interaction model for an interactive internal tool. Not "A SageMaker multi-model endpoint...": MME amortizes cost across many models on shared instances; with a single model and idle time it still pays for running instances. Not "...minimum capacity of one instance": a floor of one instance is exactly the idle cost the team wants to eliminate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/serverless-endpoints.html

prompt: A pipeline submits 200 MB documents for summarization. Each request takes several minutes of model processing, and the calling service cannot hold a synchronous connection that long. Which SageMaker AI inference option is designed for this?

options.text: Batch Transform with a scheduled job that polls the Amazon S3 input prefix and starts a new transform for each arriving document.
Real-time Inference behind an Application Load Balancer configured with an extended idle connection timeout.
Asynchronous Inference, which queues requests, accepts large payloads, and notifies the caller when results land in Amazon S3.
Serverless Inference, which provisions capacity per request and is designed for long-running, large-payload invocations.

explanation: Asynchronous Inference exists for exactly this profile: large payloads, long processing times, a request queue, and completion notification, with the ability to scale to zero when the queue drains. Not "Serverless Inference...": it has payload and duration limits and is aimed at short, spiky, small-payload traffic. Not "Real-time Inference behind an Application Load Balancer...extended idle connection timeout": real-time endpoints have their own invocation timeout that a load balancer setting cannot extend. Not "Batch Transform with a scheduled job...": Batch Transform suits scheduled bulk sweeps, not per-document requests arriving continuously from a calling service. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/async-inference.html

prompt: A team self-hosts an open-weights LLM on SageMaker AI GPU instances and wants to lower cost per generated token for sustained, high-volume inference. The model architecture is supported by the AWS Neuron SDK. What should they evaluate first?

options.text: Compiling the model with the AWS Neuron SDK and serving it on AWS AI-chip instances (Inferentia2 or Trainium) to improve price-performance per token.
Enabling SageMaker Model Monitor on the endpoint so that data-quality drift no longer inflates the number of retries.
Increasing the tensor parallelism degree to match the total GPU count on the instance so no accelerator sits idle.
Moving the endpoint to a larger on-demand GPU instance type so that each individual request completes sooner.

explanation: AWS designs its own AI chips, programmed through the AWS Neuron SDK, to lower inference cost: Inferentia chips target high performance at the lowest cost for deep learning and generative AI inference, and Trainium is now positioned for both training and inference with better cost per token at scale. Evaluating a Neuron-compiled model on those instances is the standard first step for cutting cost per token on sustained self-hosted inference. Not "Moving the endpoint to a larger on-demand GPU instance type...": a bigger GPU instance raises the hourly bill and does not by itself lower the cost of each generated token. Not "Enabling SageMaker Model Monitor...": Model Monitor detects drift and quality issues; it does not reduce inference cost. Not "Increasing the tensor parallelism degree to match the total GPU count...": raising TP to the full GPU count is often the wrong direction - if the model fits in fewer GPUs, a lower degree lets multiple replicas run per instance and raises utilization. Read more: https://aws.amazon.com/ai/machine-learning/inferentia/

prompt: An LLM endpoint on SageMaker AI autoscales on the InvocationsPerInstance metric. Under load, latency degrades badly long before the scaling threshold is reached, because each request occupies a GPU for a highly variable amount of time. Which scaling signal is more appropriate?

options.text: Scale on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel, which reflects how many requests are in flight rather than how many arrived.
Scale on the CPUUtilization metric, which rises predictably as more generation work queues up on the instance.
Scale on the Invocations metric for the endpoint as a whole, aggregated across every instance behind it.
Scale on InvocationsPerInstance but substantially shorten the cooldown period so the policy reacts before latency degrades.

explanation: Generative workloads have wildly variable per-request service time, so a request-rate metric is a poor proxy for load. Concurrency - how many requests are actually in flight per model - tracks GPU saturation directly, which is why it is the recommended autoscaling signal for LLM endpoints. Not "Scale on the CPUUtilization metric...": on GPU-served LLMs the CPU is not the bottleneck and stays low while GPUs saturate. Not "...shorten the cooldown period...": a faster reaction to the wrong signal still reacts to the wrong signal. Not "Scale on the Invocations metric for the endpoint as a whole...": an endpoint-wide total does not express per-instance load and is unsuitable for a per-instance scaling decision. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling.html

prompt: A RAG assistant's p95 latency is dominated by retrieval. Profiling shows the vector query returns 50 chunks, a reranker then scores all 50, and the top 5 go to the model. Quality measurements show no benefit beyond the top 20 candidates. What is the best first optimization?

options.text: Switch the vector index from approximate nearest neighbor to exact search so fewer candidates need to be considered.
Remove the reranker entirely and pass the top 5 vector-similarity results straight into the prompt as context.
Reduce the number of candidates retrieved and reranked to 20, keeping the reranker and the final top 5 unchanged.
Increase the number of retrieved candidates to 100 so the reranker has more material and can stop scanning earlier.

explanation: The reranker cost scales with candidate count, and the evidence says candidates beyond 20 add no quality. Cutting the candidate set to 20 removes 60% of the rerank work with no measured quality loss - the textbook retrieval-latency optimization. Not "Remove the reranker entirely...": that trades away relevance the team has not shown to be expendable; the reranker is not the thing the data indicts. Not "Increase the number of retrieved candidates to 100...": more candidates means strictly more rerank work; rerankers do not stop early. Not "Switch...to exact search...": exact k-NN is slower than ANN at scale and does not reduce the number of candidates reranked. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-reranking.html

prompt: A team must reduce spend on a high-volume summarization workload that runs a fixed, well-tested prompt against a large model. Output quality on a labeled test set must not regress. Latency is not a concern. Which approach gives the largest sustainable cost reduction?

options.text: Apply explicit prompt caching to the fixed prompt, so that the whole prompt is billed at the cache-read rate on every later call.
Distill the large model into a smaller custom model on this task's traffic, then validate it against the labeled test set.
Reduce maxTokens so summaries are shorter, then instruct the model to compensate by writing more densely.
Move the workload to a cross-Region inference profile so requests are served from the lowest-cost available Region.

explanation: Model distillation transfers task-specific behavior from a large teacher to a small student, so per-token cost drops by the model-price gap permanently, and the labeled test set is exactly the gate that protects quality. Latency being irrelevant removes the usual objection. Not "Apply explicit prompt caching to the fixed prompt...": caching helps, but a single fixed prompt is usually short and the discount applies only to the repeated input prefix - not to output tokens, which dominate a summarization bill. Not "Reduce maxTokens so summaries are shorter...": that changes the deliverable and will regress the test set. Not "Move the workload to a cross-Region inference profile...": cross-Region inference targets capacity and resilience, and does not select Regions by price. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-distillation.html

prompt: An operations team needs to be alerted when Amazon Bedrock token consumption for an application deviates sharply from its normal daily pattern, including gradual weekday-versus-weekend variation, without hand-tuning a static threshold. What should they configure?

options.text: A CloudWatch static threshold alarm on the Bedrock token count metrics, set just above the highest value observed last month.
An AWS Config rule that evaluates the account's Bedrock invocation quota and reports when consumption approaches it.
AWS Budgets with a monthly cost threshold and an alert action that notifies the operations team by email.
A CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm on the Bedrock token count metrics, which learns the metric's expected band over time.

explanation: CloudWatch anomaly detection builds a model of a metric's expected range, including daily and weekly seasonality, and alarms on deviation from that band - which is what "no hand-tuned static threshold" and "weekday-versus-weekend variation" call for. Not "A CloudWatch static threshold alarm...above the highest value observed last month": a static ceiling is exactly what the requirement excludes, and it misses drops and mid-range anomalies. Not "AWS Budgets with a monthly cost threshold...": Budgets tracks spend against a fixed target on a monthly cycle, far too coarse to catch a token burst. Not "An AWS Config rule...": Config evaluates resource configuration compliance, not time-series metric behavior. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-cw.html

prompt: A team wants to bound worst-case cost per request on an open-ended generation endpoint, where occasional runaway generations produce thousands of tokens of repetitive filler. Which combination most directly bounds the cost, and why?

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with a denied topics policy that blocks responses exceeding the expected length.
Enable prompt caching with a 1-hour TTL, so repeated filler text is served from cache at the cache-read rate.
Set maxTokens to a ceiling derived from the task, and add stop sequences so normal completions terminate before that ceiling.
Set temperature to 0 and top-p to a low value, so that decoding converges quickly and the model stops emitting repetitive filler.

explanation: maxTokens is the hard ceiling on output tokens and therefore on worst-case output cost; stop sequences make well-behaved completions end naturally before that ceiling, so the cap is a safety net rather than a truncation tool. Not "Set temperature to 0 and top-p to a low value...": low-temperature decoding actually makes repetitive loops more likely, and it provides no upper bound at all. Not "Enable prompt caching with a 1-hour TTL...": caching discounts repeated input prefixes; generated output tokens are never served from the prompt cache. Not "Enable Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with a denied topics policy...": Guardrails filters content by topic and category, not by response length. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-parameters.html

prompt: A team ingests a 30-million-chunk corpus into a vector store and finds that storage and query cost are both higher than budgeted. The embedding model supports 1024, 512 and 256 output dimensions, and an offline test shows retrieval quality is statistically unchanged at 512. What should they do?

options.text: Keep the 1024-dimension vectors and reduce the index replica count so the storage footprint of the cluster falls by half.
Re-embed the corpus at 256 dimensions, since lower dimensionality always improves both cost and recall together.
Re-embed the corpus at 512 dimensions, which roughly halves vector storage and reduces per-query distance computation.
Keep 1024-dimension vectors and apply the 512-dimension setting only to query embeddings at search time.

explanation: Embedding models such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 support selectable output dimensions. Halving dimensionality roughly halves vector storage and shrinks the per-comparison distance computation, and the offline test is the evidence that quality holds at 512. Not "...reduce the index replica count...": replicas exist for availability and query throughput; cutting them trades resilience for cost and does nothing about per-vector size. Not "...apply the 512-dimension setting only to query embeddings": query and document vectors must share a dimensionality and embedding space or similarity search breaks outright. Not "Re-embed the corpus at 256 dimensions...always improves both cost and recall": lower dimensionality trades away representational capacity; the team measured 512, not 256. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/titan-embedding-models.html

prompt: A multi-step agent workflow calls four independent tools whose results are all needed before the model can produce its final answer. Each tool takes roughly 800 ms. End-to-end latency is about 3.5 seconds and users complain. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Merge the four tools into a single composite tool definition so the model issues one call instead of four sequential ones.
Invoke the four independent tools concurrently and wait for all results, so tool latency is bounded by the slowest call.
Enable latency-optimized inference on the agent's model, which shortens the time spent inside each tool invocation.
Increase the agent's maximum iteration limit so it does not spend turns re-planning between successive tool calls.

explanation: The calls are independent, so they have no ordering constraint. Running them in parallel collapses roughly 3.2 seconds of serialized tool time to about 800 ms - bounded by the slowest call - which is where nearly all the latency lives. Not "Merge the four tools into a single composite tool definition...": it can help, but unless that merged implementation also parallelizes internally, the same four operations still run back to back. Not "Enable latency-optimized inference on the agent's model...": it speeds up model inference, not the tool executions that dominate this budget. Not "Increase the agent's maximum iteration limit...": raising the iteration ceiling permits more turns; it does not make the existing ones faster. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-how.html

prompt: An enterprise wants a single place to see Amazon Bedrock latency, invocation counts, token throughput and error rates across every application in an account, with the ability to drill into a specific model's behavior. Which approach requires the least custom instrumentation?

options.text: Build CloudWatch dashboards on the metrics Amazon Bedrock publishes to the AWS/Bedrock namespace, dimensioned by model.
Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for Bedrock and build an Amazon QuickSight dashboard over the delivered trail files.
Instrument every application with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry and export custom spans to CloudWatch for aggregation.
Enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3 and derive every operational metric with scheduled Amazon Athena queries.

explanation: Bedrock publishes operational metrics - invocation counts, latency, token counts and errors - to the AWS/Bedrock CloudWatch namespace with a model dimension, at no instrumentation cost. Dashboards over those metrics are the lowest-effort path to the stated view. Not "Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for Bedrock...QuickSight dashboard...": CloudTrail records API activity for audit, not latency or token throughput. Not "Enable model invocation logging...Athena queries": invocation logs carry full prompt and response payloads for analysis and troubleshooting; deriving operational metrics from them duplicates what CloudWatch already emits. Not "Instrument every application with the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry...": distributed tracing is valuable for end-to-end request flow, but it is far more work than consuming metrics Bedrock already publishes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-cw.html

prompt: A regulated firm commits to Provisioned Throughput for a base model to guarantee capacity. Six weeks later, Amazon Bedrock introduces a newer version of that model that the firm wants to adopt. Which statement about the commitment is correct?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput can be transferred between model versions at any time without affecting the purchased commitment term.
Provisioned Throughput is purchased for a specific model version, so adopting the new version requires provisioning for it.
Provisioned Throughput follows the model family, so the purchased model units automatically serve the newer version.
Provisioned Throughput applies at the account level, so any model the account can invoke draws on the purchased units.

explanation: Provisioned Throughput is bought against a specific model (including a specific custom or base model version), and commitment terms lock that purchase for the term. Moving to a new model version means provisioning throughput for that version - which is why version-upgrade planning has to account for the commitment. Not "...follows the model family...automatically serve the newer version": capacity is not portable across versions. Not "...can be transferred between model versions at any time...": there is no such free transfer. Not "...applies at the account level...": PT is per-model dedicated capacity, not an account-wide pool. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A global application uses a cross-Region inference profile together with explicit prompt caching. During regional demand peaks, operators observe cacheWriteInputTokens rising and cache hit rate falling, with no change to the application's prompts. What is the explanation?

options.text: Cache checkpoints expire faster under load, because the TTL is scaled down in proportion to current Region utilization.
Cross-Region inference may route requests to a different Region during peaks, and those Regions do not share the cache.
Cross-Region inference rewrites the prompt prefix with Region metadata, which changes the bytes being hashed for the cache.
Cross-Region inference disables prompt caching during peaks to preserve capacity, so no cache reads occur at all.

explanation: Cross-Region inference selects the optimal Region within the geography to serve each request. At times of high demand those routing decisions shift, and because a cache is warmed where the request landed, shifting traffic produces more cache writes and fewer hits. The behavior is documented and is the accepted trade-off for the added capacity. Not "...disables prompt caching during peaks...": caching is not switched off; writes increase, which is the observed symptom. Not "Cache checkpoints expire faster under load...TTL is scaled down...": TTL is a fixed per-request setting, not utilization-scaled. Not "...rewrites the prompt prefix with Region metadata...": no Region metadata is injected into the prompt. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: Which TWO measures most directly reduce the input token cost of a RAG application without changing the retrieval quality the model sees? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Drop retrieved chunks that a reranker scores below a validated relevance threshold before assembling the final prompt.
Reduce the maxTokens setting so the model produces shorter answers from the same retrieved context.
Place a cache checkpoint after the static system prompt and tool definitions so that prefix is billed at the cache-read rate.
Lower the model's temperature so that it consumes the retrieved context more efficiently during generation.
Increase the chunk overlap during ingestion so that fewer chunks are needed to cover the same source material.

explanation: Caching the static prefix converts repeated system and tool tokens to the cache-read rate, and dropping chunks the reranker has already judged irrelevant removes input tokens that were contributing nothing - both cut input cost while leaving the useful retrieved context intact. Not "Lower the model's temperature...": temperature affects sampling, not token accounting. Not "Reduce the maxTokens setting...": that bounds output tokens, not input. Not "Increase the chunk overlap during ingestion...": more overlap duplicates text across chunks, which increases the tokens sent for a given amount of source material. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: Which TWO signals should a team track to decide whether an Amazon Bedrock workload should move from on-demand to Provisioned Throughput? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The distribution of stopReason values returned by the model, which shows how often completions reach the token ceiling.
The rate of ThrottlingException responses during peak periods, which shows whether on-demand quota is the binding constraint.
The ratio of cacheReadInputTokens to cacheWriteInputTokens, which shows how effectively the prompt cache is being reused.
The average number of retrieved chunks per request, which determines the prompt size sent to the model on each call.
Sustained token throughput over time, which determines how many model units a provisioned commitment would need.

explanation: The decision is a capacity-and-commitment decision: throttling rate tells you whether best-effort on-demand capacity is actually failing you, and sustained token throughput tells you how much dedicated capacity you would have to buy for the commitment to pay off. Not "The ratio of cacheReadInputTokens to cacheWriteInputTokens...": cache efficiency is a cost lever within either purchasing model, not a signal about capacity guarantees. Not "The average number of retrieved chunks per request...": prompt size affects cost and context budget, not whether dedicated capacity is warranted. Not "The distribution of stopReason values...": stop reasons diagnose truncation and prompt design, not capacity. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A team must choose between two foundation models for a customer-facing summarization feature. They have 800 prompts with expert-written reference summaries, and they need scored, explainable comparisons rather than a side-by-side eyeball test. Which Amazon Bedrock evaluation approach fits?

options.text: A model evaluation job that uses human workers, who rate each pair of responses against the reference summaries.
A retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job, scoring the summaries against the reference texts supplied as ground truth.
An automatic model evaluation job using a built-in dataset, which supplies both prompts and reference outputs for scoring.
A model evaluation job that uses a judge model, scoring each response on built-in metrics with a per-response explanation.

explanation: An LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation job scores a generator model's responses with a second model against built-in metrics and returns an explanation for each score. Supplying reference responses as ground truth in the prompt dataset lets metrics such as Builtin.Correctness and Builtin.Completeness take them into account. Not "...uses human workers...": human evaluation is the right tool for subjective judgments, but it is slow and costly for an 800-prompt comparison that built-in metrics can score. Not "A retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job...": RAG evaluation scores a knowledge base or RAG source; this feature has no retrieval component. Not "An automatic model evaluation job using a built-in dataset...": a built-in dataset discards the team's own 800 task-specific prompts, which are the whole point. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-judge.html

prompt: In an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation of a RAG assistant, Builtin.Faithfulness scores are high while Builtin.Correctness scores are low. What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: The model is staying within the supplied context, but that context is leading it to answers that are not actually right.
The judge model lacks access to ground truth, so faithfulness and correctness cannot be compared in the same job.
The prompts are too long for the judge model, so it scores faithfulness on a truncated view of the supplied context.
The model is inventing content that is not present in the supplied context, while still landing on the right final answers.

explanation: Faithfulness asks whether the response contains information not found in the prompt - that is, whether the model stuck to its context. Correctness asks whether the answer is right, taking any supplied reference response into account. High faithfulness with low correctness means the model is loyally reporting what it retrieved and the retrieval is feeding it wrong or irrelevant material - so the fix belongs in the retrieval layer, not in the prompt or decoding settings. Not "...inventing content that is not present in the supplied context...": that is the opposite pattern, low faithfulness. Not "The judge model lacks access to ground truth...": both metrics are available in the same job, and ground truth is optional. Not "The prompts are too long for the judge model...": nothing here indicates truncation, and it would not produce this specific split. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-metrics.html

prompt: A team wants to compare three chunking configurations of the same Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base purely on whether the right passages come back, without letting differences in a generator model's writing confound the comparison. Which evaluation should they run?

options.text: A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job, which scores the retrieved passages and involves no response generation at all.
A retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job, holding the generator model constant across all three configurations.
A human evaluation job, in which reviewers read each generated answer and rank the three configurations by quality.
An LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation job, using the retrieved passages as the prompts fed to the generator model.

explanation: A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job bases its report solely on what the RAG source retrieved, which is precisely how you isolate retrieval quality from generation quality when comparing chunking strategies. Not "A retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job...": holding the generator constant helps, but generation still sits between the retrieval change and the score, adding variance the team explicitly wants to remove. Not "An LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation job...": that evaluates a model's responses, not a knowledge base's retrieval. Not "A human evaluation job...": reviewers would again be judging generated answers, reintroducing the confound. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A retrieve-only RAG evaluation reports low context relevance and high context coverage. Which conclusion and remedy follow?

options.text: The ground truth texts are malformed, because context coverage cannot be computed without valid ground truth.
Retrieval is returning the needed material plus a lot of irrelevant material; cut the result count or add a reranker.
The generator model is diluting the retrieved context; shorten the prompt template and re-run the evaluation job.
Retrieval is missing much of the expected material; raise the result count and widen the chunk size during ingestion.

explanation: Context relevance measures whether retrieved chunks actually address the query's intent - it is the precision side. Context coverage measures how completely the retrieved chunks cover the ground truth texts - the recall side. High coverage with low relevance is the classic over-retrieval signature: the answer is in there, buried in noise. Retrieving fewer candidates or reranking to promote the relevant ones is the fix. Not "Retrieval is missing much of the expected material...": that would show as low coverage, and raising the result count would make the relevance problem worse. Not "The ground truth texts are malformed...": coverage requires ground truth and a score was produced, so ground truth was present. Not "The generator model is diluting the retrieved context...": a retrieve-only job has no generator in it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A CI pipeline must fail a build when a prompt change degrades output quality. Outputs are free-form text, so exact string comparison against stored expected answers produces constant false failures even when quality is fine. What should the quality gate assert instead?

options.text: Byte-equality against stored reference outputs, with temperature pinned to 0 so that generation becomes fully reproducible.
That the model returns no Guardrails intervention, which confirms the response met the configured quality policy.
That the response length stays within one standard deviation of the length distribution recorded on the main branch.
Scores from an automated evaluation over a curated golden dataset, failing the build when a metric drops below a threshold.

explanation: A golden dataset scored by automated evaluation - LLM-as-a-judge metrics, or task-specific scorers - turns a subjective quality question into a thresholded number a build can gate on. That is the standard regression-testing pattern for generative output. Not "Byte-equality against stored reference outputs...": temperature 0 reduces variation but does not guarantee identical output, and byte-equality is precisely the brittle check that is already failing. Not "That the response length stays within one standard deviation...": length is not quality; a fluent wrong answer passes and a terse right answer fails. Not "That the model returns no Guardrails intervention...": Guardrails enforces safety and topic policy, not answer quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html

prompt: A team sets temperature to 0 for a regression suite and still sees occasional wording differences between runs on identical inputs, causing flaky failures. What is the correct response?

options.text: Accept that greedy decoding is not a determinism guarantee, and assert on semantic similarity and required facts instead.
Set top-k to 1 in addition to temperature 0, which removes the one remaining source of nondeterminism from the sampler.
Disable cross-Region inference, because responses differ systematically between the Regions serving the requests.
Pin the model to a Provisioned Throughput endpoint, which serves every request from identical dedicated hardware.

explanation: Temperature 0 makes sampling greedy, which sharply reduces variation, but it is not a contractual guarantee of byte-identical output across runs - batching, hardware and serving-stack details can still shift a token. Regression suites for generative systems should assert on meaning: semantic similarity to a reference, presence of required facts, schema validity. Not "Set top-k to 1 in addition to temperature 0...": it further constrains sampling but still does not make output contractually reproducible. Not "Pin the model to a Provisioned Throughput endpoint...": PT guarantees capacity, not bit-identical generation. Not "Disable cross-Region inference...": the same model version is served in each Region; this is not a systematic regional difference. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-parameters.html

prompt: Before replacing the model behind a live assistant, a team wants to see how the candidate model responds to real production traffic, measured against the current model, with zero risk of a bad response reaching a user. Which technique should they use?

options.text: A/B testing: split users into two cohorts and compare downstream business metrics between the candidate and current model.
Blue/green deployment: stand up the candidate model alongside the current one and cut over all traffic at once.
Canary deployment: route a small percentage of live user traffic to the candidate model and monitor the error rate.
Shadow testing: mirror a copy of live requests to the candidate model, log its responses, and never return them to users.

explanation: Shadow (mirror) testing sends a copy of live traffic to the candidate while the user continues to be served by the incumbent. The candidate's responses are logged for comparison and never surface, which is the only one of these options with genuinely zero user-facing risk. Not "Canary deployment...": a canary serves real responses to a small slice of real users, so the risk is small but not zero. Not "A/B testing...": A/B also serves the candidate to real users, and is aimed at measuring outcome differences rather than pre-release validation. Not "Blue/green deployment...cut over all traffic at once": it makes rollback fast but exposes every user the moment it cuts over. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html

prompt: An agent completes most tasks successfully, but for a specific class of request it picks the wrong tool and then reports a confident, wrong answer. The team needs to see which reasoning step went wrong before changing anything. What should they inspect first?

options.text: The CloudWatch metrics for the agent, which record per-step latency and error counts across all recent sessions.
The CloudTrail event history, which records each tool invocation along with the parameters the agent supplied.
The Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs, which record the full final prompt and the response text for the agent session.
The agent's trace, which records the model's reasoning, the tool it selected, and the inputs and outputs at each step.

explanation: Agent traces expose the orchestration itself - the rationale, the chosen action group or tool, the parameters, and the observation returned at each step. That is the only artifact here that shows why a tool was selected, which is the question being asked. Not "The CloudTrail event history...": CloudTrail records AWS API activity for audit; it does not capture an agent's internal reasoning or tool-selection rationale. Not "...model invocation logs...full final prompt and the response text...": invocation logs are valuable, but they show the request and response payloads, not the step-by-step decision path. Not "The CloudWatch metrics for the agent...": aggregate latency and error counts tell you that something is wrong, never which reasoning step caused it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-test.html

prompt: A document assistant intermittently fails with a ValidationException stating the input is too long, but only for a minority of documents. The prompt template and model are unchanged. What is the correct diagnosis and fix?

options.text: The documents contain characters the tokenizer rejects; sanitize the input down to a restricted character set before sending it.
The account's tokens-per-minute quota is exhausted by large documents; request a quota increase for the model.
The maxTokens setting is too low for those documents; raise it so the larger inputs are accepted by the model.
Total prompt tokens exceed the model's context window for large documents; chunk the input or summarize before the final call.

explanation: A ValidationException about input length is a context-window overflow: the serialized prompt (instructions, retrieved context and document together) exceeds what the model accepts. The remedy is to reduce what is sent - chunk the document, retrieve selectively, or summarize in a first pass and reason over the summary. Not "The maxTokens setting is too low...": maxTokens bounds the completion; it neither admits nor rejects longer input. Not "The account's tokens-per-minute quota is exhausted...": quota exhaustion surfaces as a ThrottlingException, not a validation error, and would not correlate with document size. Not "The documents contain characters the tokenizer rejects...": the error names input length, and the correlation with document size points at size, not encoding. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/troubleshooting.html

prompt: A summarization service returns answers that stop in mid-sentence for about 5% of requests. The team needs a programmatic way to distinguish genuine truncation from summaries that legitimately ended. What should they check on each response?

options.text: The stopReason field: a value indicating the token limit was reached means truncation, while an end-turn value means completion.
The latency of the response, since truncated responses return measurably faster than fully generated responses do.
The outputTokens count: any response whose output token count is within 10% of the maxTokens ceiling is truncated.
Whether the final character is terminal punctuation, which reliably separates truncated text from completed responses.

explanation: The response's stop reason is the authoritative signal. A max-tokens stop reason means the model was cut off at the ceiling; an end-turn stop reason means it finished on its own. Branching on that field is the correct programmatic check, and a rising rate of max-tokens stops is the metric to alarm on. Not "The outputTokens count...within 10% of the maxTokens ceiling...": a heuristic that both false-positives on naturally long answers and false-negatives on other stop conditions. Not "Whether the final character is terminal punctuation...": truncation frequently lands on a period mid-document, and valid outputs such as JSON or lists often do not end in punctuation. Not "The latency of the response...": a truncated response hit the ceiling and is typically the slowest, not the fastest. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/API_runtime_Converse.html

prompt: A Bedrock-backed API begins returning ThrottlingException under load spikes. The team must improve success rates without buying dedicated capacity. Which TWO measures should they implement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Lower the temperature setting, so the model spends less compute per request and completes more requests per second.
Enable model invocation logging, so throttled requests are queued to Amazon S3 and replayed once capacity returns.
Invoke through a cross-Region inference profile, so requests can be served from additional Regions during peaks.
Retry throttled calls with exponential backoff and jitter, so bursts of retries do not resynchronize into new spikes.
Increase the maxTokens setting, so fewer requests are needed to produce the same total volume of output text.

explanation: Exponential backoff with jitter is the standard SDK-level response to throttling and prevents retry storms; a cross-Region inference profile increases the on-demand capacity available to the workload without any commitment purchase. Together they address both sides of the problem. Not "Increase the maxTokens setting...": output ceiling has no relationship to request-rate throttling. Not "Lower the temperature setting...": temperature does not change per-request compute or throughput. Not "Enable model invocation logging...queued to Amazon S3 and replayed...": invocation logging records prompts and responses for analysis; it is not a queue and replays nothing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A team runs a self-managed RAG pipeline: their own ingestion code embeds documents into an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector index. They switched the query path to a different embedding model with the same vector dimensions, and retrieval quality collapsed: queries return near-random passages, though no errors are reported. What is the cause?

options.text: The vector index is caching prior query embeddings, so the cache must be invalidated before new results appear.
The new embedding model outputs a different similarity metric, so the vector index must be switched to cosine distance.
The new embedding model requires a larger number of results, so retrieval must request more candidates per query.
Existing vectors were produced by the previous embedding model, so the corpus must be re-embedded with the new model and re-indexed.

explanation: Query embeddings and document embeddings must come from the same model and therefore live in the same vector space. Changing the embedding model leaves the stored vectors in the old space, so similarity comparisons become meaningless. The corpus has to be re-embedded and re-indexed - which is why embedding-model choice is a costly decision to revisit. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base guards against this by design: its embedding model is part of `knowledgeBaseConfiguration`, which UpdateKnowledgeBase cannot change, so switching models there means creating a new knowledge base and ingesting again. Not "...different similarity metric...switched to cosine distance": a metric mismatch degrades ranking somewhat; it does not produce near-random results across a whole corpus. Not "The vector index is caching prior query embeddings...": there is no such query embedding cache to invalidate. Not "...requires a larger number of results...": retrieving more of the wrong thing does not repair a broken vector space. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_agent_UpdateKnowledgeBase.html

prompt: Evaluation of a RAG assistant shows that answers are frequently missing information that sits at the end of a retrieved passage, and reviewers can see the relevant sentence was split across two chunks. Which ingestion change addresses this most directly?

options.text: Increase numberOfResults at query time, so more chunks are retrieved and the missing half is more likely included.
Enable a reranker, so the chunk containing the more relevant half is promoted above the other half in the results.
Increase the fixed chunk size substantially, so each chunk contains far more of the surrounding document.
Introduce chunk overlap, or move to semantic chunking, so a sentence is not split across a chunk boundary.

explanation: The failure is a boundary artifact: a unit of meaning is being cut in two. Overlap keeps a window of text shared between adjacent chunks so the split sentence survives intact in at least one, and semantic chunking places boundaries at natural breaks in the first place. Not "Increase the fixed chunk size substantially...": bigger chunks move the boundary rather than removing it, and dilute the embedding of each chunk. Not "Increase numberOfResults at query time...": retrieving more chunks may pull in the other half, but it treats a symptom and adds noise and cost. Not "Enable a reranker...": reranking reorders candidates; it cannot reassemble a sentence that ingestion split. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking-parsing.html

prompt: A team wants to analyze the exact prompts and responses of Amazon Bedrock calls from the previous week to diagnose a prompt-design problem. They have CloudTrail enabled organization-wide but find no prompt text in it. What must they do?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail data events for Amazon Bedrock, which adds the full prompt and response payloads to the existing trail.
Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging, which captures request and response payloads; it is off by default and not retroactive.
Query the CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace, which retain prompt and completion text for 15 months.
Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the calling service, which records the full request body of each Bedrock call.

explanation: CloudTrail records who called which API and when - it never contains prompt or completion text. Model invocation logging is the feature that captures full request and response payloads to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs, it must be explicitly enabled, and it only covers invocations made after it is turned on. Last week's payloads are gone. Not "Enable CloudTrail data events for Amazon Bedrock...": data events add object-level API activity, not model payloads, and would not apply retroactively either. Not "Query the CloudWatch metrics...retain prompt and completion text": metrics are numeric time series; they hold no text. Not "Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing...": X-Ray captures timing and trace segments, not model request bodies. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A GenAI feature spans Amazon API Gateway, two AWS Lambda functions, a knowledge base retrieval call and a Bedrock invocation. Users report occasional multi-second responses, and the team cannot tell which hop is responsible. What should they implement?

options.text: CloudWatch alarms on the p99 latency of each individual service, so the slowest service raises an alarm on its own.
A CloudWatch dashboard showing each service's average latency over the same time window for visual comparison.
Model invocation logging to Amazon S3, then an Athena query correlating request timestamps to response timestamps.
AWS X-Ray tracing across the services, so each request produces a segmented trace attributing latency to each hop.

explanation: X-Ray produces a per-request trace with a segment per hop, which is what attributes an individual slow response to the specific service that caused it.
