Tracing across service boundaries is the documented approach for observability in composed GenAI applications. Not "CloudWatch alarms on the p99 latency of each individual service...": per-service alarms tell you a service is slow in aggregate, not that it caused this request's latency. Not "Model invocation logging...Athena query...": that covers only the Bedrock call and says nothing about the other four hops. Not "A CloudWatch dashboard showing each service's average latency...": averages hide the tail, and visual comparison does not correlate hops within one request. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring.html

prompt: A team runs a RAG evaluation and finds a high rate of unsupported claims in generated answers. They want the system itself to block such answers at runtime, with a tunable sensitivity they can set from the evaluation data. What should they configure?

options.text: A Guardrails denied topics policy, listing the subject areas in which unsupported claims were observed during evaluation.
A Guardrails word filter, populated with the specific phrases that appeared in the unsupported claims during evaluation.
A Guardrails contextual grounding policy, with grounding and relevance thresholds tuned against the evaluation results.
A Guardrails sensitive information filter, configured to block responses containing entities absent from the source documents.

explanation: Contextual grounding checks compare the model's response against the retrieved source material and the user's query, and block responses whose grounding or relevance scores fall below configurable thresholds. Evaluation data is exactly what you use to pick those thresholds. Not "A Guardrails denied topics policy...": denied topics blocks subject areas regardless of whether a claim is supported; unsupported claims are a grounding problem, not a topic problem. Not "A Guardrails sensitive information filter...": that detects and redacts PII and similar sensitive entities, not ungrounded assertions. Not "A Guardrails word filter...": blocklists catch known strings; hallucinated claims are novel text by nature. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html

prompt: A downstream system requires strictly valid JSON matching a fixed schema. Parsing currently fails on a small percentage of responses because the model wraps the JSON in prose or omits a field. Which approach most reliably enforces the contract?

options.text: Post-process with a regular expression that extracts the first JSON object found anywhere in the response body.
Use Amazon Bedrock structured outputs: supply the JSON schema in the request (Converse `outputConfig.textFormat`), or define the output as a tool marked `strict: true`.
Use a Guardrails policy that blocks any response which fails JSON schema validation before returning it to the caller.
Append "Return only valid JSON and nothing else" to the system prompt and set the temperature to 0 for all calls.

explanation: Structured outputs ensure the model response conforms to the JSON schema you supply (`outputConfig.textFormat` in Converse), and `strict: true` on a tool definition makes tool calls follow the tool input schema. That turns a formatting request into an enforced contract; a tool definition without `strict` only describes the schema. Not "...to the system prompt and set the temperature to 0 for all calls": prompt instructions plus greedy decoding reduce the failure rate but guarantee nothing, which is the situation the team is already in. Not "Post-process with a regular expression...": extraction may recover the wrapped-in-prose case, but it cannot supply a field the model omitted. Not "Use a Guardrails policy that blocks any response which fails JSON schema validation...": Guardrails evaluates content safety policies; it does not perform JSON schema validation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/structured-output.html

prompt: An evaluation of an agent must report how often it finishes the user's task, not merely whether each individual model call returned successfully. Which measurement framework is appropriate?

options.text: Mean tokens consumed per session, tracked over time and compared against the baseline recorded before the change.
Task completion rate over a suite of representative goals, combined with tool-usage correctness along each trajectory.
The ratio of successful HTTP responses to total invocations across the agent's action group Lambda functions.
The proportion of sessions in which the agent produced a final response before reaching its configured iteration limit.

explanation: Agent quality is an end-to-end property. Task completion rate over representative goals measures whether the agent achieved what the user wanted, and examining the trajectory tells you whether it selected and used the right tools to get there - the pair of measures the exam guide names for agent performance frameworks. Not "The ratio of successful HTTP responses...": every tool call can return HTTP 200 while the agent still fails the task. Not "Mean tokens consumed per session...": an efficiency metric that says nothing about correctness. Not "The proportion of sessions in which the agent produced a final response before reaching its configured iteration limit": not hitting the ceiling is not the same as succeeding. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-test.html

prompt: A team maintains several prompt versions in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management and needs to know which version a given production response came from when investigating a quality complaint. What should they do?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail so that each prompt invocation records the full prompt text used for that particular request.
Store every prompt version in Amazon S3 with versioning enabled and reconcile against response timestamps afterwards.
Invoke a specific prompt version by its identifier and record that identifier alongside each response in application logs.
Invoke the prompt by name so the latest draft is always used, and rely on the Prompt Management change history for attribution.

explanation: Prompt Management versions prompts so a specific, immutable version can be invoked by identifier. Logging that identifier with each response gives you exact attribution at investigation time - the basis for prompt version comparison and regression analysis. Not "Invoke the prompt by name so the latest draft is always used...": if production always follows the moving draft, you cannot reconstruct what a past response actually used. Not "Store every prompt version in Amazon S3...reconcile against response timestamps": timestamp reconciliation is fragile and breaks around deployments, which is when you need it most. Not "Enable CloudTrail so that each prompt invocation records the full prompt text...": CloudTrail records API activity, never prompt payloads. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: Six months after launch, a RAG assistant's retrieval quality has degraded on newer queries, though no code or configuration changed. The corpus has grown and now uses product names and terminology that did not exist at launch. What is the most likely cause and the right investigation?

options.text: Vector index fragmentation caused by continual incremental ingestion; rebuild the index from scratch and re-run the retrieval tests.
Gradual expiry of cached embeddings for older documents; re-ingest the full corpus so all embeddings are regenerated.
Query and content drift against a fixed embedding space; re-measure retrieval on a refreshed golden query set and reassess the embedding model.
Silent model deprecation of the generator model; pin an explicit model version and re-run the retrieval evaluation.

explanation: The corpus and the query distribution have both moved while the embedding space stayed fixed - the standard drift failure mode. The disciplined response is to measure it: refresh the golden query set with current terminology, re-run retrieval evaluation, and decide from the numbers whether the embedding model still fits the domain. Not "Vector index fragmentation...": index maintenance can affect latency; it does not make semantically correct matches stop matching. Not "Gradual expiry of cached embeddings...": stored embeddings do not expire. Not "Silent model deprecation of the generator model...": the symptom is in retrieval, which happens before the generator is involved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A product team already runs offline evaluation and automated LLM-as-a-judge scoring on a sample of production traffic. They now want direct feedback from end users on real responses, in a form that lets them trace a poor rating back to its cause and prioritize fixes. Which mechanism should they build?

options.text: A second automated LLM-as-a-judge job scoring a larger random daily sample of production responses, with no human input in the loop.
A per-response rating and comment interface, with ratings stored alongside the request identifier, prompt version and retrieved sources.
A CloudWatch alarm on the assistant's error rate, so degradations in quality surface as operational alerts to the team.
A monthly survey emailed to active users asking them to rate the assistant's overall helpfulness on a five-point scale.

explanation: Inline per-response feedback captured with the context that produced the response - request identifier, prompt version, retrieved sources - is what lets you trace a bad rating back to a cause and prioritize the fix. That linkage is the point; a rating with no context is not actionable. Not "A monthly survey emailed to active users...": aggregate periodic sentiment cannot be attributed to specific responses or changes. Not "A CloudWatch alarm on the assistant's error rate...": errors and quality are different failure classes; a confidently wrong answer is not an error. Not "An automated LLM-as-a-judge job...with no human input in the loop": automated scoring is already in place; more of it adds no direct end-user feedback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-human.html

prompt: A nightly deployment pipeline updates the model version behind a customer-facing assistant. The team wants automated validation that catches GenAI-specific regressions before traffic shifts, beyond checking that the endpoint returns HTTP 200. Which validation should gate the rollout?

options.text: Synthetic user workflows whose outputs are scored for hallucination rate and consistency against a reference set, gating promotion.
A canary that shifts 10% of traffic to the new version and rolls back automatically if the 5xx error rate exceeds a threshold.
A smoke test asserting that the new model version returns a non-empty response for one representative prompt.
A load test that confirms the new model version sustains the expected requests per second at the target p99 latency.

explanation: The regressions that matter here are semantic - hallucination rate, response drift, inconsistency - and none of them show up as an error code. Running synthetic workflows and scoring their outputs against a reference set is the AI-specific deployment validation the exam guide describes, and it is the only option that can fail a build for being wrong rather than broken. Not "A load test...": performance validation, orthogonal to output quality. Not "A smoke test asserting...a non-empty response...": a non-empty wrong answer passes. Not "A canary that shifts 10% of traffic to the new version...if the 5xx error rate exceeds a threshold": canarying is good practice, but a 5xx-based trigger is blind to a model that answers fluently and incorrectly. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html

prompt: Which TWO findings from a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation would specifically indicate that the problem lies in generation rather than retrieval? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Low faithfulness scores, indicating the response asserts information that is not present in the retrieved context.
Low context relevance scores, indicating the retrieved passages do not address the intent of the query.
High retrieval latency at p95, indicating the vector search is returning candidates more slowly than the target.
Low completeness scores while the retrieved context demonstrably contains all the information the question required.
Low context coverage scores, indicating the retrieved passages omit much of the expected ground truth material.

explanation: Faithfulness and completeness are both properties of the generated response given its context. Low faithfulness means the generator went beyond its context; low completeness with demonstrably sufficient context means the generator failed to use what it was given. Both indict generation. Not "Low context relevance scores...": that is a retrieval precision problem. Not "Low context coverage scores...": that is a retrieval recall problem. Not "High retrieval latency at p95...": a performance symptom in the retrieval path, unrelated to output quality. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A team must evaluate a RAG system that runs entirely outside AWS, using their own retriever and their own self-hosted model, but they want Amazon Bedrock's scored RAG metrics and report. Is this possible, and how?

options.text: Yes: point the RAG evaluation job at the external retriever's endpoint, and Bedrock will call it directly during the job.
Yes: bring your own inference response data into a RAG evaluation job, and Bedrock scores the supplied retrievals and responses.
No: RAG evaluation jobs can only score an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base, so the corpus would first have to be ingested into one.
No: external systems must be evaluated with an LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation job, which has no RAG-specific metrics.

explanation: RAG evaluation jobs accept your own inference response data from an external RAG source, in both retrieve-only and retrieve-and-generate modes. Bedrock skips the invocation step and scores the data you supply, so the metrics and report are available without moving the system onto AWS. Not "No: RAG evaluation jobs can only score an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base...": external RAG sources are explicitly supported. Not "Yes: point the RAG evaluation job at the external retriever's endpoint...": Bedrock does not call arbitrary external retrievers; you supply the data. Not "No: external systems must be evaluated with an LLM-as-a-judge model evaluation job...": judge-based model evaluation also accepts bring-your-own response data, so the premise is wrong twice over. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A team needs a metric that specifically detects whether a model declines to answer prompts it should be able to handle, after a Guardrails configuration change appeared to make the assistant overly cautious. Which built-in LLM-as-a-judge metric targets this?

options.text: Builtin.Refusal, which determines whether the response declines to answer or rejects the request with reasons.
Builtin.FollowingInstructions, which measures how closely the response respects the directions given in the prompt.
Builtin.Helpfulness, which measures how useful the response is, including coherence and anticipation of user needs.
Builtin.Harmfulness, which evaluates whether the response contains content that could be considered harmful.

explanation: Builtin.Refusal is defined precisely as detecting responses that decline to answer or reject the request - the direct measure of over-refusal after a safety configuration change. Not "Builtin.Harmfulness...": it scores harmful content in the output, the opposite failure from over-caution. Not "Builtin.FollowingInstructions...": a refusal can be scored as instruction-following if the instructions permit declining, so it does not isolate the behavior. Not "Builtin.Helpfulness...": a refusal would drag helpfulness down, but so would a dozen other defects, making it a lagging and non-specific signal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-metrics.html

prompt: An LLM-as-a-judge evaluation must score responses against a company-specific rubric - adherence to an internal style guide and correct use of regulated product terminology - that no built-in metric covers. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Run a human evaluation job, because judge-model evaluations support only the built-in metric set that Bedrock provides.
Define a custom metric with your own judge prompt and rating scale, and run the evaluation job with a supported evaluator model.
Run the job with Builtin.ProfessionalStyleAndTone, which can be parameterized with the company's own style guide as input.
Fine-tune the evaluator model on the style guide first, then run a standard built-in-metric evaluation against it.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock supports custom metrics for judge-based evaluations: you author the prompt that instructs the evaluator model and define the rating scale, then run the job with one of the evaluator models that supports custom metrics. That is the supported path for a bespoke rubric. Not "Run the job with Builtin.ProfessionalStyleAndTone...parameterized with the company's own style guide": built-in metrics use fixed prompts and take no rubric parameter. Not "Run a human evaluation job, because judge-model evaluations support only the built-in metric set": the premise is false - custom metrics exist. Not "Fine-tune the evaluator model on the style guide first...": evaluation jobs do not require or expect a fine-tuned judge, and this is far more effort than authoring a metric prompt. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-custom-metrics-create-job.html

prompt: A knowledge base ingestion job reports partial success: most documents ingest, a subset consistently fails, and the team needs to know which documents failed and why. Where should they look?

options.text: The Amazon S3 server access logs for the data source bucket, which show which objects the service failed to read.
The CloudTrail event for the StartIngestionJob call, which includes the list of documents that the job was unable to process.
The knowledge base ingestion job's CloudWatch logs, which record per-document failure reasons for the data source sync.
The Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs, which record the embedding calls that failed during the ingestion job.

explanation: Knowledge base data source sync emits per-document ingestion results to CloudWatch Logs, including the reason a given document failed - unsupported format, size limit, parsing error. That is the designed troubleshooting surface for partial ingestion failures. Not "The CloudTrail event for the StartIngestionJob call...": CloudTrail records that the job was started and by whom, not per-document outcomes. Not "The Amazon S3 server access logs...": those show request-level access to objects, which does not explain a parsing or format rejection after a successful read. Not "The Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs...": ingestion embedding calls are not what invocation logging surfaces for this purpose, and a format rejection never reaches the embedding step. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-ingestion-monitoring.html

prompt: Which TWO practices best isolate whether a quality regression after a release came from the prompt change or the model version change, when both shipped together? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Re-run the golden dataset with the previous prompt against the new model version, holding everything else constant.
Increase the golden dataset size so that the combined effect of both changes is measured with tighter confidence intervals.
Compare the p95 latency of the new release against the previous release across the same production traffic mix.
Re-run the golden dataset with the new prompt against the previous model version, holding everything else constant.
Re-run the golden dataset with the new prompt and new model at temperature 0 to remove sampling as a variable.

explanation: Isolating a confounded change means varying one factor at a time. Running new prompt with old model, and old prompt with new model, against the same golden dataset attributes the regression to whichever cell reproduces it - the standard controlled comparison. Not "...new prompt and new model at temperature 0...": reducing sampling variance is good hygiene but still measures both changes together. Not "Compare the p95 latency...": latency is not the regression being investigated. Not "Increase the golden dataset size...": a tighter estimate of the combined effect still does not decompose it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html

prompt: A team must monitor a production assistant for a rise in hallucination rate over time, and be alerted when it degrades, without a human reading every response. Which approach is workable at production volume?

options.text: Route every production response through a human review queue, and alarm when reviewers flag more responses than the baseline rate.
Score a continuous random sample of production traffic with an automated grounding or faithfulness check, and alarm on the trend.
Alarm on the rate of change in average output token count, which rises when the model begins fabricating extra detail.
Alarm on the count of Guardrails interventions, which rises in proportion to the rate of hallucinated content in responses.

explanation: Continuous sampling with an automated grounding or faithfulness scorer, trended over time and alarmed on, is the production-scale way to watch hallucination rate - it costs a fraction of full coverage while still detecting a shift in the population. Not "Route every production response through a human review queue...": full human review does not scale to production volume and adds unacceptable latency. Not "Alarm on the count of Guardrails interventions...": interventions count blocked policy violations, which is a different population from ungrounded claims - unless contextual grounding is configured to block, and even then it measures blocks rather than rate. Not "Alarm on the rate of change in average output token count...": output length is not a hallucination signal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html

prompt: An agent deployed on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore must be debugged in production: the team needs per-session traces of the agent's execution path, plus token usage and error rates, and wants the data in their existing OpenTelemetry-based monitoring stack. What should they rely on?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging, which records each agent session's spans and token counts into Amazon S3.
AWS X-Ray active tracing configured on the AgentCore runtime, which is the only supported way to capture agent spans.
AgentCore Observability, which emits OTEL-compatible telemetry and stores spans, metrics and logs in Amazon CloudWatch.
AWS CloudTrail with data events enabled for AgentCore, which records each agent step as an auditable API event.

explanation: AgentCore Observability provides built-in metrics, spans and logs for agent, gateway and memory resources, stores them in CloudWatch, and emits them in standardized OpenTelemetry-compatible format specifically so they can be consumed by an existing observability stack. Session count, latency, duration, token usage and error rates are among the built-in metrics. Not "AWS CloudTrail with data events enabled for AgentCore...": CloudTrail is an audit record of API activity, not an execution-path trace. Not "Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging...records each agent session's spans...": invocation logging captures model request and response payloads; it does not produce spans. Not "AWS X-Ray active tracing...the only supported way to capture agent spans": AgentCore emits its own telemetry natively, so X-Ray is not required and is certainly not the only path. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability.html

prompt: A German health insurer is building a claims-summarisation service in eu-central-1 on Amazon Bedrock. The chosen model can be invoked from eu-central-1 through inference profiles, not by its Regional model ID. Regulators require prompts and responses to be processed in AWS Regions inside the EU. Traffic is unpredictable, and the insurer wants to pay per token with no hourly charge. The organisation's SCP denies every action whose aws:RequestedRegion is not eu-central-1, and the security team insists that no other AWS service becomes usable outside eu-central-1 as a result of this project. Which combination of design decisions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Invoke the model through its global inference profile, and allow the role to invoke the profile and the foundation-model ARNs it needs.
Invoke the model through its geographic inference profile, and allow the role to invoke the profile and the model in each destination Region.
Widen the aws:RequestedRegion values that the Region-deny SCP allows so that the routed model evaluations of the profile pass.
Add an exception to the Region-deny SCP for requests whose bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matches the chosen inference profile.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model in the source Region, and invoke the provisioned model ARN in place of a profile.

explanation: The model is reachable only through inference profiles and processing must stay in the EU, so the design must "Invoke the model through its geographic inference profile": a geographic profile keeps requests inside its geography and is billed per token at on-demand rates. The role needs bedrock:InvokeModel on the profile and on the foundation model in the source Region and in every destination Region. Because the SCP allows only eu-central-1, the evaluations for the other EU Regions would be denied. AWS documents that bedrock:InferenceProfileArn is populated on those foundation-model evaluations, so the fix is to "Add an exception to the Region-deny SCP" for that profile, which exempts the routing without opening any Region to other services. "Invoke the model through its global inference profile" fails the residency rule, because global profiles route to commercial Regions worldwide. The option to "Widen the aws:RequestedRegion values" would add the other EU Regions to the allowlist for every service, which the security team forbids. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput" fails because the stem rules out an hourly charge and the model cannot be invoked here by its Regional ID; inference profiles do not support Provisioned Throughput. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/geographic-cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A US media company is building a headline-generation service in us-east-1 on Amazon Bedrock. It has no data residency obligations, and the product owner wants the lowest available per-token price for the chosen model, with no hourly charge, because traffic is unpredictable. The organisation's SCP denies every action whose aws:RequestedRegion is not us-east-1 or us-west-2. SCPs are generated by a central policy tool that supports the AWS global condition keys (those prefixed aws:) and rejects service-specific condition keys, and the cloud team will not hand-edit its output. Which combination of design decisions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Invoke the model through its global inference profile, and allow the role to invoke the profile and the foundation-model ARNs it needs.
Invoke the model through its geographic inference profile, and allow the role to invoke the profile and the model in each destination Region.
Widen the aws:RequestedRegion values that the Region-deny SCP allows so that the routed model evaluations of the profile pass.
Add an exception to the Region-deny SCP for requests whose bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matches the chosen inference profile.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model in the source Region, and invoke the provisioned model ARN in place of a profile.

explanation: With no residency obligation and a goal of the lowest per-token price, the company should "Invoke the model through its global inference profile": AWS states that global cross-Region inference saves approximately 10% compared with geographic profiles, is priced on the source Region and has no hourly charge. The role needs the profile ARN, the foundation-model ARN in us-east-1 and the foundation-model ARN that has no Region. For that last evaluation Amazon Bedrock sets aws:RequestedRegion to the literal value unspecified, which the Region list in the SCP denies. AWS documents two fixes: allow unspecified in the Region condition, or add an exception on bedrock:InferenceProfileArn. The policy tool accepts only global condition keys, so the workable fix is to "Widen the aws:RequestedRegion values" by adding unspecified, which uses an aws: key and opens no additional Region. The option to "Add an exception to the Region-deny SCP" relies on a service-specific condition key that the tool rejects. "Invoke the model through its geographic inference profile" is billed at standard pricing, so it misses the lowest-price requirement. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput" is billed by the hour, which the product owner ruled out for unpredictable traffic. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A logistics company runs three generative AI proofs of concept (shipment-delay emails, customs-form extraction and a driver FAQ) from one AWS account in us-east-1. All three were written with the OpenAI SDK and call the same model through the Responses API on the bedrock-runtime endpoint; the team has three weeks and will not rewrite the calls for another API. Each use case already runs in its own AWS Lambda function with its own execution role. Finance wants the model spend of each use case to appear as billed cost in AWS Cost Explorer, grouped by use case, and the company will not change its account structure. Which approach meets these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the existing system?

options.text: Create an application inference profile for each use case, tag each profile, and pass the profile ARN as the model ID in every request.
Create a member account for each use case in AWS Organizations, and run each use case in its own account so that costs group by linked account.
Enable model invocation logging, pass attribution tags in requestMetadata on each request, and compute spend from token counts with a scheduled query.
Give each use case its own IAM role with a use-case tag, and activate that tag as an IAM principal cost allocation tag in AWS Billing.

explanation: The deciding constraint is the Responses API on bedrock-runtime. AWS documents that application inference profiles are not supported by the Responses API, while IAM principal attribution is. IAM principal attribution needs no change to the calls. Amazon Bedrock records the calling role for every request, and tags on the role, once activated as IAM principal cost allocation tags, appear in Cost Explorer and CUR 2.0. Each use case already has its own execution role, so the work is to "Give each use case its own IAM role with a use-case tag" and activate the tag. "Create an application inference profile for each use case" is the usual answer for Converse or InvokeModel, but a Responses API request that names an application inference profile is rejected with a 400 error, and the team will not rewrite the calls. "Enable model invocation logging" with requestMetadata does not meet the finance requirement: AWS states that request metadata is not delivered as a cost allocation tag and does not appear in Cost Explorer, so the result is an estimate computed from logs, not billed cost. "Create a member account for each use case" would separate the costs but changes the account structure, which the company ruled out. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-mgmt-iam-principal-tracking.html

prompt: A SaaS company's support product calls one Amazon Bedrock model through the Converse API from a single AWS account in us-east-1. It serves about 9,000 customer tenants through one shared service role. Product managers want an internal dashboard that shows an estimated model cost for each individual support ticket within minutes of the ticket closing, broken down by tenant and by feature. Finance has confirmed that an estimate based on published token prices is acceptable for this dashboard and that invoice-level reporting is handled elsewhere. The company does not want to create an AWS resource for each tenant. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an application inference profile for each use case, tag each profile, and pass the profile ARN as the model ID in every request.
Create a member account for each use case in AWS Organizations, and run each use case in its own account so that costs group by linked account.
Enable model invocation logging, pass attribution tags in requestMetadata on each request, and compute spend from token counts with a scheduled query.
Give each use case its own IAM role with a use-case tag, and activate that tag as an IAM principal cost allocation tag in AWS Billing.

explanation: The requirement is per-ticket cost within minutes, by tenant and feature, with an estimate accepted. Per-request metadata is built for this: the Converse API accepts a requestMetadata object of key-value pairs on each call, the values are written to the model invocation log record beside the input and output token counts, and a CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena query can group tokens by any metadata key and multiply by the published rates. Nothing has to be created per tenant. So the team should "Enable model invocation logging" and tag each call. "Create an application inference profile for each use case" produces cost allocation tags, but billing data is aggregated, takes up to 24 hours to appear and has no per-request grain; it would also mean a resource for each tenant. "Give each use case its own IAM role" has the same grain problem: AWS states that IAM principal attribution is aggregated per usage type per day and does not produce per-request cost, and all tenants share one role. "Create a member account for each use case" gives linked-account totals only and is another resource per tenant. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-mgmt-request-metadata.html

prompt: A platform team supports 40 product teams that build generative AI workloads on Amazon Bedrock in their own AWS accounts. Reviews are done in slide decks today. The architecture board has ruled that a review in the AWS Well-Architected Tool must fit into one 90-minute session: a single lens of no more than 30 questions, each written in the company's control language and mapped to an internal control ID. The questions must cover the generative AI practices that the board selected as well as 14 internal controls, such as the mandatory guardrail. Each review must produce risks with an improvement plan, be repeatable in every account, and show progress between quarters. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Apply the Generative AI Lens from the Lens Catalog to each workload, add a shared custom lens for internal questions, and save milestones.
Create a review template with pre-filled answers for the shared platform controls, share it with the organization, and define workloads from it.
Author one custom lens that holds the company's own wording of its generative AI and internal questions, share it, and save milestones.
Apply the Generative AI Lens from the Lens Catalog to each workload, attach a profile that describes business priorities, and save milestones.

explanation: The board's ruling fixes the shape of the review: one lens, at most 30 questions, in the company's own wording. A custom lens is the feature for that. AWS describes custom lenses as having their own pillars, questions, best practices and improvement plan, tailored to governance needs; they can be shared with other AWS accounts, and milestones track progress over time. So the team should "Author one custom lens" that combines the selected generative AI questions with the 14 internal controls. The option that applies the catalog lens and adds "a shared custom lens for internal questions" is the natural design when a full review against the AWS lens is wanted, but here it means two lenses, and the catalog lens brings its complete AWS-worded question set, which breaks the single-lens and 30-question limits. The option to "attach a profile that describes business priorities" prioritises questions of the AWS lens for a workload; it does not add the internal controls or reword anything. "Create a review template" pre-fills answers to questions that already exist; it supplies no new questions and so cannot carry the internal controls. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/lenses-custom.html

prompt: A platform team supports 40 product teams that build generative AI workloads on a shared landing zone. Reviews in the AWS Well-Architected Tool already use the Framework lens and a company custom lens of 14 generative AI governance questions. For every workload, about 35 of the questions have the same answer, because the platform provides the control centrally (the mandatory guardrail, invocation logging, encryption keys), yet each team retypes these answers and the answers often contradict each other. The platform team wants the common answers entered once and applied consistently to every new workload review in every account, without changing the set of questions. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST ongoing effort?

options.text: Apply the Generative AI Lens from the Lens Catalog to each workload, add a shared custom lens for internal questions, and save milestones.
Create a review template with pre-filled answers for the shared platform controls, share it with the organization, and define workloads from it.
Author one custom lens that holds the company's own wording of its generative AI and internal questions, share it, and save milestones.
Apply the Generative AI Lens from the Lens Catalog to each workload, attach a profile that describes business priorities, and save milestones.

explanation: The problem is repeated, inconsistent answers to existing questions, not missing questions. Review templates address exactly that: AWS describes them as containing pre-filled answers for Well-Architected Framework and custom lens best practice questions, to reduce the need to fill in the same answers across workloads and to drive consistency. A template can be shared with an account, an organization or an organizational unit, and a workload can be defined from it. So the team should "Create a review template" that carries the platform answers once, and have teams define their workloads from it. The option that adds "a shared custom lens for internal questions" on top of the catalog lens changes the question set, which the stem excludes, and pre-fills nothing. "Author one custom lens" likewise creates a new set of questions that every team still answers by hand. The option to "attach a profile that describes business priorities" changes which questions are prioritised for a workload; it does not supply answers, so the 35 common answers would still be retyped. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/review-templates.html

prompt: A travel company wants an assistant that answers employee questions about its expense policy. The policy is one 60-page handbook (about 40,000 tokens) that is revised once a quarter. Its clauses refer to each other heavily: in a pilot that retrieved the five most relevant passages, a third of the answers missed an exception stated elsewhere in the handbook. The assistant receives about 2,000 questions an hour during the working day. The four developers have no ML engineers and no labelled data, and they do not want to operate a data store or an ingestion job. The architect applies the Well-Architected Generative AI Lens guidance on when to customise models. Which design is MOST consistent with that guidance and meets the requirements?

options.text: Fine-tune a small model on prompt-and-response pairs that a larger model generates from the company's own inputs.
Place the full reference material in the system prompt of a large-context model, and enable prompt caching for it.
Use prompt engineering on a base model, and add retrieval from a knowledge base that is re-synchronised after changes.
Use prompt engineering alone on a base model, with the instructions and a few examples held in a managed prompt.

explanation: The lens best practice GENOPS05-BP01 says to start with the least resource-intensive option, prompt engineering, to evaluate RAG next, and to customise a model only if those fall short. Here the knowledge is small (about 40,000 tokens) and the answers depend on clauses spread across the handbook, so the fitting design is to "Place the full reference material in the system prompt": the model sees every cross-reference, no model is trained, and there is no store or ingestion job. Prompt caching suits a long prefix that is reused many times; at 2,000 questions an hour the cache stays warm, which lowers input cost and latency, and a quarterly revision only causes one new cache write. Retrieval "from a knowledge base that is re-synchronised after changes" is ruled out by the stem: the pilot's passage-level retrieval missed exceptions, and the team will not run a data store. "Use prompt engineering alone" with instructions and a few examples leaves the model without the policy text. "Fine-tune a small model" jumps to customisation with no labelled data and no ML engineers, and the weights would be stale after each quarterly revision. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/genops05-bp01.html

prompt: A fintech company classifies 3 million support messages a day into 40 routing codes. A large model with a long, carefully engineered prompt reaches the accuracy target, but its latency is three times the limit and its cost is over budget. The team has already spent two months on prompt engineering for a small model, including few-shot examples, and the small model stays eight points below the target. The task needs no outside knowledge: everything required is in the message, and the routing codes change about once a year. The team has 20,000 representative messages but no human-labelled answers. The architect applies the Well-Architected Generative AI Lens guidance on when to customise models. Which design is MOST consistent with that guidance and meets the requirements?

options.text: Fine-tune a small model on prompt-and-response pairs that a larger model generates from the company's own inputs.
Place the full reference material in the system prompt of a large-context model, and enable prompt caching for it.
Use prompt engineering on a base model, and add retrieval from a knowledge base that is re-synchronised after changes.
Use prompt engineering alone on a base model, with the instructions and a few examples held in a managed prompt.

explanation: GENOPS05-BP01 puts prompt engineering first and RAG second, and says to choose fine-tuning when a specific task requires improved performance. That is the situation here: the cheaper steps have been tried or do not apply, and a narrow, stable task needs a small model to perform better. The team should "Fine-tune a small model" on pairs produced by the large model from its 20,000 messages; the large model already meets the target, so its outputs stand in for the human labels the team lacks, which is how model distillation works on Amazon Bedrock. "Use prompt engineering alone" is what the team did for two months, and the small model stayed eight points short. Retrieval "from a knowledge base that is re-synchronised after changes" adds knowledge, but the stem says the task needs none; it would lengthen each prompt without closing the gap. "Place the full reference material in the system prompt" of a large-context model keeps the workload on a large model, which is the source of the latency and cost problem. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/genops05-bp01.html

prompt: A legal-tech company fine-tuned an open-weight text-embedding model on its own GPU cluster to improve clause search. The weights are in Amazon S3 in us-east-1 in Hugging Face safetensors format with config and tokenizer files (2 GB in total). The search service sends a steady 40 queries a second throughout the business day, and each query must be embedded within 100 ms so that results appear as the user types. The existing weights were validated against a benchmark of 5,000 legal queries and must be reused as they are. The team already operates other Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints. Which deployment design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on GPU instances with auto scaling, and call InvokeEndpoint.
Submit an Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import job that points to the S3 location, and call the imported model with InvokeModel.
Run an Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning job on a supported base model with the original training data, and call the custom model.
Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI asynchronous inference endpoint that scales to zero, and read results from S3.

explanation: The weights are an embedding model, and that decides the question. Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import accepts safetensors weights from S3 for a list of generative architectures, but AWS states that Custom Model Import does not support embedding models, so the option to "Submit an Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import job" cannot host this model even though the file format and Region fit. The remaining way to reuse the weights unchanged is SageMaker AI. Real-time inference is described by AWS as the option for online inference with low latency or high throughput requirements on a persistent endpoint that handles sustained traffic, which matches 40 queries a second at 100 ms. So the team should "Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint". The "asynchronous inference endpoint that scales to zero" queues requests and writes results to S3; it is meant for large payloads and long processing times, not a 100 ms interactive path. "Run an Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning job" would train a new model on a Bedrock base model, which breaks the requirement to reuse the validated weights. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html

prompt: A legal-tech company fine-tuned an open-weight Llama 3.1 8B model on its own GPU cluster to draft contract clauses. The weights are in Amazon S3 in us-east-1 in Hugging Face safetensors format with config and tokenizer files (16 GB in total). The company's application already calls Amazon Bedrock models with InvokeModel on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. Traffic for the new model is interactive and spiky, with long idle periods, and the three-person team does not want to operate inference endpoints, instances or scaling policies. The existing weights passed a legal review and must be reused as they are. Which deployment design meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on GPU instances with auto scaling, and call InvokeEndpoint.
Submit an Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import job that points to the S3 location, and call the imported model with InvokeModel.
Run an Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning job on a supported base model with the original training data, and call the custom model.
Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI asynchronous inference endpoint that scales to zero, and read results from S3.

explanation: Custom Model Import brings a model that was customised elsewhere into Amazon Bedrock. Every condition is met: Llama 3.1 is a supported architecture, the files are safetensors weights with config and tokenizer files in S3, us-east-1 is a supported Region, and 16 GB is far below the 200 GB limit for text models. The imported model is used with on-demand throughput through InvokeModel or InvokeModelWithResponseStream, so the application keeps its existing integration and the team runs no endpoints. That is why the team should "Submit an Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import job". "Deploy the weights to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint" also reuses the weights, but the team would own instances, scaling policies and a second invocation path, which the stem excludes. The "asynchronous inference endpoint that scales to zero" handles idle periods well, but it queues requests and returns results through S3, which does not suit interactive drafting, and it is still an endpoint to operate. "Run an Amazon Bedrock fine-tuning job" creates a different model on a Bedrock base model; it does not reuse the reviewed weights. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html

prompt: A Dutch insurer must choose between three Amazon Bedrock models for summarising insurance-law case files written in Dutch. Public leaderboards rank the three models differently. The team has 600 anonymised case files with reference summaries written by its lawyers, five lawyers who can each spare two hours, and one week. The decision must rest on the insurer's own documents, must score each summary against its reference with a written explanation of the score, and must include the lawyers' judgement of legal tone. The team must not have to build a test harness or run the models' inference itself. Which combination of steps should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run model evaluation jobs that use a judge model, with the company's prompts and reference summaries as a custom prompt dataset.
Run programmatic model evaluation jobs for the text summarization task type with the built-in prompt dataset that Amazon Bedrock provides.
Run a model evaluation job that uses human workers, with the company's own experts as the work team rating a sample of outputs.
Run programmatic model evaluation jobs for the text summarization task type with a custom prompt dataset, scored by BERTScore.
Run model evaluation jobs that use a judge model on a prompt dataset that already contains each response in modelResponses.

explanation: Two requirements map to two job types. A judge-model job takes a custom prompt dataset in JSON Lines on Amazon S3, with up to 1,000 prompts and an optional referenceResponse; Amazon Bedrock invokes each candidate, and the judge scores each response and provides an explanation for it. That covers the insurer's 600 files, the reference summaries and the written explanations, with no harness to build, so the team should "Run model evaluation jobs that use a judge model" with its own dataset. For legal tone, a job "that uses human workers" lets employees or subject-matter experts rate outputs, which brings the lawyers into the decision within their two hours. The programmatic job "with a custom prompt dataset, scored by BERTScore" uses the insurer's data but returns a similarity number with no explanation of the score. The programmatic job "with the built-in prompt dataset" measures general summarisation, not the insurer's Dutch case files. The judge job on a dataset "that already contains each response in modelResponses" requires the team to run inference itself first, which the stem excludes; that mode exists for models hosted outside Amazon Bedrock. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html

prompt: A Dutch bank is choosing between two models for summarising loan files. One is an Amazon Bedrock model that was scored last month by a judge-model evaluation job on the bank's 800 loan files and reference summaries. The other is an open-weight model that the bank fine-tuned and hosts on its own GPU cluster, outside Amazon Bedrock; its summaries of the same 800 files are already stored in Amazon S3. The bank wants the same judge-based metrics for the self-hosted model. In addition, its model-risk committee requires a deterministic, algorithmic similarity score against the reference summaries for the Bedrock model, with no LLM or human judgement involved. No subject-matter experts are available. Which combination of steps should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run model evaluation jobs that use a judge model, with the company's prompts and reference summaries as a custom prompt dataset.
Run programmatic model evaluation jobs for the text summarization task type with the built-in prompt dataset that Amazon Bedrock provides.
Run a model evaluation job that uses human workers, with the company's own experts as the work team rating a sample of outputs.
Run programmatic model evaluation jobs for the text summarization task type with a custom prompt dataset, scored by BERTScore.
Run model evaluation jobs that use a judge model on a prompt dataset that already contains each response in modelResponses.

explanation: The self-hosted model cannot be invoked by Amazon Bedrock, but Bedrock evaluations can score responses that were generated elsewhere. The prompt dataset then carries a modelResponses entry for each prompt, with the response and a modelIdentifier, and Amazon Bedrock skips the model-invoke step. So the bank should run judge jobs "on a prompt dataset that already contains each response in modelResponses" to obtain the same judge-based metrics for that model. The committee's requirement for an algorithmic score with no LLM or human involved points to a programmatic job: for the text summarization task type the accuracy metric is BERTScore, and the job accepts a custom prompt dataset, so the bank should run it "with a custom prompt dataset, scored by BERTScore" for the Bedrock model. The judge job with "the company's prompts and reference summaries as a custom prompt dataset" has Bedrock invoke the model, which it cannot do for the self-hosted one, and the Bedrock model already has those scores. The job "that uses human workers" needs experts the bank does not have. The programmatic job "with the built-in prompt dataset" does not use the bank's loan files. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-prompt-datasets-judge.html

prompt: A retailer runs two workloads on the same Amazon Bedrock model. A customer-facing chat assistant serves shoppers worldwide around the clock at a steady 400,000 input and 60,000 output tokens per minute and has missed its latency target on standard on-demand inference. The company wants capacity reserved for the assistant and accepts a three-month term, but when a promotion pushes traffic above the reserved level, the excess must be served automatically at standard on-demand rates. A nightly job summarises 2 million product reviews, one independent prompt per review with no tool use; the records already sit in Amazon S3, nobody waits for the result, and the team wants no client process running overnight to send requests. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move the chat assistant to the Reserved service tier, with input and output tokens-per-minute capacity sized for its load.
Keep the chat assistant on on-demand inference, and set the service tier of its requests to priority.
Convert the nightly job to an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job that reads JSONL records from Amazon S3.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month commitment for the chat assistant, and invoke the provisioned model.
Keep the nightly job on the Converse API, and set the service tier of its requests to flex.

explanation: The chat assistant is a steady, 24x7, mission-critical load for which the company wants reserved capacity and accepts a term. The Reserved tier fits: capacity is reserved for 1 or 3 months with separate input and output tokens-per-minute allocations (the minimums are 100,000 and 10,000, which this load exceeds), and when the application needs more than it reserved, the service automatically overflows to the Standard tier. So the retailer should "Move the chat assistant to the Reserved service tier". Setting the tier "to priority" gives faster responses but reserves nothing; AWS positions it for workloads that do not warrant a 24x7 reservation. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month commitment" buys a fixed number of model units behind a provisioned model, and AWS documents automatic overflow to Standard for the Reserved tier, not for Provisioned Throughput. For the reviews, the team should "Convert the nightly job to an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job": one request submits the S3 records, results are written to S3, and no client loop runs overnight. Setting the nightly requests "to flex" lowers the price, but each request is still a synchronous Converse call that a running client must send. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html

prompt: A retailer runs two workloads on the same Amazon Bedrock model. A customer-facing chat assistant is busy only from 09:00 to 18:00 on weekdays, peaks at about 30,000 input tokens per minute, and has missed its latency target in busy hours on standard on-demand inference. A nightly agentic job enriches product records by calling tools through the Converse API in a multi-turn loop; it may take several hours, and nobody waits for it. The company will not sign a capacity reservation or a term commitment for either workload, and it wants the nightly job to cost as little as possible without rewriting its tool loop. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move the chat assistant to the Reserved service tier, with input and output tokens-per-minute capacity sized for its load.
Keep the chat assistant on on-demand inference, and set the service tier of its requests to priority.
Convert the nightly job to an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job that reads JSONL records from Amazon S3.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month commitment for the chat assistant, and invoke the provisioned model.
Keep the nightly job on the Converse API, and set the service tier of its requests to flex.

explanation: Service tiers are chosen per request. Priority delivers the fastest response times for a price premium and requires no reservation; AWS describes it for customer-facing workflows that do not warrant a 24x7 capacity reservation, which is a chat assistant that is busy only in office hours. So the retailer should keep on-demand inference and set the chat requests "to priority". Flex offers a pricing discount to workloads that can handle longer processing times, and AWS names agentic workflows as an example; flex requests are ordinary Converse calls, so the tool loop is unchanged, and the nightly requests should be set "to flex". "Move the chat assistant to the Reserved service tier" breaks the no-commitment rule: Reserved is a 1-month or 3-month reservation with a minimum of 100,000 input tokens per minute, more than three times this peak. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput with a 1-month commitment" is also a term commitment and is billed for every hour, including nights and weekends when chat is idle. "Convert the nightly job to an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job" is not possible for this job, because batch inference does not support tool calling: each record is processed independently with no multi-turn exchange. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html

prompt: A media company serves article tagging from a custom model that it fine-tuned in January 2026 on an Amazon Bedrock base model in us-east-1. The custom model is served through an on-demand custom model deployment. AWS has notified the company that the base model has entered the Legacy state, with an end-of-life (EOL) date seven months away. The tagging service is being replaced by a feature of a new publishing suite and will be switched off in three months, well before the EOL date. Accuracy is acceptable, traffic is flat, and the two engineers are fully assigned to the move to the new suite. Which plan is consistent with how Amazon Bedrock handles models in the Legacy state and requires the LEAST effort?

options.text: Keep the current on-demand deployment as it is until the service is switched off, and make no change to the model.
Keep serving the custom model, fine-tune an Active base model with the labelled examples, and cut over before the EOL date.
Keep serving the custom model, move tagging to an Active base model with few-shot examples in its prompt, and cut over before EOL.
Keep serving the custom model, fine-tune an open-weight model elsewhere, bring it in with Custom Model Import, and cut over before EOL.

explanation: Legacy does not stop a model from working. AWS states that when a base model enters the Legacy state, a customer who customised it earlier may continue using existing on-demand deployments and may even create a new custom model deployment for on-demand inference; what is blocked is new fine-tuning jobs and new Provisioned Throughput on the Legacy base. Requests fail only after the EOL date. This service is retired four months before that date, accuracy is fine and traffic is flat, so the plan to "Keep the current on-demand deployment as it is until the service is switched off" is both valid and the least work. The other three plans are sound migrations in other circumstances, but each spends engineering time the stem says is unavailable on a service with three months to live. The plan to "fine-tune an Active base model with the labelled examples" adds a training and evaluation cycle. The plan with "few-shot examples in its prompt" still needs prompt work, testing and a cutover. The plan to "fine-tune an open-weight model elsewhere" is the heaviest of all, with training infrastructure and an import job. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-lifecycle.html

prompt: A media company serves article tagging from a custom model that it fine-tuned in January 2026 on an Amazon Bedrock base model in us-east-1, served through an on-demand custom model deployment. AWS has notified the company that the base model has entered the Legacy state and has announced its end-of-life (EOL) date. The service must keep running after that date. The original training set was deleted under a data-retention rule, and only 40 labelled articles remain. In tests, a current Active base model that is given those 40 examples in its prompt already tags more accurately than the custom model. The team has no ML engineers and wants to stay on Amazon Bedrock serverless inference. Which plan is consistent with how Amazon Bedrock handles models in the Legacy state and meets the requirements?

options.text: Keep the current on-demand deployment as it is until the service is switched off, and make no change to the model.
Keep serving the custom model, fine-tune an Active base model with the labelled examples, and cut over before the EOL date.
Keep serving the custom model, move tagging to an Active base model with few-shot examples in its prompt, and cut over before EOL.
Keep serving the custom model, fine-tune an open-weight model elsewhere, bring it in with Custom Model Import, and cut over before EOL.

explanation: After the EOL date the base model is removed and requests fail, and AWS states that migration does not happen automatically, so the company must move to an Active model before then. During the Legacy period the existing on-demand deployment keeps working, which gives time for a cutover. The stem supplies the target: an Active base model with the 40 remaining examples in its prompt already beats the custom model, needs no training data or ML engineers, and runs on serverless on-demand inference. The plan with "few-shot examples in its prompt" therefore meets every requirement. The plan to "fine-tune an Active base model with the labelled examples" is the usual migration, but the training set is gone, 40 articles are too few to train on, and the test shows customisation is unnecessary. The plan to "fine-tune an open-weight model elsewhere" has the same data problem and needs ML skills the team lacks. The plan to "Keep the current on-demand deployment as it is" fails the requirement to keep running after EOL; new fine-tuning jobs on the Legacy base are not allowed either. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-lifecycle.html

prompt: A SaaS company exposes a text-generation API through Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. The model ID for each customer tier is hard-coded, so each model change needs a code release. The function already reads its other settings from Systems Manager Parameter Store through the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension, and an existing change-approval pipeline validates and writes those parameters. During a model incident, operators must be able to switch a tier to another model for all traffic within five minutes, without updating or redeploying the function. Any AWS service that is new to the company needs an eight-week security review, and the change is due in two weeks. Which solution meets these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the existing system?

options.text: Keep the mapping in an AWS AppConfig configuration profile with a validator, and deploy changes with a strategy that monitors a CloudWatch alarm.
Keep the mapping in Lambda environment variables, and have a pipeline update the function configuration when a change is approved.
Keep the mapping in a Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter, and read it through the Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension with a short TTL.
Publish a Lambda function version for each change, and shift a weighted alias to it gradually with AWS CodeDeploy, which can roll the alias back.

explanation: Everything needed is already in place. The function reads settings through the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension, which caches each parameter and fetches it again when its time-to-live expires; the TTL is configurable from 0 to 300 seconds, so a changed value reaches all execution environments within five minutes without touching the function. The existing pipeline already validates and writes parameters. So the team should "Keep the mapping in a Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter" and read it with a short TTL. "Keep the mapping in an AWS AppConfig configuration profile" is the stronger design when validators, gradual deployment and alarm-driven rollback are required, but none of those is asked for here, and AppConfig is a new service that would need an eight-week review against a two-week deadline. "Keep the mapping in Lambda environment variables" means every switch is an update of the function configuration, which the stem excludes, and it needs a new pipeline. "Publish a Lambda function version for each change" keeps the mapping in code, so a switch is still a release, and a gradual alias shift is the opposite of switching all traffic at once. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/ps-integration-lambda-extensions.html

prompt: A SaaS company exposes a text-generation API through Amazon API Gateway and an AWS Lambda function that calls Amazon Bedrock. Each model the company adopts needs its own prompt template, request-building code and response parser, so every model change is a code change that ships as a new build of the function. Last quarter a new parser failed on production traffic that the tests had not covered. The company now wants each model change to reach a small share of live requests first, to increase that share in steps, and to return all traffic to the previous build automatically if a CloudWatch alarm on the function's error rate goes into alarm. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Keep the mapping in an AWS AppConfig configuration profile with a validator, and deploy changes with a strategy that monitors a CloudWatch alarm.
Keep the mapping in Lambda environment variables, and have a pipeline update the function configuration when a change is approved.
Keep the mapping in a Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter, and read it through the Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension with a short TTL.
Publish a Lambda function version for each change, and shift a weighted alias to it gradually with AWS CodeDeploy, which can roll the alias back.

explanation: Here a model change is a code change: a new parser and request builder ship with it. The thing to roll out gradually is therefore a build of the function, and Lambda does that with versions and a weighted alias. An alias can split traffic between two published versions, and AWS CodeDeploy shifts the weights in canary or linear steps; the CodeDeploy deployment group manages the rolling deployment and the rollback, which CloudWatch alarms can trigger. So the team should "Publish a Lambda function version for each change" and shift the alias with CodeDeploy. "Keep the mapping in an AWS AppConfig configuration profile" gives validated, gradual, alarm-monitored rollout of configuration data, which would be right if only a model ID changed, but a configuration value cannot carry a new parser, and the parser is what failed. "Keep the mapping in a Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter" has the same limit and applies a new value to all traffic once the cache expires. "Keep the mapping in Lambda environment variables" updates every invocation at once, with no traffic split and no automatic rollback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuring-alias-routing.html

prompt: A bank's AWS Step Functions workflow calls a large Amazon Bedrock model to draft replies to customer complaints. About one execution in 200 fails at the model task: these complaints include long attachments, the request is larger than the model accepts, and every retry of the same request fails in the same way. The model is healthy for all other executions, and the failures are unrelated to each other. The bank wants each affected execution to produce its draft from a second model with a larger context window, within the same execution, without delaying or diverting the other 199. The architecture board will not approve a new data store for this workflow. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Raise MaxAttempts in the Retry block of the model task, with a higher BackoffRate and full jitter so that retries are spread over time.
Add a Catch for States.ALL to the model task so that, once retries are exhausted, the execution moves to a task that invokes a second model.
Put an Amazon SQS queue with a dead-letter queue in front of the workflow, and limit how many executions can start at the same time.
After repeated failures, write an item with an expiry time to a DynamoDB table; executions read it first and skip the model until it expires.

explanation: The failures are isolated and deterministic: one oversized request fails however often it is retried, while the model stays healthy for everyone else. The fitting tool is a fallback state. In Step Functions a Task state can have a Catch field; when retries do not resolve the error, the execution transitions to the state named in the catcher. So the team should "Add a Catch for States.ALL to the model task" that leads to a task invoking the larger-context model. Only the failing execution takes that path, and nothing is stored outside the workflow. The circuit breaker, which would "write an item with an expiry time to a DynamoDB table", is designed for a callee that is down or slow for everyone: an open circuit would divert the 199 healthy executions too, and it needs the data store that the board refuses. The option to "Raise MaxAttempts in the Retry block" suits transient errors; repeating a request that is too large only adds delay. "Put an Amazon SQS queue with a dead-letter queue in front of the workflow" controls how fast executions start, but the oversized request still fails and produces no draft. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-error-handling.html

prompt: A bank's AWS Step Functions workflow calls an Amazon Bedrock model to draft replies to customer complaints. At the top of each hour a reporting job in the same account uses most of the model's quota for about 40 seconds, and model tasks that start in that window fail with ThrottlingException. The current Retry block gives up after two quick attempts, so those executions fail. Drafts may be delayed by several minutes. Compliance has approved only this one model for customer correspondence. The executions are started by another team's system through StartExecution, and that system cannot be changed this quarter. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Raise MaxAttempts in the Retry block of the model task, with a higher BackoffRate and full jitter so that retries are spread over time.
Add a Catch for States.ALL to the model task so that, once retries are exhausted, the execution moves to a task that invokes a second model.
Put an Amazon SQS queue with a dead-letter queue in front of the workflow, and limit how many executions can start at the same time.
After repeated failures, write an item with an expiry time to a DynamoDB table; executions read it first and skip the model until it expires.

explanation: A 40-second burst of throttling is a transient error, and AWS Prescriptive Guidance names throttling (429) as the case for the retry with backoff pattern. Step Functions implements it in configuration: MaxAttempts sets how many retries are made, BackoffRate multiplies the wait after each attempt, and JitterStrategy FULL randomises the waits so that the executions caught in the same window do not all retry at the same moment. A few more attempts with a growing interval carry each execution past the 40 seconds, well inside the delay the bank accepts, so the team should "Raise MaxAttempts in the Retry block". The option to "Add a Catch for States.ALL" depends on a second model, and compliance has approved only one. The circuit breaker that would "write an item with an expiry time to a DynamoDB table" makes executions skip the model during a cool-down, which produces no draft and fits long outages, not a short quota squeeze. "Put an Amazon SQS queue with a dead-letter queue in front of the workflow" requires the upstream system to send messages instead of calling StartExecution, and that system cannot be changed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/retry-backoff.html

prompt: A company calls an Amazon Bedrock model from us-east-1. To lower its token cost, it changes the model ID from the us. geographic inference profile to the global. inference profile of the same model. Data residency is not a concern. The organisation's SCP denies all actions unless aws:RequestedRegion is us-east-1, us-east-2, us-west-2 or unspecified; the security team added the last value a month ago for another team, which uses global inference profiles successfully. The role's IAM policy allows bedrock:InvokeModel on the global inference profile ARN in us-east-1 and on the foundation-model ARNs in us-east-1, us-east-2 and us-west-2. Requests through the global. profile fail with an AccessDeniedException which reports that no identity-based policy allows the action. What should the company change?

options.text: Add the value unspecified to the aws:RequestedRegion values that the Region-deny statement of the SCP allows.
Exempt requests whose bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matches this global inference profile from the Region deny in the SCP.
Invoke the model through the us. geographic inference profile again, and leave the SCP and the IAM policy as they are.
Add the foundation-model ARN that has no Region and no account ID to the bedrock:InvokeModel statement of the role's IAM policy.

explanation: A global inference profile needs a three-part IAM policy: the profile ARN in the source Region, the foundation-model ARN in the source Region, and the global foundation-model ARN of the form arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/..., which has no Region and no account ID. AWS states that all three are required. This role has the first two and the Regional model ARNs that a geographic profile needs, but not the Region-less ARN, and the error says that no identity-based policy allows the action. The fix is to "Add the foundation-model ARN that has no Region and no account ID" to the role's policy. The option to "Add the value unspecified" addresses an SCP that blocks the Region-less evaluation, but this SCP already allows unspecified and another team uses global profiles under it. The option to "Exempt requests whose bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matches" is the alternative SCP fix for the same problem; an SCP exemption grants nothing, so the missing IAM allow would remain. "Invoke the model through the us. geographic inference profile again" would work, but it gives up the lower price that was the reason for the change. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A company calls an Amazon Bedrock model from us-east-1. To lower its token cost, it changes the model ID from the us. geographic inference profile to the global. inference profile of the same model. The role's IAM policy allows bedrock:InvokeModel on the global inference profile ARN in us-east-1, on the foundation-model ARN in us-east-1, and on the foundation-model ARN that has no Region and no account ID. Requests through the global. profile fail with an AccessDeniedException that cites an explicit deny in a service control policy. The SCP denies all actions unless aws:RequestedRegion is us-east-1, us-east-2 or us-west-2. Data residency is not a concern, but the security team will accept a change only if it applies to this one model's profile and does not let other teams' global inference profiles start working. What should the company change?

options.text: Add the value unspecified to the aws:RequestedRegion values that the Region-deny statement of the SCP allows.
Exempt requests whose bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matches this global inference profile from the Region deny in the SCP.
Invoke the model through the us. geographic inference profile again, and leave the SCP and the IAM policy as they are.
Add the foundation-model ARN that has no Region and no account ID to the bedrock:InvokeModel statement of the role's IAM policy.

explanation: For a global inference profile, Amazon Bedrock authorises the profile, the foundation model in the source Region, and a Region-agnostic foundation-model ARN. For that last evaluation the service sets aws:RequestedRegion to the literal value unspecified, so an SCP that denies everything outside a list of Region names denies it.
