AWS documents two fixes: allow unspecified in the Region condition, or keep the list and add an exception on bedrock:InferenceProfileArn, which is populated on the foundation-model evaluations. The security team wants the change limited to this model's profile, so the company should "Exempt requests whose bedrock:InferenceProfileArn matches this global inference profile". The option to "Add the value unspecified" also unblocks the call, but it does so for every global inference profile in the organisation, which the security team will not accept. The option to "Add the foundation-model ARN that has no Region and no account ID" changes nothing: the role already has it, and an IAM allow does not override an SCP deny. "Invoke the model through the us. geographic inference profile again" avoids the SCP but gives up the saving of roughly 10% that prompted the change. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A team load-tests a contract-review feature on Amazon Bedrock with on-demand inference in us-east-1. The model has a 1:1 burndown rate for output tokens, and its quotas are 2,000,000 tokens per minute and 1,000 requests per minute. At 60 evenly spaced requests per minute the test starts to return ThrottlingException (HTTP 429). Each request has about 4,000 input tokens, sets max_tokens to 400 and returns about 300 output tokens; prompt caching is not used. The feature's own logs account for about 260,000 tokens per minute. Over the same period, the account-level CloudWatch metrics InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount for this model in us-east-1 add up to about 1,900,000 tokens per minute. What is the MOST likely cause of the throttling?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock deducts input tokens plus max_tokens from the quota when each request starts, so the requests reserve more than the quota.
Output tokens of this model are multiplied by a burndown rate when usage is settled, so real quota consumption exceeds the quota.
Another workload in the same account and Region draws on the same model quota, so combined consumption exceeds the quota.
Requests arrive in short bursts within each minute, so the request rate momentarily exceeds the requests-per-minute quota.

explanation: The numbers rule out the feature itself. At the start of each request Amazon Bedrock deducts input tokens plus max_tokens: 4,000 + 400 = 4,400, so 60 requests reserve about 264,000 tokens a minute, far below 2,000,000. With a 1:1 burndown rate the settled usage is about 4,300 per request, or 258,000 a minute, which matches the feature's logs. Yet the CloudWatch metrics for the model in this account and Region show about 1,900,000 tokens a minute. The tokens-per-minute quota is set at the model level for the account, so the difference of roughly 1.6 million comes from somewhere else in the account, and the test's extra load pushes the total over the quota: "Another workload in the same account and Region draws on the same model quota". The explanation that the service "deducts input tokens plus max_tokens" describes a real mechanism, but max_tokens is only 400 here. The explanation that output tokens "are multiplied by a burndown rate" does not apply to a model with a 1:1 rate. The explanation that requests "arrive in short bursts" contradicts the evenly spaced test, and 60 requests is far below the 1,000 request quota. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html

prompt: A team load-tests a report-drafting feature on Amazon Bedrock with on-demand inference in us-east-1. No other workload uses the model in this account. The model's quotas are 2,000,000 tokens per minute and 1,000 requests per minute, and its documentation lists a 10x burndown rate for output tokens. At 100 evenly spaced requests per minute the test starts to return ThrottlingException (HTTP 429). Each request has about 2,000 input tokens, sets max_tokens to 2,000 and returns about 1,900 output tokens; prompt caching is not used. During the test, the CloudWatch metrics InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount for the model add up to about 390,000 tokens per minute. What is the MOST likely cause of the throttling?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock deducts input tokens plus max_tokens from the quota when each request starts, so the requests reserve more than the quota.
Output tokens of this model are multiplied by a burndown rate when usage is settled, so real quota consumption exceeds the quota.
Another workload in the same account and Region draws on the same model quota, so combined consumption exceeds the quota.
Requests arrive in short bursts within each minute, so the request rate momentarily exceeds the requests-per-minute quota.

explanation: Token quotas are not consumed one for one on this model. At the end of each request Amazon Bedrock settles usage as input tokens plus cache-write tokens plus output tokens multiplied by the burndown rate. Here that is 2,000 + 1,900 x 10 = 21,000 quota tokens per request, so 100 requests consume about 2,100,000 a minute, above the 2,000,000 quota, even though the raw token metrics show only 390,000. That is the statement that output tokens "are multiplied by a burndown rate when usage is settled". The explanation that the service "deducts input tokens plus max_tokens" when each request starts is true of the mechanism, but the reservation here is 2,000 + 2,000 = 4,000 per request, or 400,000 a minute, nowhere near the quota; max_tokens is already close to the real completion size. The explanation that "Another workload in the same account and Region" shares the quota is excluded by the stem, which says no other workload uses the model. The explanation that requests "arrive in short bursts" contradicts the evenly spaced test, and 100 requests a minute is a tenth of the request quota. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html

prompt: A SaaS vendor fine-tuned an open-weight Llama 3.1 8B model with one LoRA adapter for each of three bank customers. Each bank's contract requires that its requests are served by compute that no other customer's requests touch, that its model artefacts are encrypted with its own KMS key, and that its capacity scales on its own traffic, so that one bank's month-end peak cannot slow another bank. Each bank's auditors will inspect the hosting resources that are dedicated to it. Traffic for every bank is steady during business hours, and the vendor already operates Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints. Which deployment meets these requirements?

options.text: Merge each adapter into the base weights, and deploy one SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for each customer with its own auto scaling policy.
Deploy one SageMaker AI endpoint whose custom container loads the adapters from Amazon S3 at start-up and selects one for each request.
Deploy the base model as an inference component on one endpoint, and create an adapter inference component for each customer that references it.
Merge each adapter into the base weights, and bring each merged model into Amazon Bedrock with Custom Model Import, one for each customer.

explanation: The contracts demand isolation: dedicated compute, a separate key and independent scaling for each bank, in a form auditors can inspect. With three customers and steady traffic, the direct way to provide that is to merge each adapter into the base weights and "deploy one SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for each customer with its own auto scaling policy": each endpoint has its own instances, its own model artefact and its own scaling. The design with "an adapter inference component for each customer" is the efficient choice when customers may share a fleet, because AWS states that an adapter inference component uses the compute resources of the base inference component; that sharing is what these contracts forbid. The endpoint "whose custom container loads the adapters from Amazon S3 at start-up" shares one fleet and one scaling policy in the same way. Bringing each merged model into Amazon Bedrock "with Custom Model Import" removes endpoint operations, but the models then run on on-demand throughput inside a managed service, so the vendor has no dedicated hosting resources or per-bank scaling policy to show an auditor. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/realtime-endpoints-adapt.html

prompt: A SaaS vendor fine-tuned an open-weight Llama 3.1 8B model with one LoRA adapter for each of four enterprise customers. Each customer uses its model for a few short bursts a day and is idle otherwise. The vendor's application already calls Amazon Bedrock models with InvokeModel, and its two engineers do not want to operate endpoints, GPU instances, containers or scaling policies for this feature. Each request must be answered with the calling customer's fine-tuned behaviour, and the adapters are retrained about twice a year. All workloads run in us-east-1. Which deployment meets these requirements?

options.text: Merge each adapter into the base weights, and deploy one SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for each customer with its own auto scaling policy.
Deploy one SageMaker AI endpoint whose custom container loads the adapters from Amazon S3 at start-up and selects one for each request.
Deploy the base model as an inference component on one endpoint, and create an adapter inference component for each customer that references it.
Merge each adapter into the base weights, and bring each merged model into Amazon Bedrock with Custom Model Import, one for each customer.

explanation: The deciding constraints are that the team will not operate endpoints, instances, containers or scaling policies, and that the application already uses InvokeModel. Custom Model Import fits: it accepts fine-tuned models in supported architectures, which include Llama 3.1, as safetensors weights from S3 in us-east-1, and an imported model is used with on-demand throughput through InvokeModel. With four customers and retraining twice a year, merging each adapter and importing four models is a small, infrequent task, and the application selects the customer's model by its model ARN. So the vendor should bring each merged model into Amazon Bedrock "with Custom Model Import". The design with "an adapter inference component for each customer" stores the base weights once and is the better choice for many adapters on a busy shared fleet, but it is a SageMaker AI endpoint with GPU instances that run through the idle hours and must be scaled by the team. The endpoint "whose custom container loads the adapters from Amazon S3 at start-up" adds a container to maintain. Deploying "one SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for each customer" means four mostly idle GPU fleets to operate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html

prompt: An ML platform team retrains a domain-specific fine-tuned model every month and serves it to customers from an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Today an engineer copies the new artifact over the old one in Amazon S3 and recreates the endpoint by hand. The risk officer must sign off each version after reading its evaluation report before it can be deployed, and each version must be catalogued with its metrics. Once a version is signed off, deployment must be automatic, must expose only a small share of customer traffic to the new version at first, and must return all traffic to the previous fleet without human action if error-rate or latency alarms fire. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Register each trained model as a version in a SageMaker Model Registry model group, and start the deployment when a reviewer sets its status to Approved.
Add a condition step to the SageMaker pipeline that compares the evaluation metric with a threshold and continues to deployment when it passes.
Add each new model to the endpoint as a second production variant with a small traffic weight, and change the weights after comparing the variants.
Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses canary traffic shifting, a baking period and CloudWatch alarms for auto-rollback.
Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that shifts all traffic at once, with CloudWatch alarms for auto-rollback during a baking period.

explanation: The sign-off requirement points to Model Registry. Versions are catalogued in a model group with their metrics, a version can be registered as PendingManualApproval, and changing its status to Approved can initiate CI/CD deployment, so the risk officer's decision is the trigger: "Register each trained model as a version" and deploy on Approved. For the rollout, deployment guardrails update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment. Canary traffic shifting sends a small portion of traffic to the new fleet first and confines the blast radius of a bad update; if any specified CloudWatch alarm trips during the baking period, SageMaker AI rolls all traffic back to the old fleet automatically. That is the deployment "that uses canary traffic shifting". The option to "Add a condition step" is an automatic gate on a metric, which bypasses the human sign-off the stem requires. The deployment "that shifts all traffic at once" exposes every customer request to the new version from the first moment. Adding the model "as a second production variant with a small traffic weight" limits exposure, but changing weights and reverting are manual actions, not an automatic rollback. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deployment-guardrails-blue-green.html

prompt: An ML platform team retrains an internal document-tagging model every night and serves it to back-office tools from an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Nobody is available to review versions at night, so a version must go live without human action whenever its F1 score on a fixed test set is at least 0.92 and must be discarded otherwise. Each endpoint update should finish as quickly as possible and keep the time during which two fleets are billed to a minimum, because the GPU instances are expensive and the internal callers tolerate a brief regression. All traffic must still return to the old fleet automatically if the error-rate alarm fires. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Register each trained model as a version in a SageMaker Model Registry model group, and start the deployment when a reviewer sets its status to Approved.
Add a condition step to the SageMaker pipeline that compares the evaluation metric with a threshold and continues to deployment when it passes.
Add each new model to the endpoint as a second production variant with a small traffic weight, and change the weights after comparing the variants.
Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that uses canary traffic shifting, a baking period and CloudWatch alarms for auto-rollback.
Update the endpoint with a blue/green deployment that shifts all traffic at once, with CloudWatch alarms for auto-rollback during a baking period.

explanation: With no reviewer at night, the gate has to be automatic. A condition step in a SageMaker pipeline evaluates a property such as an evaluation metric and decides which steps run next, so the team should "Add a condition step" that continues to deployment only when F1 is at least 0.92. For the update itself, AWS recommends all-at-once traffic shifting to minimise update time and cost: traffic moves to the new fleet in a single step, and alarms during the baking period still trigger an automatic rollback to the old fleet. That is the deployment "that shifts all traffic at once". The deployment "that uses canary traffic shifting" is safer for customer-facing traffic, but AWS notes that both fleets are operational in parallel for the entire deployment, which is the cost the stem wants to minimise for callers that tolerate a brief regression. Starting deployment "when a reviewer sets its status to Approved" needs a person who is not there. Adding the model "as a second production variant with a small traffic weight" keeps two variants running until someone compares them and changes the weights by hand. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deployment-guardrails-blue-green.html

prompt: A fintech company uses a large Amazon Bedrock model to turn each dispute ticket into a structured settlement proposal. Many different proposals can be valid for one ticket. The cost per ticket is three times the budget, and the large model's proposals pass the company's policy-rule engine only 80 percent of the time. The company has 12,000 production prompts in Amazon S3 but no stored responses and no human-written proposals. An AWS Lambda function that wraps the rule engine can score any proposal in under a second. The company wants every ticket served by a smaller, cheaper model on Amazon Bedrock whose proposals pass the rule engine more often than the large model's do today. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a supervised fine-tuning job for a smaller model, with prompt-and-response pairs as the training dataset.
Create a model distillation job with the large model as teacher, a smaller model as student, and the prompts as input.
Create a reinforcement fine-tuning job for a smaller model, with the prompts and a reward function in AWS Lambda.
Create a prompt router that uses intelligent prompt routing between the large model and a smaller model of the same family.

explanation: The company has prompts, no labels, and a program that can score any output. That is the case for reinforcement fine-tuning: the model generates several responses per prompt, a reward function grades them, and training optimises the model to maximise the reward. AWS lists as ideal the scenarios with multiple valid solutions, success that can be verified programmatically, and labelled examples that are impractical to collect, and the reward function can be custom code in Lambda. So the company should "Create a reinforcement fine-tuning job" that uses the rule-engine function as the grader. The "model distillation job with the large model as teacher" is the usual way to shrink a model without labels, but the student learns from the teacher's responses, and the teacher passes the rule engine only 80 percent of the time; the goal is to do better than that. The "supervised fine-tuning job" needs prompt-and-response pairs, and no proposals exist. The "prompt router" trains nothing: it sends each request to one of two models, so some tickets still go to the large model and the pass rate does not rise. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/reinforcement-fine-tuning.html

prompt: A fintech company answers customer support questions in English with a large Amazon Bedrock model. Quality is good, but the average cost per answer is twice the budget. Analysis shows that about 70 percent of the questions are simple and that a smaller model of the same family answers them just as well, while the remaining questions need the large model's quality. A change freeze starts in one week, so there is no time to prepare training data, run a customisation job and evaluate a custom model. The company has 12,000 production prompts in Amazon S3 but no stored responses. It wants the application to keep calling a single model ID. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a supervised fine-tuning job for a smaller model, with prompt-and-response pairs as the training dataset.
Create a model distillation job with the large model as teacher, a smaller model as student, and the prompts as input.
Create a reinforcement fine-tuning job for a smaller model, with the prompts and a reward function in AWS Lambda.
Create a prompt router that uses intelligent prompt routing between the large model and a smaller model of the same family.

explanation: The company does not need a new model; it needs the simple 70 percent of questions to go to the cheaper model and the rest to stay on the large one, behind one ID, within a week. Intelligent prompt routing does that: a prompt router is a single serverless endpoint that predicts the response quality of two models in the same family for each request and routes the request to optimise quality and cost. It needs no training data, and its documented limit, that it is optimised for English prompts, is met. So the company should "Create a prompt router". The "model distillation job with the large model as teacher" could produce a cheap custom model from the 12,000 prompts, but it is a customisation job followed by evaluation, which does not fit before the freeze, and a single small model would also serve the hard 30 percent. The "reinforcement fine-tuning job" has the same timing problem and needs a reward function that nobody has written. The "supervised fine-tuning job" needs prompt-and-response pairs, and the company kept no responses. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-routing.html

prompt: A company fine-tuned an Amazon Nova model on Amazon Bedrock in us-east-1 in March 2025 to rewrite product descriptions in its brand voice. The custom model is served from a no-commitment Provisioned Throughput of two model units. Amazon CloudWatch shows that a catalogue pipeline now invokes the model around the clock at close to the full capacity of both model units, and the business has confirmed the same volume for at least the next year. The fine-tuned behaviour passed a formal brand review and must not change, and the company will not repeat the customisation job. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to serve this model?

options.text: Keep Provisioned Throughput for the custom model, sized for the measured load, and move it to a 6-month commitment term.
Create a custom model deployment for on-demand inference, use the deployment ARN as the model ID, and delete the Provisioned Throughput.
Delete the custom model, and add few-shot examples of the brand voice to prompts that call the base model with on-demand inference.
Keep no-commitment Provisioned Throughput, and create and delete it on a schedule so that it exists only around the hours of use.

explanation: Two facts decide this. First, the model was customised in March 2025. A custom model deployment for on-demand inference requires that the model was customised on or after 16 July 2025, so the option to "Create a custom model deployment for on-demand inference" is not available for this model unless the customisation job is repeated, which the company refuses. The model therefore stays on Provisioned Throughput. Second, the load is constant, close to full capacity, and confirmed for a year. Provisioned Throughput is billed hourly, and AWS states that the longer the commitment, the more discounted the hourly price; the choices are no commitment, 1 month and 6 months. With guaranteed round-the-clock use, the cheapest valid choice is to "Keep Provisioned Throughput for the custom model" and move it to the 6-month term. The option to "create and delete it on a schedule" saves money only when there are idle hours, and this model has none. "Delete the custom model" and prompt the base model replaces the reviewed behaviour with something different, which the brand review forbids. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A company fine-tuned an Amazon Nova model on Amazon Bedrock in us-east-1 in March 2025 to rewrite product descriptions in its brand voice. The custom model is served from a no-commitment Provisioned Throughput of two model units that has run continuously since launch. Amazon CloudWatch shows that a single scheduled catalogue job invokes the model between 01:00 and 03:00 each night and that the model is idle for the other 22 hours of the day. The fine-tuned behaviour passed a formal brand review and must not change, and the company will not repeat the customisation job. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to serve this model?

options.text: Keep Provisioned Throughput for the custom model, sized for the measured load, and move it to a 6-month commitment term.
Create a custom model deployment for on-demand inference, use the deployment ARN as the model ID, and delete the Provisioned Throughput.
Delete the custom model, and add few-shot examples of the brand voice to prompts that call the base model with on-demand inference.
Keep no-commitment Provisioned Throughput, and create and delete it on a schedule so that it exists only around the hours of use.

explanation: The model is used two hours a day at a known time and paid for 24. Paying per request would be ideal, but a custom model deployment for on-demand inference requires that the model was customised on or after 16 July 2025; this one dates from March 2025 and the company will not repeat the job, so the option to "Create a custom model deployment for on-demand inference" is not available. Within Provisioned Throughput, billing is hourly and continues until the Provisioned Throughput is deleted, and a no-commitment purchase can be deleted at any time. The job is scheduled, so the company can "Keep no-commitment Provisioned Throughput, and create and delete it on a schedule": automation purchases it before 01:00 and deletes it after the job, and the idle 22 hours are no longer billed. Moving to "a 6-month commitment term" lowers the hourly price but cannot be deleted during the term, so all 24 hours are paid for every day. "Delete the custom model" and prompt the base model replaces the reviewed behaviour, which the brand review forbids. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/deploy-custom-model-on-demand.html

prompt: A retailer's nightly ETL job copies product records from a JDBC database to a curated Amazon S3 prefix, and an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base is synchronised from that prefix every morning on a fixed schedule. The ETL job is built and operated by an external vendor, and under the contract the retailer's data team cannot change the job or its script. Truncated extracts with empty descriptions have reached the knowledge base and produced poor answers. The data team wants the quality of each night's curated data measured after it lands, and wants the knowledge base to be synchronised only on days when the quality score meets its threshold, so that on bad days the assistant keeps answering from the previous index. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Schedule an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset to run against the Data Catalog table of the curated prefix after each nightly load.
In the ETL job, set the data quality action so that the job fails without loading the target when the ruleset fails.
Add an Evaluate Data Quality transform before the S3 target with row-level rules, and route rows to curated or quarantine by outcome.
Publish the data quality results of the ETL job to Amazon CloudWatch, and notify the data team from an alarm on the quality metrics.
Start the knowledge base sync from an Amazon EventBridge rule on the data quality results, through a Lambda function that checks the score.

explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality has two entry points: ETL jobs, for data in transit, and the Data Catalog, for data at rest. The data team cannot touch the vendor's job, so it must use the second: "Schedule an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset to run against the Data Catalog table of the curated prefix" after each load. Data quality for the Data Catalog integrates with Amazon EventBridge, so the result of each evaluation can drive the next step. Replacing the fixed morning schedule, the team should "Start the knowledge base sync from an Amazon EventBridge rule on the data quality results": a small function starts the ingestion only when the score meets the threshold, and on a bad day no sync runs, so the previous index stays in use. The three remaining options all modify the vendor's ETL job, which the contract forbids: the action under which "the job fails without loading the target", the "Evaluate Data Quality transform before the S3 target", and publishing "the data quality results of the ETL job" to CloudWatch. A notification alone would not hold back the sync in any case. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/glue-data-quality.html

prompt: A retailer's nightly AWS Glue ETL job, owned by its data team, copies product records from a JDBC database to a curated Amazon S3 prefix. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base is synchronised from that prefix each morning, and that schedule must stay as it is. Records with an empty description, a duplicate SKU or a description shorter than 20 characters have been reaching the knowledge base and producing poor answers. The data team wants failing records kept out of the curated prefix and written to a quarantine prefix for data stewards, wants the valid records to keep flowing and to be synchronised every night, and wants a notification when the nightly quality score drops. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Schedule an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset to run against the Data Catalog table of the curated prefix after each nightly load.
In the ETL job, set the data quality action so that the job fails without loading the target when the ruleset fails.
Add an Evaluate Data Quality transform before the S3 target with row-level rules, and route rows to curated or quarantine by outcome.
Publish the data quality results of the ETL job to Amazon CloudWatch, and notify the data team from an alarm on the quality metrics.
Start the knowledge base sync from an Amazon EventBridge rule on the data quality results, through a Lambda function that checks the score.

explanation: In an ETL job, AWS Glue Data Quality evaluates data in transit, which lets a pipeline filter bad data before it is loaded. The Evaluate Data Quality transform can output the original rows with added columns that list the rules each row passed and failed and give a row-level Passed or Failed result, so the job can write passed rows to the curated prefix and failed rows to quarantine. Completeness, uniqueness and length checks are evaluated per row. So the team should "Add an Evaluate Data Quality transform before the S3 target with row-level rules". The job can also publish its results to CloudWatch, which covers the notification: "Publish the data quality results of the ETL job" and alarm on them. Running a ruleset "against the Data Catalog table of the curated prefix" checks data after the bad records have already landed, and AWS notes that identifying failed records is not supported for the Data Catalog entry point. The action under which "the job fails without loading the target" keeps bad records out but stops the valid ones too. Gating "the knowledge base sync" on the score changes the schedule that must stay and withholds valid records on a bad night. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/tutorial-data-quality.html

prompt: A contact centre stores 20,000 recorded calls a day in Amazon S3. The telephony platform mixes both parties into single-channel audio. Each call has one agent and one customer and is in either US English or US Spanish, and the language of each call is recorded in the IVR metadata. A foundation model will summarise each call, and the summariser needs to know who said what. Product names such as 'Zentrix Q7' must be transcribed correctly. The privacy office has ruled that card numbers and personal names must be removed and that no transcript containing them may be written to any bucket, including buckets with restricted access. Which Amazon Transcribe batch configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Set the language code, and enable speaker partitioning, a custom vocabulary, and PII redaction that outputs the redacted transcript alone.
Set the language code, and enable channel identification, a custom vocabulary, and PII redaction that outputs the redacted transcript alone.
Set the language code, and enable speaker partitioning, a custom vocabulary, and PII redaction that outputs redacted and unredacted transcripts.
Set the language code, and enable channel identification, a custom vocabulary, and PII redaction that outputs redacted and unredacted transcripts.

explanation: Two choices have to be made: how speakers are separated, and what the redaction feature writes. The audio has one channel, so speakers must be separated by speaker partitioning (diarization), which labels each speaker in the transcript. Channel identification transcribes each channel separately and applies when the audio has two channels; it cannot split two people who share one channel, which rules out both configurations that "enable channel identification". For PII, Amazon Transcribe replaces each detected instance with [PII] and can produce the redacted transcript only, or the redacted and the unredacted transcript in the same output bucket. The privacy office forbids storing any unredacted transcript, so the output must be "the redacted transcript alone". The configuration with speaker partitioning that "outputs redacted and unredacted transcripts" separates the speakers correctly but writes the verbatim text, with card numbers and names, to S3. Batch redaction supports both en-US and es-US, the language code comes from the IVR metadata, and a custom vocabulary improves recognition of product names in every configuration. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/pii-redaction-batch.html

prompt: A contact centre stores 20,000 recorded calls a day in Amazon S3. The telephony platform records two-channel audio, with the agent on one channel and the customer on the other, and the two often talk over each other. Each call is in either US English or US Spanish, and the language is recorded in the IVR metadata. A foundation model will summarise each call from a transcript in which card numbers and personal names are removed, and the summary must state reliably which party is the agent. Product names such as 'Zentrix Q7' must be transcribed correctly. The disputes team is required by its regulator to keep the verbatim transcript of every call for 90 days and reads it from the transcription output location. Which Amazon Transcribe batch configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Set the language code, and enable speaker partitioning, a custom vocabulary, and PII redaction that outputs the redacted transcript alone.
Set the language code, and enable channel identification, a custom vocabulary, and PII redaction that outputs the redacted transcript alone.
Set the language code, and enable speaker partitioning, a custom vocabulary, and PII redaction that outputs redacted and unredacted transcripts.
Set the language code, and enable channel identification, a custom vocabulary, and PII redaction that outputs redacted and unredacted transcripts.

explanation: Two choices have to be made: how speakers are separated, and what the redaction feature writes. The audio has two channels with one party on each, so channel identification applies: Amazon Transcribe transcribes each channel separately and labels the output ch_0 and ch_1. Because the agent is always on the same channel, the label says reliably who the agent is, and speech that overlaps is kept apart with its own timestamps on each channel. Speaker partitioning assigns generic labels such as spk_0 and spk_1 by voice, which does not say which one is the agent, so both configurations that "enable speaker partitioning" are weaker here. For PII, Transcribe can write the redacted transcript only, or both transcripts to the same output location. The model needs the redacted one and the disputes team must keep the verbatim one, so the job must be the one that "outputs redacted and unredacted transcripts". The configuration with channel identification that "outputs the redacted transcript alone" leaves the disputes team without the record its regulator requires. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/transcribe/latest/dg/channel-id.html

prompt: An insurer receives 15,000 scanned claim forms a day as PDFs that mix printed text, tables and handwriting. A rules engine needs a fixed set of 40 fields in a consistent form (dates as YYYY-MM-DD, amounts as numbers), and any field read with low certainty must go to a human reviewer. The insurer already runs a document pipeline for other form types on Amazon Textract, AWS Lambda and AWS Step Functions, with a review queue. Its security office has approved those services for claimant data; Amazon Bedrock is not yet approved for this data class, approval takes six months, and the new form type must be live in six weeks. The team has no annotated sample forms. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint whose field descriptions state the formats, and route fields by confidence score.
Send each document to a multimodal model as a document block in the Converse API, with a prompt that asks for the fields as JSON in the required formats.
Extract forms and tables with Amazon Textract, normalise the values in AWS Lambda, orchestrate the steps with AWS Step Functions, and route by confidence.
Use Amazon Textract Queries with an adapter trained on annotated sample forms, normalise the answers in AWS Lambda, and route by confidence.

explanation: The approval constraint decides this. Amazon Bedrock is not approved for claimant data and cannot be within the six-week deadline, which removes both Bedrock designs: the "Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint", which would otherwise be the least-effort answer for fixed fields with per-field confidence, and sending each document "to a multimodal model as a document block in the Converse API". Among the approved services, Amazon Textract analysis returns form data as key-value pairs and tables from scanned documents, distinguishes handwriting from printed text, and reports a confidence score for what it recognises. Lambda functions can normalise dates and amounts, and Step Functions with the existing review queue handles low-confidence fields. So the team should "Extract forms and tables with Amazon Textract" and reuse its pipeline pattern. The option to "Use Amazon Textract Queries with an adapter trained on annotated sample forms" also stays within approved services, but an adapter is created by annotating sample documents and training on them, and the team has no annotated samples. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/textract/latest/dg/how-it-works-analyzing.html

prompt: A claims handler's desktop tool lets the handler upload one supporting letter at a time (a PDF of two or three pages, under 2 MB) and type which facts to pull out, for example 'the date the claimant first reported the damage and whether liability is accepted'. The requested fields differ for every request and often call for a judgement that is implied by the wording instead of printed as a labelled value. The handler waits for the answer, so it must come back within a few seconds, and reads the result directly, so no confidence-based review queue is wanted. About 200 letters a day are processed, and the team does not want to maintain extraction assets for each kind of request. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint whose field descriptions state the formats, and route fields by confidence score.
Send each document to a multimodal model as a document block in the Converse API, with a prompt that asks for the fields as JSON in the required formats.
Extract forms and tables with Amazon Textract, normalise the values in AWS Lambda, orchestrate the steps with AWS Step Functions, and route by confidence.
Use Amazon Textract Queries with an adapter trained on annotated sample forms, normalise the answers in AWS Lambda, and route by confidence.

explanation: The fields are not known in advance: the handler types them for each letter, and many require reading meaning from prose. A multimodal model handles that directly. The Converse API accepts a PDF as a document block of up to 4.5 MB in a user message together with a text block, so one synchronous call can carry the letter and the handler's request and return JSON in a few seconds, with nothing to maintain between requests. So the team should "Send each document to a multimodal model as a document block in the Converse API". The "Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint" is the stronger choice for a fixed field set at volume, but a blueprint is a saved list of field names, types and descriptions for a class of file; fields that change on every request would mean a new blueprint each time, which is the asset maintenance the team rejects. The option to "Extract forms and tables with Amazon Textract" returns labelled key-value pairs and tables, not a judgement such as whether liability is accepted, and adds a pipeline. "Amazon Textract Queries with an adapter" needs annotated samples and training for a fixed set of questions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Message.html

prompt: A developer uses the AWS SDK for Python to call the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with a model that supports document input. The request has a system field with one text block that holds the instructions, an inferenceConfig, and one message with the role user. The content array of that message holds a single block: a document with the format pdf, the name claims_2026.q3-final, and the raw bytes of a 3.9 MB PDF file in source.bytes. The call is rejected with a validation error before the model runs. The developer has confirmed that the file opens correctly as a PDF. Which changes are required to make the request valid? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a text block that contains the instruction for the model to the same content array as the document block.
Rename the document so that the name contains only letters, digits, single spaces, hyphens, parentheses and square brackets.
Split the PDF so that each document block carries no more than 4.5 MB, which is the size limit for one document.
Move the document block into the user message that holds the question, because documents are accepted in user messages.
Change the format field of the document block so that it matches the actual type of the file that is being sent.

explanation: The request breaks two documented rules for document blocks. First, if the content array of a message includes a document, it must also include a block with a text field; here the document is the only block, and the instructions in the system field do not satisfy the rule. The developer must "Add a text block" to the same content array. Second, a document name may contain only alphanumeric characters, whitespace characters (no more than one in a row), hyphens, parentheses and square brackets. The underscore and the period in claims_2026.q3-final are not allowed, so the developer must "Rename the document". The option to "Split the PDF" is not needed, because a document may be up to 4.5 MB and this file is 3.9 MB. The option to "Move the document block into the user message" changes nothing, because the block is already in a message with the role user. The option to "Change the format field" is not needed either: the file is a PDF, the format is pdf, and pdf is a valid value. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_DocumentBlock.html

prompt: A developer uses the AWS SDK for Python to call the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with a model that supports document input. The request has a system field with one text block and two messages. The first message has the role user and holds one text block with the question. The second has the role assistant and holds a single document block, which the developer placed there so that the model would treat the file as something it had already read. The block has the format pdf, the name Claims report 2026 Q3, and the raw bytes of a 6.1 MB PDF file in source.bytes. The call is rejected with a validation error before the model runs. Which changes are required to make the request valid? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a text block that contains the instruction for the model to the same content array as the document block.
Rename the document so that the name contains only letters, digits, single spaces, hyphens, parentheses and square brackets.
Split the PDF so that each document block carries no more than 4.5 MB, which is the size limit for one document.
Move the document block into the user message that holds the question, because documents are accepted in user messages.
Change the format field of the document block so that it matches the actual type of the file that is being sent.

explanation: The request breaks two documented rules for message content. First, images and documents can be included only if the role of the message is user; this document sits in an assistant message. The developer must "Move the document block into the user message that holds the question", which also places it beside a text block, as the API requires for any message that contains a document. Second, each document must be no larger than 4.5 MB, and this file is 6.1 MB. A message may hold up to five documents, so the developer can "Split the PDF" into parts that each fit the limit. The option to "Add a text block" is already satisfied once the document is in the user message, which has the question as a text block. The option to "Rename the document" is not needed: Claims report 2026 Q3 uses only letters, digits and single spaces, all of which are allowed. The option to "Change the format field" is not needed, because the file is a PDF and pdf is a valid format value. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Message.html

prompt: A developer builds an order-status assistant on an Amazon Nova model with the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and client-side tool use. The first request contains the customer's question and a toolConfig that defines the tool get_order_status. The response has the stopReason tool_use and an assistant message with a toolUse block whose toolUseId is tooluse_7Kp and whose input is the order ID A-1182. The developer's code calls the order system, which returns HTTP 404 because no such order exists. The developer wants the model to know that the lookup failed, so that it explains the problem and asks the customer to check the order ID, and does not present an error payload as if it were an order status. Which next request is formatted correctly for this purpose?

options.text: Append the assistant message, then a user message with a toolResult block that carries the toolUseId and the order status as json content.
Append the assistant message, then a user message with a toolResult block that carries the toolUseId, a text explanation and the status error.
Append the assistant message, then a user message with a text block that gives the model the detail it asked the customer for.
Send the original user message again, with toolChoice in the toolConfig set to the specific tool get_order_status.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock keeps no conversation state for Converse, so the next request must carry the exchange: the assistant message with its toolUse block is appended, followed by a message with the role user whose content holds a toolResult block. The toolResult carries the toolUseId of the request it answers, here tooluse_7Kp, and its content. When the tool fails, the block can also carry the status error, which Amazon Nova and Anthropic Claude models support; AWS's own example returns a text description of the failure with that status. That is the request with "a text explanation and the status error", and it tells the model that the lookup did not succeed. The request that carries "the order status as json content" has the right shape for a successful call, but there is no order status to send, and returning the 404 payload as an ordinary result is what the developer wants to avoid. The request with "a text block that gives the model the detail it asked the customer for" leaves the model's tool request unanswered. Sending "the original user message again" discards the turn and makes the model request the same failing lookup. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/tool-use-client-side.html

prompt: A developer builds an order-status assistant on an Amazon Nova model with the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and client-side tool use. The first request contains the customer's question 'Has order A-1182 shipped?' and a toolConfig that defines the tool get_order_status, with toolChoice left at its default of auto. The response has the stopReason end_turn and an assistant message with a single text block which says that the order has shipped. It contains no toolUse block, and the developer's code never called the order system. Company policy requires that every order status given to a customer comes from the order system. The developer wants the next request to make the model request the tool before it answers. Which next request is formatted correctly for this purpose?

options.text: Append the assistant message, then a user message with a toolResult block that carries the toolUseId and the order status as json content.
Append the assistant message, then a user message with a toolResult block that carries the toolUseId, a text explanation and the status error.
Append the assistant message, then a user message with a text block that gives the model the detail it asked the customer for.
Send the original user message again, with toolChoice in the toolConfig set to the specific tool get_order_status.

explanation: With toolChoice set to auto, which is the default, the model decides whether to call a tool or to generate text, and here it answered from nothing. The Converse API lets the caller remove that choice: toolChoice can be set to any, meaning the model must request at least one tool, or to tool, meaning the model must request the specified tool, an option supported by Amazon Nova and Anthropic Claude models. The fix is to "Send the original user message again, with toolChoice in the toolConfig set to the specific tool get_order_status"; the response will then contain a toolUse block that the code can execute. Both requests that append the assistant message and then send "a toolResult block" are malformed for this conversation: a toolResult must carry the toolUseId of a tool request the model made, and the model made none, so there is no ID to reference; they would also keep the unverified claim in the history. The request with "a text block that gives the model the detail it asked the customer for" does not apply, because the model asked for nothing, and it leaves toolChoice at auto. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_ToolChoice.html

prompt: An airline maintenance team feeds 50,000 technician notes a night into a foundation model that drafts reliability reports. Technicians do not type part codes: a handheld scanner inserts each code into the note in one fixed format, PN-00000-A, so the codes contain no spelling variants or typos. The problem is that the scanners still accept the labels of withdrawn parts, and the model then reports on parts that are no longer in the 6,000-code master list. Data stewards want to inspect every note that mentions a code missing from the master list before the model sees it, while all other notes continue to the model unchanged. The team has no annotated documents and does not want to train or host a model. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Train an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer from an entity list of the part codes and the note archive, and run it as a nightly asynchronous job.
Extract the part codes in the nightly AWS Glue job with a regular expression that matches the format in which the codes are written.
Run Amazon Comprehend built-in entity detection as a nightly asynchronous job, and keep the entities of the preset types that it returns.
Add an AWS Lambda function that maps each detected part code to its master-list form before the prompt for the model is assembled.
Route notes whose part codes are absent from the master list to a review prefix, and send the remaining notes on to the model.

explanation: The codes are machine-written in one fixed format, so finding them is a pattern-matching task: the team should "Extract the part codes in the nightly AWS Glue job with a regular expression". Nothing has to be trained. The real requirement is validation against reference data: a note with a code that is not in the master list must be held for the stewards, and the others pass through, so the team should "Route notes whose part codes are absent from the master list to a review prefix". The option to "Train an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer" earns its cost when entities appear with typos or new conventions that string matching misses; with scanner-inserted codes it adds a model to train, which the team does not want. The option to "Run Amazon Comprehend built-in entity detection" relies on preset types such as COMMERCIAL_ITEM, described as a branded product, which are not the airline's part codes. The Lambda function "that maps each detected part code to its master-list form" solves a different problem: these codes are already canonical, and a withdrawn code has no master-list form to map to. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/custom-entity-recognition.html

prompt: An airline maintenance team feeds 50,000 free-text technician notes a night into a foundation model that drafts reliability reports. Technicians type the airline's part codes by hand, in many spellings and sometimes with typos ('PN 44-871A', 'pn44871a', 'part 44817-A'), and the model treats the variants as different parts. The team has a master list of 6,000 part codes and a large archive of notes, but no annotated documents. It wants the part codes identified in every note, including the misspelt ones, and passed to the model in one canonical form. Every note must reach the model on the night it is written, because the reports are used at the morning maintenance briefing. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Train an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer from an entity list of the part codes and the note archive, and run it as a nightly asynchronous job.
Extract the part codes in the nightly AWS Glue job with a regular expression that matches the format in which the codes are written.
Run Amazon Comprehend built-in entity detection as a nightly asynchronous job, and keep the entities of the preset types that it returns.
Add an AWS Lambda function that maps each detected part code to its master-list form before the prompt for the model is assembled.
Route notes whose part codes are absent from the master list to a review prefix, and send the remaining notes on to the model.

explanation: There are two tasks: find a company-specific entity that is written inconsistently, then normalise it. Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognition identifies entity types that are not among the preset types, such as product codes. It can be trained from an entity list plus unannotated documents that contain those entities, which is what the team has, and the trained model runs in asynchronous entity detection jobs. AWS notes that string matching will not detect entities that have typos or follow new naming conventions, while a custom model can. So the team should "Train an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer" and then "Add an AWS Lambda function that maps each detected part code to its master-list form", so that every variant reaches the model as one code. Extracting codes "with a regular expression" is the string-matching approach that misses typed variants and typos. Built-in detection returns "the preset types", such as COMMERCIAL_ITEM for a branded product, not the airline's codes. The option to "Route notes whose part codes are absent from the master list to a review prefix" would hold back most hand-typed notes, which breaks the rule that every note reaches the model that night. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/custom-entity-recognition.html

prompt: A law firm is building a research assistant over 90 million archived case memos in Amazon S3 with an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Paralegals ask about 200 questions per day in two short bursts, and every question, including the first of each burst, must get its retrieval results within one second. The firm will not pay for compute capacity that sits idle between bursts. Queries are conceptual, so no exact-term matching is needed, and results are filtered only by an exact `practice_area` value. The firm embeds with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 as float32 vectors, runs no database or search cluster today, and has no staff to size or patch one. Which vector store design is MOST cost-effective for this workload?

options.text: An Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector search collection with a faiss index of float32 vectors and a filterable metadata field.
An Amazon S3 vector index that stores float32 vectors with cosine distance and a filterable metadata key.
An Amazon OpenSearch Service managed domain with a faiss index of binary vectors, Hamming distance and a keyword metadata field.
An Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with pgvector, an HNSW index on the embedding column and a GIN index on the metadata column.

explanation: AWS describes Amazon S3 Vectors as cost-optimized vector storage that is best suited to infrequent query workloads: there is no infrastructure to provision, you pay for what you use, and infrequent queries return in under a second. With 200 queries a day, a one-second target, semantic-only search and an equality filter, 'an Amazon S3 vector index that stores float32 vectors with cosine distance and a filterable metadata key' meets every requirement at the lowest cost. The 'OpenSearch Serverless vector search collection' also needs no cluster administration, but it cannot meet both burst constraints: with a minimum of 0 OCUs it scales to zero after 10 idle minutes and AWS says to expect 10 to 30 seconds of latency on the first request while capacity is restored, and with a non-zero minimum those OCUs are provisioned regardless of traffic, which is the idle compute the firm will not pay for; its hybrid search is also unused because no exact-term matching is required. The 'OpenSearch Service managed domain' fails the stated constraint that the firm has no staff to size or patch a cluster, and the firm embeds float32 vectors, not binary ones. The 'Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with pgvector' likewise introduces a database that someone must size and operate, with an HNSW index over 90 million rows, for a workload of two short bursts a day. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/s3-vectors.html

prompt: A publisher is moving 70 million article chunks into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Its search team already operates an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain on engine version 2.17 with public access and fine-grained access control, and the domain has spare capacity that is already paid for. An evaluation showed that binary embeddings from Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 give acceptable recall for this corpus at a fraction of the memory of float32 vectors. Retrieval runs at a steady 80 queries per second with a 100 ms budget, and the architecture board will not approve an additional data store service. Which vector store design is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: An Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector search collection with a faiss index of float32 vectors and a filterable metadata field.
An Amazon S3 vector index that stores float32 vectors with cosine distance and a filterable metadata key.
An Amazon OpenSearch Service managed domain with a faiss index of binary vectors, Hamming distance and a keyword metadata field.
An Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with pgvector, an HNSW index on the embedding column and a GIN index on the metadata column.

explanation: The existing domain already satisfies what Bedrock Knowledge Bases requires of an OpenSearch managed cluster: public network access, engine version 2.16 or later for binary embeddings, and a faiss index. Storing binary vectors with the Hamming space type uses the spare, already paid-for capacity and far less memory than float32, so 'an Amazon OpenSearch Service managed domain with a faiss index of binary vectors' adds no new service and the least new cost. The 'OpenSearch Serverless vector search collection' is an additional data store service, which the architecture board will not approve, and as described it holds float32 vectors, giving up the memory saving the evaluation justified. The 'Amazon S3 vector index' is also a new store; S3 Vectors supports only floating-point embeddings and is best suited to infrequent queries, with latency of about 100 ms at best for frequent ones, which leaves no margin at a steady 80 queries per second. The 'Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with pgvector' is again a new service, and it cannot hold binary embeddings: only OpenSearch Serverless and OpenSearch managed clusters store binary vectors for a knowledge base. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A manufacturer runs its order and parts systems on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, operated by a platform team of experienced PostgreSQL administrators. It is adding an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over 3 million maintenance bulletins. Technicians search with exact part numbers such as `PN-88417-C` mixed with natural-language symptoms, so retrieval must combine keyword matching with semantic matching. Newly synced bulletins must be queryable as soon as a sync finishes. Company policy is that new workloads reuse the existing database engine, backup tooling and runbooks, and the team will not take on a search engine it has never operated. Which vector store should the team choose?

options.text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, using an HNSW index on the embedding column and a GIN index on the text column.
Amazon S3 Vectors, using a float32 vector index with cosine distance and filterable metadata keys for document attributes.
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, using a vector search collection with a faiss vector index and a filterable text field.
Amazon Neptune Analytics, using a graph that has a vector search index and is populated through the GraphRAG option.

explanation: Hybrid search in Bedrock Knowledge Bases is supported for Amazon RDS (Aurora), OpenSearch Serverless and MongoDB stores that have a filterable text field. 'Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector', with a GIN index on the text column for the keyword side and an HNSW index for vectors, gives keyword plus semantic matching while reusing the engine, tooling and runbooks the policy demands. It is also the store for which the documentation does not warn of a few minutes' delay before newly synced embeddings can be queried, which matches the freshness requirement. 'Amazon S3 Vectors' fails the keyword requirement: it is not one of the stores that support hybrid search, so the query falls back to semantic search and part numbers would be missed. 'Amazon OpenSearch Serverless' does support hybrid search, but it is a search engine the team has never operated, which the stem rules out, and newly ingested data can take a few minutes to become queryable. 'Amazon Neptune Analytics' with GraphRAG connects entities across documents, which nobody asked for; it is not listed for hybrid search and is another engine the administrators do not know. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A pharmaceutical company keeps 700 clinical study reports in one Amazon S3 bucket and wants an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for its medical writers. Typical questions need facts joined across reports, for example which investigators ran studies of compounds that share an adverse event with a named compound. Chunk retrieval in a pilot returned each fact separately and the answers missed the links between them. Queries are conceptual, with no exact-term matching, and the company runs no relational database on AWS. The team wants Bedrock to identify the entities and relationships during ingestion instead of building that logic itself. Which vector store should the team choose?

options.text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, using an HNSW index on the embedding column and a GIN index on the text column.
Amazon S3 Vectors, using a float32 vector index with cosine distance and filterable metadata keys for document attributes.
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, using a vector search collection with a faiss vector index and a filterable text field.
Amazon Neptune Analytics, using a graph that has a vector search index and is populated through the GraphRAG option.

explanation: The stated problem is multi-hop reasoning: facts sit in different reports and the answer depends on the relationships between entities. GraphRAG in Bedrock Knowledge Bases identifies entities and relationships automatically during ingestion and, after the initial vector search, traverses the graph to pull in related chunks. 'Amazon Neptune Analytics, using a graph that has a vector search index and is populated through the GraphRAG option' is therefore the fit; GraphRAG supports S3 data sources, and 700 files sit inside the default of 1,000 files per data source. 'Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector' returns the nearest chunks independently, which is exactly what the pilot showed to be insufficient, and the company runs no relational database on AWS; its GIN text index serves hybrid search, which is not needed for conceptual queries. 'Amazon S3 Vectors' is also plain similarity retrieval with metadata filters and cannot connect facts across reports. 'Amazon OpenSearch Serverless' adds keyword matching through its filterable text field, but the stem says no exact-term matching is required and the links between entities would still be missing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-build-graphs.html

prompt: A SaaS company serves 600 customers from one Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector 0.8.0. Each chunk carries a `tenant_id` in the `custom_metadata` JSONB column, which has a GIN index, and every `Retrieve` call applies an `equals` filter on `tenant_id` with `numberOfResults` set to 10. Large tenants receive 10 results. Small tenants, which each own under 0.1% of the rows but still have hundreds of relevant chunks, usually receive one or two results and sometimes none. Query latency is normal, no errors are logged, and the questions are conceptual with no identifiers in them. Which change should the team make?

options.text: Recreate the GIN index on the text column with the `'english'` dictionary in place of the `'simple'` dictionary.
Set the override search type to `HYBRID` so that the raw chunk text is searched together with the vector embeddings.
Create an expression index on the numeric key in the custom metadata column that the range filters compare against.
Enable HNSW iterative index scans for the database so that the scan continues until enough filtered rows are found.

explanation: With pgvector, the HNSW index scan returns a limited candidate set and the metadata filter is applied afterwards. For a tenant that owns a tiny share of the rows, most candidates are discarded, so fewer results than requested come back without any error. AWS recommends that knowledge bases using metadata filtering 'enable HNSW iterative index scans' (pgvector 0.8.0 or later, for example `hnsw.iterative_scan = 'relaxed_order'`), which keeps scanning until enough filtered rows are found. That matches the symptom: large tenants are fine and small tenants are starved. The option to 'create an expression index on the numeric key' is AWS's advice for frequent range filters over numbers and improves speed; here the filter is an equality on a string, latency is already normal, and the number of rows returned would not change. The option to 'set the override search type to `HYBRID`' adds keyword matching, but the questions contain no identifiers and the filter would still be applied after the scan. Recreating the text index 'with the `'english'` dictionary' tunes hybrid search accuracy for English content and has no effect on how many filtered rows a semantic query returns. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: An engineering standards body runs an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector 0.8.0, and HNSW iterative index scans are already enabled. Each chunk has an `effective_year` number in the `custom_metadata` JSONB column, which has the required GIN index. Most `Retrieve` calls add a `greaterThan` or `lessThan` filter on `effective_year`. These calls return the full 10 requested results and reviewers rate the results as relevant, but they take about four seconds, while unfiltered calls return in 200 ms. Users ask conceptual questions and searches run as semantic search. Which change should the team make?

options.text: Recreate the GIN index on the text column with the `'english'` dictionary in place of the `'simple'` dictionary.
Set the override search type to `HYBRID` so that the raw chunk text is searched together with the vector embeddings.
Create an expression index on the numeric key in the custom metadata column that the range filters compare against.
Enable HNSW iterative index scans for the database so that the scan continues until enough filtered rows are found.

explanation: The symptom is slow range filtering, not missing or irrelevant results. AWS's setup guidance for Aurora says that if you frequently use range filters over numerical metadata, you should 'create an expression index on the numeric key', for example on `(custom_metadata->>'year')::double precision`, to optimize performance. The GIN index on the JSONB column serves key-value lookups, so a dedicated expression index on `effective_year` is what speeds up `greaterThan` and `lessThan` comparisons. The option to 'enable HNSW iterative index scans' addresses selective filters returning too few rows; the stem says iterative scans are already enabled and every call returns the full 10 results. The option to 'set the override search type to `HYBRID`' adds a keyword search over the chunk text, which helps exact-term queries, but these users ask conceptual questions and the delay comes from the metadata filter, so hybrid search would add work without removing it. Recreating the text index 'with the `'english'` dictionary' improves hybrid search accuracy and latency for English content, which is irrelevant while searches run as semantic search and the results are already rated relevant. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A legal-tech SaaS provider hosts contract documents for 400 customers in one S3 bucket, organised by a prefix per customer, and indexes them in a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on OpenSearch Serverless. Users sign in through Amazon Cognito, and the chat backend runs on AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway. An audit requires that a user can never receive chunks from another customer's documents, even if the user tampers with the request body or writes a manipulative prompt. The provider will keep a single knowledge base and will not operate one per customer. Which combination of actions meets the requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a reranking configuration to each query so that a reranker model reorders the retrieved chunks by relevance.
Store a `.metadata.json` sidecar file beside each document that sets its attributes, and then sync the data source.
Configure `implicitFilterConfiguration` with the attribute schema so that a model derives the filter from each query.
Create one knowledge base per group of documents, and have the backend choose the knowledge base for each query.
Have the backend read attribute values from verified token claims and set an explicit metadata filter on each query.

explanation: Isolation inside a shared knowledge base needs two things: every chunk must carry the tenant attribute, and the filter must be set by trusted code from a verified identity. For an S3 data source the attribute comes from 'a `.metadata.json` sidecar file beside each document', which becomes filterable metadata after a sync. The backend must then 'read attribute values from verified token claims and set an explicit metadata filter on each query', so other tenants' chunks are excluded before anything reaches the model and nothing in the request body or prompt can change the tenant. Using '`implicitFilterConfiguration`' lets a model generate the filter from the query text, so a manipulative prompt could name another customer, which the audit forbids. The option to 'create one knowledge base per group of documents' would isolate tenants, but the provider has ruled out one knowledge base per customer. 'A reranking configuration' only reorders chunks that were already retrieved; it is not an access control and other customers' chunks could still be returned. Note that anyone with `bedrock:Retrieve` permission can read all synced data, so only the backend role should hold it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/s3-data-source-connector.html

prompt: A manufacturer indexes 40,000 internal audit reports from Amazon S3 in one Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Every employee may read every report, and the search page is a single text box with no drop-down fields. Users type requests such as 'audit findings from the 2024 Lisbon plant', but results come from other years and plants, and the wanted reports are often missing from the retrieved set altogether. The year and plant of each report are known in the document management export, yet the indexed chunks carry no attributes. Sign-in tokens hold only the employee's identity, and the team will not split the corpus across knowledge bases. Which combination of actions meets the requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a reranking configuration to each query so that a reranker model reorders the retrieved chunks by relevance.
Store a `.metadata.json` sidecar file beside each document that sets its attributes, and then sync the data source.
Configure `implicitFilterConfiguration` with the attribute schema so that a model derives the filter from each query.
Create one knowledge base per group of documents, and have the backend choose the knowledge base for each query.
Have the backend read attribute values from verified token claims and set an explicit metadata filter on each query.

explanation: The year and plant live in the user's wording, not in any identity or form field, so the search must be restricted by a filter generated from the query. Implicit metadata filtering does this: with '`implicitFilterConfiguration`' and a schema that describes each attribute, a model builds and applies a retrieval filter from the query text. A filter needs something to filter on, so each report also needs 'a `.metadata.json` sidecar file' holding its year and plant, followed by a sync. The option to 'read attribute values from verified token claims' cannot work here because the tokens hold only the employee's identity, not the year or plant being asked about, and every employee may read everything. 'A reranking configuration' reorders the chunks that were retrieved, but the stem says the wanted reports are often absent from the retrieved set, so there is nothing to promote. The option to 'create one knowledge base per group of documents' is excluded because the team will not split the corpus, and with a single text box the backend would have no field from which to choose. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A media company runs its own RAG retrieval layer on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain with six data nodes. A new k-NN index for article embeddings will hold about 90 GiB including indexing overhead, with little growth expected, and the workload is read-heavy with a strict search latency objective. The team first created the index with the service default shard settings and saw shards spread unevenly across the nodes, with one node running hot. Because the primary shard count of an existing index cannot easily be changed, the team will reindex once into a new index. Which shard configuration follows AWS sizing guidance for this index?

options.text: 6 primary shards, each with 1 replica shard.
12 primary shards, each with 1 replica shard.
5 primary shards, each with 2 replica shards.
1 primary shard, with 5 replica shards.

explanation: AWS guidance is to keep shards between 10 and 30 GiB when search latency is the key objective, and to choose a shard count that distributes the index evenly across all data nodes. For 90 GiB on six nodes, '6 primary shards' gives 15 GiB per shard, inside the range, and exactly one primary per node, with one replica as the second copy. '12 primary shards' would give 7.5 GiB shards, below the recommended range for this 90 GiB index; AWS warns that many small shards consume CPU and memory needlessly. '5 primary shards' is the service default the team already tried: 18 GiB shards are a fine size, but five primaries cannot be spread evenly over six nodes, which is the hot-node problem in the stem, and extra replicas do not change that. '1 primary shard' makes a single 90 GiB shard, three times the upper bound for a search-latency workload, so every query scans one very large shard and recovery after a failure is slow. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/bp-sharding.html

prompt: A retailer hosts product-search embeddings for its RAG assistant on an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain with six data nodes. A rebuilt k-NN index will hold about 200 GiB including indexing overhead, the catalogue is stable so little growth is expected, and the assistant has a strict search latency objective with few writes. An earlier attempt with the service default shard settings left one node much busier than the others. The primary shard count cannot easily be changed later, so the team wants to choose it correctly before reindexing. Which shard configuration follows AWS sizing guidance for this index?

options.text: 6 primary shards, each with 1 replica shard.
12 primary shards, each with 1 replica shard.
5 primary shards, each with 2 replica shards.
1 primary shard, with 5 replica shards.

explanation: AWS guidance is to keep shards between 10 and 30 GiB when search latency is the key objective (30 to 50 GiB is for write-heavy workloads such as log analytics) and to distribute the index evenly across the data nodes. For 200 GiB on six nodes, '12 primary shards' gives about 17 GiB per shard, inside the range, and two primaries per node, with one replica as the second copy. '6 primary shards' would also spread evenly, but each shard would be about 33 GiB, above the 30 GiB bound for a search-latency workload with a 200 GiB index.
