'5 primary shards' is the default that was already tried: 40 GiB shards are too large for search and five primaries cannot be divided evenly over six nodes, which is why one node was busier; adding a second replica changes neither fact. '1 primary shard' creates one 200 GiB shard, far outside the range, which slows every query and makes recovery from a node failure difficult, however many replicas exist. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/bp-sharding.html

prompt: An engineering firm keeps design standards in a third-party document management system (DMS) that has no native Amazon Bedrock connector. The DMS calls a webhook when a document is published, revised or withdrawn, and exposes an API that returns document text and attributes. Withdrawn standards must stop appearing in the RAG assistant within 5 minutes, and revisions must be searchable in the same window. The team wants Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to keep doing the chunking, embedding and retrieval, and security policy forbids copying the standards into an S3 bucket. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an S3 data source on the bucket, and run `StartIngestionJob` once on an Amazon EventBridge schedule.
Create an S3 data source, and have S3 event notifications invoke a Lambda function that calls `IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments` per object.
Create a custom data source, and have a Lambda function call `IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments` or `DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments` per change.
Create an S3 data source, and have S3 event notifications invoke a Lambda function that calls `StartIngestionJob` per object.

explanation: A custom data source exists for sources without a connector. Documents are added, updated or removed with the KnowledgeBaseDocuments operations, content and metadata can be supplied inline, and no sync is needed: each change becomes part of the data source and the knowledge base in one step. So 'a custom data source' with a webhook-driven Lambda function that calls '`IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments` or `DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments` per change' meets the 5-minute window while Bedrock still chunks, embeds and retrieves. All three other options begin with 'create an S3 data source', which requires the standards to be copied into a bucket, and security policy forbids that. Beyond that, the option that runs '`StartIngestionJob` once on an Amazon EventBridge schedule' is a batch pattern that would need a very short schedule to meet 5 minutes. The option that calls '`IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments` per object' from S3 events is direct ingestion for S3 sources, where AWS warns the bucket must be kept in step or the next sync overwrites the change. The option that calls '`StartIngestionJob` per object' starts a full incremental scan for every event, which is more jobs to run and monitor. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-direct-ingestion.html

prompt: A hospital group licenses clinical guidelines from a publisher whose only delivery method is a nightly export: at 01:00 the publisher's job rewrites all 40,000 guideline files in an S3 bucket in the hospital's account and removes withdrawn ones. The publisher offers no webhook and no per-document API. The hospital wants the guidelines in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, and content that is up to 24 hours old is acceptable. The bucket is governed by the publisher's integration contract, which does not allow event notifications or other configuration changes on it. Which approach keeps the knowledge base current with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an S3 data source on the bucket, and run `StartIngestionJob` once on an Amazon EventBridge schedule.
Create an S3 data source, and have S3 event notifications invoke a Lambda function that calls `IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments` per object.
Create a custom data source, and have a Lambda function call `IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments` or `DeleteKnowledgeBaseDocuments` per change.
Create an S3 data source, and have S3 event notifications invoke a Lambda function that calls `StartIngestionJob` per object.

explanation: The only signal available is that a complete export lands once a night, and day-old content is acceptable. A sync is incremental: it processes documents added, modified or deleted since the last sync, so one job after the export picks up revisions and removes withdrawn guidelines. 'An S3 data source on the bucket' with '`StartIngestionJob` once on an Amazon EventBridge schedule' is a single scheduled action with nothing else to operate. The two options in which 'S3 event notifications invoke a Lambda function' cannot be used, because the integration contract does not allow event notifications on the bucket. Even if it did, calling '`StartIngestionJob` per object' would attempt 40,000 job starts a night where one is enough, and calling '`IngestKnowledgeBaseDocuments` per object' would replace one sync with 40,000 direct-ingestion calls. The option to 'create a custom data source' needs something to drive the per-change calls, but the publisher offers no webhook and no per-document API, so the hospital would have to write its own comparison of each night's export to work out what changed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-data-source-sync-ingest.html

prompt: A bank indexes 1.8 million product rate sheets from Amazon S3 in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Each rate sheet is a `.csv` file with a `.metadata.json` sidecar file, and the data source uses default chunking with no custom transformation. Each quarter a job updates a `review_status` attribute by rewriting only the sidecar files, leaving the content objects and the data source untouched, and then starts a sync. The team expected the sync to merge the new metadata into the existing vectors, but the embedding model's invocation count shows that every document is embedded again each quarter. What is the MOST likely reason?

options.text: The data source uses a custom transformation Lambda function, so the metadata-only update path is not applied to its documents.
The content files are CSV files, which are ingested again in full whenever their metadata files are updated.
The job deletes and re-creates the data source, so the first sync of the new data source ingests every document.
The job also rewrites the content files, so the sync treats every document as modified and ingests it again.

explanation: Bedrock can apply a metadata-only change without calling the embedding model, by fetching the existing vectors, merging the new metadata and writing them back, but only when three conditions all hold: only `metadata.json` files changed, the content files are not CSV, and the data source has no custom transformation Lambda function. These rate sheets are CSV. A CSV file's metadata carries `documentStructureConfiguration`, which controls which columns are indexed, and Bedrock cannot tell whether that changed without re-processing the file, so 'CSV files' are 'ingested again in full whenever their metadata files are updated'. The option blaming 'a custom transformation Lambda function' names a real condition, but the stem says the data source has no custom transformation. The option that the job 'deletes and re-creates the data source' would also cause full ingestion, but the stem says the data source is left untouched. The option that the job 'also rewrites the content files' is excluded because only the sidecar files are rewritten and the content objects are unchanged. Limiting the job to sidecars whose status really changed would reduce the cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-data-source-sync-ingest.html

prompt: An insurer indexes 1.2 million PDF policy documents from Amazon S3 in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Each PDF has a `.metadata.json` sidecar file, and the data source, created two years ago and never replaced, uses fixed-size chunking with no custom transformation. Each quarter a job updates a `review_status` attribute. To keep things simple, it re-renders every PDF with the new status printed in its footer, regenerates the sidecar files, and then runs `aws s3 cp --recursive` from a staging prefix, which uploads every PDF and every sidecar, before starting a sync. The embedding model's invocation count shows that every document is embedded again each quarter. What is the MOST likely reason?

options.text: The data source uses a custom transformation Lambda function, so the metadata-only update path is not applied to its documents.
The content files are CSV files, which are ingested again in full whenever their metadata files are updated.
The job deletes and re-creates the data source, so the first sync of the new data source ingests every document.
The job also rewrites the content files, so the sync treats every document as modified and ingests it again.

explanation: Sync is incremental: unchanged documents are skipped, and a document whose content or metadata changed is re-parsed, re-chunked, re-embedded and re-indexed. The metadata-only optimization, which merges new metadata into existing vectors without calling the embedding model, applies only when no content files are changed. Here the job re-renders and uploads every PDF, so 'the job also rewrites the content files' and the sync treats every document as modified. Leaving the PDFs alone and uploading only the sidecar files would let the optimization apply, because these are PDFs with no custom transformation. The option blaming 'a custom transformation Lambda function' describes a genuine exclusion from the metadata-only path, but the stem says this data source has no custom transformation. The option that 'the content files are CSV files' describes the other genuine exclusion, yet these documents are PDFs. The option that the job 'deletes and re-creates the data source' would explain a full ingestion, but the data source was created two years ago and never replaced, and the job only copies objects and starts a sync. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-data-source-sync-ingest.html

prompt: An insurer wants its claims assistant to answer questions that connect facts across documents, so it will build an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with Amazon Neptune Analytics (GraphRAG). Its 6,500 claim files already sit under one prefix of an S3 bucket and will be embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 at 1,024 dimensions. The platform team proposes reusing an existing Neptune Analytics graph that was created last year for fraud analytics without any vector search settings; its capacity has ample headroom and the corpus is static. The application will reach the data only through `RetrieveAndGenerate`. Which actions must the team plan for? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a new Neptune Analytics graph whose vector search index dimension matches the embedding model's output.
Create a private graph endpoint in the team's VPC so that the application can run openCypher queries on the graph.
Allocate enough m-NCUs for the expected corpus, and plan to change the graph's capacity manually as it grows.
Split the files across folders or data sources, or request an increase in the files-per-data-source limit.
Move the documents into an Amazon S3 bucket, and connect that bucket to the knowledge base as its data source.

explanation: Two documented constraints collide with this plan. First, GraphRAG needs an empty Neptune Analytics graph with a vector search index, the index can be created only when the graph is created, and its dimension must match the embedding model. The fraud graph has no vector search settings, so the team must 'create a new Neptune Analytics graph whose vector search index dimension matches', here 1,024. Second, each GraphRAG data source holds up to 1,000 files by default, raisable on request to 10,000, or the bucket can be partitioned into folders of up to 1,000 files; 6,500 files under one prefix therefore mean the team must 'split the files across folders or data sources, or request an increase'. The option to 'allocate enough m-NCUs' and resize manually is real, since graphs do not autoscale, but the stem says capacity has ample headroom and the corpus is static. The option to 'move the documents into an Amazon S3 bucket' is unnecessary because the files are already in S3. 'A private graph endpoint' is not needed: Bedrock creates its own connection to the graph, and the application uses only `RetrieveAndGenerate`. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-build-graphs.html

prompt: A consultancy wants a research assistant that connects facts across its project reports, so it will build an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with Amazon Neptune Analytics (GraphRAG). The 300 reports are pages in a wiki, and the count will reach about 900 over two years. For the pilot, an engineer has already created an empty graph with the smallest capacity and a 1,024-dimension vector search index, matching Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, and assumes the graph will scale by itself as reports are added. The application will reach the data only through `RetrieveAndGenerate`. Which actions must the team plan for? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a new Neptune Analytics graph whose vector search index dimension matches the embedding model's output.
Create a private graph endpoint in the team's VPC so that the application can run openCypher queries on the graph.
Allocate enough m-NCUs for the expected corpus, and plan to change the graph's capacity manually as it grows.
Split the files across folders or data sources, or request an increase in the files-per-data-source limit.
Move the documents into an Amazon S3 bucket, and connect that bucket to the knowledge base as its data source.

explanation: Two documented limitations apply here. GraphRAG supports only Amazon S3 as the data source, so wiki pages cannot be connected directly: the team must 'move the documents into an Amazon S3 bucket, and connect that bucket to the knowledge base'. And autoscaling is not supported for Neptune Analytics graphs, so the engineer's assumption is wrong: the team must 'allocate enough m-NCUs for the expected corpus, and plan to change the graph's capacity manually' as the corpus triples. The option to 'create a new Neptune Analytics graph' with a matching vector index is not needed, because the pilot graph was created empty with a 1,024-dimension index that already matches the embedding model. The option to 'split the files across folders or data sources' addresses the default of 1,000 files per data source, which 300 reports growing to about 900 never reach. 'A private graph endpoint' for openCypher queries is unnecessary: Bedrock creates the network connection to the graph itself, and the application reaches the data only through `RetrieveAndGenerate`. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-build-graphs.html

prompt: A retailer stores sales, returns and inventory tables in Amazon Redshift Serverless. Regional managers want to ask questions such as 'which five stores had the highest return rate last quarter' in a chat assistant. Answers must be computed from current table data, not from a periodic export. A data governance rule requires every generated SQL statement to pass an in-house policy checker, which blocks access to salary and customer columns, before the statement is executed. The team wants to write and maintain as little text-to-SQL logic as possible. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Unload the tables to files in S3 each night, index them in a vector knowledge base, and answer with `RetrieveAndGenerate`.
Create a knowledge base with a structured data store on Redshift, and call `RetrieveAndGenerate` to produce and run the SQL.
Create a knowledge base with a structured data store on Redshift, call `GenerateQuery`, and run the returned SQL from the application.
Have a Lambda function send the table schemas to the Converse API to produce SQL, and run that SQL from the function.

explanation: A knowledge base connected to a structured data store uses Amazon Redshift as the query engine and converts natural-language questions into SQL from the table metadata. `GenerateQuery` decouples that conversion from retrieval: it returns the SQL without running it, so the application can pass the statement to the policy checker and execute it against live tables only if it passes. The option to 'call `GenerateQuery`, and run the returned SQL from the application' therefore satisfies current data, the pre-execution check and minimal custom text-to-SQL logic. The option to 'call `RetrieveAndGenerate` to produce and run the SQL' uses the same knowledge base, but conversion and execution happen inside one call, leaving no point at which the checker can inspect the statement first. The option to 'unload the tables to files in S3 each night' answers from a periodic export, which the stem forbids, and vector retrieval of rows cannot compute a ranking of return rates. The option in which a Lambda function will 'send the table schemas to the Converse API' can honour the governance rule, but the team would own the prompt, schema handling and examples, which is the logic it wants to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-generate-query.html

prompt: An appliance maker keeps 2 million free-text service notes in an Amazon Redshift table, one note per row with a ticket ID. Support engineers want to ask an assistant for notes that describe a symptom, for example 'units where the door seal swells after a hot cycle', and read a summary with links to the matching tickets. Customers describe the same fault in many different words, so column predicates do not find the notes. Notes that are a day old are acceptable. The warehouse team does not allow model-generated SQL to run on the warehouse, and no totals or rankings are needed. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Unload the tables to files in S3 each night, index them in a vector knowledge base, and answer with `RetrieveAndGenerate`.
Create a knowledge base with a structured data store on Redshift, and call `RetrieveAndGenerate` to produce and run the SQL.
Create a knowledge base with a structured data store on Redshift, call `GenerateQuery`, and run the returned SQL from the application.
Have a Lambda function send the table schemas to the Converse API to produce SQL, and run that SQL from the function.

explanation: The need is to find rows by meaning, not to compute over columns. Embedding the notes and searching by similarity matches different wordings of the same fault, and a nightly export is acceptable because day-old notes are fine. So the team should 'unload the tables to files in S3 each night, index them in a vector knowledge base, and answer with `RetrieveAndGenerate`', which returns a generated summary with citations to the source files. Both options that 'create a knowledge base with a structured data store on Redshift' work by converting the question into SQL: with '`RetrieveAndGenerate` to produce and run the SQL' the generated statement runs on the warehouse, which the warehouse team does not allow, and with '`GenerateQuery`' the application would still run model-generated SQL there. In either case the SQL can only apply column predicates, which the stem says do not find notes written in different words. The option in which a Lambda function will 'send the table schemas to the Converse API to produce SQL' has the same two faults: it executes model-generated SQL on the warehouse and matches text by predicate, not by meaning. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-build-structured.html

prompt: An investigations firm indexes 25,000 narrative incident reports in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base whose vector store is an S3 vector index, chosen for cost. Reports run to 30 pages of continuous prose without headings, and the subject changes in mid-page. A pilot with token-count chunks returned passages that started or ended halfway through an explanation, and reviewers rejected the answers. The team wants each chunk to hold one coherent topic, with boundaries placed where the meaning shifts, and has budget approval for foundation model usage during ingestion. The vector store will not be changed. Which chunking strategy should the team configure?

options.text: Fixed-size chunking with a maximum of about 300 tokens per chunk and a 20% overlap between consecutive chunks.
Hierarchical chunking with small child chunks for matching and larger parent chunks returned for context.
Semantic chunking with a maximum token size, a buffer size and a breakpoint percentile threshold.
No chunking, so that each file in the data source is embedded and returned as a single chunk.

explanation: Semantic chunking divides text by meaning instead of by token count: it compares each sentence, plus a buffer of surrounding sentences, with its neighbours and draws a breakpoint where dissimilarity passes the configured percentile threshold. That is exactly a boundary placed where the meaning shifts, so 'semantic chunking with a maximum token size, a buffer size and a breakpoint percentile threshold' fits. It uses a foundation model and costs extra, which the stem says is approved. 'Fixed-size chunking' is the token-count approach the pilot already showed to cut explanations in half; overlap softens the cut but does not move it to a topic boundary. 'Hierarchical chunking' returns larger parents for context, but its boundaries are still token sizes, and AWS does not recommend it when the vector store is an S3 vector bucket, because parent-child context is stored as metadata and can exceed the metadata size limits; the stem fixes the store. 'No chunking' would embed each 30-page report as one chunk, far too coarse to match a single topic, and it also removes page numbers from citations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A software vendor's documentation pipeline already splits its support content into 180,000 short articles, one file per article, each between 400 and 1,200 tokens and each written to stand alone. Every file has a `.metadata.json` sidecar with product and version attributes. The licence audit for the knowledge base requires exactly one vector per file, so that a retrieved result maps to one article and the article is returned whole. Citations need the article's file location but not page numbers, and the team does not want to pay for foundation model usage during ingestion. Which chunking strategy should the team configure for the Amazon Bedrock knowledge base?

options.text: Fixed-size chunking with a maximum of about 300 tokens per chunk and a 20% overlap between consecutive chunks.
Hierarchical chunking with small child chunks for matching and larger parent chunks returned for context.
Semantic chunking with a maximum token size, a buffer size and a breakpoint percentile threshold.
No chunking, so that each file in the data source is embedded and returned as a single chunk.

explanation: AWS documents this case directly: you might pre-process documents by splitting them into separate files and then choose no chunking, so that each document is treated as a single chunk. With 'no chunking, so that each file in the data source is embedded and returned as a single chunk', every article yields exactly one vector and comes back whole, and no foundation model is used during ingestion. The cost of this strategy, losing page numbers in citations and the page-number metadata filter, does not matter because only the file location is needed. 'Fixed-size chunking' at about 300 tokens would cut most of these 400 to 1,200-token articles into several chunks, breaking the one-vector-per-file requirement. 'Hierarchical chunking' embeds several child chunks per file, so it also produces more than one vector per article, and it can return fewer results than requested when children share a parent. 'Semantic chunking' would split articles at meaning shifts into multiple chunks and uses a foundation model, which is the ingestion cost the team wants to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A pump manufacturer indexes 9,000 PDF datasheets in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Each datasheet mixes a few paragraphs with specification tables and performance charts. With the current configuration, answers about flow rates and pressure limits are wrong because the table values and chart content never reach the index. The team wants tables returned as Markdown and each chart described with its axis units, and it needs to state those instructions itself. Paragraph-sized chunks are acceptable, no metadata filtering is planned, and the team will not write or operate ingestion code. Which ingestion configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Semantic chunking with a buffer size of 1, plus a `.metadata.json` sidecar file for each source file in the bucket.
A foundation model parser with a customised extraction prompt, combined with the default chunking strategy.
The no-chunking strategy with a custom transformation Lambda function and an intermediate S3 bucket.
Fixed-size chunking with a small token limit and no overlap, plus a `.metadata.json` sidecar file for each source file.

explanation: The content is lost at parsing, before chunking happens. The default parser outputs only text, and AWS recommends Bedrock Data Automation or a foundation model as the parser when documents include figures, charts or tables. Of those, the foundation model parser is the one that lets you customize the prompt used for extraction, which is how the team states that tables become Markdown and charts are described with axis units. 'A foundation model parser with a customised extraction prompt, combined with the default chunking strategy' therefore fits, since paragraph-sized chunks are acceptable. 'Semantic chunking' and 'fixed-size chunking' change only where the parsed text is split; with the default parser the table and chart content still never reaches the index, and their sidecar files add file-level attributes that nobody plans to filter on. 'The no-chunking strategy with a custom transformation Lambda function' is for chunking logic or chunk metadata of your own; the function receives content that has already been parsed, and it is ingestion code, which the team will not write or operate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-advanced-parsing.html

prompt: A contact-centre company indexes call transcripts in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Each transcript is one JSON file in S3 that holds a list of speaker turns with timestamps. Retrieval quality is poor because chunks cut across turns and lose the speaker. The team needs chunks that follow the topic segments computed by its own segmentation algorithm, with `speaker_role` and `start_time` stored as metadata on each individual chunk for filtering. Citations must point to the original transcript file, so the files cannot be pre-split into many S3 objects. The team is willing to maintain a small amount of ingestion code. Which ingestion configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Semantic chunking with a buffer size of 1, plus a `.metadata.json` sidecar file for each source file in the bucket.
A foundation model parser with a customised extraction prompt, combined with the default chunking strategy.
The no-chunking strategy with a custom transformation Lambda function and an intermediate S3 bucket.
Fixed-size chunking with a small token limit and no overlap, plus a `.metadata.json` sidecar file for each source file.

explanation: When chunking logic is not natively supported, Knowledge Bases lets you choose the no-chunking strategy and specify a custom transformation Lambda function with an S3 bucket for intermediate files. Bedrock writes the parsed file to that bucket, the function applies the team's segmentation, writes the chunks back with per-chunk `contentMetadata`, and returns references for the rest of ingestion. The source document stays the single transcript file, so citations point to it, and `speaker_role` and `start_time` exist on each chunk. 'The no-chunking strategy with a custom transformation Lambda function and an intermediate S3 bucket' is therefore the answer. 'Semantic chunking' uses Bedrock's own sentence-similarity boundaries, not the team's algorithm, and a sidecar file describes the whole file, so every chunk would share one speaker and one start time. 'A foundation model parser with a customised extraction prompt' controls how content is extracted from a file; the default chunking strategy still decides the boundaries and adds no per-chunk attributes. 'Fixed-size chunking with a small token limit' splits by token count, which only approximates turns and ignores topic segments, and again offers only file-level metadata. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-custom-transformation.html

prompt: A publisher's Amazon Bedrock knowledge base holds 70 million chunks embedded with Amazon Titan Embeddings G1 - Text as 1,536-dimension float32 vectors in an OpenSearch Service managed domain on engine version 2.17. Memory-optimized data nodes are the largest line in the bill. An evaluation shows that binary embeddings give acceptable recall for this corpus when a reranker is applied, whereas shorter float32 vectors did not meet the accuracy target. The domain also serves other search applications, so the team must stay on it. Which actions are required to make this change? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a new knowledge base that uses Titan Text Embeddings V2 with the `BINARY` embedding data type, and ingest again.
Create a new knowledge base that uses Titan Text Embeddings V2 with 256-dimension float32 vectors, and ingest again.
Create a vector index whose vector field uses the binary data type and the Hamming space type on the faiss engine.
Create a vector index whose vector field has 256 dimensions and uses the l2 space type on the faiss engine.
Create an S3 vector index for float32 vectors with cosine distance, and point a new knowledge base at that index.

explanation: Titan Embeddings G1 - Text produces floating-point vectors only, whereas Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports binary output, so the embedding model must change. The embedding model and its configuration belong to the knowledge base configuration, which `UpdateKnowledgeBase` cannot change, so the team must 'create a new knowledge base that uses Titan Text Embeddings V2 with the `BINARY` embedding data type, and ingest again'. On the store side, a managed cluster supports binary embeddings from engine version 2.16, which 2.17 satisfies, and the index must declare 'the binary data type and the Hamming space type on the faiss engine'. The two options built on 256-dimension float32 vectors, a knowledge base 'with 256-dimension float32 vectors' and an index that 'has 256 dimensions and uses the l2 space type', are a valid way to shrink an index, but the evaluation found that shorter float32 vectors missed the accuracy target. The option to 'create an S3 vector index' is ruled out because the team must stay on the existing domain, and S3 Vectors stores only floating-point embeddings, so the binary saving would be lost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A legal publisher's Amazon Bedrock knowledge base holds 40 million chunks embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 as 1,024-dimension float32 vectors in an OpenSearch Service managed domain on engine version 2.17. The team must cut the memory used by the index. An evaluation found that binary embeddings lose too much recall on its citation-heavy queries, even with a reranker, while 256-dimension float32 vectors from the same model stay within the accuracy target. The domain is shared with other search applications, so the team must keep using it. Which actions are required to make this change? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a new knowledge base that uses Titan Text Embeddings V2 with the `BINARY` embedding data type, and ingest again.
Create a new knowledge base that uses Titan Text Embeddings V2 with 256-dimension float32 vectors, and ingest again.
Create a vector index whose vector field uses the binary data type and the Hamming space type on the faiss engine.
Create a vector index whose vector field has 256 dimensions and uses the l2 space type on the faiss engine.
Create an S3 vector index for float32 vectors with cosine distance, and point a new knowledge base at that index.

explanation: Titan Text Embeddings V2 can produce 1,024, 512 or 256 dimensions, so a quarter-size float32 vector is available from the same model. The dimension is part of the knowledge base's embedding configuration, which `UpdateKnowledgeBase` cannot change, and vectors of different sizes cannot share an index field, so the team must 'create a new knowledge base that uses Titan Text Embeddings V2 with 256-dimension float32 vectors, and ingest again' and 'create a vector index whose vector field has 256 dimensions and uses the l2 space type on the faiss engine'; l2 is the space type AWS specifies for float embeddings on a managed cluster. The two binary options, a knowledge base 'with the `BINARY` embedding data type' and an index using 'the binary data type and the Hamming space type', would save more memory, but the evaluation found binary embeddings lose too much recall on these queries even with a reranker. The option to 'create an S3 vector index' fails the constraint that the team must keep using the shared domain; it moves the vectors to a different store instead of shrinking the index there. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A furniture retailer wants shoppers to find products by appearance. Its catalogue in Amazon S3 holds 300,000 product photos and short silent demonstration clips, with only a product code as text. In the mobile app a shopper uploads a photo of a chair seen elsewhere, and the backend calls `Retrieve` on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base to return visually similar products; shoppers may also type a short description. No generated answers are needed, and none of the media contains speech. The knowledge base will be created in US East (N. Virginia). Which knowledge base configuration should the team choose?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser, a text embedding model, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.
Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings as the embedding model, the default parser, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.
The default parser, a text embedding model, and no multimodal storage destination for the knowledge base.
A foundation model parser with a customised prompt, a text embedding model, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.

explanation: The decisive requirements are an image as the query and matching by visual similarity. Nova Multimodal Embeddings embeds media natively, without converting it to text, supports text queries or image queries, and is the approach AWS recommends for product catalogues, visual similarity search and image discovery; it requires a multimodal storage destination and is available in US East (N. Virginia). So 'Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings as the embedding model, the default parser, and a multimodal storage destination in S3' fits. Its documented weaknesses, speech content and `RetrieveAndGenerate` limited to text, do not matter here because the media is silent and no generated answers are needed. 'Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser' converts media to text and supports text queries only, so a shopper's uploaded photo could not be used as the query and matching would rest on descriptions, not appearance. 'A foundation model parser' likewise turns images into text for a text embedding model, cannot take an image query, and does not handle video clips. 'The default parser' with no multimodal storage processes only text, which here is just a product code. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-multimodal-choose-approach.html

prompt: An industrial equipment maker has 20,000 PDF service manuals in Amazon S3. Much of the important content is in wiring diagrams and torque tables, and there are no audio or video files. Technicians type questions and expect generated answers with citations from `RetrieveAndGenerate`; nobody searches by uploading an image. In a trial, extracted diagram content was too vague, so the team needs to give its own extraction instructions, for example to list every connector and pin label shown in a diagram. Token-based parsing charges are acceptable. Which knowledge base configuration should the team choose?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser, a text embedding model, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.
Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings as the embedding model, the default parser, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.
The default parser, a text embedding model, and no multimodal storage destination for the knowledge base.
A foundation model parser with a customised prompt, a text embedding model, and a multimodal storage destination in S3.

explanation: The manuals need their diagrams and tables turned into text that can be searched and used for generated answers, and the team must control how that extraction is done. Both advanced parsers handle figures, charts and tables in PDFs, but only the foundation model parser gives the option to customize the prompt used for data extraction; it is billed by input and output tokens, which the stem accepts, and it handles images although not audio or video, of which there are none. So 'a foundation model parser with a customised prompt, a text embedding model, and a multimodal storage destination in S3' fits. 'Amazon Bedrock Data Automation as the parser' processes multimodal data without any prompting, so there is nowhere to state the instruction about connectors and pin labels. 'Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings' targets visual similarity and image queries, which nobody uses here, and its `RetrieveAndGenerate` support is limited to text content, so diagram content would not feed the generated answers. 'The default parser' outputs only text, so the diagrams and table graphics would be dropped, which is worse than the trial. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-advanced-parsing.html

prompt: A company runs Amazon OpenSearch Service for product search: a managed domain on engine version 2.11 with public access and fine-grained access control, whose existing k-NN indexes use the nmslib engine. The search team wants this managed domain to be the vector store for a new Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that embeds with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 as float32 vectors. The company intends to keep one search technology, and the team wants to set HNSW parameters such as `m` and `ef_construction` itself. Which changes must the team make before the knowledge base can be created on this domain? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Provide a domain that uses public network access in place of a domain that is inside a VPC.
Replace the domain with an OpenSearch Serverless collection that is reached through a VPC endpoint.
Upgrade the domain to a later engine version before creating the vector index for the knowledge base.
Create a vector index whose vector field uses the binary data type with the Hamming space type.
Create a vector index that uses the faiss engine and the HNSW method in place of the nmslib index.

explanation: For OpenSearch managed clusters, Bedrock Knowledge Bases documents three requirements: public network access, engine version 2.13 or higher to create the k-NN index (2.16 or later for binary embeddings), and a vector field on the faiss engine, because nmslib is not supported. This domain already has public access, and fine-grained access control is recommended but optional, so the gaps are the version and the engine: the team must 'upgrade the domain to a later engine version', from 2.11 to at least 2.13, and 'create a vector index that uses the faiss engine and the HNSW method in place of the nmslib index'. The sample mapping exposes `m` and `ef_construction`, which is where the team does its tuning. The option to 'provide a domain that uses public network access' describes a real requirement that this domain already meets. The option with 'the binary data type with the Hamming space type' is for binary embeddings; the stem says the knowledge base embeds float32 vectors, which use the l2 space type. The option to 'replace the domain with an OpenSearch Serverless collection' contradicts the intention to keep one search technology on the managed domain. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A company runs an Amazon OpenSearch Service managed domain on engine version 2.17 that is deployed inside a VPC. The search team has already built a faiss HNSW index of float32 vectors there and wants a managed domain to be the vector store for a new Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. To reduce memory, the knowledge base will embed with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 using the binary embedding data type. The company intends to keep managed domains as its one search technology, and the team wants to keep setting HNSW parameters itself. Which changes must the team make before the knowledge base can be created? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Provide a domain that uses public network access in place of a domain that is inside a VPC.
Replace the domain with an OpenSearch Serverless collection that is reached through a VPC endpoint.
Upgrade the domain to a later engine version before creating the vector index for the knowledge base.
Create a vector index whose vector field uses the binary data type with the Hamming space type.
Create a vector index that uses the faiss engine and the HNSW method in place of the nmslib index.

explanation: Bedrock Knowledge Bases states that for a managed cluster you must choose public access, because OpenSearch domains behind a VPC are not supported; fine-grained access control is recommended, to restrict what the knowledge base service role can do, but optional. The team must therefore 'provide a domain that uses public network access in place of a domain that is inside a VPC'. Because the knowledge base will produce binary embeddings, the index must declare 'the binary data type with the Hamming space type'; the existing float32 index cannot hold them. The option to 'upgrade the domain to a later engine version' is unnecessary: binary embeddings need version 2.16 or later and the domain runs 2.17. The option to create a faiss HNSW index 'in place of the nmslib index' does not apply, since the team's index already uses faiss and there is no nmslib index to replace. The option to 'replace the domain with an OpenSearch Serverless collection that is reached through a VPC endpoint' would give private connectivity, but the company intends to keep managed domains as its one search technology. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-setup.html

prompt: A software vendor's support assistant uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on OpenSearch Serverless. The application calls `Retrieve` with `numberOfResults` set to 5 and then the Converse API. Evaluation shows two problems. Questions that quote exact identifiers, such as error code `E-4471` or a CLI flag, often miss the one article that contains that string. For conceptual questions the best article frequently sits between positions 6 and 20 of the similarity ranking, so it never reaches the model. Token cost means at most five chunks may be sent to the model, the articles cover a single product and release, and retrieved passages are long enough to answer from. Which changes address these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` so that the raw chunk text is searched together with the vector embeddings.
Raise `numberOfResults` to 25, and pass every returned chunk to the model in the Converse request.
Have the application add a metadata filter on a document attribute whose value it already knows for the user.
Raise `numberOfResults` to 25, and add a reranking configuration that returns the 5 highest-scoring chunks.
Re-create the data source with hierarchical chunking so that matched chunks are returned as larger parent chunks.

explanation: The two symptoms have different causes. Exact identifiers are a keyword-matching problem: hybrid search, which OpenSearch Serverless supports when the text field is filterable, queries the raw text as well as the embeddings, so setting '`overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID`' lets a literal string such as `E-4471` match. The ranking problem is solved by retrieving a wider candidate set and letting a reranker score each chunk against the query: 'raise `numberOfResults` to 25, and add a reranking configuration that returns the 5 highest-scoring chunks' pulls the best article up from positions 6 to 20 while keeping the five-chunk budget. The option to 'pass every returned chunk to the model' would also expose the article, but it breaks the stated limit of five chunks. The option to 'add a metadata filter on a document attribute' has nothing to narrow, because the articles cover a single product and release. The option to use 'hierarchical chunking' returns larger parent passages, but the stem says passages are already long enough; the article is missing or ranked too low, not too short. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A network vendor's support assistant uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on OpenSearch Serverless with default chunking. The application calls `Retrieve` with `numberOfResults` set to 5 and then the Converse API. Evaluation shows two problems. The top results often describe a different firmware release from the one the signed-in customer runs; each article has a `release` attribute, the customer's release is in the account record, and customers rarely mention it in the question. And when the right passage is ranked first, it is too short: the model does not see the prerequisites in the surrounding section. Questions are conceptual and quote no identifiers, and at most five chunks may be sent to the model. Which changes address these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` so that the raw chunk text is searched together with the vector embeddings.
Raise `numberOfResults` to 25, and pass every returned chunk to the model in the Converse request.
Have the application add a metadata filter on a document attribute whose value it already knows for the user.
Raise `numberOfResults` to 25, and add a reranking configuration that returns the 5 highest-scoring chunks.
Re-create the data source with hierarchical chunking so that matched chunks are returned as larger parent chunks.

explanation: The first problem is scope: results come from the wrong release, and the correct release is known to the application from the account record. An explicit filter in the retrieval configuration restricts the search to matching documents, so the team should 'have the application add a metadata filter on a document attribute whose value it already knows for the user'. The second problem is context: the matched chunk is right but too small. Hierarchical chunking matches on small child chunks and replaces them with their larger parents at retrieval time, so to 're-create the data source with hierarchical chunking' gives the model the surrounding prerequisites; chunking cannot be edited on an existing data source, hence the re-creation. Setting '`overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID`' helps exact strings, but these questions quote no identifiers. The option to add 'a reranking configuration that returns the 5 highest-scoring chunks' scores chunks against the question text, which rarely names the release, and the right passage is already ranked first, so neither problem changes. The option to 'pass every returned chunk to the model' exceeds the five-chunk limit. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A wholesaler built an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over its product sheets with an Amazon S3 vector index as the vector store, chosen for low cost. Ingestion succeeds and semantic retrieval works, and inspection of the stored chunks shows that SKU codes such as `KX-20417` are present in the chunk text. To improve matching on SKU codes, a developer sets `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` in `Retrieve` requests. The calls succeed without errors, but the results and scores are identical to those returned for `SEMANTIC`, even with `numberOfResults` raised to 100, and SKU lookups still fail. What is the MOST likely cause, and what should the team do?

options.text: The vector store is of a type that does not support hybrid search, so the query runs as semantic search; move to a store type that supports it.
The text field of the vector index is not filterable, so the query runs as semantic search; create an index with a filterable text field.
The keyword matches are found but rank below the cut-off; raise `numberOfResults` and add a reranking configuration to the query.
The codes are missing from the indexed text because the parser did not extract them; use a parser that extracts that content.

explanation: Hybrid search is supported only for Amazon RDS (Aurora), OpenSearch Serverless and MongoDB vector stores that contain a filterable text field. The documentation states that if you use a different vector store, the query uses semantic search. An S3 vector index is a different store type, which explains both symptoms: no error, and results identical to `SEMANTIC`. So 'the vector store is of a type that does not support hybrid search', and the fix is a store type that does. The option that 'the text field of the vector index is not filterable' describes the other documented fallback, but it applies to a store that supports hybrid search; with S3 Vectors no text-field setting would enable it. The option that 'the keyword matches are found but rank below the cut-off' is contradicted by the identical results and scores, which show that no keyword search ran, and by the failure persisting at 100 results. The option that 'the codes are missing from the indexed text' is contradicted by the inspection, which found the SKU codes in the chunk text. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A wholesaler built an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over supplier catalogues in PDF, using an OpenSearch Serverless collection and the default parser. To improve matching on SKU codes such as `KX-20417`, a developer sets `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` in `Retrieve` requests. Results and scores now differ from those returned for `SEMANTIC`, which shows that the raw text is being searched, but SKU lookups still fail even with `numberOfResults` raised to 100. Inspection of the stored chunks shows product descriptions but no SKU codes: in the catalogues the codes appear only inside label images and table graphics. What is the MOST likely cause, and what should the team do?

options.text: The vector store is of a type that does not support hybrid search, so the query runs as semantic search; move to a store type that supports it.
The text field of the vector index is not filterable, so the query runs as semantic search; create an index with a filterable text field.
The keyword matches are found but rank below the cut-off; raise `numberOfResults` and add a reranking configuration to the query.
The codes are missing from the indexed text because the parser did not extract them; use a parser that extracts that content.

explanation: Keyword search can match only text that was indexed. The default parser parses only text, and AWS recommends Bedrock Data Automation or a foundation model as the parser when documents include figures, charts, tables or images, because those parsers extract such elements. Here the SKU codes exist only inside label images and table graphics, and inspection confirms that no stored chunk contains them, so 'the codes are missing from the indexed text because the parser did not extract them'; the data source needs a parser that extracts that content, followed by re-ingestion. The option that 'the vector store is of a type that does not support hybrid search' does not apply: OpenSearch Serverless is a supported type, and the results differ from `SEMANTIC`. The option that 'the text field of the vector index is not filterable' is ruled out for the same reason, since a fallback to semantic search would return identical results. The option that 'the keyword matches are found but rank below the cut-off' fails because lookups still miss at 100 results and no chunk holds the code, so a reranker would have nothing to promote. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-advanced-parsing.html

prompt: An electronics retailer's assistant calls `Retrieve` on a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base and then generates the answer with its own Converse request, which carries a tuned system prompt, three tools and a citation format that the legal team approved. Simple questions are answered well. Compound questions such as 'Is the X200 or the X300 cheaper to repair out of warranty, and which has the longer battery warranty?' produce answers about one product only, because all top results come from that product's documents at any `numberOfResults` up to 20. Legal requires that the final answer keeps coming from the existing Converse request. What should the team do?

options.text: Call `RetrieveAndGenerate` with the query transformation type set to `QUERY_DECOMPOSITION` in the orchestration configuration.
Add a reranking configuration to the retrieval request so that a reranker model reorders a wider set of candidates.
Re-create the data source with hierarchical chunking so that each result returns a larger passage of the document.
Have the application split the question with a Converse call, and call `Retrieve` once for each sub-question.

explanation: One search for a two-product question returns chunks dominated by one product, so the question has to be broken into sub-queries that are searched separately. The built-in query decomposition does this, but it is configured in the orchestration configuration of `RetrieveAndGenerate`, which also generates the answer from the knowledge base's own prompt template. Legal requires the final answer to keep coming from the existing Converse request, so the option to 'call `RetrieveAndGenerate` with the query transformation type set to `QUERY_DECOMPOSITION`' is ruled out. The team should 'have the application split the question with a Converse call, and call `Retrieve` once for each sub-question', then pass the combined chunks to its existing request. The option to 'add a reranking configuration' cannot help, because a reranker only reorders retrieved candidates and the stem says the other product's chunks are absent even at 20 results. The option to use 'hierarchical chunking' returns larger passages, but they are larger passages about the one product that dominated the ranking, and it needs the data source to be re-created. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: An electronics retailer's assistant calls `RetrieveAndGenerate` on a customer-managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with `numberOfResults` set to 5, the most that its latency budget allows to be passed to the model. Customers ask about one product at a time, for example 'How do I reset the X200 after a firmware failure?'. Offline tests show that the passage with the answer is usually retrieved when 25 results are requested, but it ranks between positions 8 and 20 by vector similarity, behind passages that merely mention the product. The passages themselves are long enough to answer from, and the team wants no new application components. What should the team do?

options.text: Call `RetrieveAndGenerate` with the query transformation type set to `QUERY_DECOMPOSITION` in the orchestration configuration.
Add a reranking configuration to the retrieval request so that a reranker model reorders a wider set of candidates.
Re-create the data source with hierarchical chunking so that each result returns a larger passage of the document.
Have the application split the question with a Converse call, and call `Retrieve` once for each sub-question.

explanation: The right passage is being retrieved but ranked too low to be among the five that reach the model. A reranker model scores each candidate against the query and reorders them, and it is configured inside the retrieval configuration of the same `RetrieveAndGenerate` call: retrieve 25 candidates and return the 5 highest after reranking. The option to 'add a reranking configuration to the retrieval request so that a reranker model reorders a wider set of candidates' therefore fixes the ranking within the five-passage budget and adds no components. The option to set '`QUERY_DECOMPOSITION`' breaks a complex question into sub-queries, but these customers ask about one product at a time, so there is nothing to decompose and the similarity ranking of each search would be unchanged. The option to 'have the application split the question with a Converse call' has the same flaw and adds application components, which the team does not want. The option to use 'hierarchical chunking' returns larger passages, yet the stem says passages are already long enough; the answer passage would still sit at positions 8 to 20. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-retrieve-generate.html

prompt: A bank's policy desk assistant is built on the Converse API with a compliance-approved system prompt and its own citation format. Every question it receives is a policy question, and compliance requires that every answer is grounded in passages from the policy knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock: the model must not be able to answer without a search having been performed for that question. The answer must be produced by exactly one model generation under the approved system prompt, and the team wants the lowest response latency, with no additional model round trips. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Call `RetrieveAndGenerate` for each user message, and return its generated answer and citations to the user.
Add a tool whose handler calls `RetrieveAndGenerate`, and return the generated answer to the model as the tool result.
Add a search tool to `toolConfig`, and when the model requests it, call `Retrieve` and return the chunks as the tool result.
Call `Retrieve` for each user message before Converse, and place the returned chunks in the request with the question.

explanation: Because every question is a policy question and a search is mandatory, retrieval should be done by the application, not left to the model. `Retrieve` returns the relevant chunks with their source locations and generates nothing, so the option to 'call `Retrieve` for each user message before Converse, and place the returned chunks in the request with the question' guarantees a search for every question, keeps the approved system prompt and citation format, and uses exactly one model generation with no extra round trip. The option to 'add a search tool to `toolConfig`' lets the model decide when a tool is needed, so it could answer without searching, and each search adds a second model call after the tool result is returned. The option whose handler 'calls `RetrieveAndGenerate`' has the same optional search and also produces the answer in two generations, one of them under the knowledge base's prompt template. The option to 'call `RetrieveAndGenerate` for each user message' always searches, but its answer and citations come from the knowledge base's own template, not the compliance-approved system prompt and format. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-retrieve.html

prompt: A small charity wants a question-and-answer page over its grant guidelines, which are indexed in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. Two volunteers maintain the site. They have no existing chat application, no prompt of their own and no tools, and they want Amazon Bedrock to perform the search, build the prompt, generate the answer and supply citations to the source documents in a single API call. Follow-up questions should keep the context of the conversation without the site storing message history. Every question is about the guidelines. Which design requires the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Call `RetrieveAndGenerate` for each user message, and return its generated answer and citations to the user.
Add a tool whose handler calls `RetrieveAndGenerate`, and return the generated answer to the model as the tool result.
Add a search tool to `toolConfig`, and when the model requests it, call `Retrieve` and return the chunks as the tool result.
Call `Retrieve` for each user message before Converse, and place the returned chunks in the request with the question.

explanation: `RetrieveAndGenerate` queries the knowledge base, generates a response from the retrieved chunks with a built-in prompt template and returns citations to the original source data, all in one call. It also returns a `sessionId` that can be sent with the next request to continue the conversation, so the site stores no history. The option to 'call `RetrieveAndGenerate` for each user message, and return its generated answer and citations to the user' is therefore the least code for volunteers who have no prompt or application of their own. The option to 'call `Retrieve` for each user message before Converse' would make them write the prompt, the citation handling and the storage of message history, which is what they want Bedrock to do. The option to 'add a search tool to `toolConfig`' requires a tool-use loop in application code, and letting the model decide when to search has no value when every question is about the guidelines. The option whose handler 'calls `RetrieveAndGenerate`' needs the same loop and generates each answer twice, for no benefit. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-retrieve-generate.html

prompt: A bank's platform team owns a customer-service prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with `{{customer_tier}}` and `{{question}}` variables. Compliance has approved version 4, and Prompt Management must remain the only place where the prompt text is stored. The mobile-banking team's assistant already runs a Converse tool-use loop with three account-lookup tools in `toolConfig`, and it sets `maxTokens` in each request according to the customer's tier. That loop must stay as it is. Later edits to the working draft must not change production behaviour. How should the application use the approved prompt?

options.text: Call `GetPrompt` for a numbered prompt version, fill in the variables in code, and send the text to Converse with request-level settings.
Call `GetPrompt` for the working draft at start-up, fill in the variables in code, and send the text to Converse with request-level settings.
Call Converse with the ARN of a numbered prompt version as the model ID, and pass the variable values in `promptVariables`.
Call `InvokeFlow` on a flow alias whose prompt node references the prompt, and pass the variable values as the flow input.

explanation: When Converse is called with a Prompt Management prompt as the model ID, the request cannot include `toolConfig`, `inferenceConfig`, `system` or `additionalModelRequestFields`; those must be defined in Prompt Management. This application needs its own `toolConfig` and a per-request `maxTokens`, so the option to 'call Converse with the ARN of a numbered prompt version as the model ID' would be rejected for the existing loop. `GetPrompt` with the `promptVersion` parameter returns a specific version, which is a snapshot that later draft edits do not alter, so the application should 'call `GetPrompt` for a numbered prompt version, fill in the variables in code, and send the text to Converse with request-level settings'. Prompt Management stays the single store of the text, and the tool-use loop is unchanged. The option to call '`GetPrompt` for the working draft' reads the mutable draft, so later edits would reach production. The option to 'call `InvokeFlow` on a flow alias' runs the prompt inside a flow, which replaces the Converse tool-use loop that must stay as it is. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-test.html

prompt: A bank's platform team owns a customer-service prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. It defines the assistant's role in a system instruction, the model and the inference parameters, and it has `{{customer_tier}}` and `{{question}}` variables. Compliance has approved version 4. Application teams must continue to call the Converse API and append each conversation's messages; they use no tools. The audit requirement is that an application cannot alter the approved system instruction or inference parameters in a request, and that later edits to the working draft do not change production behaviour. How should the applications invoke the prompt?

options.text: Call `GetPrompt` for a numbered prompt version, fill in the variables in code, and send the text to Converse with request-level settings.
Call `GetPrompt` for the working draft at start-up, fill in the variables in code, and send the text to Converse with request-level settings.
Call Converse with the ARN of a numbered prompt version as the model ID, and pass the variable values in `promptVariables`.
Call `InvokeFlow` on a flow alias whose prompt node references the prompt, and pass the variable values as the flow input.

explanation: The Converse API accepts the ARN of a prompt version as the model ID and fills the template from `promptVariables`; messages in the request are appended after those defined in the prompt. When a managed prompt is used this way, the request cannot include `system`, `inferenceConfig`, `toolConfig` or `additionalModelRequestFields`, which is exactly the enforcement the audit wants, and a version is a snapshot, so draft edits do not reach production. The applications should 'call Converse with the ARN of a numbered prompt version as the model ID, and pass the variable values in `promptVariables`'. The option to 'call `GetPrompt` for a numbered prompt version' and send the text 'with request-level settings' pins the text, but the application then builds its own request and can set any system instruction or inference parameters, which the audit forbids. The option to call '`GetPrompt` for the working draft' has that fault and also reads the mutable draft. The option to 'call `InvokeFlow` on a flow alias' moves the teams off the Converse API, which they must continue to call while appending conversation messages. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Converse.html

prompt: A parcel carrier's tracking assistant handles 1,500 requests per second at peak. Each request runs a six-step workflow (classify, look up the parcel, retrieve policy text, generate, validate, format) that finishes within 20 seconds, and Amazon API Gateway must return the workflow's result in the same HTTP response. Each conversation is a single exchange, so no history is loaded during a request, but the full transcript must be kept server-side for seven years for regulatory audits, read only a few times a year with retrieval in seconds, and then removed automatically. The regulator requires the stored transcripts to be protected by a write-once-read-many (WORM) control for that period. Which design choices are MOST cost-effective? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store each turn as an item in a DynamoDB table keyed by session ID and turn timestamp, with TTL on an epoch-seconds attribute.
Write each session's transcript to an S3 object keyed by session ID, with a lifecycle rule that expires the objects.
Run each request as a Step Functions Standard workflow that sends the message with a task token and waits for the callback.
Run each request as a synchronous Step Functions Express workflow that returns its result directly to the caller.
Have the client application hold the conversation history, and send the full history to the backend with every request.

explanation: The workflow is short, high-volume and must answer in the same HTTP response. Synchronous Express Workflows start a workflow, wait until it completes and return the result, can be invoked from API Gateway, and are priced by executions, duration and memory, so 'a synchronous Step Functions Express workflow' fits. Transcripts are written once, rarely read and kept for seven years, which is archival data: 'an S3 object keyed by session ID, with a lifecycle rule that expires the objects' stores it cheaply and S3 deletes expired objects on your behalf. 'A Step Functions Standard workflow' starts asynchronously, so its result cannot be returned in the same HTTP response; it is also billed per state transition, which is costly for six steps at 1,500 requests per second, and its task-token wait serves long pauses that this 20-second workflow does not have. 'A DynamoDB table' with TTL is designed for fast lookups during conversations; no history is loaded here, and DynamoDB offers no write-once-read-many control, whereas S3 Object Lock stores objects under a WORM model for a retention period, after which the lifecycle rule can expire them. Having 'the client application hold the conversation history' fails the requirement that transcripts are kept server-side for audits. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html

prompt: A utilities company is building a service-request assistant. An Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API invokes stateless Lambda functions that call the Converse API. Conversations span many turns and can resume from another device, so each turn must be appended as it happens and the latest turns loaded by session ID with very low latency. History must be removed automatically some time after the session ends, without scheduled clean-up jobs. When a request is ambiguous, for example a missing meter number, the workflow must send the customer a clarifying question by SMS, pause for up to 48 hours, and resume exactly where it stopped when the reply arrives. Which design choices meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store each turn as an item in a DynamoDB table keyed by session ID and turn timestamp, with TTL on an epoch-seconds attribute.
Write each session's transcript to an S3 object keyed by session ID, with a lifecycle rule that expires the objects.
Run each request as a Step Functions Standard workflow that sends the message with a task token and waits for the callback.
Run each request as a synchronous Step Functions Express workflow that returns its result directly to the caller.
Have the client application hold the conversation history, and send the full history to the backend with every request.

explanation: History for stateless compute belongs in a key-value store that any device's request can reach. 'A DynamoDB table keyed by session ID and turn timestamp' lets each turn be appended as one item and a session's turns read in order with one query, and TTL deletes expired items automatically without consuming write throughput; the TTL attribute must be a Number holding Unix epoch time in seconds. For the clarification step, the callback pattern pauses a task until the task token is returned, and Standard workflows can run for up to a year, so 'a Step Functions Standard workflow that sends the message with a task token and waits for the callback' covers the 48-hour pause and resumes at the same state. 'A synchronous Step Functions Express workflow' fails because Express workflows run for at most five minutes and do not support the callback pattern. 'An S3 object keyed by session ID' would have to be rewritten on every turn and suits archives, not per-turn appends and low-latency reads. Having 'the client application hold the conversation history' breaks resuming from another device. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/TTL.html

prompt: A healthcare company manages production prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management in a dedicated production account. After an incident in which an engineer edited a prompt and published a new version directly, the security team sets two requirements. First, there must be a durable record of who created, modified or versioned each prompt, and when. Second, no person may change or publish a prompt in production directly; a version may be created only after a reviewer has approved the change. Engineers keep read access to prompts for debugging. The account has no trail configured today. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a CloudTrail trail that delivers management events to S3, which records `UpdatePrompt` and `CreatePromptVersion` calls.
Enable model invocation logging to an S3 bucket, which records each request and response with the caller's identity.
Add CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::Prompt` resource type, which records each `RenderPrompt` event.
Create CloudWatch alarms on invocation metrics for the models that the prompts use, and notify the security team.
Allow `UpdatePrompt` and `CreatePromptVersion` in IAM only for a pipeline role that runs after a manual approval action.

explanation: Edits to prompts are control-plane calls such as `UpdatePrompt` and `CreatePromptVersion`, which CloudTrail records as management events with the caller's identity and time. Event history shows only recent events, so the durable record is 'a CloudTrail trail that delivers management events to S3'. Prevention is an IAM matter: engineers keep read actions such as `GetPrompt`, while the write actions are allowed 'only for a pipeline role that runs after a manual approval action', so a version cannot be created until a reviewer approves and the pipeline resumes. 'Model invocation logging' captures the inputs and outputs of model invocations; it does not record edits to prompt resources and prevents nothing. 'CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::Prompt` resource type' record `RenderPrompt`, the permission-only action that fires when a managed prompt is rendered for inference; that tracks usage, whereas the requirement concerns who created, modified or versioned a prompt. 'CloudWatch alarms on invocation metrics' show counts and latency without identities, and observing behaviour afterwards neither records who changed a prompt nor stops a direct change. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

prompt: A healthcare company manages production prompts in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, and applications invoke them through the Converse API with prompt version ARNs. Change control is already in place: only an approved pipeline role can edit or version prompts, and a CloudTrail trail delivers management events to S3. An auditor now sets two further requirements. First, each time a managed prompt is rendered for inference, an event must be recorded against that prompt resource with the calling principal. Second, the full input and output of every model invocation must be retained, with the calling identity, so that a disputed answer can be reconstructed. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a CloudTrail trail that delivers management events to S3, which records `UpdatePrompt` and `CreatePromptVersion` calls.
Enable model invocation logging to an S3 bucket, which records each request and response with the caller's identity.
Add CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::Prompt` resource type, which records each `RenderPrompt` event.
Create CloudWatch alarms on invocation metrics for the models that the prompts use, and notify the security team.
Allow `UpdatePrompt` and `CreatePromptVersion` in IAM only for a pipeline role that runs after a manual approval action.

explanation: Both new requirements concern inference, not change control. `RenderPrompt` is the permission-only action performed when a Prompt Management prompt is rendered for `Converse` or `InvokeModel`, and CloudTrail logs it only as a data event, which is not recorded by default; the team must 'add CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::Prompt` resource type'. Reconstructing a disputed answer needs the content itself: 'model invocation logging to an S3 bucket' collects the full request data, response data and metadata, including the ARN of the principal that made the request, for Converse and InvokeModel calls, and it is disabled until configured. The option to 'create a CloudTrail trail that delivers management events to S3' is already in place according to the stem, and management events hold neither `RenderPrompt` events nor prompt and response bodies. The option to allow write actions 'only for a pipeline role' is also already in place and governs edits, not usage. 'CloudWatch alarms on invocation metrics' give counts and latency per model, with no principal, no prompt resource and no content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A travel company keeps its itinerary-summary prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management and releases new versions through AWS CodePipeline. Twice, a wording change fixed one complaint but broke date formatting for multi-city trips, and nobody noticed until customers reported it. The team has a golden dataset of 400 inputs whose expected properties are exact: required JSON fields are present and dates match one format. These must be verified by code assertions, not by a model's judgement. Every candidate version must be checked against the whole dataset within five minutes, the pass rate must be tracked over time, and the release must stop when the rate drops. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Compare the candidate with the current prompt as variants in the prompt builder on sample inputs before saving a version.
Run an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job in which a judge model scores responses to the dataset on selected metrics.
Add a pipeline stage that runs a Step Functions Map state over the dataset, where Lambda checks each output and publishes a CloudWatch metric.
Attach a guardrail with contextual grounding checks to the application, using the source record as the grounding source.

explanation: Prompt regression testing means re-running a fixed set of cases against every candidate and comparing results with expectations before release. A Step Functions Map state runs the same steps for each item of a dataset in parallel, so 400 cases finish quickly; a Lambda function invokes the candidate version for each case and applies the exact assertions; and a CloudWatch metric for the pass rate gives the history and a threshold on which the stage can fail.
