So the team should 'add a pipeline stage that runs a Step Functions Map state over the dataset, where Lambda checks each output and publishes a CloudWatch metric'. The 'model evaluation job in which a judge model scores responses' rates qualities such as correctness or helpfulness by model judgement, whereas the stem demands code assertions on JSON fields and date formats. The option to 'compare the candidate with the current prompt as variants in the prompt builder' is a manual authoring aid on a few sample inputs; it covers neither 400 cases nor a pipeline gate. 'A guardrail with contextual grounding checks' acts at run time on grounding and relevance, not on JSON fields or date formats, and gives no pre-release signal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-map.html

prompt: A travel company's itinerary-summary prompt is released through AWS CodePipeline, and every candidate version already passes an automated regression suite over a golden dataset before release. Even so, production inputs are far more varied than the dataset, and twice last quarter a summary sent to a customer mentioned a flight that was not in the booking record supplied to the model. The compliance team now requires that any summary containing information not supported by the booking record is blocked before it reaches the customer, for every request, without waiting for a later review. Summaries are generated in single non-streaming Converse calls. Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Compare the candidate with the current prompt as variants in the prompt builder on sample inputs before saving a version.
Run an Amazon Bedrock model evaluation job in which a judge model scores responses to the dataset on selected metrics.
Add a pipeline stage that runs a Step Functions Map state over the dataset, where Lambda checks each output and publishes a CloudWatch metric.
Attach a guardrail with contextual grounding checks to the application, using the source record as the grounding source.

explanation: The requirement is a run-time control on every response, not another pre-release test. Contextual grounding checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails score a model response against a supplied reference source; any new information the response introduces is treated as ungrounded, and responses scoring below the configured threshold are blocked. Summarization is a supported use case, and with non-streaming calls the response is checked before it is returned. So the team should 'attach a guardrail with contextual grounding checks to the application, using the source record as the grounding source', here the booking record. The option to 'add a pipeline stage that runs a Step Functions Map state over the dataset' is the kind of regression suite that already exists; it tests candidate prompts on fixed inputs and cannot block an individual production summary. The 'model evaluation job in which a judge model scores responses' is likewise an offline job over a dataset, reported after the fact. The option to 'compare the candidate with the current prompt as variants' is an authoring-time check on sample inputs; none of these three inspects each live request before the customer sees it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html

prompt: An insurer's claims-extraction workload sends each claim text to a model through the Converse API with a 700-token prompt that it reads from Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. The prompt was rewritten with prompt optimization for the current model last month, and reviewers confirm that the extracted values are correct. However, about 2% of responses cannot be parsed by the downstream system: a field name is misspelled, a required field is omitted, or text precedes the JSON. The team has no labelled training set, the model supports structured outputs, and the requirement is that every response can be parsed without retries. What should the team do?

options.text: Configure structured output with a JSON schema on the Converse request so that each response conforms to the schema.
Enable prompt caching on the static part of the prompt so that the repeated prefix is read from the cache.
Run prompt optimization for the model, compare the result with the original as variants, and save a version.
Fine-tune the model on labelled prompt and completion pairs so that it learns the expected output.

explanation: The values are right; the defect is that output shape is only requested in the prompt, and prompt-based formatting has a residual error rate. Structured outputs constrain the model's response to a user-defined JSON schema, which AWS describes as ensuring schema compliance and removing the error rates and retry loops of prompt-based approaches; on the Converse API it is set in `outputConfig.textFormat`. The team should 'configure structured output with a JSON schema on the Converse request so that each response conforms to the schema'. The option to 'run prompt optimization for the model' was already done last month, and another rewrite is still a prompt-based approach that cannot guarantee that every response parses. The option to 'fine-tune the model on labelled prompt and completion pairs' needs a labelled training set, which the team does not have, and a tuned model still does not guarantee conformance. The option to 'enable prompt caching' reduces latency and input token cost for a repeated prefix; it does not change what the model generates, and a 700-token prompt is below the caching minimum of several models. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/structured-output.html

prompt: An insurer's claims-triage assistant calls a model through the Converse API about 40 times per minute. Every call sends the same 6,000 tokens of underwriting rules and worked examples from a prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management, followed by a short claim text that differs each time. Reviewers are satisfied with the accuracy and the output format, and the model supports prompt caching. The finance team wants the input token cost reduced and the operations team wants lower response latency, with no change to the model's behaviour and no training project. What should the team do?

options.text: Configure structured output with a JSON schema on the Converse request so that each response conforms to the schema.
Enable prompt caching on the static part of the prompt so that the repeated prefix is read from the cache.
Run prompt optimization for the model, compare the result with the original as variants, and save a version.
Fine-tune the model on labelled prompt and completion pairs so that it learns the expected output.

explanation: Prompt caching exists for workloads with long, repeated context: it reduces inference latency and input token cost by reading a static prompt prefix from a cache, with tokens read from the cache billed at the lower cache-read rate. Here 6,000 identical tokens precede a short variable claim text, the calls arrive far more often than the default five-minute time to live, which resets on each hit, and Prompt Management lets you enable caching when you create or modify a prompt. The team should 'enable prompt caching on the static part of the prompt so that the repeated prefix is read from the cache'; the model's behaviour is unchanged. The option to 'run prompt optimization for the model' rewrites the prompt, which changes behaviour that reviewers are satisfied with and does not remove the repeated tokens. The option to 'configure structured output with a JSON schema' addresses output format, which is already acceptable, and saves no input tokens. The option to 'fine-tune the model on labelled prompt and completion pairs' is a training project, which the stem excludes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: An insurer's developers are building an invoice-checking flow in Amazon Bedrock Flows (called Prompt Flows in the exam guide) in a development account. The flow input is an array of invoice line items; every item must go through the same extraction prompt from Prompt Management, and the flow must return all the extracted results together. The developers run an automated test harness after each saved change and want the harness to exercise the latest saved definition immediately, without publishing anything; nothing in this account is used by production. They want as little custom code as possible. Which design decisions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Connect the upstream prompt node to a condition node whose conditions test its output and whose default leads to a fallback path.
Add a Lambda function node that contains the processing logic and calls the Converse API with the appropriate prompt.
Use an iterator node to send each array item through the prompt node, and a collector node to return the results as an array.
Have the caller send `InvokeFlow` requests to the test alias `TSTALIASID`, which points to the working draft of the flow.
Publish a version of the flow, point an alias at that version, and have the caller send `InvokeFlow` requests to the alias.

explanation: An iterator node takes an array and returns its items one by one to the downstream node, and a collector node downstream gathers the iterated outputs back into an array, so 'an iterator node to send each array item through the prompt node, and a collector node to return the results as an array' applies the same Prompt Management prompt to every line item with no code. When a flow is created, a working draft and a test alias, `TSTALIASID`, that points to the draft are created, and changes apply to the draft; having the harness 'send `InvokeFlow` requests to the test alias `TSTALIASID`' therefore always exercises the latest saved definition without publishing. The option to 'publish a version of the flow, point an alias at that version' is the production deployment pattern; versions are immutable snapshots, so every change would need a new version, which the developers want to avoid. 'A condition node' routes data to different paths by condition, but every item here takes the same path. 'A Lambda function node that contains the processing logic' would work but is the custom code the team wants to minimise. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows-nodes.html

prompt: An insurer wants to automate first-line handling of claim emails with Amazon Bedrock Flows (called Prompt Flows in the exam guide). A prompt classifies each email as `new_claim`, `status_query` or `other`. New claims go to an extraction prompt, status queries go to a knowledge base lookup followed by a reply-drafting prompt, and everything else gets a generic reply. Each flow invocation handles one email, and the prompts are maintained in Prompt Management. The operations team wants as little custom code as possible and must be able to return production to the previous flow definition within minutes without changing the calling application. Which design decisions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Connect the upstream prompt node to a condition node whose conditions test its output and whose default leads to a fallback path.
Add a Lambda function node that contains the processing logic and calls the Converse API with the appropriate prompt.
Use an iterator node to send each array item through the prompt node, and a collector node to return the results as an array.
Have the caller send `InvokeFlow` requests to the test alias `TSTALIASID`, which points to the working draft of the flow.
Publish a version of the flow, point an alias at that version, and have the caller send `InvokeFlow` requests to the alias.

explanation: A condition node sends data from the previous node to different downstream nodes according to conditions written with relational and logical operators; conditions are evaluated in order and a default condition catches everything else. So 'a condition node whose conditions test its output and whose default leads to a fallback path' gives the three-way routing on the classifier's output with no code. For deployment, a flow version is an immutable snapshot and an alias points to a version; the application calls `InvokeFlow` on the alias, so to 'publish a version of the flow, point an alias at that version' lets operations roll back by repointing the alias to the previous version, with no application change. Sending requests 'to the test alias `TSTALIASID`' runs the mutable working draft, so every edit reaches production at once and there is no earlier definition to return to. 'An iterator node' with a collector processes the items of an array along one path; each invocation handles a single email and the need is to choose between paths. 'A Lambda function node that contains the processing logic' would work but moves the branching into custom code, which the team wants to minimise. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows-deploy.html

prompt: A research firm built a due-diligence agent with Strands Agents. One investigation is a single session that stays continuously active for up to 3 days while the agent crawls filings and answers an analyst's follow-up requests. Between requests the agent keeps working files on local disk and large search indexes in process memory, and rebuilding the indexes takes hours. The security team requires that the compute, memory and filesystem used by one investigation are not shared with any other investigation. The platform team has two engineers and does not want to build session routing or manage the lifecycle of the compute. Which hosting option meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Package the agent as an AWS Lambda function that loads each session's state from Amazon DynamoDB at the start of a request and saves it at the end.
Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime on microVM compute and have clients pass the same runtimeSessionId for a session.
Run the agent as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions on the target group.
Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime on Instances compute through a capacity provider, with one runtimeSessionId per session.

explanation: The deciding constraint is a session that is continuously active for up to 3 days with state held in process memory. On AgentCore Runtime a session on the Instances compute type is an isolated EC2 instance that AgentCore provisions, patches and tears down in the firm's account, and it can run for up to 14 days, so the option to deploy 'on Instances compute through a capacity provider' gives isolation, routing by `runtimeSessionId` and managed lifecycle for the whole investigation. Deploying 'on microVM compute' gives the same isolation, but a microVM lives for at most 8 hours; the session would resume on new compute and the in-memory indexes would be lost several times during a 3-day investigation. The 'AWS Lambda function that loads each session's state from Amazon DynamoDB' cannot hold large in-memory indexes between requests and is limited to 15 minutes per invocation. The 'Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate' with sticky sessions keeps a client on one task, but each task serves many investigations, so compute and filesystem are shared, which the security team forbids. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-instances-how-it-works.html

prompt: An insurer built a policy-FAQ agent with Strands Agents. Each request finishes in under 20 seconds, and the only state between requests is a conversation record of a few kilobytes. Traffic is a few hundred requests a day with idle periods that last days. The business unit's AWS account is governed by a service control policy that allows only AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon API Gateway and Amazon Bedrock model invocation; adding any other service requires a security review that takes months. The team runs no container platform and wants to reuse its existing Lambda deployment pipeline. Which hosting option is the MOST cost-effective and requires the FEWEST changes to the existing environment?

options.text: Package the agent as an AWS Lambda function that loads each session's state from Amazon DynamoDB at the start of a request and saves it at the end.
Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime on microVM compute and have clients pass the same runtimeSessionId for a session.
Run the agent as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions on the target group.
Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime on Instances compute through a capacity provider, with one runtimeSessionId per session.

explanation: Every constraint points at the services the account may already use. The agent is short-lived and its state is a small record, so the option to package it 'as an AWS Lambda function that loads each session's state from Amazon DynamoDB' fits inside the 15-minute Lambda limit, costs nothing during the idle days, uses only services on the allow list and reuses the existing pipeline. Both AgentCore options, 'on microVM compute' and 'on Instances compute through a capacity provider', would give session isolation and managed lifecycle, but Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a separate service that the service control policy does not allow, so neither can be deployed without the months-long review; nothing in the workload needs per-session compute or sessions that outlive a request. The 'Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer' is also outside the allow list, needs a container platform the team does not run, and keeps tasks billed through idle periods that last days. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html

prompt: A wealth-management firm hosts an advisor assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with microVM compute and default lifecycle settings. The agent keeps the conversation history in a Python list and does not use AgentCore Memory. Advisors report that when they reopen a client conversation the next morning, the agent has forgotten it. The web client generates a new runtimeSessionId at every login. Compliance requires that the agent can show the exact wording of earlier turns, not a paraphrase. The firm also wants each advisor's stated preferences, such as report format, to be recalled in new conversations weeks later, and one advisor's preferences must not be retrievable for another advisor. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a summary memory strategy whose namespace includes {actorId} and {sessionId}, and load the session's summary records when a conversation resumes.
Write each turn to AgentCore Memory with CreateEvent under the user's actorId and the conversation's sessionId, and reload the events on resume.
Raise idleRuntimeSessionTimeout and maxLifetime to 28,800 seconds so that the microVM behind each session stays available through a working day.
Add a user preference memory strategy whose namespace includes {actorId}, and retrieve that user's records at the start of new conversations.
Configure session storage on the runtime and write working data under its mount path so that the files persist when a session stops and resumes.

explanation: Two needs are stated: verbatim turns that survive the compute and a new `runtimeSessionId`, and per-advisor preferences across conversations. The option to 'Write each turn to AgentCore Memory with CreateEvent' stores raw events keyed by actor and conversation, independent of any Runtime session, so the exact wording can be reloaded the next morning. The option to 'Add a user preference memory strategy whose namespace includes {actorId}' extracts preferences from those events into records scoped to one advisor, which satisfies the isolation rule. The 'summary memory strategy' produces condensed summaries of a session, which compliance rules out because it is a paraphrase. Raising the timeouts 'to 28,800 seconds' cannot bridge an overnight gap, since 8 hours is the maximum for a microVM, and it does nothing for recall weeks later. The option to 'Configure session storage on the runtime' persists files across the stop and resume of the same session, but the client starts a new session ID at every login, so the stored files are not the ones the new session sees, and files do not give per-advisor preference retrieval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/user-preference-memory-strategy.html

prompt: An engineering company hosts a code-review agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with microVM compute. The agent already writes every turn to AgentCore Memory with CreateEvent, and no memory strategies are configured. An engineer stops work in the evening and invokes the same runtimeSessionId about 15 hours later. Two problems are reported. The cloned repository and build outputs that the agent wrote to local disk are gone when the session resumes. And reloading thousands of raw events on resume fills the model's context window, so the team wants a condensed recap of that session instead. The agent does not need to remember anything about an engineer across different sessions. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a summary memory strategy whose namespace includes {actorId} and {sessionId}, and load the session's summary records when a conversation resumes.
Write each turn to AgentCore Memory with CreateEvent under the user's actorId and the conversation's sessionId, and reload the events on resume.
Raise idleRuntimeSessionTimeout and maxLifetime to 28,800 seconds so that the microVM behind each session stays available through a working day.
Add a user preference memory strategy whose namespace includes {actorId}, and retrieve that user's records at the start of new conversations.
Configure session storage on the runtime and write working data under its mount path so that the files persist when a session stops and resumes.

explanation: The first problem is the filesystem: a microVM's disk lasts only for the compute lifecycle, and after 15 idle hours the session has stopped. The option to 'Configure session storage on the runtime' gives a mount path whose data persists across stop and resume of the same session, and the engineer does reuse the same `runtimeSessionId`. The second problem is context size: the option to 'Add a summary memory strategy whose namespace includes {actorId} and {sessionId}' generates condensed summaries at session level from the events that are already being written, so the agent loads a recap instead of the full history. The option to 'Write each turn to AgentCore Memory with CreateEvent' is already in place and reloading those events is the cause of the second problem. Raising the timeouts 'to 28,800 seconds' cannot cover a 15-hour gap, because 8 hours is the maximum for microVM compute. The 'user preference memory strategy' builds a profile of a user across sessions, which the stem says is not needed, and it does not produce a recap of one session. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/summary-strategy.html

prompt: A health insurer assigns diagnosis codes to clinical notes with foundation models on Amazon Bedrock. It tested three models from different providers. Each takes about 3 seconds per note. One model reaches 97% accuracy on radiology notes, another 96% on discharge summaries and the third 96% on pathology reports, but each is below 85% outside its strong note type. On the notes that the models get wrong, they tend to get the same notes wrong. The note type is recorded reliably in each note's header. The inference budget covers one model invocation per note, and the claims system allows 6 seconds per note. Which design gives the GREATEST accuracy within these constraints?

options.text: Call one model three times in parallel at a temperature of 0.7, accept the code that appears most often, and flag notes without a majority.
Put a classifier in front of the models that predicts which model is strongest for each note type, and send the note to that model.
Invoke three models from different providers in parallel, accept the code that the majority returns, and flag split votes for review.
Send the note to one model, then have a second model review and correct the first model's code before the answer is stored.

explanation: The data says the models' strengths are tied to note type and their errors are correlated, and the budget allows one invocation per note. That is a model selection problem: the option to 'Put a classifier in front of the models that predicts which model is strongest for each note type' sends each note to the model that scores 96 to 97% on it, with a single 3-second call. Voting designs need independent errors and several calls. The option to 'Invoke three models from different providers in parallel' spends three invocations per note, which the budget does not cover, and a majority of models that fail on the same notes is still wrong, while two weak models can outvote the strong one. The option to 'Call one model three times in parallel' also uses three invocations and repeats one model's weakness outside its strong note type. The design in which 'a second model' reviews the first uses two invocations per note, again over budget, and takes about 6 seconds, leaving no margin within the limit. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/gencost01-bp01.html

prompt: A hospital network assigns diagnosis codes to clinical notes with a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Its data processing agreement covers one model provider, and notes must not be sent to any other provider's model. Evaluation shows that this model's mistakes vary from run to run: when the same note is sampled several times at a non-zero temperature, the correct code is usually the most frequent answer. One call takes about 3 seconds, the coding system allows 4 seconds per note, and there is no limit on the number of concurrent invocations. Notes on which the system is unsure must be routed to a human coder. Which design gives the GREATEST accuracy improvement within these constraints?

options.text: Call one model three times in parallel at a temperature of 0.7, accept the code that appears most often, and flag notes without a majority.
Put a classifier in front of the models that predicts which model is strongest for each note type, and send the note to that model.
Invoke three models from different providers in parallel, accept the code that the majority returns, and flag split votes for review.
Send the note to one model, then have a second model review and correct the first model's code before the answer is stored.

explanation: Only one provider's model may see the notes, its errors are not repeated consistently across samples, and calls can run concurrently. That is the case for a self-consistency vote: the option to 'Call one model three times in parallel at a temperature of 0.7' keeps latency near a single 3-second call, takes the most frequent code, and uses the absence of a majority as the signal for a human coder. The option to 'Invoke three models from different providers in parallel' would send notes to providers outside the data processing agreement. The 'classifier in front of the models' has nothing to choose between when one model is permitted, and it returns a single answer with no disagreement signal for routing unsure notes. The design in which 'a second model' reviews the first runs two calls in sequence, about 6 seconds, which exceeds the 4-second limit, and a different reviewing model is not covered by the agreement. In a workflow, the three samples can run as branches of a Step Functions Parallel state. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-parallel.html

prompt: A logistics company runs a dispatch agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Last week an engineer updated the runtime with a test build and production traffic used it at once. The security team now requires that test builds run in a separate AWS account whose execution role has no access to production data. Partner integrations and IAM policies reference one fixed production runtime ARN, and that ARN must not change when a build is promoted. Promotion to production must be an explicit action taken after tests pass. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a second AgentCore Runtime for testing, and promote a build by applying the same update to the production runtime after tests pass.
Keep clients on the DEFAULT endpoint, promote a build by updating the runtime, and roll back by updating it again with the earlier image URI.
Create a named endpoint pinned to a tested version, point production clients at it, and move it with UpdateAgentRuntimeEndpoint.
Deploy each build as its own AgentCore Runtime, and move clients between runtime ARNs with an AWS AppConfig gradual deployment strategy.

explanation: The decisive constraints are that test builds run in a different AWS account and that the production runtime ARN stays fixed. Versions and endpoints belong to one runtime in one account, so testing has to happen on a separate runtime: the option to 'Create a second AgentCore Runtime for testing' places test builds in the other account with their own execution role, and promotion is an explicit update of the unchanged production runtime. The option to 'Create a named endpoint pinned to a tested version' is the usual way to separate test and production traffic, but every version and endpoint of that runtime lives in the production account with access governed there, which the security team rules out. The option to 'Keep clients on the DEFAULT endpoint' means each update, including a test build, reaches production immediately, because `DEFAULT` follows the latest version. The option to 'Deploy each build as its own AgentCore Runtime' gives every build a new ARN, which breaks the partner integrations and IAM policies that reference a fixed one. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agent-runtime-versioning.html

prompt: A ride-hailing company runs a pricing agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. Its client services already read the agent's ARN from AWS AppConfig. After a faulty build reached every client at once, the reliability team requires that a new build is first used by about 10% of client services, that the share grows in steps over an hour, and that the rollout is reverted automatically if an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on agent errors fires. All clients must end up on the same build when the rollout completes. Which approach meets these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the client services?

options.text: Create a second AgentCore Runtime for testing, and promote a build by applying the same update to the production runtime after tests pass.
Keep clients on the DEFAULT endpoint, promote a build by updating the runtime, and roll back by updating it again with the earlier image URI.
Create a named endpoint pinned to a tested version, point production clients at it, and move it with UpdateAgentRuntimeEndpoint.
Deploy each build as its own AgentCore Runtime, and move clients between runtime ARNs with an AWS AppConfig gradual deployment strategy.

explanation: The requirement is a stepped rollout to a share of clients with automatic rollback on an alarm. An AgentCore Runtime endpoint references one version at a time, so moving an endpoint moves every client that uses it at once. The option to 'Deploy each build as its own AgentCore Runtime, and move clients between runtime ARNs with an AWS AppConfig gradual deployment strategy' uses what the clients already do: an AppConfig deployment strategy releases the new ARN to a growing percentage of callers over the deployment time and rolls back if a CloudWatch alarm fires. The option to 'Create a named endpoint pinned to a tested version' makes promotion explicit, but `UpdateAgentRuntimeEndpoint` switches all production clients together, so there is no 10% stage. The option to 'Keep clients on the DEFAULT endpoint' also moves every client with each update, and rollback is a manual second update. The option to 'Create a second AgentCore Runtime for testing' separates testing from production, yet promotion still applies the build to all production traffic in one step. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appconfig/latest/userguide/appconfig-creating-deployment-strategy.html

prompt: A fintech company has 14 internal REST operations described in OpenAPI specifications and 3 AWS Lambda functions that its agents should call. Agent teams use Strands Agents and LangGraph and want one MCP endpoint instead of framework-specific integrations, without writing or hosting wrapper code. The model risk team requires that each agent's complete tool list is fixed and logged when the agent starts and that every tool definition is present in every model call, so that evaluation runs are reproducible. The latency budget does not allow an extra tool-discovery round trip before a tool is called. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with semantic search enabled, add OpenAPI and Lambda targets, and have agents use its search tool.
Build MCP servers with an MCP SDK that wrap each group of tools, run them on Amazon ECS, and register the servers in each agent's MCP client.
Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, add OpenAPI and Lambda targets, and have each agent call tools/list at startup and bind the tools.
Define the tools as action groups on Amazon Bedrock Agents from their OpenAPI schemas, and call those agents from the other agent frameworks.

explanation: With 17 tools, the definitions fit comfortably in a prompt, and the model risk team wants the full, fixed list in every call. The option to 'Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, add OpenAPI and Lambda targets, and have each agent call tools/list at startup and bind the tools' turns the existing specifications and functions into MCP tools behind one endpoint with no wrapper code, and gives each agent a complete list that can be logged at startup. The gateway 'with semantic search enabled' is designed for large tool catalogs: agents call `x_amz_bedrock_agentcore_search` with a query and receive the relevant tools, which adds the discovery round trip the latency budget forbids and makes the tool set vary by query instead of being fixed. The option to 'Build MCP servers with an MCP SDK' is the wrapper code and hosting the teams want to avoid, and it produces several endpoints. The option to 'Define the tools as action groups on Amazon Bedrock Agents' does not give Strands and LangGraph an MCP endpoint and adds an agent hop to every call. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/gateway-using-mcp-semantic-search.html

prompt: A shipping line wants its Strands Agents and LangGraph agents to use a legacy booking mainframe through MCP. The mainframe has no REST API and no OpenAPI specification; tools drive terminal sessions over a proprietary protocol. A single tool call can run for 25 minutes while a manifest is reconciled and must send progress notifications to the agent. Each tool call depends on a terminal connection that is opened earlier in the same MCP session and held in memory between calls, because re-authenticating to the mainframe takes several minutes. The team accepts writing and operating integration code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with semantic search enabled, add OpenAPI and Lambda targets, and have agents use its search tool.
Build MCP servers with an MCP SDK that wrap each group of tools, run them on Amazon ECS, and register the servers in each agent's MCP client.
Create an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, add OpenAPI and Lambda targets, and have each agent call tools/list at startup and bind the tools.
Define the tools as action groups on Amazon Bedrock Agents from their OpenAPI schemas, and call those agents from the other agent frameworks.

explanation: The tools here are stateful and long-running, and no API description exists to convert. The option to 'Build MCP servers with an MCP SDK that wrap each group of tools, run them on Amazon ECS' gives long-lived containers that can hold a terminal connection in memory across the calls of an MCP session, run a 25-minute call and stream progress notifications, and both frameworks reach them with a standard MCP client. Both gateway options, with 'semantic search enabled' or with 'tools/list at startup', rely on 'OpenAPI and Lambda targets': there is no OpenAPI specification, and a Lambda function cannot run for more than 15 minutes or keep an open connection in memory from one invocation to the next, so the 25-minute reconciliation and the held session both fail. The option to 'Define the tools as action groups on Amazon Bedrock Agents from their OpenAPI schemas' has the same gap, since there are no schemas and action group fulfilment would again be a Lambda function, and it does not expose an MCP endpoint to the agents. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-mcp-protocol-contract.html

prompt: A manufacturer hosts an assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and is configuring AgentCore Identity for two tools. The first tool reads a shared engineering document store. It is used by an unattended nightly run that indexes all published documents; no employee is signed in during the run, and the store's administrator has registered the agent as an application with read access to published documents. The second tool calls an inventory API to post stock adjustments. Adjustments are made only in interactive sessions, the API enforces each employee's own entitlements, and its audit log must record the employee as the actor. The inventory API accepts OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens and does not issue static keys. Which combination of configurations meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use an OAuth credential provider with the authorization code grant for the document store so that tokens are bound to each consenting user.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the client credentials grant for the inventory API so that the agent authenticates as a service client.
Use an API key credential provider for the inventory API so that the agent retrieves the key from the token vault when it calls the API.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the client credentials grant for the document store so that the agent authenticates as a service client.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the authorization code grant for the inventory API so that tokens are bound to each consenting user.

explanation: The document tool runs with no user present and the store has registered the agent as an application, which is machine-to-machine access: 'the client credentials grant for the document store' lets the agent authenticate as that service client during the nightly run. The inventory tool must act as the signed-in employee so that entitlements and the audit log apply to that person, which is user-delegated access: 'the authorization code grant for the inventory API' has the employee consent and binds the token to that user. The 'authorization code grant for the document store' needs an interactive user to consent, and the nightly run has none. The 'client credentials grant for the inventory API' would make every adjustment appear as the agent's service identity, so per-employee entitlements and the audit actor are lost. The 'API key credential provider for the inventory API' cannot be used because the API accepts OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens and issues no static keys, and a shared key would not identify the employee either. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/identity-authentication.html

prompt: A consulting firm hosts an assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and is configuring AgentCore Identity for two tools. Employees sign in through the corporate identity provider. The first tool reads files from a cloud document store and must see only the files that the signed-in employee is allowed to see; it is used only while an employee is chatting. The second tool calls an internal inventory API that accepts only registered service clients through OAuth 2.0 and does not issue static keys; the tool is also used by scheduled runs when no employee is present. Security policy forbids long-lived secrets in agent code, environment variables or prompts. Which combination of configurations meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use an OAuth credential provider with the authorization code grant for the document store so that tokens are bound to each consenting user.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the client credentials grant for the inventory API so that the agent authenticates as a service client.
Use an API key credential provider for the inventory API so that the agent retrieves the key from the token vault when it calls the API.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the client credentials grant for the document store so that the agent authenticates as a service client.
Use an OAuth credential provider with the authorization code grant for the inventory API so that tokens are bound to each consenting user.

explanation: The document tool must act on behalf of the signed-in employee, which is user-delegated access: 'the authorization code grant for the document store' has each employee consent, and the token held in the token vault is bound to that user, so the agent sees only that employee's files. The inventory API admits registered service clients and is called when no one is signed in, which is machine-to-machine access: 'the client credentials grant for the inventory API' lets the agent authenticate as a service client. In both cases the credential provider holds the secrets, which satisfies the policy. The 'client credentials grant for the document store' makes the agent act as an application, so access is no longer limited to what one employee may see. The 'authorization code grant for the inventory API' needs a user to consent, which fails for scheduled runs, and the API accepts service clients, not end users. The 'API key credential provider for the inventory API' does not apply because the API authenticates clients through OAuth 2.0 and issues no static keys. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/identity-authentication.html

prompt: A retailer's refund tool is an AWS Lambda function. Three support agents call it through an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, and the returns web portal and a nightly reconciliation job invoke the same function directly without passing through the gateway. Each agent's system prompt says refunds above 500 USD are not allowed, but a red-team exercise used prompt injection to make an agent issue a 2,000 USD refund. The company needs one control that applies to every caller of the tool on every path, does not depend on what a model generates, and rejects an over-limit refund outright unless the signed token passed with the call carries a supervisor role. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for large refunds to each agent's model calls, and review its trace before blocking.
Check the refund amount and the caller's role claim inside the refund tool's AWS Lambda function, and reject calls that break the rule.
Attach an AgentCore Policy engine to the gateway with Cedar policies that test the refund amount and the caller's role claim on each call.
Have the refund tool start an AWS Step Functions execution that holds refunds above the limit at a callback task until a supervisor decides.

explanation: The control has to hold for every path into the tool, and two of the three paths bypass the gateway. The option to 'Check the refund amount and the caller's role claim inside the refund tool's AWS Lambda function' puts one deterministic check at the only point all callers share, independent of any model output. The option to 'Attach an AgentCore Policy engine to the gateway' is deterministic and defined once for the agents, but Policy in AgentCore evaluates traffic that passes through the gateway; the web portal and the nightly job invoke the function directly and would not be checked. The 'Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic' evaluates the text of prompts and responses on each agent's model calls; it does not evaluate a tool call's numeric argument or a role claim, and it does not cover the non-agent callers. The option that 'holds refunds above the limit at a callback task until a supervisor decides' builds an approval flow, whereas the requirement is to reject over-limit refunds outright unless the caller already holds the supervisor role. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/policy.html

prompt: A travel company's support agents, built by three teams, issue refunds through one refund tool that is reachable only through an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Refunds above 500 USD are legitimate but must wait until a duty supervisor approves them in a back-office console, which can take up to 24 hours. Once approved, the refund must be executed automatically, without the customer or the agent asking again; if the supervisor declines, it must be cancelled. The behaviour must not depend on what a model generates, and refunds at or below the limit must run immediately. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic for large refunds to each agent's model calls, and review its trace before blocking.
Check the refund amount and the caller's role claim inside the refund tool's AWS Lambda function, and reject calls that break the rule.
Attach an AgentCore Policy engine to the gateway with Cedar policies that test the refund amount and the caller's role claim on each call.
Have the refund tool start an AWS Step Functions execution that holds refunds above the limit at a callback task until a supervisor decides.

explanation: Over-limit refunds are not to be refused; they are to be held, decided by another person up to a day later, and then completed automatically. The option to 'Have the refund tool start an AWS Step Functions execution that holds refunds above the limit at a callback task until a supervisor decides' does that: a Standard workflow pauses at a `.waitForTaskToken` task with no polling, the console returns the token with `SendTaskSuccess` or `SendTaskFailure`, and the workflow then issues or cancels the refund, all outside the model. The option to 'Attach an AgentCore Policy engine to the gateway' permits or forbids a tool call when it is made; a forbidden refund is simply not executed, and nothing holds it for a supervisor or completes it after approval. The option to 'Check the refund amount and the caller's role claim inside the refund tool's AWS Lambda function' and 'reject calls' likewise discards the legitimate refund. The 'Amazon Bedrock guardrail with a denied topic' acts on model text, which the requirement excludes, and it cannot queue an action for approval. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html

prompt: A payment processor wants a ReAct-style agent that triages declined transactions. Each run asks a model on Amazon Bedrock for a thought and an action, runs the chosen tool, and feeds the observation back, for at most 6 iterations; a run finishes in under 45 seconds. About 40,000 runs start every hour. The tools are read-only lookups, so running a step twice is harmless. Risk officers review and approve the control flow as a state machine definition in Workflow Studio, and they accept per-step records in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The company wants the LOWEST cost per run. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: An Express workflow in AWS Step Functions that loops through a Bedrock InvokeModel task, a Choice state on the answer and a counter, and a tool task.
A Standard workflow in AWS Step Functions that loops through a Bedrock InvokeModel task, a Choice state on the answer and a counter, and a tool task.
A Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime that runs the loop in code with an iteration limit and emits each step as a trace span.
A single AWS Lambda function that runs the loop in code with an iteration counter and writes each step to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

explanation: The risk officers approve the control flow as a state machine definition, so the loop must be expressed in Step Functions; the choice is then between workflow types. Runs are short, very frequent and idempotent, which is the profile of the 'Express workflow': it can run for up to five minutes, is priced by executions, duration and memory instead of by state transition, and its steps can be inspected through CloudWatch Logs, which the officers accept. The 'Standard workflow' with the same loop also works, but it is priced per state transition, and tens of transitions on each of 40,000 runs an hour makes it the costlier choice; its exactly-once semantics and long duration are not needed for 45-second read-only runs. The 'Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime' and the 'single AWS Lambda function' both run the loop in code, so there is no state machine definition for the risk officers to review in Workflow Studio. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html

prompt: A bank is deploying a ReAct-style agent that investigates reconciliation breaks. The loop is already implemented and tested with Strands Agents, and the bank wants to reuse that code without re-expressing it in another form. One investigation runs for up to 3 hours. Between iterations the agent keeps several hundred megabytes of ledger extracts in process memory, and reloading them at every step would be too slow. Each investigation's memory and files must be isolated from other investigations. Risk officers require a step-by-step view of every thought, action and observation, and a run must stop after a fixed number of iterations. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: An Express workflow in AWS Step Functions that loops through a Bedrock InvokeModel task, a Choice state on the answer and a counter, and a tool task.
A Standard workflow in AWS Step Functions that loops through a Bedrock InvokeModel task, a Choice state on the answer and a counter, and a tool task.
A Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime that runs the loop in code with an iteration limit and emits each step as a trace span.
A single AWS Lambda function that runs the loop in code with an iteration counter and writes each step to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

explanation: The loop exists as Strands code, a run lasts hours, and working data stays in process memory between iterations. The 'Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime' hosts that code unchanged: each session gets its own microVM with isolated memory and filesystem, a session can last up to 8 hours, the iteration limit lives in the agent code, and trace spans give the step-by-step view. The 'Standard workflow in AWS Step Functions' could run for 3 hours and records each state, but it requires re-expressing the loop as states, and its tasks are separate invocations that do not share process memory, so the ledger extracts would have to be reloaded at every step. The 'Express workflow' has the same drawbacks and can run for at most five minutes. The 'single AWS Lambda function' would keep the code, but an invocation cannot exceed 15 minutes, far short of a 3-hour investigation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-sessions.html

prompt: An agent orchestrated by an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow calls a partner pricing API through a tool Lambda function. During a partner outage each tool call hung until the function's 15-minute timeout, the workflow retried the task, and the model then asked for the same tool again. Hundreds of executions stayed open for hours. Healthy tool calls return in under 5 seconds; healthy runs can legitimately take 30 minutes and many iterations because of other steps. Prices change every minute, so a stale price must not be used, and when the API is unavailable a run should tell the user promptly instead of being deferred. The team wants to fail fast on a hung call and to stop sending traffic to the API while it is known to be down. Which combination of changes meets these goals? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set a short TimeoutSeconds on the tool task and the function, with a bounded Retry and a Catch that returns an error observation to the model.
Send each tool request to an Amazon SQS queue with the .waitForTaskToken pattern, and let a worker call the API and return the result with the token.
Record repeated tool failures in an Amazon DynamoDB item with a TTL, and check the item before the tool task to skip the call while the circuit is open.
Add a Catch on the tool task that routes to a fallback task, which returns the most recent price for the product from an Amazon DynamoDB cache.
Set TimeoutSeconds on the state machine and keep an iteration counter in the state that a Choice state checks before each model call.

explanation: Two safeguards are missing. A call that normally returns in 5 seconds should not hang for 15 minutes: the option to 'Set a short TimeoutSeconds on the tool task and the function, with a bounded Retry and a Catch' raises `States.Timeout` quickly, limits the retries and hands the model an error observation so the run can tell the user promptly. To stop traffic during the outage, the option to 'Record repeated tool failures in an Amazon DynamoDB item with a TTL' is the circuit breaker from AWS Prescriptive Guidance: the workflow checks the item first and skips the call until the record expires. The option to send requests 'to an Amazon SQS queue with the .waitForTaskToken pattern' defers work until the API recovers, which the stem rules out. The fallback that 'returns the most recent price' from a cache serves a stale price, which is not allowed. The option to 'Set TimeoutSeconds on the state machine' with an iteration counter caps a whole run, but healthy runs legitimately take 30 minutes and many iterations, so a hung call would still wait and calls would still reach the dead API. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/circuit-breaker.html

prompt: An agent orchestrated by an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow produces insurance quotes by calling a partner rating API through a tool Lambda function. The partner allows 5 requests per second and answers immediately with HTTP 429 when the rate is exceeded; calls do not hang. Under load, most tool calls are rejected and quotes are abandoned. The contract requires that every accepted quote request is eventually completed with a live rate, even if that takes hours, and cached rates must not be used. Separately, some executions never finish: the model keeps requesting tools for more than 150 iterations, and model spend on those runs is unbounded. Which combination of changes addresses both problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set a short TimeoutSeconds on the tool task and the function, with a bounded Retry and a Catch that returns an error observation to the model.
Send each tool request to an Amazon SQS queue with the .waitForTaskToken pattern, and let a worker call the API and return the result with the token.
Record repeated tool failures in an Amazon DynamoDB item with a TTL, and check the item before the tool task to skip the call while the circuit is open.
Add a Catch on the tool task that routes to a fallback task, which returns the most recent price for the product from an Amazon DynamoDB cache.
Set TimeoutSeconds on the state machine and keep an iteration counter in the state that a Choice state checks before each model call.

explanation: The first problem is a rate limit combined with a must-complete requirement. The option to 'Send each tool request to an Amazon SQS queue with the .waitForTaskToken pattern' buffers requests, lets a worker drain the queue at the partner's rate, and pauses the Standard workflow without polling until the worker returns the result with the token, so every quote completes with a live rate. The second problem is a runaway loop: the option to 'Set TimeoutSeconds on the state machine and keep an iteration counter' gives an explicit stopping condition and an upper bound on run time and spend. A 'short TimeoutSeconds on the tool task' with a bounded Retry does not help because calls return immediately and are not hung, and its Catch would hand the model an error and abandon the quote. The DynamoDB circuit breaker would 'skip the call while the circuit is open', which drops quote requests that the contract says must complete. The fallback that 'returns the most recent price' from a cache is excluded because cached rates must not be used. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html

prompt: A retailer runs an analytics agent whose only tool is an AWS Lambda function that executes model-generated SQL in Amazon Athena. The agent needs the orders and customers tables in the sales_curated database, and the tool's execution role is already limited to that database. A document uploaded by a user contained hidden instructions, and the agent returned the card_number and email columns of the customers table, which analysts using the agent must not see. The agent must keep access to the other columns of the same tables. The security team wants a preventive control that holds even if the model is manipulated again and that does not depend on recognizing the text of a malicious query. Which change BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Scope the tool's execution role to the approved database's AWS Glue Data Catalog resources, its Amazon S3 prefix and one Athena workgroup.
Parse each generated statement in the tool function and run it if it is a single SELECT statement that references tables on an allow list.
Register the data with AWS Lake Formation and grant the tool's role SELECT on the approved tables with the sensitive columns excluded.
Run the tool's queries in a dedicated Athena workgroup with a per-query data scanned limit so that queries over the limit are cancelled.

explanation: The agent legitimately needs the tables but must be unable to read two columns in them, whatever SQL the model produces. AWS Lake Formation enforces database, table and column-level permissions for Athena queries on registered data, so the option to 'Register the data with AWS Lake Formation and grant the tool's role SELECT on the approved tables with the sensitive columns excluded' makes a query that names those columns fail on authorization, not on text inspection. The option to 'Scope the tool's execution role to the approved database's AWS Glue Data Catalog resources' is already in place and stops at the table: IAM resource-level access to the catalog cannot separate the card_number column from the rest of the customers table. The option to 'Parse each generated statement in the tool function' depends on recognizing query text, which the security team rules out, and a table allow list would still admit the customers table. The 'per-query data scanned limit' is a cost control; a small query that selects the sensitive columns stays under any limit. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/security-athena-lake-formation.html

prompt: A media company runs an analytics agent whose only tool is an AWS Lambda function that executes model-generated SQL in Amazon Athena. The tool's execution role is already limited to the clickstream_curated database, and every column in it is approved for the agent's users. The problem is cost: the model sometimes writes queries without a partition filter that scan the full 3 TB events table, and several such queries ran in one afternoon. Legitimate questions scan less than 5 GB. The finance team wants a preventive control that stops an oversized query however the SQL is written, without inspecting the SQL text and without changing what data the agent may read. Which change BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Scope the tool's execution role to the approved database's AWS Glue Data Catalog resources, its Amazon S3 prefix and one Athena workgroup.
Parse each generated statement in the tool function and run it if it is a single SELECT statement that references tables on an allow list.
Register the data with AWS Lake Formation and grant the tool's role SELECT on the approved tables with the sensitive columns excluded.
Run the tool's queries in a dedicated Athena workgroup with a per-query data scanned limit so that queries over the limit are cancelled.

explanation: Access is already correct here; the risk is the volume of data a generated query scans. Athena workgroups support a per-query data usage control: if a query in the workgroup exceeds the configured amount of data scanned, Athena cancels it. The option to 'Run the tool's queries in a dedicated Athena workgroup with a per-query data scanned limit' therefore stops a full-table scan regardless of how the SQL was written, while questions that scan under 5 GB are unaffected. The option to 'Scope the tool's execution role' to the approved database is already in place and says nothing about how much of an approved table a query reads. The Lake Formation grant 'with the sensitive columns excluded' changes what data the agent may read, which finance does not want, and column permissions do not limit bytes scanned. The option to 'Parse each generated statement in the tool function' inspects the SQL text, which the requirement excludes, and a single SELECT on an allowed table can still omit the partition filter. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/workgroups-setting-control-limits-cloudwatch.html

prompt: A procurement company uses an agent in an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow to draft supplier contracts. Before a contract is sent, it must be approved by both a finance reviewer and a legal reviewer, each independently. Reviewers record their decisions only in a third-party ticketing product. That product cannot call AWS APIs or send webhooks; an existing job copies each ticket's status into an Amazon DynamoDB table every 10 minutes. Reviewers never open any other application. Overdue tickets are chased by the ticketing product's own reminders, so the workflow needs no deadline or escalation of its own. Which combination of design elements meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Place the approval step in a Parallel state with one branch per required approver so that the workflow continues after every branch completes.
Make the approval step a task that uses .waitForTaskToken, and have the decision endpoint call SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with the token.
Set HeartbeatSeconds on the approval task and have the review application call SendTaskHeartbeat while a reviewer has the item open.
Set TimeoutSeconds on the approval task and add a Catch for States.Timeout that routes the execution to an escalation step.
Follow the notification with a Wait state and a task that reads the decision from a table, looping through a Choice state until one exists.

explanation: Two facts drive the design: two independent approvals are required, and the only place a decision appears is a table that a job refreshes every 10 minutes. The option to 'Place the approval step in a Parallel state with one branch per required approver' models the finance and legal approvals so that the contract proceeds only when both branches finish. Inside each branch, the option to 'Follow the notification with a Wait state and a task that reads the decision from a table' is the workable mechanism, because polling the table is the only way the workflow can learn of a decision. The '.waitForTaskToken' task needs something to call `SendTaskSuccess` or `SendTaskFailure`, and the ticketing product cannot call AWS APIs or send webhooks. Setting 'HeartbeatSeconds' requires a review application that sends `SendTaskHeartbeat`; reviewers use only the ticketing product, so the task would time out. The 'TimeoutSeconds on the approval task' with a Catch adds a deadline and escalation that the stem says the workflow does not need, since the ticketing product chases overdue tickets. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-parallel.html

prompt: A legal-tech company uses an agent in an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow to draft contract amendments. Before an amendment is sent to a counterparty, one lawyer must approve or reject it from a link in an email; the link calls an Amazon API Gateway endpoint backed by a Lambda function that the company controls. Lawyers usually respond within hours but may take up to 3 business days, and the workflow must continue as soon as the decision arrives. If nobody decides within 5 days, the amendment must be passed to a partner. The company does not want state transitions spent on checking for a decision while the workflow waits, and lawyers use no application other than email. Which combination of design elements meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Place the approval step in a Parallel state with one branch per required approver so that the workflow continues after every branch completes.
Make the approval step a task that uses .waitForTaskToken, and have the decision endpoint call SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with the token.
Set HeartbeatSeconds on the approval task and have the review application call SendTaskHeartbeat while a reviewer has the item open.
Set TimeoutSeconds on the approval task and add a Catch for States.Timeout that routes the execution to an escalation step.
Follow the notification with a Wait state and a task that reads the decision from a table, looping through a Choice state until one exists.

explanation: The callback pattern fits a single human decision that arrives at an unknown time. The option to 'Make the approval step a task that uses .waitForTaskToken, and have the decision endpoint call SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with the token' pauses the Standard workflow with no polling and resumes it the moment the lawyer clicks the link. Without a limit the task would wait until the one-year execution quota, so the option to 'Set TimeoutSeconds on the approval task and add a Catch for States.Timeout' provides the 5-day hand-off to a partner. The 'Parallel state with one branch per required approver' is for several independent approvals, and one lawyer decides here. Setting 'HeartbeatSeconds' needs a review application that calls `SendTaskHeartbeat`; lawyers act from email only, so no heartbeat would arrive and the task would fail early. The 'Wait state and a task that reads the decision from a table' is polling: it spends state transitions on checks and delays the workflow until the next check instead of continuing as soon as the decision arrives. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html

prompt: A subscription business has an Amazon Bedrock agent with an action group whose cancelSubscription action is fulfilled by an AWS Lambda function. The company is moving billing to a provider whose cancellation API can be called only from the mobile app through the provider's on-device SDK, using the customer's signed-in session; the session token must not leave the device, so the Lambda function can no longer perform the cancellation. The app must show the customer the exact action and parameters before it runs, and the agent must be told the outcome, including a refusal, so that it can continue the conversation. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Change the action group to return control, and have the app carry out the action itself and send the outcome in returnControlInvocationResults.
Have the action's Lambda function start an AWS Step Functions execution that waits at a callback task for approval, and return a pending status.
Enable user confirmation on the action, and have the app show the returned invocationInputs and reply with a confirmationState of CONFIRM or DENY.
Add an instruction to the agent to restate the action and its parameters and to ask the customer to reply YES before it calls the action.

explanation: The cancellation can now be executed only on the device, so the agent has to hand the action to the application. With return of control, the `InvokeAgent` response returns the action and its parameters in `invocationInputs`; the option to 'Change the action group to return control, and have the app carry out the action itself and send the outcome in returnControlInvocationResults' lets the app display the details, call the provider's SDK with the on-device session, and report success or the customer's refusal back to the agent. The option to 'Enable user confirmation on the action' also shows a confirm or deny prompt, but after `CONFIRM` the agent invokes the action group's Lambda function, which cannot reach the provider's API. The option in which the 'Lambda function' starts 'an AWS Step Functions execution' keeps execution in the backend as well, where the session token is not available. The option to 'Add an instruction to the agent' relies on the model's wording, gives the app no structured parameters to display, and still ends with the Lambda function being called. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-returncontrol.html

prompt: A B2B software vendor has an Amazon Bedrock agent with an action group whose cancelSubscription action is fulfilled by an AWS Lambda function that contains the billing logic. After several costly cancellations, the vendor requires that a cancellation of an enterprise contract is approved by the customer's account manager, who is a different person from the user chatting with the agent and who typically responds by email the next day. The agent should tell the requester that the cancellation is pending and end the conversation. The billing logic must stay in the backend, the cancellation must run automatically once approved, and the control must not depend on the model following an instruction. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Change the action group to return control, and have the app carry out the action itself and send the outcome in returnControlInvocationResults.
Have the action's Lambda function start an AWS Step Functions execution that waits at a callback task for approval, and return a pending status.
Enable user confirmation on the action, and have the app show the returned invocationInputs and reply with a confirmationState of CONFIRM or DENY.
Add an instruction to the agent to restate the action and its parameters and to ask the customer to reply YES before it calls the action.

explanation: The approver is a third party who answers hours later, outside the chat session. The option to 'Have the action's Lambda function start an AWS Step Functions execution that waits at a callback task for approval, and return a pending status' keeps the billing logic in the backend: a Standard workflow pauses at a `.waitForTaskToken` task until the account manager's decision returns the token, then runs or abandons the cancellation, while the agent immediately tells the requester that it is pending. The option to 'Enable user confirmation on the action' asks the user of the application to confirm or deny within the same agent exchange; it has no way to route the decision to another person the next day. The option to 'Change the action group to return control' moves execution into the app, but the billing logic must stay in the backend and the app's user is still not the approver. The option to 'Add an instruction to the agent' asks the chatting customer for a YES and depends on the model obeying, which the requirement excludes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-to-resource.html

prompt: A retailer's Strands agent uses a model on Amazon Bedrock with two Lambda-backed tools, get_order_status and get_order_history. Traces show that the model picks the right tool and passes well-formed 10-digit order IDs. Two problems remain. About 2% of calls fail because the order service behind the tools returns HTTP 503 for a few seconds during deployments; the same call succeeds when it is repeated, but today the function raises the error and the agent tells the customer that the order cannot be found. And for business accounts with thousands of orders, get_order_history returns the full records as several megabytes of JSON, which exceeds the model's input limit. Many conversations start with questions that need no tool. Which combination of changes MOST improves reliability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Validate the arguments in the function and return a tool result with an error status and a message that states the expected format.
Wrap the backend call in retries with exponential backoff and jitter so that a failed request is repeated before a result is returned.
Rewrite each tool description to say when to use it and what it returns, and constrain the parameter in the input schema with a pattern.
Return a trimmed set of fields from the tool, with a page size limit and a cursor parameter that the model uses to request further results.
Set toolChoice on the first model call of each conversation so that the model must request a named tool before it writes any text.

explanation: Both problems sit behind the tool interface, not in tool selection. The 503 responses are transient and succeed on a repeat, so the option to 'Wrap the backend call in retries with exponential backoff and jitter' absorbs them inside the function before the model sees a failure. The oversized history is a result-shaping problem: the option to 'Return a trimmed set of fields from the tool, with a page size limit and a cursor parameter' keeps each tool result within the model's input limit and lets the model ask for more when needed. The option to 'Validate the arguments in the function and return a tool result with an error status' targets malformed input, but the traces show the arguments are well formed. The option to 'Rewrite each tool description' and add a schema pattern targets wrong tool choice and bad arguments, neither of which occurs here. Setting 'toolChoice on the first model call' forces a tool request even though many conversations start with questions that need no tool, and it fixes neither the 503 errors nor the payload size. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/retry-backoff.html

prompt: A retailer's Strands agent uses a model on Amazon Bedrock with two Lambda-backed tools, get_order_status and get_order_history. Both tool descriptions read 'Gets order information', and order_id is declared as a plain string. Traces show the model passing values such as 'order #12345' or a customer email as order_id; the function then raises an unhandled exception and the customer receives a generic failure. In other traces the model calls get_order_history when the customer asked where a parcel is. Order IDs are 10 digits. The order service itself is healthy and responds in milliseconds, and its responses are a few hundred bytes. Many conversations start with questions that need no tool. Which combination of changes MOST improves reliability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Validate the arguments in the function and return a tool result with an error status and a message that states the expected format.
Wrap the backend call in retries with exponential backoff and jitter so that a failed request is repeated before a result is returned.
Rewrite each tool description to say when to use it and what it returns, and constrain the parameter in the input schema with a pattern.
Return a trimmed set of fields from the tool, with a page size limit and a cursor parameter that the model uses to request further results.
Set toolChoice on the first model call of each conversation so that the model must request a named tool before it writes any text.

explanation: The faults are in the tool definitions and the error path. The model chooses a tool and fills its parameters from the name, description and input schema, so the option to 'Rewrite each tool description to say when to use it and what it returns, and constrain the parameter in the input schema with a pattern' fixes the confusion between the two tools and reduces malformed IDs. For arguments that still arrive malformed, the option to 'Validate the arguments in the function and return a tool result with an error status and a message that states the expected format' uses the `status` field of the Converse `toolResult` block so that the model can correct the value or ask the customer, instead of an unhandled exception. The 'retries with exponential backoff and jitter' repeat a deterministic failure on the same bad input; the service is healthy, so nothing transient exists to retry. Returning 'a trimmed set of fields' with paging solves a payload-size problem, and responses here are a few hundred bytes. Setting 'toolChoice on the first model call' forces a tool request in conversations that need none and does not improve which tool or which argument is chosen. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_ToolResultBlock.html

prompt: A media company exposes two sets of tools to its agents through MCP. Both sets are already implemented as MCP servers with an MCP SDK, and the company wants to reuse that server code as it is. The first set performs lookups against Amazon DynamoDB that finish in under a second. The second set calls a rights-pricing API; each call takes 5 to 20 seconds, and the only data carried between calls is a small JSON cursor that can be stored anywhere. Traffic for both sets is bursty, with idle periods that last hours. The company wants the MOST cost-effective hosting that meets these needs. Which approach should it choose?

options.text: Host both sets as stateless MCP servers on AWS Lambda behind function URLs, and keep any data shared between calls in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Host both sets as MCP servers in one Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with session affinity enabled.
Host the first set as a stateless MCP server on AWS Lambda and the second set as an MCP server on Amazon ECS with session affinity enabled.
Implement both sets as AWS Lambda function handlers and expose them as Lambda targets on an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: Both tool sets are short-running and hold no in-process state, traffic is bursty with long idle periods, and the existing MCP server code is to be reused. The option to 'Host both sets as stateless MCP servers on AWS Lambda behind function URLs, and keep any data shared between calls in an Amazon DynamoDB table' fits each constraint: calls of up to 20 seconds are well inside the Lambda limit, the cursor is stored externally, and nothing is billed while idle.
