The option to 'Host both sets as MCP servers in one Amazon ECS service' keeps tasks running, and billed, through the idle hours. The split option that puts 'the second set as an MCP server on Amazon ECS' has the same idle cost for a tool set that needs neither long calls nor in-memory sessions. The option to 'Implement both sets as AWS Lambda function handlers and expose them as Lambda targets' on a gateway is also pay-per-use, but Lambda targets are plain function handlers with tool schemas, so the existing MCP server code would be replaced instead of reused. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-mcp-protocol-contract.html

prompt: A media company exposes two sets of tools to its agents through MCP. The first set performs lookups against Amazon DynamoDB and receives a steady 300 requests per second around the clock from a large fleet of agents. The second set drives headless browser sessions: one tool call can run for 25 minutes, streams progress notifications, and relies on a browser process that is kept in memory across calls in the same MCP session. The platform team already operates Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate with one deployment pipeline, runs nothing on AWS Lambda, and wants a single deployable unit. Which approach meets the technical needs with the FEWEST changes to the existing platform?

options.text: Host both sets as stateless MCP servers on AWS Lambda behind function URLs, and keep any data shared between calls in an Amazon DynamoDB table.
Host both sets as MCP servers in one Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with session affinity enabled.
Host the first set as a stateless MCP server on AWS Lambda and the second set as an MCP server on Amazon ECS with session affinity enabled.
Implement both sets as AWS Lambda function handlers and expose them as Lambda targets on an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway.

explanation: The browser tools need a long-lived process: a call lasts 25 minutes and depends on a browser held in memory across the calls of a session. The lookup tools have steady traffic with no idle time to save on. The platform team runs ECS only and wants one deployable unit, so the option to 'Host both sets as MCP servers in one Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer with session affinity enabled' meets the technical needs with the existing pipeline. Hosting 'both sets as stateless MCP servers on AWS Lambda' fails for the browser tools, because an invocation cannot exceed 15 minutes and a running browser process cannot be kept in a DynamoDB table between invocations. The option to implement both sets 'as AWS Lambda function handlers' behind a gateway has the same 15-minute and in-memory limits. The split design with 'the first set as a stateless MCP server on AWS Lambda' is technically sound, but it adds a second hosting model and pipeline to a team that runs nothing on Lambda, for lookups whose constant load leaves no idle cost to recover. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html

prompt: A software company is building an outage-investigation system with Strands Agents. Specialist agents cover networking, databases, deployments and security. Which specialist is needed next depends on what the previous one finds, and the team has been unable to map the possible sequences in advance; an investigation often returns to a specialist that worked on it earlier. An earlier design in which a coordinating agent relayed every exchange lost detail in its re-summaries and doubled the number of model calls, so specialists must pass the investigation directly to one another together with the accumulated findings. Which multi-agent pattern BEST fits these requirements?

options.text: A Graph in which the agents are nodes and developers define the edges and their conditions, including edges that loop back to earlier nodes.
A Swarm in which the agents share working context and each agent decides when to hand the task off to another agent it judges more suitable.
An orchestrator agent that is given the specialist agents as tools and decides at run time which specialist to call for each request.
A Workflow in which the agents' tasks form a dependency graph that is fixed in advance and independent tasks are executed in parallel.

explanation: The path cannot be mapped in advance, specialists must hand work directly to each other with the accumulated findings, and a central relay has already proved lossy and costly. That describes the 'Swarm in which the agents share working context and each agent decides when to hand the task off': the route emerges from autonomous handoffs, shared context travels with the task, and an agent can hand back to one that worked earlier. The 'Graph in which the agents are nodes and developers define the edges' needs the transitions to be defined by developers beforehand, which the team could not do. The 'orchestrator agent that is given the specialist agents as tools' is the coordinating design that failed: every exchange passes through the orchestrator, which re-summarises results and adds a model call per hop. The 'Workflow in which the agents' tasks form a dependency graph that is fixed in advance' is a predetermined, acyclic task graph, so it can neither choose the next specialist from findings nor return to an earlier one. Read more: https://strandsagents.com/docs/user-guide/sdk/multi-agent/multi-agent-patterns/

prompt: A retail bank is building a customer assistant with Strands Agents. One front agent must own the whole conversation with the customer and write every reply, because compliance reviews a single prompt for tone and disclosures. Specialist agents for mortgages, cards and foreign exchange each answer one focused question and return their result; they keep no conversation state and must not address the customer or call one another. Most requests need exactly one specialist, chosen from the content of the request, and there is no fixed sequence of steps. The team wants the pattern that needs the LEAST orchestration code. Which multi-agent pattern BEST fits these requirements?

options.text: A Graph in which the agents are nodes and developers define the edges and their conditions, including edges that loop back to earlier nodes.
A Swarm in which the agents share working context and each agent decides when to hand the task off to another agent it judges more suitable.
An orchestrator agent that is given the specialist agents as tools and decides at run time which specialist to call for each request.
A Workflow in which the agents' tasks form a dependency graph that is fixed in advance and independent tasks are executed in parallel.

explanation: One agent keeps the conversation and the final wording, and specialists behave like functions: called with a focused question, returning a result, never talking to the customer or to each other. That is the 'orchestrator agent that is given the specialist agents as tools and decides at run time which specialist to call', which the Strands documentation describes as the simplest composition, so it also needs the least orchestration code. In the 'Swarm in which the agents share working context', control is handed from agent to agent and the specialist that ends up holding the task produces the answer, which breaks the rule that only the front agent writes replies and that specialists do not call one another. The 'Graph in which the agents are nodes and developers define the edges' passes control along predefined edges and requires the team to build and maintain a flow, although the stem says there is no fixed sequence. The 'Workflow in which the agents' tasks form a dependency graph that is fixed in advance' runs the same predetermined tasks every time, whereas each request here needs one specialist chosen from its content. Read more: https://strandsagents.com/docs/user-guide/sdk/multi-agent/multi-agent-patterns/

prompt: A tax-preparation company extracts data from uploaded documents with a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock, invoked by AWS Lambda functions while the customer waits on the screen. During the 5-week filing season, volume is steady and well above the on-demand quota, the functions receive ThrottlingException errors, and a further quota increase was declined. Outside the season, on-demand capacity is sufficient. Contracts require that prompts are processed only in the current Region, and the validated prompts must keep using this model, which supports Provisioned Throughput. Finance wants the LOWEST cost that guarantees the throughput for the season. Which option meets these requirements?

options.text: Switch the functions to a geographic cross-Region inference profile for the same model so that requests can draw on capacity in other Regions.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model with no commitment, and invoke the provisioned model ARN from the functions.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model with a 6-month commitment, and invoke the provisioned model ARN from the functions.
Write the prompts to Amazon S3 and process them with batch inference jobs for the same model, reading the results from Amazon S3.

explanation: The need is guaranteed real-time throughput for one model in one Region, for about 5 weeks. Provisioned Throughput buys model units at an hourly price, and the option to purchase it 'with no commitment' can be deleted when the season ends, so the company pays for the capacity only while it is needed. The same purchase 'with a 6-month commitment' has a lower hourly price, but it cannot be deleted until the term is over, so the company would pay for roughly five months of capacity that on-demand already covers. The 'geographic cross-Region inference profile' may relieve throttling, but it processes requests in other Regions, which the contracts forbid, and it remains on-demand capacity instead of a guarantee. The option to process prompts 'with batch inference jobs' is asynchronous, with results written to Amazon S3 when a job completes, which does not work while a customer waits on the screen. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A claims processor runs two workloads on one foundation model in Amazon Bedrock in a single AWS Region. Interactive requests during the day stay within the on-demand quota. Each night, AWS Lambda functions also re-extract a back-file of about 2 million archived documents; these calls receive ThrottlingException errors, and a further quota increase was declined. Nobody waits for the back-file results, which are needed by the next morning. Contracts require that prompts are processed only in that Region, and the validated prompts must keep using this model. Finance will not pay for capacity that is billed around the clock but used for a few hours a night. Which option is the MOST cost-effective way to complete the nightly work?

options.text: Switch the functions to a geographic cross-Region inference profile for the same model so that requests can draw on capacity in other Regions.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model with no commitment, and invoke the provisioned model ARN from the functions.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model with a 6-month commitment, and invoke the provisioned model ARN from the functions.
Write the prompts to Amazon S3 and process them with batch inference jobs for the same model, reading the results from Amazon S3.

explanation: The throttled work is a large set of prompts that is known up front and has no one waiting on it. The option to 'Write the prompts to Amazon S3 and process them with batch inference jobs for the same model' submits them as an asynchronous job and writes the responses to Amazon S3, which suits a next-morning deadline, keeps the same model and Region, and takes the back-file out of the real-time invocation path that is being throttled. Both Provisioned Throughput options would remove the throttling, but Provisioned Throughput is billed hourly until it is deleted, so 'with no commitment' or 'with a 6-month commitment' the company pays around the clock for capacity used a few hours a night, which finance has ruled out; the 6-month term also cannot be deleted early. The 'geographic cross-Region inference profile' sends requests to other Regions, which breaks the contractual rule that prompts are processed only in the current Region. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/batch-inference.html

prompt: A law firm distilled a clause-classification model that it hosts itself on Amazon SageMaker AI because the weights must stay in the firm's account. The model is 300 MB, runs on CPU and classifies a clause in about 400 milliseconds. The firm's intake web form calls the model and must receive the label in the same HTTP response within a few seconds; request payloads are under 1 MB. About 200 requests arrive per day in bursts during business hours and none overnight or at weekends. An occasional slower first request after an idle period is acceptable. The firm wants the LOWEST cost that meets these needs. Which deployment should it use?

options.text: A real-time endpoint on a GPU instance with target tracking auto scaling and a minimum of one instance, invoked synchronously.
An Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero instances on queue backlog and publishes completion notices through Amazon SNS.
A Serverless Inference endpoint with 6 GB of memory that is invoked synchronously and is billed for the compute used per request.
A batch transform job, started on a schedule, that reads the accumulated inputs from Amazon S3 and writes the outputs to Amazon S3.

explanation: The model is small and CPU-based, the caller needs a synchronous answer, traffic is intermittent with long idle periods, and cold starts are tolerated. That is the profile of the 'Serverless Inference endpoint with 6 GB of memory': it supports payloads up to 4 MB and processing times up to 60 seconds, scales down to zero when there are no requests, and bills for the compute used per request. The 'real-time endpoint on a GPU instance' with a minimum of one instance also answers synchronously, but it is billed through every night and weekend for a model that does not need a GPU. The 'Asynchronous Inference endpoint' can scale to zero, but it queues requests and delivers results to Amazon S3 with a notification, so the web form would not get the label in the same HTTP response. The 'batch transform job, started on a schedule' processes accumulated inputs offline, which cannot serve an interactive form. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/serverless-endpoints.html

prompt: A law firm fine-tuned an open-weight LLM that it hosts itself on Amazon SageMaker AI because the weights must stay in the firm's account. The model summarizes deposition transcripts on a GPU instance, and one summary takes several minutes. Court reporters upload the day's transcripts, about 3,000 files, to Amazon S3 by 20:00, and paralegals need all summaries by 07:00 the next morning; nobody requests a summary during the day. The firm's small team wants no endpoint, request queue or scaling policy to exist between the nightly runs, and it wants the LOWEST cost that meets these needs. Which deployment should it use?

options.text: A real-time endpoint on a GPU instance with target tracking auto scaling and a minimum of one instance, invoked synchronously.
An Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero instances on queue backlog and publishes completion notices through Amazon SNS.
A Serverless Inference endpoint with 6 GB of memory that is invoked synchronously and is billed for the compute used per request.
A batch transform job, started on a schedule, that reads the accumulated inputs from Amazon S3 and writes the outputs to Amazon S3.

explanation: All inputs are available up front each evening, the deadline is the next morning, and the team wants nothing left running or configured between runs. A 'batch transform job, started on a schedule' is intended for offline processing when large amounts of data are available upfront and no persistent endpoint is needed: it starts GPU instances for the job, reads the transcripts from Amazon S3, writes the summaries and releases the instances. The 'Asynchronous Inference endpoint' handles long processing times and can scale to zero, but it is a persistent endpoint with a request queue and scaling policies to maintain, which the team has ruled out. The 'real-time endpoint on a GPU instance' with a minimum of one instance is billed all day although nobody requests summaries then, and regular responses are limited to 60 seconds of processing. The 'Serverless Inference endpoint' does not support GPUs and limits processing to 60 seconds, so it cannot run summaries that take minutes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model-options.html

prompt: A team is deploying a 70-billion-parameter open-weight LLM to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on a multi-GPU instance with a large model inference (LMI) container. The artifacts are a single 140 GB model.tar.gz object in Amazon S3. Endpoint creation runs for a long time and then fails. Amazon CloudWatch Logs show the artifact still being downloaded and extracted, followed by a health check timeout; there are no out-of-memory messages, and the same model loads on the same instance type in a notebook. The weights have been validated and must be deployed without modification. Which combination of changes will MOST likely allow the endpoint to reach InService? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move the production variant to an instance type with more total GPU memory and let the container shard the model across the GPUs.
Upload the artifacts uncompressed under an S3 prefix and reference them through ModelDataSource with CompressionType set to None.
Call the endpoint with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream so that tokens are returned as a stream while the model generates.
Increase ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds and ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds on the production variant.
Quantize the weights to a lower-precision format with a SageMaker AI inference optimization job before deploying the model.

explanation: The logs point to load time, not capacity: 140 GB cannot be downloaded, extracted and loaded before the default timeouts expire. AWS recommends deploying very large models uncompressed, so the option to 'Upload the artifacts uncompressed under an S3 prefix and reference them through ModelDataSource with CompressionType set to None' removes the extraction step. AWS also documents raising `ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds` for models larger than 40 GB and `ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds` when logs show a health check timeout on a correctly configured container, which is the option to increase both on the production variant. Moving to 'an instance type with more total GPU memory' addresses out-of-memory errors, and the logs show none; the model already loads on this instance type. Calling the endpoint 'with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream' affects invocations of an endpoint that is InService, and this one fails during creation. The option to 'Quantize the weights' would shrink the artifacts, but the validated weights must be deployed without modification, and a quantized model might be less accurate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/large-model-inference-hosting.html

prompt: A team is deploying a 70-billion-parameter open-weight LLM to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with a large model inference (LMI) container. The artifacts are already stored uncompressed under an S3 prefix and download in about 9 minutes, well inside the configured timeouts. Endpoint creation fails shortly after the download: Amazon CloudWatch Logs show a CUDA out-of-memory error while the container loads the weights onto the instance's four 24 GB GPUs. In tests on a larger instance in a notebook the model loads, but long-document generations take up to 4 minutes, and the application's InvokeEndpoint calls would fail at 60 seconds. The weights have been validated and must be deployed at full precision. Which combination of changes addresses both problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move the production variant to an instance type with more total GPU memory and let the container shard the model across the GPUs.
Upload the artifacts uncompressed under an S3 prefix and reference them through ModelDataSource with CompressionType set to None.
Call the endpoint with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream so that tokens are returned as a stream while the model generates.
Increase ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds and ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds on the production variant.
Quantize the weights to a lower-precision format with a SageMaker AI inference optimization job before deploying the model.

explanation: Two separate limits are hit. The weights do not fit in 96 GB of GPU memory, so the option to 'Move the production variant to an instance type with more total GPU memory and let the container shard the model across the GPUs' fixes the load failure, as the notebook test confirmed. Real-time inference allows 60 seconds of processing for regular responses and 8 minutes for streaming responses, so the option to 'Call the endpoint with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream' lets 4-minute generations complete. The option to 'Upload the artifacts uncompressed under an S3 prefix' is already in place. Increasing 'ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds and ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds' targets download and health check timeouts, but the download finishes in 9 minutes and the failure is an out-of-memory error. The option to 'Quantize the weights to a lower-precision format' would reduce the memory needed, but the validated weights must be deployed at full precision, and AWS notes that a quantized model might be less accurate than its source. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model-options.html

prompt: A company hosts three fine-tuned 7-billion-parameter models, each on its own Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with one ml.g5.12xlarge instance (4 GPUs). Each model fits on a single GPU and average GPU utilization is below 15%. The models belong to three business units, and a compliance rule forbids them from sharing an instance. Staff around the world use the tools at a low, constant rate 24 hours a day; applications call the endpoints synchronously, expect an answer within 2 seconds, and a failed request is not acceptable. The models are budgeted to run unchanged for at least three years. Which combination of actions gives the LARGEST reduction in hosting cost within these constraints? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploy the three models as inference components on one endpoint, with each component reserving one accelerator on shared instances.
Purchase a SageMaker AI Savings Plan with a one-year term sized to the endpoints' steady hourly instance usage.
Move each endpoint to a single-GPU instance type of the same family, such as ml.g5.2xlarge, with one model per instance.
Set the endpoint's managed instance scaling minimum to zero and add a step scaling policy on a CloudWatch alarm to scale out from zero.
Move each model to an Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero instances when its request queue is empty.

explanation: The endpoints must stay separate, always on and synchronous, so the savings have to come from the size and the price of the instances. Each model uses one of four GPUs, so the option to 'Move each endpoint to a single-GPU instance type of the same family' removes the three idle GPUs per endpoint. Because usage is constant and budgeted for years, the option to 'Purchase a SageMaker AI Savings Plan with a one-year term' lowers the price of that steady instance usage in exchange for a commitment the company can make. The option to 'Deploy the three models as inference components on one endpoint' places them on shared instances, which the compliance rule forbids. Setting the 'managed instance scaling minimum to zero' means requests fail for several minutes while an instance is provisioned, which is not acceptable, there is no idle period to exploit, and scaling to zero requires inference components. The 'Asynchronous Inference endpoint' queues requests and returns results through Amazon S3, so applications would not get a synchronous answer within 2 seconds. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/latest/userguide/what-is-savings-plans.html

prompt: A company hosts three fine-tuned 7-billion-parameter models for internal tools, each on its own Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with one ml.g5.12xlarge instance (4 GPUs). Each model fits on a single GPU, average GPU utilization is below 15%, and the tools are used only during business hours. The tools call the endpoints synchronously and their integration cannot be changed. Users have agreed that the first requests after an idle period may fail and be retried for a few minutes while capacity starts. The tools may be retired within months, so finance will not sign any term commitment. Which combination of actions gives the LARGEST reduction in hosting cost without changing the models? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploy the three models as inference components on one endpoint, with each component reserving one accelerator on shared instances.
Purchase a SageMaker AI Savings Plan with a one-year term sized to the endpoints' steady hourly instance usage.
Move each endpoint to a single-GPU instance type of the same family, such as ml.g5.2xlarge, with one model per instance.
Set the endpoint's managed instance scaling minimum to zero and add a step scaling policy on a CloudWatch alarm to scale out from zero.
Move each model to an Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero instances when its request queue is empty.

explanation: Two sources of waste exist: twelve GPUs for three models that need one each, and instances that run all night. The option to 'Deploy the three models as inference components on one endpoint, with each component reserving one accelerator' packs the models onto one 4-GPU instance. An endpoint that hosts inference components can also scale in to zero instances: the option to set the 'managed instance scaling minimum to zero and add a step scaling policy on a CloudWatch alarm' removes the overnight cost, and the failed first requests during provisioning are accepted by the users. The 'SageMaker AI Savings Plan with a one-year term' is a commitment that finance has ruled out. Moving 'each endpoint to a single-GPU instance type' still leaves three instances running every night and weekend, and those separate endpoints cannot scale to zero because that requires inference components. The 'Asynchronous Inference endpoint' also scales to zero, but it exchanges requests and results through a queue and Amazon S3, which would change the tools' synchronous integration. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling-zero-instances.html

prompt: A contact center serves a self-hosted LLM from an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with response streaming. Auto scaling uses target tracking on SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance. Every weekday at 08:00, when the day shift logs in, traffic rises tenfold within 2 minutes and then stays flat until the evening. A new GPU instance takes about 7 minutes to become ready, so time to first token is poor for the first several minutes of every shift. Managers require that latency is within target from the first minute of the shift, and the traffic pattern has been the same for a year. Which change BEST addresses the problem?

options.text: Lower the target value for SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance so that the existing policy adds instances at a smaller request count.
Use target tracking on the SageMakerVariantConcurrentRequestsPerModelHighResolution metric so that scaling follows requests in flight.
Add scheduled scaling actions that raise the minimum instance count ahead of the hours of the day when the load is known to rise.
Use target tracking on a customized metric specification for the average GPU utilization that the endpoint's instances report.

explanation: The surge arrives at a known time, completes in 2 minutes, and a new instance needs 7 minutes. Any policy that waits for a metric to rise starts provisioning after the surge has begun, so capacity is late whatever the metric is. The option to 'Add scheduled scaling actions that raise the minimum instance count ahead of the hours of the day when the load is known to rise' has the instances InService before 08:00, which is the only way to meet the latency target from the first minute. Target tracking on 'SageMakerVariantConcurrentRequestsPerModelHighResolution' reacts faster than standard metrics because it emits data every 10 seconds, but it is still reactive: it would trigger at about 08:00 and the capacity would arrive about 7 minutes later. The option to 'Lower the target value' of the existing policy and the 'customized metric specification for the average GPU utilization' have the same flaw, since both respond only after load has risen, and a lower target also over-provisions during the flat part of the day. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling-add-code-define.html

prompt: A search company serves a self-hosted embedding model from an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Every request embeds one fixed-size passage and occupies a GPU for about 80 milliseconds, so load is proportional to the request count. Auto scaling uses target tracking on SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance with a target that was set for an older, larger instance type; load tests show that the current instances saturate at well below that value, so latency degrades before instances are added. Traffic rises and falls gradually over tens of minutes with no fixed daily pattern. Under the company's change policy, parameter changes to an existing scaling policy are pre-approved, while new policies or metrics need a four-week review. Which change addresses the problem with the FEWEST changes?

options.text: Lower the target value for SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance so that the existing policy adds instances at a smaller request count.
Use target tracking on the SageMakerVariantConcurrentRequestsPerModelHighResolution metric so that scaling follows requests in flight.
Add scheduled scaling actions that raise the minimum instance count ahead of the hours of the day when the load is known to rise.
Use target tracking on a customized metric specification for the average GPU utilization that the endpoint's instances report.

explanation: Requests are uniform, so invocations per instance is a faithful measure of load here; the policy scales late only because its target is above the point at which the current instances saturate. The option to 'Lower the target value for SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance' corrects that with a parameter change to the existing policy, which is pre-approved, and gradual traffic changes give a one-minute metric ample time to react. Target tracking on 'SageMakerVariantConcurrentRequestsPerModelHighResolution' is valuable when request durations vary widely or traffic spikes within seconds; neither applies, and it is a new policy and metric that would wait four weeks for review. The 'scheduled scaling actions' assume the load rises at known hours, but the stem says there is no fixed daily pattern. The 'customized metric specification for the average GPU utilization' is likewise a new metric that needs the review and must be tested before production use, with no benefit over a correctly set request-count target for uniform requests. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling-add-code-define.html

prompt: A telecom's support assistant sends every question to a large model on Amazon Bedrock. The questions cover a narrow domain: plans, billing and device settings. A new service-level agreement requires a p95 response time of 1.5 seconds for every question, and the large model takes about 4 seconds even on simple ones. A smaller model from the same family meets the latency target but scores 71% on the company's evaluation set against 93% for the large model. Model invocation logging has captured 200,000 prompts with the large model's responses, and the company has an ML engineer available. It must also cut inference cost substantially. Which approach BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Send each question to the small model first, and call the large model when the small model's structured output flags that its confidence is low.
Create an Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt router over the two models, and send every question to the router's endpoint.
Distill the large model into the small model with Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation, using the logged prompts, and serve the distilled model.
Keep the large model for every question, and place a prompt cache checkpoint after the static policy text at the start of each prompt.

explanation: The service-level agreement applies to every question, and the large model takes 4 seconds, so no design that still calls the large model can comply. The only way to get the large model's quality at the small model's speed and price is to move that quality into the small model: the option to 'Distill the large model into the small model with Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation, using the logged prompts' fine-tunes the student on the teacher's responses for this narrow use case, and the invocation logs already hold the training data. The option to 'Send each question to the small model first' still escalates the hard questions to the large model, which then take more than 4 seconds and breach the 1.5-second target. The 'intelligent prompt router' has the same flaw whenever it selects the large model. The option to 'Keep the large model for every question' with a prompt cache checkpoint keeps the 4-second model on every request, so it fails the latency requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-distillation.html

prompt: A legal research firm's assistant sends every question to a large model on Amazon Bedrock. Each prompt begins with the same 30,000-token policy manual, followed by a short question; questions arrive continuously, seconds apart, and input tokens for the repeated manual dominate the bill. In the firm's evaluation, a smaller model fails the quality bar on about 80% of questions, because nearly all of them need multi-step reasoning over the manual. Client agreements forbid using client conversations to train or customize any model. The firm must cut inference cost substantially while answer quality must not drop. Which approach BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Send each question to the small model first, and call the large model when the small model's structured output flags that its confidence is low.
Create an Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt router over the two models, and send every question to the router's endpoint.
Distill the large model into the small model with Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation, using the logged prompts, and serve the distilled model.
Keep the large model for every question, and place a prompt cache checkpoint after the static policy text at the start of each prompt.

explanation: Nearly every question needs the large model, and the cost is dominated by a long prefix that is identical on every request. The option to 'Keep the large model for every question, and place a prompt cache checkpoint after the static policy text at the start of each prompt' lets Amazon Bedrock read the manual from the cache on subsequent requests at a reduced rate, and with questions arriving seconds apart the cache stays warm, so cost falls with no change in quality. The option to 'Send each question to the small model first' pays for a small-model call and then escalates about 80% of questions anyway, so it saves little and adds latency. The 'intelligent prompt router' would send most of these questions to the large model for the same reason, and each of those requests still carries the full uncached manual. The option to 'Distill the large model into the small model' uses logged prompts as training data, which the client agreements forbid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: A marketplace company fine-tuned an open-weight text embedding model in an Amazon SageMaker AI training job; the weights are in Amazon S3 in Hugging Face safetensors format. Its product search service will call the model about 150 times per second around the clock and needs each embedding back in the same request with a p99 latency of 60 milliseconds, which load tests show requires a GPU. The company's other generative AI features call Amazon Bedrock models through InvokeModel, and the team would prefer not to operate endpoints, but the latency target is fixed. Which deployment option meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on a GPU instance and call it from the application through InvokeEndpoint.
Import the weights with Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import and invoke the imported model on demand through InvokeModel.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero, and exchange requests and results through Amazon S3.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint with 6 GB of memory and call it through InvokeEndpoint.

explanation: The model is an embedding model with steady, heavy, latency-critical traffic that needs a GPU. A 'SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on a GPU instance' is the option built for online inference with low latency and sustained traffic, and with constant load there is no idle time to pay for. The option to 'Import the weights with Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import' would match the team's preference for `InvokeModel` and no endpoints, but Custom Model Import does not support embedding models, so this model cannot be imported. The 'Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero' queues requests and delivers results through Amazon S3, which cannot return an embedding within a 60-millisecond synchronous call, and with traffic around the clock there is nothing to scale to zero for. The 'Serverless Inference endpoint with 6 GB of memory' does not support GPUs, which the load tests show are required, and it can incur cold starts that break a p99 target. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-customization-import-model.html

prompt: A startup fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B in an Amazon SageMaker AI training job and packaged it in its own inference container together with an OCR pre-processing stage and a constrained-decoding post-processor that the output depends on. Each request is a bundle of scanned contracts of up to 300 MB and takes about 20 minutes on a GPU. A few dozen bundles arrive per day in clusters, with idle gaps of several days, and the results are collected by a downstream job later. The startup does not want to pay for an instance while no bundle is being processed. Its other features call Amazon Bedrock models through InvokeModel. Which deployment option BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on a GPU instance and call it from the application through InvokeEndpoint.
Import the weights with Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import and invoke the imported model on demand through InvokeModel.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero, and exchange requests and results through Amazon S3.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI Serverless Inference endpoint with 6 GB of memory and call it through InvokeEndpoint.

explanation: The workload has very large payloads, long processing times, no caller waiting, long idle gaps, and a custom container that must run as a unit. The 'SageMaker AI Asynchronous Inference endpoint that scales to zero' is designed for this: it queues requests, supports payloads up to 1 GB and processing times up to one hour, runs the startup's own container on a GPU instance, and can scale down to zero instances when the queue is empty. The option to 'Import the weights with Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import' imports model weights only; the OCR stage and the constrained-decoding post-processor in the custom container would not run, so outputs would differ. The 'real-time endpoint on a GPU instance' supports payloads up to 25 MB and 60 seconds of processing for regular responses, and it bills for the instance through idle gaps of several days. The 'Serverless Inference endpoint with 6 GB of memory' is limited to 4 MB payloads and 60 seconds and does not support GPUs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deploy-model-options.html

prompt: A logistics company's order-management system publishes OrderDelayed events to a custom Amazon EventBridge event bus, and three other teams consume them through their own rules. A new team must draft a customer message for each event with an Amazon Bedrock model. An order can be delayed several times in one day, and each draft quotes the previous message for that order, so events for the same order must be processed strictly one at a time, in the order in which the new team's consumer receives them, with each event (including its retries) finished before the next one begins, while different orders are processed in parallel. The publisher and the existing consumers must not be changed. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a rule that targets an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, using the order ID as the message group ID, and consume the queue with a Lambda event source mapping.
Add a rule that targets an Amazon SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue, and consume the queue with a Lambda event source mapping that sets a maximum concurrency.
Add a rule that invokes a Lambda function asynchronously, and configure the function with a retry policy and an on-failure destination for failed events.
Add a rule that starts an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow for each event, and call the model from a Bedrock task that has Retry and Catch.

explanation: The deciding constraint is that events for the same order must be handled one at a time, in the order received, while other orders run in parallel. An EventBridge rule can target a FIFO queue and set the message group, so the option to target 'an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, using the order ID as the message group ID' gives exactly that: Amazon SQS delivers messages of one group to Lambda in order, and Lambda finishes all retries on a group's messages before it receives more from that group, while separate groups are processed concurrently. EventBridge itself gives no ordering guarantee when it delivers events to targets, so the sequence is fixed where messages enter the queue; from there the FIFO queue preserves it within each order. Adding a rule leaves the publisher and the other consumers untouched. The 'Amazon SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue' buffers bursts well, but a standard queue does not preserve order and several function instances can work on two events of one order at once. The rule that 'invokes a Lambda function asynchronously' has the same problem: each event becomes an independent invocation with no sequencing per order. The rule that 'starts an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow for each event' creates independent executions that run side by side, so a second delay can be drafted before the first has finished. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-scaling.html

prompt: A freight broker's dispatch system publishes ShipmentDelayed events to a custom Amazon EventBridge event bus that two other teams already consume through their own rules. A new team must draft an apology with an Amazon Bedrock model for each event, about 300 events a day. Every draft must then wait for a duty manager's approval, which can take up to two days, before a final step sends it, and auditors want to open any event and see each step with its input and output. The team does not want to build its own state tracking, and the publisher and the existing consumers must not be changed. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a rule that targets an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, using the order ID as the message group ID, and consume the queue with a Lambda event source mapping.
Add a rule that targets an Amazon SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue, and consume the queue with a Lambda event source mapping that sets a maximum concurrency.
Add a rule that invokes a Lambda function asynchronously, and configure the function with a retry policy and an on-failure destination for failed events.
Add a rule that starts an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow for each event, and call the model from a Bedrock task that has Retry and Catch.

explanation: The deciding constraints are the approval that can take up to two days and the step-by-step record, both without custom state tracking. The rule that 'starts an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow for each event' fits: Standard workflows can run for up to one year, a task can pause for a callback until the approval arrives, and the full execution history of every state can be retrieved for up to 90 days after an execution completes. The Bedrock task's Retry and Catch handle model errors, and adding a rule changes nothing for the publisher or the other consumers. The three Lambda-based options all end the work inside one function invocation, which lasts at most 15 minutes. The 'Amazon SQS standard queue with a dead-letter queue' and the 'Amazon SQS FIFO queue' designs would buffer 300 events a day without difficulty, but the function cannot stay paused for a two-day approval, so the team would have to store and resume each draft's state itself, and neither queue shows the steps of one event. The rule that 'invokes a Lambda function asynchronously' with an on-failure destination keeps failed events but has the same gap. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html

prompt: A SaaS ticketing platform calls a company's webhook for every new ticket and expects HTTP 200 within 3 seconds; otherwise it retries and eventually disables the webhook. The company wants to add a summary and a suggested priority from an Amazon Bedrock model (8 to 25 seconds per call) and write the result back through the platform's REST API, which uses OAuth client credentials. The write-back endpoint validates each update synchronously and takes 10 to 20 seconds to respond. About 2,000 tickets arrive per day, far below the API's rate limit. The security team forbids fetching or handling the OAuth client secret in function code. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an Amazon API Gateway Lambda integration: the function calls Bedrock, posts the result to the SaaS API with a credential from AWS Secrets Manager, and then returns 200.
Have a webhook Lambda function put the item on an EventBridge bus and return 200; an enrichment function's result event goes to an API destination that uses a connection.
Have a webhook Lambda function send the item to an SQS queue and return 200; a consumer function calls Bedrock, reads the SaaS credential from AWS Secrets Manager, and posts the result.
Have a webhook Lambda function start a Step Functions Express workflow and return 200; the workflow invokes Bedrock and posts the result with an HTTP Task that uses a connection.

explanation: Three constraints decide this: the 3-second acknowledgement, the ban on handling the OAuth secret in function code, and a write-back endpoint that needs 10 to 20 seconds to answer. Starting 'a Step Functions Express workflow' and returning 200 satisfies the first. The HTTP Task authenticates through an EventBridge connection, which stores the OAuth parameters in AWS Secrets Manager and applies them itself, so no function touches the secret, and an HTTP Task request is allowed 60 seconds before it times out; the whole run fits inside the five-minute limit of an Express workflow. The design that sends the result event to 'an API destination that uses a connection' also keeps the secret out of code, but EventBridge times out an API destination request when the endpoint takes longer than 5 seconds, so every 10 to 20 second write-back would be cut off and retried. The design in which the consumer 'reads the SaaS credential from AWS Secrets Manager' is the credential handling in code that security forbids. The 'Amazon API Gateway Lambda integration' keeps the platform waiting through the model call, far beyond 3 seconds, and it also reads the credential in code. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/call-https-apis.html

prompt: A field-service platform calls a company's webhook for every new work order and expects HTTP 200 within 3 seconds; otherwise it retries and eventually suspends the webhook. The company wants to add a parts list suggested by an Amazon Bedrock model (8 to 25 seconds per call) and write it back through the platform's REST API. That API does not accept OAuth, basic authentication or a static API key: every request must carry an HMAC-SHA256 signature computed over that request's body and timestamp with a shared secret, which the company keeps in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation. Bursts reach 200 work orders per second. Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an Amazon API Gateway Lambda integration: the function calls Bedrock, posts the result to the SaaS API with a credential from AWS Secrets Manager, and then returns 200.
Have a webhook Lambda function put the item on an EventBridge bus and return 200; an enrichment function's result event goes to an API destination that uses a connection.
Have a webhook Lambda function send the item to an SQS queue and return 200; a consumer function calls Bedrock, reads the SaaS credential from AWS Secrets Manager, and posts the result.
Have a webhook Lambda function start a Step Functions Express workflow and return 200; the workflow invokes Bedrock and posts the result with an HTTP Task that uses a connection.

explanation: The deciding constraint is the authentication scheme: a signature that must be computed over each request's body and timestamp. That needs code, so the design in which a consumer function 'reads the SaaS credential from AWS Secrets Manager, and posts the result' is the one that works: the webhook function acknowledges within 3 seconds, the SQS queue absorbs bursts of 200 work orders per second, and the consumer computes the HMAC with the current secret before each call. The two designs that rely on 'a connection' cannot do this. An EventBridge connection, which both API destinations and the Step Functions HTTP Task use for authorization, supports the Basic, OAuth and API key schemes; each adds fixed or token-based credentials to a request, and none computes a per-request signature over the body. The 'Amazon API Gateway Lambda integration' could sign the request in code, but it returns 200 only after the 8 to 25 second model call and the write-back, so the platform's 3-second limit is missed on every work order and the webhook is eventually suspended. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-target-connection.html

prompt: A media company's platform team in eu-central-1 must give 60 developers access to one Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock for drafting public marketing copy. Legal has confirmed that this content may be processed in any commercial AWS Region, and finance requires the routing option with the lowest per-token price. Developers must sign in with the corporate identity provider and must not hold long-lived credentials, and they must not be able to invoke any other model or to call the model outside the chosen routing option. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Allow model invocation on the EU inference profile ARN and on the foundation-model ARN in each Region of that profile, with a bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition.
Allow model invocation on the foundation-model ARN in eu-central-1, and include no statement for an inference profile ARN.
Allow model invocation on the global inference profile ARN and on the foundation-model ARNs that it requires, with a bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition.
Federate the corporate identity provider with IAM Identity Center, and assign the callers a permission set that carries the policy.
Attach the policy to the IAM role that the application's Amazon ECS tasks assume, and let the AWS SDK obtain the task role's credentials.

explanation: Two decisions are needed: which resources the policy allows, and how the callers obtain credentials. With no residency restriction and a requirement for the lowest per-token price, the global inference profile is the fit: AWS states that Global cross-Region inference saves approximately 10% compared with geographic cross-Region inference. Its policy allows 'the global inference profile ARN and on the foundation-model ARNs that it requires', and the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition on the foundation-model statements means the model can be invoked only through that profile. The callers are people who must sign in with the corporate identity provider, so federating it 'with IAM Identity Center' and assigning a permission set gives them role sessions rather than long-lived credentials. The 'EU inference profile ARN' option is sound for data residency, but it is billed at standard pricing, so it misses the price requirement. Allowing only 'the foundation-model ARN in eu-central-1' is in-Region on-demand use at standard pricing as well. Attaching the policy to 'the IAM role that the application's Amazon ECS tasks assume' serves a workload, not 60 developers signing in from their own machines. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/global-cross-region-inference.html

prompt: A German insurer's platform team must let a claims-triage service that runs on Amazon ECS in eu-central-1 call one Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock. The model is offered for on-demand use in that Region. A contract with the insurer's regulator states that prompts must be processed in Germany, so inference must not be routed to another Region. The service has no interactive users, no person may be able to obtain its permissions by signing in, and it must not use stored access keys or be able to invoke any other model. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Allow model invocation on the EU inference profile ARN and on the foundation-model ARN in each Region of that profile, with a bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition.
Allow model invocation on the foundation-model ARN in eu-central-1, and include no statement for an inference profile ARN.
Allow model invocation on the global inference profile ARN and on the foundation-model ARNs that it requires, with a bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition.
Federate the corporate identity provider with IAM Identity Center, and assign the callers a permission set that carries the policy.
Attach the policy to the IAM role that the application's Amazon ECS tasks assume, and let the AWS SDK obtain the task role's credentials.

explanation: The contract fixes where inference runs, and the caller is a workload rather than a person. Because prompts must be processed in Germany, the policy should allow only 'the foundation-model ARN in eu-central-1' with 'no statement for an inference profile ARN': the service then invokes the model on demand in that Region, cannot route elsewhere, and cannot invoke another model. For credentials, attaching the policy to 'the IAM role that the application's Amazon ECS tasks assume' lets Amazon ECS deliver the role's credentials to the containers, so there are no stored access keys and nothing a person can sign in to. The 'EU inference profile ARN' option fails the contract: an inference profile distributes requests across the Regions it contains, and the policy must allow the foundation model in each of them, so prompts could be processed outside Germany. The 'global inference profile ARN' option routes to commercial Regions worldwide, which is further still from the requirement. Federating the identity provider 'with IAM Identity Center' gives a permission set to people who sign in, which this service does not have and the requirement explicitly rules out. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles-prereq.html

prompt: A healthcare SaaS company signs users in by federating each hospital's SAML identity provider directly with an Amazon Cognito identity pool; it has no user pool. The browser calls Amazon Bedrock directly with temporary AWS credentials to keep latency low. Clinicians may invoke a large and a small model; front-desk staff may invoke only the small one. Each hospital already sends a jobFunction attribute in its signed SAML assertion, which users cannot alter. The company will not introduce a user directory of its own or maintain group memberships for 40,000 users, AWS must enforce the decision, and no backend proxy may be added. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an identity pool with one authenticated IAM role that is scoped to the permitted model ARNs, and call Bedrock from the browser with its credentials.
Use identity pool rule-based role mapping on a claim that originates in the identity provider's SAML assertion, and scope each mapped role to its model ARNs.
Route calls through Amazon API Gateway with a Cognito user pool authorizer, and have a Lambda function check the group claim before it invokes Bedrock.
Attach an IAM role to each user pool group, configure the identity pool to choose the role from the token, and scope each role to its model ARNs.

explanation: The entitlement signal is an attribute that each hospital's identity provider asserts, and the company refuses to run its own directory or maintain groups. Identity pool 'rule-based role mapping on a claim' fits: a rule names a claim, a match type, a value and an IAM role, and for SAML providers the claims are parsed from the received assertion. Users whose jobFunction claim equals the clinician value receive credentials for a role that allows both model ARNs, and everyone else receives the small-model role, so IAM enforces the difference on every direct call from the browser. Because the assertion is signed by the hospital, users cannot change the claim; AWS warns that a mapped claim that end users can modify lets any user assume the role. The option to 'attach an IAM role to each user pool group' also enforces access in IAM, but it needs a user pool and group memberships maintained for 40,000 users, which is ruled out. The 'one authenticated IAM role' option gives every user the same permissions, so it cannot separate clinicians from front-desk staff. Routing 'through Amazon API Gateway with a Cognito user pool authorizer' is the backend proxy the company excluded, and it too needs a user pool. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/role-based-access-control.html

prompt: A legal-tech company signs users in through an Amazon Cognito user pool that is federated with each law firm's SAML identity provider. Partners may use a large model on Amazon Bedrock and paralegals only a small one, according to user pool groups that the firms' administrators maintain. Every request must be combined with the company's proprietary system prompt and with clauses from a database in a private subnet; neither the system prompt nor the database may be exposed to the browser. Responses are short classifications that are returned in one piece. The rules must be enforced on the server side, not by front-end code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an identity pool with one authenticated IAM role that is scoped to the permitted model ARNs, and call Bedrock from the browser with its credentials.
Use identity pool rule-based role mapping on a claim that originates in the identity provider's SAML assertion, and scope each mapped role to its model ARNs.
Route calls through Amazon API Gateway with a Cognito user pool authorizer, and have a Lambda function check the group claim before it invokes Bedrock.
Attach an IAM role to each user pool group, configure the identity pool to choose the role from the token, and scope each role to its model ARNs.

explanation: The deciding constraint is that each request must be assembled from a proprietary system prompt and from clauses in a private database, neither of which may reach the browser. That requires a server-side component, so routing calls 'through Amazon API Gateway with a Cognito user pool authorizer' is the fit: the authorizer validates the user pool token, the Lambda function reads the group claim to pick the permitted model, adds the system prompt and the clauses, and calls Bedrock with its own role. Responses are short and returned whole, so nothing is lost by not calling Bedrock from the browser. The three identity pool options all hand the browser temporary credentials and have it call Bedrock directly. The option to 'attach an IAM role to each user pool group' and the option that uses 'rule-based role mapping on a claim' would both enforce the model split in IAM, and 'one authenticated IAM role' would not even do that, but in every one of them the browser builds the request, so the system prompt would have to be shipped to the client and the private database would have to be reachable from it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-integrate-with-cognito.html

prompt: A hospital group operates in a country that has no AWS Region. National law requires patient records and scanned documents to remain physically in the group's own data centre; the regulator accepts that de-identified text excerpts are processed by a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock in an EU Region, provided that this traffic does not cross the public internet. The group stores the documents on a storage array that it bought last year, runs a de-identification service on its virtualisation cluster, and has an AWS Direct Connect link to a VPC in eu-central-1. The board has frozen purchases of new data-centre hardware. Which architecture meets these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the existing environment?

options.text: Store documents in Amazon S3 on Outposts, de-identify them on Outposts compute, and call Bedrock through an interface VPC endpoint in the Region.
Store documents in an Amazon S3 bucket in the Region with a customer managed KMS key, and build an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on that bucket.
Keep documents on the existing on-premises storage, de-identify them on existing servers, and call the public Bedrock endpoint over the internet with TLS and SigV4.
Keep documents on the existing on-premises storage, de-identify them on existing servers, and call Bedrock through an interface VPC endpoint over AWS Direct Connect.

explanation: The group already has everything the law asks for on premises: documents on its own storage array and a de-identification service on its own cluster. What is missing is a private path for the excerpts. Calling Bedrock 'through an interface VPC endpoint over AWS Direct Connect' supplies it: an interface endpoint for the Bedrock runtime is created in the VPC with AWS PrivateLink, the on-premises service reaches it across the existing private link, and nothing on premises is replaced. An endpoint policy can additionally limit the endpoint to actions such as bedrock:InvokeModel. Storing documents 'in Amazon S3 on Outposts' would also keep the data in the data centre, because S3 on Outposts keeps objects on the Outpost, but it means buying and installing an Outposts rack and migrating documents and compute to it, which the hardware freeze and the fewest-changes goal rule out. Calling 'the public Bedrock endpoint over the internet' leaves the environment untouched but sends the excerpts across the public internet, which the regulator excludes even when they are encrypted. Storing documents 'in an Amazon S3 bucket in the Region' moves the source documents out of the country, which encryption with a customer managed key does not cure. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html

prompt: A university research institute in a country that has no AWS Region is running a three-month pilot. Ethics rules require original interview recordings and transcripts to remain on the institute's own servers; de-identified excerpts may be processed by a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock in an EU Region, and the ethics board has accepted transfer over the internet when it is encrypted in transit and every request is authenticated. The institute has no AWS Outposts, no AWS Direct Connect and no VPN to AWS, processes about 200 excerpts a day, and its grant does not cover dedicated connectivity or new hardware. Which architecture is MOST cost-effective while meeting these requirements?

options.text: Store documents in Amazon S3 on Outposts, de-identify them on Outposts compute, and call Bedrock through an interface VPC endpoint in the Region.
Store documents in an Amazon S3 bucket in the Region with a customer managed KMS key, and build an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on that bucket.
Keep documents on the existing on-premises storage, de-identify them on existing servers, and call the public Bedrock endpoint over the internet with TLS and SigV4.
Keep documents on the existing on-premises storage, de-identify them on existing servers, and call Bedrock through an interface VPC endpoint over AWS Direct Connect.

explanation: In this scenario the ethics board has explicitly accepted internet transfer that is encrypted in transit and authenticated, the originals must stay on the institute's servers, and the grant pays for neither connectivity nor hardware. Keeping documents on the existing storage and calling 'the public Bedrock endpoint over the internet with TLS and SigV4' meets every rule at the lowest cost: only de-identified excerpts leave, TLS encrypts them, SigV4 authenticates each request, and the only charge is for the 200 model invocations a day. Calling Bedrock 'through an interface VPC endpoint over AWS Direct Connect' is the right design when traffic must stay off the internet, but here it would require a dedicated connection that the institute does not have and the grant does not cover, for a three-month pilot. Storing documents 'in Amazon S3 on Outposts' requires an Outposts rack, which is new hardware and a far larger commitment than the pilot justifies. Storing documents 'in an Amazon S3 bucket in the Region' and building a knowledge base on it moves the original recordings and transcripts off the institute's servers, which the ethics rules forbid regardless of how the bucket is encrypted. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html

prompt: A fintech team ships a RAG assistant through AWS CodePipeline with the stages Source, Build, DeployStaging and DeployProd. Build already runs secret and dependency scans and scores a 200-question golden dataset, and it fails the pipeline on findings or a low score. Two gaps remain. The financial regulator requires a named compliance officer to sign off every production release after reading the evaluation report. And DeployProd fails about once a week on a transient throttling error from a third-party API; running the stage again has always succeeded, releases are scheduled overnight, and the new version must be live by morning rather than production staying on the previous release. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a manual approval action before DeployProd so that a named reviewer examines the evaluation report and the scan findings and approves or rejects each release.
Add AWS CodeBuild actions that run secret and dependency scans in Build and score the golden dataset against staging, failing the build on findings or a low score.
Enable automatic retry on stage failure for DeployProd so that a failed production deployment is attempted again without an operator.
Configure DeployProd for automatic rollback on failure, and add an On Success condition with a CloudWatchAlarm rule whose result is Rollback.
Enable model invocation logging in production, and alarm on a groundedness metric that notifies the on-call engineer through Amazon SNS.

explanation: The two gaps are a human sign-off that the regulator demands and a transient failure that should be retried, not undone. A 'manual approval action before DeployProd' stops the pipeline until the named compliance officer approves or rejects the release, which is the sign-off. 'Automatic retry on stage failure' makes CodePipeline try the failed stage once more without an operator, so the weekly throttling error no longer leaves the overnight release undeployed. The option to add 'AWS CodeBuild actions that run secret and dependency scans' and score the golden dataset describes gates that this pipeline already has in Build, so it closes neither gap. Configuring DeployProd 'for automatic rollback on failure' would return the stage to its most recent successful execution, which keeps production on the previous release, the outcome the team wants to avoid; CodePipeline also does not allow automatic stage retry together with On Failure conditions. 'Model invocation logging in production' with an alarm is monitoring after release: it neither records a sign-off nor reruns a failed deployment. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/stage-retry.html

prompt: A travel company ships a RAG assistant (Lambda code, prompt templates and infrastructure templates) through AWS CodePipeline with the stages Source, Build, DeployStaging and DeployProd. Last quarter a prompt change that lowered groundedness reached production, a release contained a hardcoded API key, and a faulty deployment stayed live for two hours until someone redeployed the previous version. The team now requires that a release is blocked when its score on a 200-question golden dataset is below a threshold, that secrets and vulnerable dependencies are detected before any deployment, and that production returns to the last good release when the stage fails or its error alarm fires. Releases go out at night with nobody on duty, so no step may wait for a person. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a manual approval action before DeployProd so that a named reviewer examines the evaluation report and the scan findings and approves or rejects each release.
Add AWS CodeBuild actions that run secret and dependency scans in Build and score the golden dataset against staging, failing the build on findings or a low score.
Enable automatic retry on stage failure for DeployProd so that a failed production deployment is attempted again without an operator.
Configure DeployProd for automatic rollback on failure, and add an On Success condition with a CloudWatchAlarm rule whose result is Rollback.
Enable model invocation logging in production, and alarm on a groundedness metric that notifies the on-call engineer through Amazon SNS.

explanation: The team needs automated gates before deployment and automated recovery after it, with nobody on duty. Adding 'AWS CodeBuild actions that run secret and dependency scans in Build and score the golden dataset against staging' creates the gates: when a scan or the evaluation script fails its command, the build fails and the release does not reach DeployProd. For recovery, a stage configured 'for automatic rollback on failure' is rolled back to its most recent successful execution, and an On Success condition with a CloudWatchAlarm rule whose result is Rollback returns the stage to the last good release when the production error alarm fires after a deployment that itself succeeded. The 'manual approval action' could catch a bad release, but the pipeline would stop and wait for a reviewer, which the night-time, nobody-on-duty constraint excludes. 'Automatic retry on stage failure' attempts the same faulty revision again instead of restoring the previous one. 'Model invocation logging in production' with an alarm that notifies an engineer detects a regression only after users see it and neither blocks the release nor restores the last good one. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/stage-conditions.html

prompt: A platform team operates a central GenAI gateway for 14 product teams that share one AWS account. Every model call goes through Amazon API Gateway to a Lambda function that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with the function's own execution role. Callers authenticate with SigV4 using their corporate federated roles, and that must remain the access control. Each product team must now get its own request rate limit and monthly request quota so that one team cannot starve the others, and finance must see each team's monthly Bedrock spend in AWS Cost Explorer without anyone querying logs. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a REST API with IAM authorization on the methods, and give each team an API key that is associated with its own usage plan.
Use an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, and configure route-level throttling values on the stage for each of the API's routes.
Create an application inference profile for each team with a cost allocation tag, and have the gateway invoke the model through the caller's profile.
Pass an identifier as request metadata on each Converse call, enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3, and query the logs with Amazon Athena.
Tag the gateway function's execution role, activate the tag for cost allocation, and use IAM principal attribution for Amazon Bedrock in AWS Cost Explorer.

explanation: The requirements are per-team limits with a monthly quota while SigV4 stays the access control, and per-team spend in Cost Explorer without log queries. A 'REST API with IAM authorization on the methods' and an API key per team in its own usage plan does the first: the usage plan applies a throttle rate, burst and quota to each key while IAM still decides who may call, which matches the AWS guidance that API keys identify clients and are not for authorization. For cost, 'an application inference profile for each team with a cost allocation tag' makes the on-demand spend of calls made through that profile appear under the team's tag. The 'HTTP API with a JWT authorizer' fails twice: the callers must keep SigV4, and route-level throttling applies to a route for everyone, with no per-client limits or quotas. Passing 'an identifier as request metadata' and querying invocation logs with Athena is the log querying finance wants to avoid. Tagging 'the gateway function's execution role' cannot separate teams, because all 14 teams' calls reach Bedrock under that one role. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-api-usage-plans.html

prompt: A retailer's mobile shopping app calls a GenAI gateway: Amazon API Gateway in front of a Lambda function that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with the function's execution role. App users sign in with the retailer's OpenID Connect identity provider and hold no AWS credentials, and the gateway itself must validate their tokens without custom authorizer code. The gateway has a chat route and a product-summary route, and each route needs its own overall request limit to protect the model quota; there are no per-customer limits or quotas. The data science team must analyse in SQL the token counts and the full prompts of individual requests for each app feature. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a REST API with IAM authorization on the methods, and give each team an API key that is associated with its own usage plan.
Use an HTTP API with a JWT authorizer, and configure route-level throttling values on the stage for each of the API's routes.
Create an application inference profile for each team with a cost allocation tag, and have the gateway invoke the model through the caller's profile.
Pass an identifier as request metadata on each Converse call, enable model invocation logging to Amazon S3, and query the logs with Amazon Athena.
Tag the gateway function's execution role, activate the tag for cost allocation, and use IAM principal attribution for Amazon Bedrock in AWS Cost Explorer.

explanation: Here the callers hold OpenID Connect tokens and no AWS credentials, limits are per route rather than per client, and the analysis needs individual requests with their prompts. An 'HTTP API with a JWT authorizer' validates the identity provider's tokens natively, and route-level throttling gives the chat route and the product-summary route their own limits. For the analysis, passing 'an identifier as request metadata on each Converse call' and enabling model invocation logging to Amazon S3 produces one record per request that contains the request metadata, the token counts and the request body, which Athena can query in SQL by feature. A 'REST API with IAM authorization' requires SigV4-signed requests, which app users without AWS credentials cannot make, and per-key usage plans answer a per-client requirement that does not exist here. 'An application inference profile for each team with a cost allocation tag' reports spend by tag in cost tools; it does not expose individual requests or prompts. Tagging 'the gateway function's execution role' for IAM principal attribution likewise yields aggregated daily cost for one role, not per-request token counts and prompts for each feature. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A law firm summarises contracts asynchronously. An upload service places a message on an Amazon SQS standard queue (visibility timeout 120 seconds, redrive policy with maxReceiveCount 5 to a dead-letter queue). A Lambda function with a 600-second timeout receives one message per invocation and calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API; long contracts take 4 to 8 minutes. Concurrency stays below 10, and Amazon CloudWatch shows no throttling and no function errors. Two problems appear: the upload service retries on network timeouts and sometimes sends the same contract twice within a few seconds, and long contracts are summarised two or three times even when they were sent once. Which combination of changes resolves these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move to an SQS FIFO queue with content-based deduplication so that an item that is sent twice within the deduplication interval is delivered once.
Increase the batch size and add a batching window so that fewer, larger invocations are made for the same number of items.
Set maximum concurrency on the event source mapping to a value that the model's Bedrock quota can sustain during the peak.
Raise the queue's visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout so that a message is not redelivered while it is being processed.
