Enable ReportBatchItemFailures, catch errors per message, and return the failed message IDs in batchItemFailures.

explanation: There are two separate causes of duplicate work. First, the producer sends the same contract twice within seconds; a standard queue accepts both messages. 'An SQS FIFO queue with content-based deduplication' removes the second copy, because a message with the same content sent again within the 5-minute deduplication interval is not introduced into the queue. Second, the visibility timeout is 120 seconds while a long contract takes 4 to 8 minutes, so the message becomes visible again and is delivered to another invocation while the first is still working. Raising 'the queue's visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout' is the AWS recommendation for a queue that feeds Lambda and stops that redelivery. Setting 'maximum concurrency on the event source mapping' addresses throttling, and the stem states there is none. 'ReportBatchItemFailures' matters when part of a batch fails, but each invocation receives one message and no errors occur. Increasing 'the batch size' makes each invocation run longer, so even more messages would outlive the visibility timeout. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-configure.html

prompt: An insurer summarises claims asynchronously. An upload service places exactly one message per claim on an Amazon SQS standard queue (visibility timeout 1,800 seconds, redrive policy with maxReceiveCount 5 to a dead-letter queue). A Lambda function with a 300-second timeout receives batches of 10 and calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API once per message. During morning peaks Lambda scales to several hundred concurrent executions, Bedrock returns ThrottlingException for some calls, and the function raises the exception. The team observes that claims that were already summarised are summarised again, and that valid claims end up in the dead-letter queue. Which combination of changes resolves these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Move to an SQS FIFO queue with content-based deduplication so that an item that is sent twice within the deduplication interval is delivered once.
Increase the batch size and add a batching window so that fewer, larger invocations are made for the same number of items.
Set maximum concurrency on the event source mapping to a value that the model's Bedrock quota can sustain during the peak.
Raise the queue's visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout so that a message is not redelivered while it is being processed.
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures, catch errors per message, and return the failed message IDs in batchItemFailures.

explanation: Two faults are visible. Nothing limits how far the event source mapping scales, so hundreds of concurrent invocations exceed the model quota; 'maximum concurrency on the event source mapping' limits the number of concurrent function instances the queue can invoke, while the queue holds the backlog. And when the function raises an error, all messages in the batch become visible again by default, including those that were processed successfully, which explains both the repeated summaries and the healthy claims that reach maxReceiveCount. With 'ReportBatchItemFailures' the function returns only the failed message IDs and the rest are deleted. 'An SQS FIFO queue with content-based deduplication' removes messages that are sent twice, but the upload service sends exactly one message per claim; the repeats come from redelivery after a failed batch. Raising 'the queue's visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout' changes nothing, because 1,800 seconds is already six times the 300-second timeout. Increasing 'the batch size' means every throttled call sends even more successful work back to the queue. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-sqs-errorhandling.html

prompt: A company exposes a text-generation endpoint to partners through an Amazon API Gateway REST API with a Lambda integration that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. Requests are well formed, but many break contract rules: each partner has its own maxTokens ceiling and its own list of permitted models, held in an Amazon DynamoDB table that account managers edit daily, and the combined length of all messages must not exceed the partner's limit. Violations currently reach Bedrock and are billed. Invalid requests must be rejected with HTTP 400 and a message that names the rule that was broken, and a changed limit must take effect as soon as the table is edited. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a schema-validation library to the Lambda function, and return HTTP 400 at the start of the handler when the request is invalid.
Define a JSON schema model for the request body, and assign a request validator for the body and parameters to the method.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the stage, and add rules that inspect the JSON body and block the requests that match.
Use a custom (non-proxy) Lambda integration with a mapping template that reshapes the request body before the function receives it.

explanation: The rules to enforce are not about the shape of the request. They depend on per-partner values in a DynamoDB table that changes daily and on a sum across all messages, and the response must name the broken rule. That is application logic, so validating 'at the start of the handler' is the fit: the function reads the partner's current limits, checks the ceiling, the permitted models and the combined length, and returns HTTP 400 with a specific message before any Bedrock call is made, so nothing is billed. 'A JSON schema model' with a request validator checks that required parameters are present and that the body conforms to a static schema; it cannot look up a partner's row, compare against a value edited that morning, or add up message lengths. 'An AWS WAF web ACL' inspects requests against rules defined in the web ACL and has the same blind spot for per-partner data, and it blocks requests rather than returning a 400 that names the rule. 'A mapping template that reshapes the request body' transforms a request on its way to the integration; it does not reject contract violations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-method-request-validation.html

prompt: A company exposes a text-generation endpoint to partners through an Amazon API Gateway REST API with a Lambda integration that calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. The function now expects a messages array and an inferenceConfig object, but 18% of traffic comes from partners that still send the original contract: a single prompt string and a top-level max_tokens number. These partners have a contractual right to keep that format for another year, so their requests must succeed rather than be rejected. The function belongs to another team whose code is frozen for a compliance audit, and the partners will not change their clients. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add a schema-validation library to the Lambda function, and return HTTP 400 at the start of the handler when the request is invalid.
Define a JSON schema model for the request body, and assign a request validator for the body and parameters to the method.
Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the stage, and add rules that inspect the JSON body and block the requests that match.
Use a custom (non-proxy) Lambda integration with a mapping template that reshapes the request body before the function receives it.

explanation: The old-format requests are not errors to be rejected; they must succeed, and neither the partners' clients nor the frozen function may change. The only place left to adapt them is the API layer. With 'a custom (non-proxy) Lambda integration', a mapping template transforms the method request before it is sent to the integration, so the template can wrap the prompt string in a messages array and move max_tokens into an inferenceConfig object, and the function receives the shape it expects. 'A JSON schema model' with a request validator would do the opposite of what the contract requires: requests that do not match the schema are failed immediately with a 400 response. 'An AWS WAF web ACL' that blocks matching requests also turns the old format away. Adding 'a schema-validation library to the Lambda function' is excluded twice: the function's code is frozen for the audit, and returning HTTP 400 denies these partners the format they are entitled to. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/models-mappings.html

prompt: A kiosk vendor is adding an ordering assistant to restaurant kiosks. The kiosk firmware, which the vendor's hardware partner controls, speaks plain WebSocket with JSON frames and has no GraphQL or server-sent events client. While Amazon Bedrock is generating a reply, the customer must be able to send a correction or a cancel message on the same connection, and the backend must be able to push a message that nobody requested when the kitchen rejects an item. Traffic is concentrated in two short meal-time peaks, and the company's architecture standard allows only pay-per-request services, with no containers or always-running compute. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an API Gateway WebSocket API, and have a Lambda function push each chunk to the client through the connection management (@connections) API.
Expose a Lambda function through a function URL in RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode, and have the client read the streamed HTTPS response.
Use AWS AppSync: a Lambda function publishes each chunk through a mutation, and clients receive the chunks over a GraphQL subscription.
Run the service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, and stream ConverseStream output as server-sent events.

explanation: The firmware dictates the protocol: plain WebSocket with JSON frames, messages in both directions on one connection, and pushes that the client did not ask for. An 'API Gateway WebSocket API' provides that. Client frames are routed to Lambda functions, and the backend sends data to a connected client at any time through the @connections API, so chunks from ConverseStream, a cancel acknowledgement and a kitchen rejection can all travel over the same connection, and the service is billed per message and connection minute with nothing running between the meal-time peaks. A 'function URL in RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode' streams a single HTTPS response to a single request; the kiosk cannot send a correction on that response, the backend cannot push unprompted, and it is not the WebSocket protocol the firmware speaks. The 'AWS AppSync' design delivers chunks in real time, but clients must issue GraphQL mutations and subscriptions, which the firmware does not support. Running the service 'on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer' needs containers that run continuously, which the architecture standard excludes, and it streams server-sent events, for which the kiosk has no client. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-websocket-api-overview.html

prompt: A research-assistant product streams answers that are generated with ConverseStream on Amazon Bedrock. A single answer can stream for up to 40 minutes while an agent works through its sources, and about 3,000 streams are open at any time of the day. The existing browser and partner clients consume server-sent events over ordinary HTTPS, and the partners' client libraries cannot be changed. The streaming service is a Python FastAPI application that the team already builds and tests as a container image. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an API Gateway WebSocket API, and have a Lambda function push each chunk to the client through the connection management (@connections) API.
Expose a Lambda function through a function URL in RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode, and have the client read the streamed HTTPS response.
Use AWS AppSync: a Lambda function publishes each chunk through a mutation, and clients receive the chunks over a GraphQL subscription.
Run the service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, and stream ConverseStream output as server-sent events.

explanation: Two constraints decide this: one response stream can last 40 minutes, and the clients consume server-sent events over ordinary HTTPS and cannot be changed. Running the existing container 'on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer' meets both: a long-running task can hold a response open for as long as the agent works, the load balancer forwards the event stream over HTTPS, and a steady 3,000 open streams suit always-on compute. The team's FastAPI image is deployed as it is. A 'function URL in RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode' also streams over plain HTTPS, but a Lambda invocation ends after at most 900 seconds, so a 40-minute answer would be cut off after 15 minutes. An 'API Gateway WebSocket API' can carry the chunks, but clients would have to open a WebSocket connection instead of reading server-sent events, and the partners' libraries cannot be changed; the Lambda function that pushes chunks is also bound by the same 15-minute limit. The 'AWS AppSync' design requires clients to subscribe with GraphQL, which is again a different client protocol from the one the partners use. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-response-streaming.html

prompt: A support assistant runs as a container on Amazon ECS behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of it. The service calls ConverseStream on Amazon Bedrock and forwards text to the browser as server-sent events. Answers that produce text continuously complete correctly, including some that stream for three minutes. When the model calls an inventory tool that takes 35 to 50 seconds, during which the service sends no bytes, the browser receives an error from CloudFront, while service logs show that the tool call and the Bedrock stream finished normally afterwards. The distribution and the load balancer use their default timeout settings. The container image comes from a vendor and cannot be modified this quarter. Which change resolves the problem?

options.text: Raise the origin response timeout on the Amazon CloudFront distribution to a value above the longest silent period.
Raise the idle timeout on the Application Load Balancer to a value above the longest silent period.
Have the service write a server-sent events comment line every 15 seconds while a tool call is in progress.
Raise the read timeout of the service's Bedrock runtime client to a value above the longest silent period.

explanation: The symptom is a connection that dies only when no bytes flow for 35 to 50 seconds, with defaults everywhere. CloudFront's origin response timeout defaults to 30 seconds, and it applies both to the wait for the first response and to the wait after one packet of a response before the next packet arrives. A 35 to 50 second silence exceeds it, so CloudFront gives up on the origin and returns an error. Raising 'the origin response timeout on the Amazon CloudFront distribution' above the longest silent period fixes this; values up to 120 seconds can be set. Raising 'the idle timeout on the Application Load Balancer' does not help, because its default is 60 seconds and the silence never lasts that long, so the load balancer is not the component closing the connection. Writing 'a server-sent events comment line every 15 seconds' would keep bytes flowing, but it is a change to the vendor's container image, which cannot be modified this quarter. Raising 'the read timeout of the service's Bedrock runtime client' targets the wrong hop: the logs show that the Bedrock stream completed normally. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html

prompt: An analyst assistant runs as a container on Amazon ECS behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of it. The service calls ConverseStream on Amazon Bedrock and forwards text to the browser as server-sent events. Answers that produce text continuously complete correctly, including some that stream for three minutes. When the model calls a data-warehouse tool that takes 70 to 100 seconds, during which the service sends no bytes, the connection is closed, while service logs show that the tool call and the Bedrock stream finished normally afterwards. Last month the team raised the distribution's origin response timeout to 120 seconds; the load balancer still uses its default settings. The container image comes from a vendor and cannot be modified this quarter. Which change resolves the problem?

options.text: Raise the origin response timeout on the Amazon CloudFront distribution to a value above the longest silent period.
Raise the idle timeout on the Application Load Balancer to a value above the longest silent period.
Have the service write a server-sent events comment line every 15 seconds while a tool call is in progress.
Raise the read timeout of the service's Bedrock runtime client to a value above the longest silent period.

explanation: Again the connection dies only during a silence, here 70 to 100 seconds, but the settings differ. CloudFront's origin response timeout has already been raised to 120 seconds, which is longer than any silent period, so CloudFront is not the component giving up. The Application Load Balancer still has its default idle timeout of 60 seconds, and it closes a connection on which no data has been sent or received for that long. Raising 'the idle timeout on the Application Load Balancer' above 100 seconds resolves the problem; the valid range is 1 to 4,000 seconds. Raising 'the origin response timeout on the Amazon CloudFront distribution' further changes nothing, because the 120-second value already covers the silence and the load balancer would still cut the connection at 60 seconds. Writing 'a server-sent events comment line every 15 seconds' would keep the connection active, but it requires changing the vendor's container image, which is not allowed this quarter. Raising 'the read timeout of the service's Bedrock runtime client' addresses a hop that is healthy: the logs show the Bedrock stream finished normally. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-load-balancer-attributes.html

prompt: A shared inference service on Amazon ECS in eu-west-1 uses one long-lived AWS SDK client for the Amazon Bedrock runtime to serve 30 tenants' interactive requests across four models. After ThrottlingException errors appeared on the most popular model, an engineer set the client to adaptive retry mode with 10 attempts; since then, whenever that model is throttled, p95 latency for the other three models rises from 2 to more than 20 seconds. Tenant contracts state that each answer must come from the model the tenant selected and that prompts are processed in eu-west-1, and the client must not hold back a request's first attempt. Demand for the popular model is steadily above its on-demand quota, and the company accepts hourly-billed dedicated capacity for it. Which change is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Create one SDK client for each model in adaptive retry mode, so that each client's rate limiter responds to a single model's throttling.
Use standard retry mode with the default maximum attempts, and send the request to a fallback model when retries are exhausted.
Use standard retry mode with the default maximum attempts, and call the throttled model through a geographic cross-Region inference profile.
Use standard retry mode with the default maximum attempts, and serve the throttled model from Provisioned Throughput.

explanation: Two things are wrong: the retry mode, and capacity for the popular model. Adaptive mode adds a client-side rate limiter and, according to the SDK guide, can delay or block the initial request, not just retries; AWS advises against it when a client sends requests to multiple resources or serves multiple tenants. Standard mode is the recommended default. Because demand is steadily above the on-demand quota and the company accepts hourly-billed capacity, serving the model 'from Provisioned Throughput' removes the cause of the throttling while every answer still comes from the selected model in eu-west-1. Creating 'one SDK client for each model in adaptive retry mode' stops the slowdown spreading between models, but each client still serves 30 tenants and may hold back first attempts, which is ruled out, and it adds no capacity. Sending the request 'to a fallback model' breaks the contract that the answer comes from the model the tenant selected. 'A geographic cross-Region inference profile' distributes requests across the Regions in the profile, so prompts would be processed outside eu-west-1. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-retry-behavior.html

prompt: A nightly enrichment service on Amazon ECS in eu-central-1 runs four pipelines, each calling a different Amazon Bedrock model, through one shared AWS SDK client in adaptive retry mode. When one model is throttled, the other three pipelines slow down although they are far below their quotas. Nobody waits for the results; the goal is that every record is eventually processed, with the client slowing its own request rate when a model throttles instead of failing records. Each pipeline's output was validated for its model, so substituting another model is not permitted; inference must stay in eu-central-1; and the budget allows no committed or hourly-billed capacity. Which change is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Create one SDK client for each model in adaptive retry mode, so that each client's rate limiter responds to a single model's throttling.
Use standard retry mode with the default maximum attempts, and send the request to a fallback model when retries are exhausted.
Use standard retry mode with the default maximum attempts, and call the throttled model through a geographic cross-Region inference profile.
Use standard retry mode with the default maximum attempts, and serve the throttled model from Provisioned Throughput.

explanation: This workload is the case adaptive retry mode is meant for, except for one mistake: a single client is shared by four models. The SDK guide describes adaptive mode as suitable when a client targets a single resource and frequent throttling is expected, and warns against it when one client sends requests to multiple resources, because its client-side rate limiter then slows everything. Creating 'one SDK client for each model in adaptive retry mode' keeps the behaviour the team wants, a client that reduces its own request rate when its model throttles so that records are delayed, not failed, and it confines each slowdown to the throttled pipeline. Nobody waits for results, so a delayed first attempt is acceptable here. The three standard-mode options each bring something the constraints forbid. Sending the request 'to a fallback model' substitutes a model whose output was not validated for that pipeline. 'A geographic cross-Region inference profile' distributes requests across several Regions, so inference would leave eu-central-1. 'Provisioned Throughput' is billed hourly, which the budget does not allow. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-retry-behavior.html

prompt: A B2B writing assistant exposes an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Each partner sends an API key and is authorized by a Lambda authorizer; a Lambda function then calls an Amazon Bedrock model with on-demand throughput. One partner's bulk script now sends 50 requests per second, which consumes the account's tokens-per-minute quota for the model, and the other partners receive HTTP 500 because the function surfaces ThrottlingException after the SDK's retries. The company requires that no partner can use more than its contracted share of requests, that users receive a slightly lower-quality answer in the same response instead of an error while the primary model is throttled, and that no committed or always-on cost is introduced. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set stage-level method throttling on the API so that the total request rate that reaches the function stays within what the backend can absorb.
Associate each caller's API key with a usage plan that sets that caller's throttle rate, burst and request quota.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the primary model with a commitment term, sized for the combined peak load.
Catch throttling errors once SDK retries are exhausted, and invoke a smaller fallback model, flagging the answer as degraded.
Return HTTP 202 with a job ID, place the request on an Amazon SQS queue that a consumer drains at the quota rate, and let callers fetch the result.

explanation: Two requirements stand out: a limit for each partner, and a degraded answer in the same response instead of an error. Per-client limits in API Gateway come from usage plans: associating 'each caller's API key with a usage plan' applies a throttle rate, burst and quota to that key, so the bulk script is throttled when it exceeds its share while the other partners are unaffected; authorization stays with the Lambda authorizer. For degradation, the function lets the SDK retry and, when throttling persists, invokes 'a smaller fallback model' with its own quota and marks the answer as degraded. Both measures are pay-per-use. 'Stage-level method throttling' limits the stage's methods for all partners together, so the noisy partner still takes most of the allowance and the others are rejected. 'Provisioned Throughput for the primary model with a commitment term' is the committed, always-on cost that is excluded, and it does not enforce contracted shares. Returning 'HTTP 202 with a job ID' makes the answer arrive later through a second call, whereas users must receive it in the same response. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-request-throttling.html

prompt: An internal document-drafting API is an Amazon API Gateway REST API with IAM authorization in front of a Lambda function that calls an Amazon Bedrock model with on-demand throughput. Forty internal applications call it; none has an API key and no application has an allowance of its own, but month-end bursts consume the model's tokens-per-minute quota and callers receive HTTP 500 after the SDK's retries. Callers can wait up to 15 minutes for a draft and already poll other internal services for results. Every draft must come from the approved primary model, the budget allows no committed capacity, and the API must reject traffic beyond the overall rate that the backend can absorb. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set stage-level method throttling on the API so that the total request rate that reaches the function stays within what the backend can absorb.
Associate each caller's API key with a usage plan that sets that caller's throttle rate, burst and request quota.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the primary model with a commitment term, sized for the combined peak load.
Catch throttling errors once SDK retries are exhausted, and invoke a smaller fallback model, flagging the answer as degraded.
Return HTTP 202 with a job ID, place the request on an Amazon SQS queue that a consumer drains at the quota rate, and let callers fetch the result.

explanation: Here the callers tolerate waiting, every draft must come from the primary model, and the only limit wanted is an overall one. Returning 'HTTP 202 with a job ID' and placing the request on an SQS queue that a consumer drains at the quota rate turns the month-end burst into a backlog: each draft is produced by the primary model when capacity is available, well within the 15 minutes callers accept, and they fetch it by polling as they already do elsewhere. 'Stage-level method throttling' gives the overall ceiling: requests beyond the configured rate are rejected at the API before they reach the backend. Associating 'each caller's API key with a usage plan' addresses per-client limits, but the applications have no API keys and no individual allowances. 'Provisioned Throughput for the primary model with a commitment term' is committed capacity, which the budget excludes. Invoking 'a smaller fallback model' returns a draft from a model other than the approved primary one, which is not permitted. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-request-throttling.html

prompt: A travel company's support assistant sends every question to the larger of two models in one provider's family on Amazon Bedrock. To cut cost, the company has adopted a policy: questions from customers on the premium tier, and any question about a booking worth more than 5,000 euros, go to the larger model; all other questions go to the smaller one. Customers write in nine languages. Auditors must be able to tell from the customer tier and the booking value alone which model answered, and product managers want to change the threshold several times a week without a code deployment. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add an AWS Step Functions Express workflow in which a small model rates each question's complexity and a Choice state selects the model that answers.
Create a configured prompt router with the two models, a fallback model and a response quality difference, and send requests to the router.
Store routing rules in AWS AppConfig, and have the application select the model for each request from the rule that matches it.
Send every question to the smaller model through a cross-Region inference profile, and keep the larger model for a manual escalation path.

explanation: The routing policy is a business rule on two known attributes, customer tier and booking value, and it must be predictable from those attributes alone and adjustable without a deployment. Storing 'routing rules in AWS AppConfig' fits: the application evaluates the current rule for each request, so the same tier and booking value always lead to the same model, and product managers change the threshold by deploying a new configuration, not new code. 'A configured prompt router' decides differently: intelligent prompt routing predicts response quality for each prompt and picks the model from that prediction, so it cannot route on customer tier or booking value and an auditor could not predict its choice from them; it is also optimized for English prompts only, while customers write in nine languages. The 'AWS Step Functions Express workflow' in which a small model rates complexity has the same flaw, because a model's rating of the question, not the policy's attributes, would determine the route. Sending 'every question to the smaller model' with a manual escalation path does not give premium customers and high-value bookings the larger model automatically. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-routing.html

prompt: A travel company's support assistant sends every question to a large model from one provider on Amazon Bedrock. Tests show that a small model from a different provider answers about 70% of questions equally well at a fraction of the cost. Static keyword rules were tried and misrouted too many unfamiliar questions, so the choice must be made from the content of each question, without a person in the loop. The company's own written rubric defines what counts as a hard question and will be refined over time, and compliance wants each routing decision logged together with the rating that led to it. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add an AWS Step Functions Express workflow in which a small model rates each question's complexity and a Choice state selects the model that answers.
Create a configured prompt router with the two models, a fallback model and a response quality difference, and send requests to the router.
Store routing rules in AWS AppConfig, and have the application select the model for each request from the rule that matches it.
Send every question to the smaller model through a cross-Region inference profile, and keep the larger model for a manual escalation path.

explanation: The choice must be made from each question's content, between models of two different providers, according to the company's own rubric, with the rating recorded. An 'AWS Step Functions Express workflow in which a small model rates each question's complexity' does that: the rating prompt carries the rubric and can be refined, a Choice state sends the question to the small or the large model, and the workflow's logging records the rating and the branch taken for each execution. 'A configured prompt router' is the managed alternative for content-based routing, but it requires exactly two models within the same family, and these two models come from different providers. Storing 'routing rules in AWS AppConfig' is static routing; the company has already found that fixed rules misroute unfamiliar questions. Sending 'every question to the smaller model' and keeping the larger one for manual escalation gives the 30% of hard questions a weaker answer unless a person intervenes, which is ruled out. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-routing.html

prompt: A document-intake service receives scanned invoices, long legal contracts and source-code files, and each kind must be processed by a different specialised foundation model on Amazon Bedrock, from three different providers. Items arrive only from three internal systems, one per kind, and each system has been verified to send nothing but its own kind. Callers wait for the result in the same request, the latency budget allows no step other than the specialised model call itself, and finance will not pay for an additional model invocation per item. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock prompt router across two models, and let intelligent prompt routing select a model for each item by predicted response quality.
Expose one Amazon API Gateway route for each kind of item, each integrated with a Lambda function that calls the model for that kind.
Write one AWS Lambda function that classifies the item with a small model, calls the matching model, and writes an audit item to Amazon DynamoDB.
Use an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow: a Bedrock task classifies the item, and a Choice state routes to model tasks with Retry and Catch.

explanation: Here the kind of each item is already known and trustworthy: every source system sends exactly one kind. The constraints then forbid anything beyond the specialised model call, in time and in cost. Exposing 'one Amazon API Gateway route for each kind of item' is static routing that meets them: each system calls its own route, the integrated Lambda function invokes the model for that kind, and the caller receives the result in the same request with no classification step. The single function that 'classifies the item with a small model' and the workflow in which 'a Bedrock task classifies the item' both add a model invocation per item, which finance has excluded and the latency budget does not allow; a Standard workflow is also started asynchronously, so the caller would not get the result in the same request. The 'Amazon Bedrock prompt router' does not apply to this routing problem: intelligent prompt routing chooses between two models of the same family by predicted response quality, whereas this service must send each kind to one of three models from three different providers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-routing.html

prompt: A document-intake service receives scanned invoices, long legal contracts and source-code files through one endpoint, and each kind must be processed by a different specialised foundation model on Amazon Bedrock, from three different providers. Client-supplied type fields have proved unreliable, so the kind must be determined from the content. Callers wait for the result in the same HTTPS request, which must complete within 20 seconds. For each item, compliance needs a record of the routing decision together with the customer ID and cost centre, queryable by those fields for seven years. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock prompt router across two models, and let intelligent prompt routing select a model for each item by predicted response quality.
Expose one Amazon API Gateway route for each kind of item, each integrated with a Lambda function that calls the model for that kind.
Write one AWS Lambda function that classifies the item with a small model, calls the matching model, and writes an audit item to Amazon DynamoDB.
Use an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow: a Bedrock task classifies the item, and a Choice state routes to model tasks with Retry and Catch.

explanation: Three constraints decide this: the kind must be read from the content, the caller waits for the answer in the same request, and the routing record must be queryable by customer ID and cost centre for seven years. The single function that 'classifies the item with a small model, calls the matching model, and writes an audit item to Amazon DynamoDB' meets all three: it runs synchronously behind the endpoint, classifies on content, and stores a record whose attributes and retention the team controls. The 'AWS Step Functions Standard workflow' routes on content just as well, but Standard workflows are started asynchronously, so the result does not come back in the caller's request, and their execution history is removed 90 days after an execution completes, far short of seven years, and cannot be queried by business fields. Exposing 'one Amazon API Gateway route for each kind of item' relies on the client choosing the right route, which is the client-supplied type information that has proved unreliable. The 'Amazon Bedrock prompt router' selects between two models of one family by predicted response quality; it cannot send items to three models from three providers according to their kind. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html

prompt: A reporting service uses a Python Lambda function with a 15-minute timeout to generate 20-page reports. The function calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with a boto3 client in its default configuration; one generation takes 3 to 6 minutes. The function log shows a ReadTimeoutError about 60 seconds after each call, followed by further attempts, although model invocation logs show that Bedrock completed every request, and token charges are several times higher than expected. Editors follow each report on a progress page that must show text within seconds of its being generated. Each report must come from a single generation, because later sections refer back to earlier ones. Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: Create the Bedrock runtime client with a botocore Config whose read_timeout is longer than the longest expected generation.
Call ConverseStream in place of Converse, and assemble the report in the function from the events as they arrive.
Split each report into sections, and generate them with separate shorter Converse calls that an AWS Step Functions workflow runs in sequence.
Submit the requests as an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job, and read the reports from the S3 output location when the job completes.

explanation: The root cause is that AWS SDK clients time out after one minute by default, and a non-streaming Converse call returns nothing until generation has finished; the client abandons the connection, retries, and Bedrock completes and bills every attempt. Several options stop that, so the extra constraints decide: text must be visible within seconds of being generated, and the report must be one generation. Calling 'ConverseStream in place of Converse' satisfies both. The response arrives as events while the model writes, so the connection is not silent for a minute, the function can forward text to the progress page as it arrives, and the report is still a single generation. A client 'whose read_timeout is longer than the longest expected generation' ends the timeouts and the duplicate charges, but the function still receives the whole report only after 3 to 6 minutes, so the progress page shows nothing meanwhile. Splitting the report 'into sections' with separate calls breaks the rule that the report comes from a single generation. A 'batch inference job' is asynchronous and delivers results to S3 when the job completes, with no incremental text at all. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-parameters-anthropic-claude-messages.html

prompt: A reporting service uses a Python Lambda function with a 15-minute timeout to generate 20-page reports. The function calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with a boto3 client in its default configuration; one generation takes 3 to 6 minutes. The function log shows a ReadTimeoutError about 60 seconds after each call, followed by further attempts, although model invocation logs show that Bedrock completed every request, and token charges are several times higher than expected. The service produces 6,000 reports each night from prompts that are ready by 20:00, and nobody reads the reports before 08:00. The prompts use no tools and no prompt caching, and finance has asked for the LOWEST inference cost. Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: Create the Bedrock runtime client with a botocore Config whose read_timeout is longer than the longest expected generation.
Call ConverseStream in place of Converse, and assemble the report in the function from the events as they arrive.
Split each report into sections, and generate them with separate shorter Converse calls that an AWS Step Functions workflow runs in sequence.
Submit the requests as an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job, and read the reports from the S3 output location when the job completes.

explanation: The timeouts come from the SDK's default one-minute read timeout on a call that returns nothing for 3 to 6 minutes; each retry is completed and billed by Bedrock. Several options stop that waste, so the deciding constraints are the workload and the cost goal: 6,000 reports, prompts ready in the evening, results not needed for twelve hours, and the lowest inference cost. Submitting the requests 'as an Amazon Bedrock batch inference job' fits. Batch inference processes prompts from S3 asynchronously and writes the responses to S3, there is no client connection to time out, and AWS prices batch inference 50% below on-demand inference. The prompts use neither tool calling nor prompt caching, which batch inference does not support. A client 'whose read_timeout is longer than the longest expected generation' removes the retries, but every report is still billed at the on-demand rate. Calling 'ConverseStream in place of Converse' also ends the timeouts at the on-demand rate, and nobody is watching the text arrive. Splitting each report 'into sections' keeps on-demand pricing, resends shared context with every call, and adds a workflow to operate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/batch-inference.html

prompt: A three-person front-end team that works in React and TypeScript, with no backend engineers, must add a feature to a seller portal in four weeks. A seller fills in a form and receives a product listing as an object with a title, five bullet points and a price suggestion, produced by a model on Amazon Bedrock. Each request is independent: there is no follow-up turn, and the exchange must not be kept as a stored conversation afterwards. The prompt template must stay on the server, and the team wants to define the backend in TypeScript next to the front-end code. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Define a conversation route with the AWS Amplify AI kit, and render it with the AIConversation component and the useAIConversation hook.
Define a generation route with the AWS Amplify AI kit, and call it from a form component that renders the typed result it returns.
Host the application on AWS Amplify, call ConverseStream from the browser with Cognito identity pool credentials, and keep the history in the browser's local storage.
Build an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API with Lambda functions and DynamoDB tables for connections and history, and write a chat component for it.

explanation: The feature is a single request that returns a structured object, with no follow-up turn and no stored conversation, and the prompt must stay on the server. An Amplify AI kit 'generation route' is that primitive: it is declared in the TypeScript data schema, it is a single synchronous request-response query that generates structured data according to the route definition, and the prompt lives in the backend definition, so the form component only renders the typed result. A 'conversation route' is the multi-turn primitive: it is a streaming, multi-turn API whose conversations and messages are automatically stored in DynamoDB, which is what this feature must not do, and a chat component is the wrong interface for a form. Calling ConverseStream 'from the browser with Cognito identity pool credentials' means the browser builds the request, so the prompt template would be shipped to the client. The 'Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API with Lambda functions and DynamoDB tables' could be made to work, but it is a hand-built backend with stored history, the most effort for a team without backend engineers. Read more: https://docs.amplify.aws/react/ai/generation/

prompt: A three-person front-end team that works in React and TypeScript, with no backend engineers, must deliver a journaling companion in four weeks. Users sign in and chat in a multi-turn interface that streams responses from a model on Amazon Bedrock. The product's privacy promise, reviewed by counsel, is that conversation text is never written to any database or storage that the company operates and that earlier conversations exist only on the device on which they took place. The prompt contains nothing confidential. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Define a conversation route with the AWS Amplify AI kit, and render it with the AIConversation component and the useAIConversation hook.
Define a generation route with the AWS Amplify AI kit, and call it from a form component that renders the typed result it returns.
Host the application on AWS Amplify, call ConverseStream from the browser with Cognito identity pool credentials, and keep the history in the browser's local storage.
Build an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API with Lambda functions and DynamoDB tables for connections and history, and write a chat component for it.

explanation: The privacy promise decides this: conversation text must never be written to storage the company operates, and history lives only on the device. Calling ConverseStream 'from the browser with Cognito identity pool credentials' and keeping the history 'in the browser's local storage' honours it. The identity pool gives signed-in users temporary AWS credentials, the browser streams responses directly from Bedrock, the multi-turn history is resent from local storage on each turn, and nothing is persisted on the company's side; since the prompt is not confidential, building the request in the browser is acceptable. A 'conversation route' would normally be the least effort for a streaming chat, but its conversations and messages are automatically stored in DynamoDB, which breaks the promise. A 'generation route' is a single synchronous request-response query for structured results, not a streaming multi-turn chat. The 'Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API with Lambda functions and DynamoDB tables' for history stores conversation text in a database the company operates and is also the most backend work for a front-end team. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html

prompt: A marketing operations team wants an assistant for campaign planners. A planner's request can be anything from a quick tagline to a multi-market brief, and the conversation continues over several turns. Depending on the request, the assistant may need to look up disclaimer text in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, check stock through an inventory API, or query a pricing API, in an order that cannot be laid out in advance, and it must remember earlier turns of the session. The team has reviewed the trade-offs and accepts that the model, not a fixed definition, decides which steps to take. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock agent with the knowledge base attached, and describe the task and the available tools in the agent's instructions.
Have developers implement the sequence as an AWS Step Functions state machine with Lambda tasks, defined in the team's infrastructure as code.
Keep a single prompt with variables in Prompt Management, and call a version of it through the Converse API with prompt variables.
Build the workflow in the Amazon Bedrock Flows visual builder with prompt, condition and knowledge base nodes, and invoke an alias of a published version.

explanation: The request types are open-ended, the order of lookups cannot be laid out in advance, and the conversation spans several turns. That is what 'an Amazon Bedrock agent with the knowledge base attached' is for: at each iteration of orchestration the foundation model predicts the API operation to invoke or the knowledge base to query, and the conversation history is preserved as the session continues through further InvokeAgent requests. The team has accepted that the model decides the steps. The 'Amazon Bedrock Flows visual builder' links prompt, condition and knowledge base nodes into paths that are fixed in the flow definition; it suits a known sequence, but here the sequence cannot be enumerated. The 'AWS Step Functions state machine with Lambda tasks' is likewise a predefined sequence, and every new kind of request would need developers to add branches. 'A single prompt with variables in Prompt Management' is one model call: it cannot query the knowledge base, call the inventory or pricing API, or hold a multi-turn session by itself. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-how.html

prompt: A marketing operations team generates campaign taglines. The task is one model call: a prompt takes a product description and a tone and returns three taglines; nothing is retrieved, and there is no branching. A prompt engineer wants to edit and version the prompt text without an application release. The application already calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, and its developers will not adopt a different invocation API or add another service to the request path, because the feature has a strict latency budget. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock agent with the knowledge base attached, and describe the task and the available tools in the agent's instructions.
Have developers implement the sequence as an AWS Step Functions state machine with Lambda tasks, defined in the team's infrastructure as code.
Keep a single prompt with variables in Prompt Management, and call a version of it through the Converse API with prompt variables.
Build the workflow in the Amazon Bedrock Flows visual builder with prompt, condition and knowledge base nodes, and invoke an alias of a published version.

explanation: The task is a single model call with two variables, the prompt must be versioned outside the application, and the developers will keep calling Converse with no additional service in the path. Keeping 'a single prompt with variables in Prompt Management' meets all of that: the prompt engineer edits and versions the prompt there, and the application specifies the prompt's ARN in the modelId parameter of Converse and supplies the values in promptVariables, so the invocation API does not change. The 'Amazon Bedrock Flows visual builder' can wrap the same prompt in a flow, but a flow is invoked with InvokeFlow, a different API, and its condition and knowledge base nodes have no use when nothing branches or is retrieved. 'An Amazon Bedrock agent' is called with InvokeAgent and adds an orchestration loop that decides on steps, which is extra latency for a one-step task. The 'AWS Step Functions state machine with Lambda tasks' puts another service in the request path and moves prompt changes back to developers and their infrastructure code. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-test.html

prompt: A mortgage lender holds 2 million archived application packets in Amazon S3: pay slips, bank statements and identity documents as scans or phone photos, many with tables and stamps. Compliance analysts need to ask free-form questions across the archive, such as which applications in a given quarter relied on a particular employer's letter, and every answer must cite the source documents. The questions are not known in advance, so there is no fixed list of fields to extract. The four-person team does not want to build its own OCR, indexing or retrieval components. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Orchestrate Amazon Textract for OCR and per-type Amazon Bedrock classification and extraction prompts in an AWS Step Functions state machine.
Create an Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint for each document type, and call InvokeDataAutomationAsync with EventBridge notifications.
Ingest the documents into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses the Data Automation parser, and query it with RetrieveAndGenerate.
Send each page image to a multimodal model through the Converse API from a Lambda function, using a JSON schema for structured output.

explanation: The analysts' need is question answering over an archive with cited sources, and the questions are not known in advance. That is retrieval-augmented generation, so ingesting the documents into 'an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses the Data Automation parser' fits: the parser handles scans with tables and stamps during ingestion, the knowledge base manages indexing and retrieval, and RetrieveAndGenerate returns responses with citations to the original source data, with no OCR or retrieval component for the team to build. 'An Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint for each document type' solves a different problem: a blueprint defines a fixed set of fields to extract from each document, and here there is no fixed field list and nothing in it answers questions across 2 million packets. Orchestrating 'Amazon Textract for OCR' with per-type prompts is also field extraction, and it is the self-built pipeline the team wants to avoid. Sending 'each page image to a multimodal model' returns structured output for one page at a time; it provides no search across the archive and no citations. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-advanced-parsing.html

prompt: A lender's mobile app lets a loan officer photograph a single document during a customer meeting. The app sends the image together with a JSON schema that the officer's workflow builds at that moment, so the requested fields differ from one request to the next and cannot be registered ahead of time. The extracted values must come back in the response to the same HTTPS request while the officer waits, shaped exactly to that schema. Volume is a few hundred images a day, and neither confidence scores nor human review are required. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Orchestrate Amazon Textract for OCR and per-type Amazon Bedrock classification and extraction prompts in an AWS Step Functions state machine.
Create an Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint for each document type, and call InvokeDataAutomationAsync with EventBridge notifications.
Ingest the documents into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that uses the Data Automation parser, and query it with RetrieveAndGenerate.
Send each page image to a multimodal model through the Converse API from a Lambda function, using a JSON schema for structured output.

explanation: The decisive facts are that the schema arrives with each request and differs every time, and that the result must return in the same request, shaped to that schema. Sending the page image 'to a multimodal model through the Converse API from a Lambda function, using a JSON schema for structured output' fits: the function passes the caller's schema in the request's output configuration, the model returns JSON that conforms to it, and one synchronous call serves a few hundred images a day. The first request that uses a new schema includes a grammar compilation step, so it takes longer than a request whose schema is already cached. 'An Amazon Bedrock Data Automation project with a blueprint for each document type' is the managed choice for a known set of document types, but blueprints are resources created ahead of time that define the fields to extract, and these fields cannot be registered in advance; its confidence scores are not needed here. Orchestrating 'Amazon Textract for OCR' with per-type classification and extraction prompts also assumes predefined types and adds several steps to a request whose response the officer is waiting for. 'An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base' requires documents to be ingested before they can be queried and returns generated answers with citations, not values shaped to a caller's schema. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/structured-output.html

prompt: A team maintains 30 Java 8 services, built with Maven, that call Amazon Bedrock. Before an audit in two weeks every service must run on Java 17 with the build passing. The team lead wants each service upgraded by an automated transformation that builds the code and produces a summary and a diff for review, and does not want developers to work through the files of each service in chat sessions. The company will not build or host its own tooling for this work. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST effort?

options.text: Run the Amazon Q Developer code transformation capability on each repository, and review the proposed changes and the transformation summary.
Create an AWS CodeBuild project that sends each pull request's changed files to an Amazon Bedrock model with the company's review prompt and posts the findings.
Use Amazon Q Developer in the IDE: chat to refactor code, unit test generation for coverage, and code reviews for secrets and vulnerabilities.
Index the repositories and the engineering wiki in an Amazon Q Business application so that developers can ask how the code should be changed.

explanation: The work is a language-version upgrade of Maven projects, and the lead wants an automated transformation per service that builds the code and yields a summary and a diff. That is the 'Amazon Q Developer code transformation capability': it upgrades Java 8 and Java 11 projects built on Maven to Java 17 or Java 21, builds the code as part of the transformation, and presents the proposed changes as a diff together with a transformation summary for review. Using 'Amazon Q Developer in the IDE' through chat, test generation and code reviews could help a developer upgrade a service, but it is the interactive, file-by-file route that the lead has ruled out, repeated 30 times. The 'AWS CodeBuild project that sends each pull request's changed files to an Amazon Bedrock model' is tooling the company would have to write, prompt and operate, which it will not do, and it reviews changes instead of performing an upgrade. 'An Amazon Q Business application' answers questions over indexed content; it does not modify code, build it or produce a diff. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/code-transformation.html

prompt: A platform team must enforce a house rule on 40 Python Lambda functions that call Amazon Bedrock: every Converse call has to pass the company's guardrail identifier and a cost-centre value in the request metadata. The check must run on every pull request and post its findings there, whichever editor the author uses; a third of the contributors are contractors who work in Vim on locked-down laptops on which no IDE plug-ins may be installed. The rule is specific to the company and is expressed in a review prompt that the platform team maintains and intends to extend. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Run the Amazon Q Developer code transformation capability on each repository, and review the proposed changes and the transformation summary.
Create an AWS CodeBuild project that sends each pull request's changed files to an Amazon Bedrock model with the company's review prompt and posts the findings.
Use Amazon Q Developer in the IDE: chat to refactor code, unit test generation for coverage, and code reviews for secrets and vulnerabilities.
Index the repositories and the engineering wiki in an Amazon Q Business application so that developers can ask how the code should be changed.

explanation: The rule is company-specific, it must be checked on every pull request regardless of the author's editor, and the findings must appear on the pull request. A pipeline-side check does that: 'an AWS CodeBuild project that sends each pull request's changed files to an Amazon Bedrock model with the company's review prompt and posts the findings' runs for every contributor, and the platform team extends the rule by editing its prompt. 'Amazon Q Developer in the IDE' offers chat, unit test generation and code reviews that detect vulnerabilities and secrets, but it runs in a developer's IDE: it cannot be enforced for contractors who work in Vim without plug-ins, and nothing in it runs automatically on each pull request. The 'Amazon Q Developer code transformation capability' performs Java upgrades and .NET porting; it does not review Python code against a house rule. 'An Amazon Q Business application' answers questions over indexed repositories and wiki pages when someone asks; it does not check each pull request or post findings on it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/code-reviews.html

prompt: A payments company screens each transaction dispute with six checks. Each check is a Lambda function that makes one Amazon Bedrock call and takes 3 to 8 seconds; the same six checks run for every dispute, and a failed check must be retried with backoff. The calling API waits for the combined result in the same request and needs it within 30 seconds. About 2 million disputes are screened each month, and there is no human step. The team wants parallelism, retries and the collection of the six results handled for it, without writing its own coordination code. Which orchestration meets these requirements?

options.text: An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow with a Map state limited to 8 concurrent iterations, task retries, and a callback task that waits for a task token.
An AWS Step Functions Express workflow, started synchronously, with a Map state limited to 8 concurrent iterations and retries on each task.
A supervisor Lambda function that runs a Strands Agents loop and calls the workers as tools, letting the model choose which workers to call.
An Amazon SQS queue with one message per worker and a maximum concurrency of 8 on the event source mapping, with results written to Amazon DynamoDB.

explanation: The decisive constraints are that the caller waits for the combined result in the same request, that the run is short and has no human step, and that the same six checks always run. An 'AWS Step Functions Express workflow, started synchronously' fits: a synchronous Express execution starts the workflow, waits until it completes and returns the result, the Map state runs the checks in parallel and gathers their outputs, Retry handles backoff, and a run of well under a minute is far inside the five-minute Express limit. Express workflows are intended for high-volume, short workloads such as this one. The 'AWS Step Functions Standard workflow' offers the same Map and Retry, but a Standard execution is started asynchronously and its result must be fetched later, so the calling API cannot receive it in the same request, and its callback task has no purpose without a human step. The 'supervisor Lambda function that runs a Strands Agents loop' lets a model choose which workers to call, whereas the six checks are fixed and must all run every time. The 'Amazon SQS queue with one message per worker' runs the checks, but collecting six results and answering the waiting caller would need the coordination code the team wants to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/choosing-workflow-type.html

prompt: A due-diligence application investigates acquisition targets with a library of 40 specialised research workers, each a Lambda function that runs for 1 to 2 minutes against Amazon Bedrock. Running all 40 for every target has proved wasteful: a typical target needs three to five of them, and which ones, and in what order, depends on what the earlier findings reveal. The team therefore wants a model to choose the next worker as findings come in. A complete investigation finishes within 10 minutes, there is no approval step, and a failed worker call can simply be attempted again by the coordinator. Which orchestration meets these requirements?

options.text: An AWS Step Functions Standard workflow with a Map state limited to 8 concurrent iterations, task retries, and a callback task that waits for a task token.
An AWS Step Functions Express workflow, started synchronously, with a Map state limited to 8 concurrent iterations and retries on each task.
A supervisor Lambda function that runs a Strands Agents loop and calls the workers as tools, letting the model choose which workers to call.
An Amazon SQS queue with one message per worker and a maximum concurrency of 8 on the event source mapping, with results written to Amazon DynamoDB.

explanation: The deciding constraint is that the set and order of workers is not known in advance: a model must pick the next worker from the findings so far. That is the agents-as-tools pattern, so 'a supervisor Lambda function that runs a Strands Agents loop and calls the workers as tools' fits. The supervisor's model sees each worker's result, decides which specialist to call next, and stops when it has enough; three to five workers of 1 to 2 minutes each finish inside the 10-minute investigation, which is within a Lambda invocation's 15-minute maximum. The two Step Functions options are built around 'a Map state', which iterates over a list that is fixed when the state starts; they would run a predetermined set of workers rather than let findings steer the choice, the Standard workflow's callback task serves an approval step that does not exist here, and an Express workflow cannot run longer than five minutes. The 'Amazon SQS queue with one message per worker' likewise needs the messages, and therefore the workers, to be chosen up front, and deciding the next step from results in DynamoDB would be coordination logic the team would have to write. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html

prompt: A RAG assistant runs as an Amazon API Gateway REST API that invokes a Lambda function; the function queries Amazon OpenSearch Service and then calls one of two models through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. Prompts contain patient data, so company policy forbids model invocation logging, and the function's code and dependencies are frozen for an audit; only configuration may change. Last week p95 latency rose from 4 to 11 seconds. The team has two hypotheses: that one of the two models became slower and now receives more input tokens, and that the function is short of memory or CPU, so that API Gateway waits longer for the integration. Which combination of steps tests both hypotheses? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the API stage and the function, instrument the function's SDK and HTTP clients, and inspect the trace timeline.
Compare the InvocationLatency and InputTokenCount metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace for each ModelId for the weeks before and after the change.
Query AWS CloudTrail for Converse events grouped by role to count the calls that each role made during the last week.
Enable API Gateway access logging with integration latency and Lambda Insights, and compare that latency with the function's memory and CPU usage.
Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query on the invocation log group that sums input.inputTokenCount by identity.arn, then read the largest prompts.

explanation: Each hypothesis needs its own evidence, and two constraints limit the tools: no model invocation logging, and no change to the function's code. For the model hypothesis, the 'InvocationLatency and InputTokenCount metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace' are published without any logging and carry the ModelId dimension, so comparing the two models before and after the change shows whether one became slower or receives more tokens. For the resource hypothesis, 'API Gateway access logging with integration latency and Lambda Insights' shows how long API Gateway waits for the function alongside the function's memory and CPU usage; Lambda Insights is added as an extension in a Lambda layer, which is configuration, not code. 'AWS X-Ray active tracing' with instrumented SDK and HTTP clients would give a detailed timeline, but instrumenting the clients means changing the frozen code and dependencies, and a trace does not report memory or CPU. The 'CloudWatch Logs Insights query on the invocation log group' depends on invocation logging, which policy forbids. 'AWS CloudTrail' events for Converse identify the caller and the model but contain no latency, token or resource figures. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-metrics.html

prompt: A RAG assistant runs as an Amazon API Gateway REST API that invokes a Lambda function; the function queries Amazon OpenSearch Service and then calls a single model through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. Model invocation logging to Amazon CloudWatch Logs is enabled, and the team may change the function's code. Two problems appeared last week. First, p95 end-to-end latency rose from 4 to 11 seconds, and the team cannot tell whether the time is spent in API Gateway, in Lambda initialisation, in retrieval or in the model call. Second, Bedrock cost doubled, and the team suspects that one of the three IAM roles that call the model has started to send much larger prompts. Which combination of steps identifies both causes MOST efficiently? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the API stage and the function, instrument the function's SDK and HTTP clients, and inspect the trace timeline.
Compare the InvocationLatency and InputTokenCount metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace for each ModelId for the weeks before and after the change.
Query AWS CloudTrail for Converse events grouped by role to count the calls that each role made during the last week.
Enable API Gateway access logging with integration latency and Lambda Insights, and compare that latency with the function's memory and CPU usage.
Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query on the invocation log group that sums input.inputTokenCount by identity.arn, then read the largest prompts.

explanation: The latency question spans several components, which is what tracing answers. With 'AWS X-Ray active tracing on the API stage and the function', each sampled request has segments for API Gateway and Lambda, including initialisation, and instrumenting the function's SDK and HTTP clients adds subsegments for the OpenSearch query and the Bedrock call, so the timeline shows where the extra seconds go; the team is free to change the code. The cost question is answered by the invocation logs: each record carries identity.arn, input.inputTokenCount and the request body, so the 'CloudWatch Logs Insights query on the invocation log group' totals input tokens by role and then shows that role's largest prompts. The 'InvocationLatency and InputTokenCount metrics' confirm that tokens rose, but their dimension is ModelId and there is one model, so they cannot separate the three roles or show time spent outside the model call. 'AWS CloudTrail' shows which role made each call but holds no token counts or prompt content. 'API Gateway access logging with integration latency and Lambda Insights' gives one latency figure for the whole integration and resource usage; it neither separates retrieval from the model call nor attributes tokens to roles. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A telecom company uses an Amazon Bedrock model to turn support-call transcripts into summaries that are written to a CRM analytics store. Policy forbids customer names, phone numbers and email addresses in that store, but every call must still produce a usable summary, so a summary cannot be discarded just because the transcript mentioned a customer. Transcripts also sometimes contain internal provisioning identifiers (TK- followed by 16 hexadecimal characters). An identifier in a summary means a privileged session was recorded, so the whole response must be withheld and replaced with a fixed message that triggers manual review. The team wants one guardrail on the inference call. Which sensitive information filter configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Set the NAME, PHONE and EMAIL PII types to block on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to anonymize on output.
Set the NAME, PHONE and EMAIL PII types to block on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to block on output.
Set the NAME, PHONE and EMAIL PII types to anonymize on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to block on output.
Set the NAME, PHONE and EMAIL PII types to anonymize on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to anonymize on output.

explanation: Sensitive information filters offer two handling modes, and both are available for built-in PII types and for custom regex entries, separately for input and output. Mask (`ANONYMIZE`) replaces each detected value with its type, such as {NAME}, and delivers the rest of the response. Block withholds the whole response and returns the configured message. Here every call must still produce a summary, so the PII types need anonymize, and an identifier must stop the whole response, so the regex needs block: 'PII types to anonymize on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to block on output'. The configuration with 'PII types to block on output' and the regex 'set to anonymize' reverses the two rules: any summary that names a customer would be discarded, and an identifier would merely be replaced while the summary reached the CRM store without review. Setting both to block also discards every summary that mentions a customer, which the stem rules out. Setting both to anonymize keeps the summaries, but a summary with an identifier would still be delivered, and the requirement is to withhold it and send the fixed message. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-sensitive-filters.html

prompt: A recruitment platform runs a public chatbot on an Amazon Bedrock model that answers candidates' questions about open positions. The model's context can include records of other applicants. If a response contains a person's name, phone number or email address, the security team treats it as a leak of another applicant's record, and the whole response must be withheld and replaced with a fixed message. Responses also sometimes include internal job reference identifiers (JR- followed by eight digits) that should not be shown to candidates. An identifier is harmless on its own, so the answer must still be delivered with the identifier replaced by a placeholder. The team wants one guardrail on the inference call. Which sensitive information filter configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Set the NAME, PHONE and EMAIL PII types to block on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to anonymize on output.
Set the NAME, PHONE and EMAIL PII types to block on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to block on output.
Set the NAME, PHONE and EMAIL PII types to anonymize on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to block on output.
Set the NAME, PHONE and EMAIL PII types to anonymize on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to anonymize on output.

explanation: Sensitive information filters support Block and Mask (`ANONYMIZE`) for both built-in PII types and custom regex patterns. Block withholds the entire response and returns the configured message; Mask replaces the matched value with a placeholder and delivers the rest. In this scenario personal data signals a leak that must stop the whole response, while a job reference identifier only needs to be hidden, so the right choice is 'PII types to block on output, and add a custom regex for the identifier pattern set to anonymize on output'. The configuration with 'PII types to anonymize on output' and the regex 'set to block' has the two rules the wrong way round for this company: a leaked applicant record would be delivered with placeholders in it, and a harmless identifier would suppress a useful answer. Setting both to block handles the leak correctly but withholds every answer that mentions a job reference, which contradicts the requirement that such answers still be delivered. Setting both to anonymize handles the identifier correctly but delivers responses that the security team requires to be withheld in full. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-sensitive-filters.html

prompt: A retail bank's mobile app shows answers from an Amazon Bedrock model. A guardrail anonymizes account numbers and email addresses in model responses, and compliance requires that an unmasked value never reaches the device. User research shows that customers abandon the chat when the screen stays blank, so the product owner requires text to appear progressively as it is generated; a small delay on each chunk is acceptable. The engineering lead wants guardrail handling to be configured in the inference request and does not want moderation or buffering logic in the application code, which is shared with three other channels. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Call Converse without streaming with the guardrail attached, and send the complete evaluated response to the client in a single message.
Call ConverseStream with the guardrail in synchronous stream processing mode, so that chunks are buffered and evaluated before they are sent.
