prompt: A utilities company is building a support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Its privacy office set two requirements. First, before an Amazon S3 bucket of 2 million historical objects is approved as a knowledge base data source, the company needs a report of which objects contain personal data or credentials. The bucket holds PDF files, Excel workbooks and ZIP archives as well as text files, and the objects must not be changed or copied at this stage. Second, at run time, a model response that contains a customer's name or email address must still be delivered, with those values replaced by placeholders. The team wants managed features and no custom detection code. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job on the bucket and review the findings that it reports for the objects.
Run an Amazon Comprehend PII detection job in ONLY_REDACTION mode that writes redacted copies of the documents to an output bucket.
Add a guardrail sensitive information filter for the NAME and EMAIL types with the output action set to block.
Run an Amazon Comprehend PII detection job in ONLY_OFFSETS mode that writes the location of each entity to an output bucket.
Add a guardrail sensitive information filter for the NAME and EMAIL types with the output action set to anonymize.

explanation: Amazon Macie automates discovery and reporting of sensitive data in Amazon S3: a sensitive data discovery job analyses the objects in a bucket and generates findings for objects that contain sensitive data, and its supported formats include PDF files, Excel workbooks and ZIP archives. It reports and leaves the objects untouched, which fits the first requirement: 'run an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job on the bucket'. At run time, a guardrail sensitive information filter with the mask action replaces each detected value with its type, such as {NAME}, and delivers the rest of the response: 'the output action set to anonymize'. The Comprehend job 'in ONLY_REDACTION mode' writes redacted copies, but the stem says objects must not be changed or copied at this stage, and it produces documents, not a report. The Comprehend job 'in ONLY_OFFSETS mode' locates PII entities in English or Spanish text documents; the stem's bucket also holds PDF files, Excel workbooks and ZIP archives, which are among the formats a Macie discovery job analyses, so Macie is the service that can report on the whole bucket. The filter with 'the output action set to block' withholds the whole response, contradicting the requirement that it still be delivered. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/discovery-jobs.html

prompt: A debt-advice charity is building a support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Its privacy office set two requirements. First, an Amazon S3 bucket holds 300,000 English plain-text call transcripts that are already known to contain clients' personal data; they must be converted in bulk into copies with the personal data removed, and only those copies may be ingested into the knowledge base. Second, the assistant is used by volunteers from partner organizations, so if a model response contains a person's name or email address, the whole response must be withheld and a fixed message shown, so that the case is escalated to a staff member. The team wants managed features and no custom detection code. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job on the bucket and review the findings that it reports for the objects.
Run an Amazon Comprehend PII detection job in ONLY_REDACTION mode that writes redacted copies of the documents to an output bucket.
Add a guardrail sensitive information filter for the NAME and EMAIL types with the output action set to block.
Run an Amazon Comprehend PII detection job in ONLY_OFFSETS mode that writes the location of each entity to an output bucket.
Add a guardrail sensitive information filter for the NAME and EMAIL types with the output action set to anonymize.

explanation: Amazon Comprehend can redact in bulk: an asynchronous PII entity detection job with `Mode` set to `ONLY_REDACTION` writes a copy of each input document to an output location in Amazon S3 with the PII entities replaced, for English or Spanish text, which matches the plain-text English transcripts: 'a PII detection job in ONLY_REDACTION mode that writes redacted copies'. At run time, a sensitive information filter with the block action withholds the whole response and returns the configured message, which is the escalation behaviour the privacy office wants: 'the output action set to block'. The 'Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job' reports which objects contain sensitive data; the stem says that is already known, and Macie's findings do not produce cleaned copies. The Comprehend job 'in ONLY_OFFSETS mode' writes the location of each entity and leaves the text unchanged, so the team would still need its own code to produce copies. The filter with 'the output action set to anonymize' would deliver the response with placeholders, while the requirement is that the whole response be withheld and the case escalated. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/redact-api-pii.html

prompt: A lender enabled Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to both an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group and an Amazon S3 bucket, because auditors require the full prompt and response of every invocation. Prompts contain applicants' national ID numbers, and the model needs the real values to complete its task. Operations engineers query the log group with CloudWatch Logs Insights and must not see the ID numbers, while a small fraud team must be able to see them. The copies in S3 must be permanently deleted 90 days after delivery; the bucket has versioning enabled. Default encryption satisfies the lender's policy. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Associate a customer managed KMS key with the log group and the bucket, and add S3 Lifecycle rules that expire current and noncurrent versions.
Add a log group data protection policy with logs:Unmask for one team, and apply an S3 Object Lock default retention period to the bucket.
Add a log group data protection policy with logs:Unmask for one team, and add S3 Lifecycle rules that expire current and noncurrent versions.
Associate a customer managed KMS key with the log group and the bucket, and apply an S3 Object Lock default retention period to the bucket.

explanation: CloudWatch Logs data protection policies detect sensitive data as it is ingested into a log group and mask it at all egress points, including Logs Insights; principals with the `logs:Unmask` permission can view the original values. That gives operations masked logs and the fraud team full access without changing what is logged. For the S3 copies, expiring an object in a versioning-enabled bucket only adds a delete marker and makes the version noncurrent, so permanent deletion also needs a `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` rule. Together: 'a log group data protection policy with logs:Unmask for one team, and ... S3 Lifecycle rules that expire current and noncurrent versions'. The options that 'associate a customer managed KMS key' encrypt the data at rest, but CloudWatch Logs decrypts it whenever it is requested, so operations engineers who can query the log group still see the ID numbers; the stem also says default encryption is sufficient. The options that 'apply an S3 Object Lock default retention period' protect object versions from deletion during the period; they do not delete anything after 90 days, which is the stated requirement. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/mask-sensitive-log-data.html

prompt: An online travel agency plans to fine-tune an Amazon Bedrock model on 500,000 English support-chat transcripts stored in Amazon S3 so that it learns the agency's tone and resolution patterns. Nearly every transcript contains a customer name, phone number or address. The privacy office requires that no customer's personal data be present in the training data, because a customized model can reproduce training examples. The data science team wants the model to keep learning the structure of a good reply, including the points in a conversation where an agent confirms a name as opposed to a phone number or an address. The platform team wants a managed feature and will not write or operate transformation code. Which approach BEST satisfies all three teams?

options.text: Run an Amazon Comprehend PII redaction job on the transcripts with the mask mode that replaces each character of an entity with a chosen character.
Run an Amazon Comprehend PII redaction job on the transcripts with the mask mode that replaces each entity with the name of its entity type.
Run an Amazon Comprehend PII job that returns entity offsets, and use an AWS Glue job to replace each located entity with a synthetic value.
Run an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job on the transcripts, and exclude every object that has a finding from the training dataset.

explanation: The privacy requirement concerns what goes into training, so the transcripts must be transformed before the customization job. An Amazon Comprehend PII job in `ONLY_REDACTION` mode writes redacted copies of English or Spanish documents, and its `MaskMode` can be `REPLACE_WITH_PII_ENTITY_TYPE`, which replaces each entity with the name of its type. The personal data is gone, but each placeholder still says what kind of information stood there, so the model can learn where an agent confirms a name as opposed to an address: 'the mask mode that replaces each entity with the name of its entity type'. The mode that 'replaces each character of an entity with a chosen character' also removes the personal data, but a run of identical characters does not distinguish a name from a phone number or an address, which loses the structure the data science team wants. The job 'that returns entity offsets' followed by an AWS Glue job could insert realistic synthetic values, but the platform team will not write or operate transformation code. The 'Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job' with exclusion would discard nearly every transcript, since the stem says almost all of them contain personal data. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/comprehend/latest/dg/redact-api-pii.html

prompt: An energy retailer plans to fine-tune an Amazon Bedrock model on 200,000 English support-chat transcripts stored in Amazon S3. explanation: An Amazon Comprehend PII job in `ONLY_REDACTION` mode writes redacted copies of English or Spanish documents. Because each character is replaced one for one, the text keeps its length, and the output carries no indication of the entity type. That satisfies the privacy policy, the alignment tool and the platform team: 'the mask mode that replaces each character of an entity with a chosen character'. The mode that 'replaces each entity with the name of its entity type' removes the personal data, but it inserts exactly the kind of label the privacy policy treats as a disclosure, and a type name rarely has the same length as the value it replaces, which breaks alignment by character position. prompt: A financial services company runs two GenAI workloads in one AWS account: a claims summarizer and an underwriting notes tool. Both call the Amazon Bedrock Converse and ConverseStream APIs directly from AWS Lambda; the company uses no agents, flows or knowledge bases. A trail delivers management events from all Regions to an Amazon S3 bucket with a 7-year retention policy, and no data event selectors are configured. The prompts contain claimants' health data, and the privacy policy forbids copying prompt or response content into any additional store. The company wants to add as little new logging volume as possible. Which change meets the requirement?

options.text: Enable model invocation logging to the S3 bucket, and query the identity.arn field of the delivered log records with Amazon Athena.
Add advanced event selectors for data events on the AWS::Bedrock::AgentAlias and AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase resource types to the existing trail.
Keep the trail's event selectors as they are, and query the Amazon Bedrock management events that it already delivers with Amazon Athena.
Add advanced event selectors for data events on the AWS::Bedrock::FlowAlias resource type to the existing trail, scoped to the production alias ARN.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock logs InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, Converse and ConverseStream as CloudTrail management events, and a trail records management events by default. Each event carries the userIdentity of the caller and the event time, so the existing trail already holds the audit record for both workloads, with 7-year retention and no new volume. "Keep the trail's event selectors as they are" and query what is there is therefore enough. "Enable model invocation logging" would also give the caller in `identity.arn`, but each record includes the full request and response bodies, which breaks the rule against copying prompt content into another store and adds the most volume. The option for "AWS::Bedrock::AgentAlias and AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase" data events records InvokeAgent, Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate calls; the company uses no agents or knowledge bases, so it adds nothing. The option for "AWS::Bedrock::FlowAlias" data events records InvokeFlow calls, and the company has no flows. Data events are also charged separately, which works against the goal of minimal new logging. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

prompt: A lender uses Amazon Bedrock to draft explanations of credit decisions. Applicants' Social Security numbers appear in the prompts. A guardrail with a sensitive information filter is attached to every Converse call, and testing confirms that the responses shown to users are masked. Model invocation logging delivers to a CloudWatch Logs log group that is retained for 7 years, and support engineers query it with CloudWatch Logs Insights. A review finds complete Social Security numbers in the logged requests. The privacy office rules that the original numbers must not be persisted in any log store, whether masked on read or encrypted, and that nobody needs the original values later. Engineers must keep their Logs Insights access, and the team is free to change application code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Deliver the invocation logs to an S3 bucket encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, and allow kms:Decrypt on that key for the compliance officers' role.
Mask the Social Security numbers in the application with the ApplyGuardrail API before each Converse call, and send the masked text that it returns to the model.
Deliver the invocation logs to an S3 bucket cataloged in AWS Glue, and grant the engineers AWS Lake Formation column permissions that exclude the request body.
Apply a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy with matching data identifiers to the log group, and grant the logs:Unmask permission to the compliance officers.

explanation: The Guardrails documentation states that in model invocation logs the `input` field contains the original, unmodified request regardless of guardrail intervention. To keep the numbers out of the log, they must be removed before the request is made. `ApplyGuardrail` evaluates text against a guardrail without invoking a model, and with an anonymize action its output is the masked text, so "Mask the Social Security numbers in the application with the ApplyGuardrail API before each Converse call" means the logged request never holds an original value, and engineers keep Logs Insights. "Apply a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy" masks values at egress, but the originals remain stored and can be revealed with `logs:Unmask`, which the privacy office excludes by ruling out masking on read. "Deliver the invocation logs to an S3 bucket encrypted with a customer managed KMS key" still persists the originals, only encrypted, and removes the engineers' Logs Insights access. "AWS Lake Formation column permissions that exclude the request body" hides the column from engineers, but the original numbers are still stored in the bucket. prompt: A fintech startup runs all of its GenAI workloads in a single standalone AWS account; the company does not use AWS Organizations and has no plan to adopt it this year. Application teams call Amazon Bedrock with InvokeModel and Converse in two Regions. The risk committee requires a baseline set of content filters and denied topics on every model invocation in the account. A request that a developer sends without any guardrail must be protected by the baseline, not rejected, and teams must remain free to attach their own stricter guardrail to a request. The baseline configuration must be immutable once it is released. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Call PutEnforcedGuardrailConfiguration with the guardrail ARN and its version in each Region where the workload account invokes Amazon Bedrock models.
Create the guardrail and a numeric version in the organization's management account, with a resource-based policy that grants bedrock:ApplyGuardrail to the member accounts.
Enable the Amazon Bedrock policy type in AWS Organizations, and attach a policy that names the guardrail ARN and its version to the OU that holds the workload accounts.

explanation: Account-level enforcement designates one version of a guardrail in an account for all Amazon Bedrock model invocations from that account. The guardrail is created in the account, a numeric version makes its configuration immutable, and `PutEnforcedGuardrailConfiguration` is called in every Region where enforcement is wanted. The guardrail is then applied automatically to inputs and outputs, including requests that carry no guardrail, and a guardrail in the request is combined with it, the most restrictive control taking precedence. So "Create the guardrail and a numeric version in the workload account" and "Call PutEnforcedGuardrailConfiguration" are the two actions. "Create the guardrail ... in the organization's management account" and "Enable the Amazon Bedrock policy type in AWS Organizations" are the organization-level route, which is not available to a standalone account without AWS Organizations. The statement that "denies InvokeModel and Converse unless bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier matches" fails twice: a request without a guardrail is rejected rather than protected, and a request has to name the baseline guardrail, so a team cannot send its own. Create the guardrail and a numeric version in the organization's management account, with a resource-based policy that grants bedrock:ApplyGuardrail to the member accounts.
Enable the Amazon Bedrock policy type in AWS Organizations, and attach a policy that names the guardrail ARN and its version to the OU that holds the workload accounts.
Create the guardrail and a numeric version in the workload account, and allow bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on that guardrail for the IAM roles that invoke models there.
Add a statement to the invoking IAM roles that denies InvokeModel and Converse unless bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier matches the guardrail ARN and its version.

explanation: Organization-level enforcement needs both parts. The guardrail is created in the management account with a numeric version, which keeps the configuration immutable for member accounts, and a resource-based policy grants `bedrock:ApplyGuardrail` to them. An AWS Organizations policy of type `BEDROCK_POLICY` that names the guardrail ARN and version is then attached to the OU. The guardrail is applied automatically to InvokeModel and Converse calls in those accounts, including requests without a guardrail, and it is combined with any guardrail in the request. That gives one centrally managed definition. "Create the guardrail and a numeric version in the workload account" with "Call PutEnforcedGuardrailConfiguration" is account-level enforcement: it would mean 40 separate definitions, each configured inside a member account where its administrators could change or remove it, which the board rules out. The statement that "denies InvokeModel and Converse unless bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier matches" rejects requests that carry no guardrail instead of protecting them, and it forces every request to name the baseline guardrail, so teams could not attach their own. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-enforcements.html

prompt: A bank fine-tunes an open-weight foundation model with Amazon SageMaker AI and registers each approved version in SageMaker Model Registry. SageMaker Clarify evaluation reports for every version are written to Amazon S3 as JSON. A regulator requires, for each model version, a record in the regulator's own JSON schema: about 60 fields that include intended uses, known limitations, a risk rating on a five-level scale and the evaluation results. Every record must be held on write-once-read-many storage so that no principal, including the account's root user, can delete or overwrite it for 10 years, and auditors want a PDF copy. The CI/CD pipeline must produce the record. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Have the pipeline store the intended use, risk rating and metric values as custom metadata properties on each model package version in SageMaker Model Registry.
Have the pipeline create a SageMaker model card for each version with the SageMaker Python SDK, reference the Clarify report in Amazon S3, and export the card to PDF.
Have the pipeline log the intended use, risk rating and metric values as parameters and metrics of a run in SageMaker managed MLflow that is linked to each version.
Have the pipeline write a JSON governance record for each version to an S3 bucket that uses S3 Versioning and Object Lock in compliance mode, and render it as a PDF.

explanation: S3 Object Lock stores objects with a write-once-read-many model. In compliance mode a protected object version cannot be overwritten or deleted by any user, including the root user, and the retention period cannot be shortened; Object Lock works on buckets with S3 Versioning. A JSON object can follow any schema, so "write a JSON governance record for each version to an S3 bucket that uses S3 Versioning and Object Lock in compliance mode" meets the regulator's format, the 10-year WORM rule and, with rendering, the PDF. "create a SageMaker model card" gives a versioned record and a PDF export, but a card follows the model card JSON schema, whose risk rating is one of unknown, low, medium or high, so it cannot be the regulator's 60-field record with a five-level scale, and it is not WORM storage. "custom metadata properties on each model package version" are key-value strings that can be updated or removed, with no retention lock. "a run in SageMaker managed MLflow" tracks parameters and metrics, but runs can be deleted through the MLflow API, so the root-proof retention rule is not met. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: An insurer fine-tunes an open-weight foundation model with Amazon SageMaker AI and registers each approved version in SageMaker Model Registry. SageMaker Clarify evaluation reports for every version are written to Amazon S3 as JSON. A deployment gate, implemented as a Lambda function, calls DescribeModelPackage and already reads a data_classification key from the custom metadata properties of the version. Governance now requires the gate to refuse any version whose risk rating is high or whose bias metric exceeds a threshold. The gate's code and IAM role are frozen for an audit, so it can only be configured to read further keys from the response it already receives. No document or PDF is required. Which solution meets these requirements with the FEWEST changes to the existing system?

options.text: Have the pipeline store the intended use, risk rating and metric values as custom metadata properties on each model package version in SageMaker Model Registry.
Have the pipeline create a SageMaker model card for each version with the SageMaker Python SDK, reference the Clarify report in Amazon S3, and export the card to PDF.
Have the pipeline log the intended use, risk rating and metric values as parameters and metrics of a run in SageMaker managed MLflow that is linked to each version.
Have the pipeline write a JSON governance record for each version to an S3 bucket that uses S3 Versioning and Object Lock in compliance mode, and render it as a PDF.

explanation: A model package version carries `CustomerMetadataProperties`, a map of up to 50 string keys and values that the pipeline can set when it registers or updates the version and that `DescribeModelPackage` returns. The gate already reads one key from that map, so "store the intended use, risk rating and metric values as custom metadata properties on each model package version" lets it enforce the new rule through configuration only, with no new code, API call or permission. "create a SageMaker model card" is the fuller governance document, but nothing here asks for a document or PDF, and a standalone card is a separate resource that the frozen gate would need new code and permissions to read. "write a JSON governance record ... to an S3 bucket that uses S3 Versioning and Object Lock" would require the gate to call Amazon S3, which its frozen role and code do not allow, and WORM retention is not a requirement. "a run in SageMaker managed MLflow" puts the values behind the MLflow API, again outside the single response the gate is allowed to use. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/APIReference/API_UpdateModelPackage.html

prompt: An insurer has an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over policy PDFs in Amazon S3. The assistant calls RetrieveAndGenerate and shows the S3 URI of each cited document. Compliance now requires every answer to display the owning business unit, the document version and the effective date of each source, taken from stored data and not from model-generated text. These attributes are mastered in the DynamoDB table of the records-management application, keyed by S3 URI, and they change several times a day as documents are superseded. Policy forbids keeping a copy of the attributes anywhere outside that table, and the values shown must be current at the moment of the answer. Each business unit already has its own knowledge base, so no retrieval filter is needed. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store the three attributes as user-defined object metadata on each PDF, call HeadObject for every cited S3 URI after each response, and render the returned headers.
Upload a .metadata.json file with the three attributes beside each PDF, sync the data source, and render the metadata of every retrieved reference in the response.
Keep the three attributes in an Amazon DynamoDB table keyed by S3 URI, call BatchGetItem for the cited S3 URIs after each response, and render the returned items.
Keep the three attributes as S3 object tags on each PDF, call GetObjectTagging for every cited S3 URI after each response, and render the returned tag values.

explanation: Each citation in a RetrieveAndGenerate response returns the location of the source it used, so the application can take the cited S3 URIs and read the attributes from the system of record. "Keep the three attributes in an Amazon DynamoDB table keyed by S3 URI" and read them with `BatchGetItem` shows the value that is current when the answer is produced and creates no second copy. "Upload a .metadata.json file" would copy the attributes into sidecar files and into the vector store, which the policy forbids, and a changed value would only appear after the next sync, so it could be stale. "Keep the three attributes as S3 object tags" is also a copy outside the records table that someone would have to keep in step. "Store the three attributes as user-defined object metadata" is a copy as well, and user-defined metadata cannot be modified after upload except by copying the object, which is a poor fit for values that change several times a day. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_agent-runtime_RetrievedReference.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMetadata.html

prompt: A reinsurer has an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over treaty PDFs in Amazon S3. The assistant calls RetrieveAndGenerate and shows the S3 URI of each cited document. Compliance now requires every answer to display the owning business unit, the document version and the effective date of each source, taken from stored data and not from model-generated text. The records team already maintains exactly these attributes as S3 object tags, which also drive its S3 Lifecycle rules, and it updates the tags whenever a document is superseded. The values shown must be current at the moment of the answer. The team may not introduce a new data store, and it may not write additional objects or new object versions to the bucket, which is mirrored to a regulator's archive. No retrieval filter is needed. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Store the three attributes as user-defined object metadata on each PDF, call HeadObject for every cited S3 URI after each response, and render the returned headers.
Upload a .metadata.json file with the three attributes beside each PDF, sync the data source, and render the metadata of every retrieved reference in the response.
Keep the three attributes in an Amazon DynamoDB table keyed by S3 URI, call BatchGetItem for the cited S3 URIs after each response, and render the returned items.
Keep the three attributes as S3 object tags on each PDF, call GetObjectTagging for every cited S3 URI after each response, and render the returned tag values.

explanation: Each citation in a RetrieveAndGenerate response returns the location of the source it used. The attributes already exist as object tags, tags can be added to or replaced on an existing object, and `GetObjectTagging` returns the tag set of an object. "Keep the three attributes as S3 object tags ... call GetObjectTagging for every cited S3 URI" therefore displays stored, current values with no new store and no new objects. "Upload a .metadata.json file" fails because it writes an extra object beside every PDF, which the bucket rule forbids, and a changed tag would not be reflected until the sidecar was rewritten and the data source synced. "Keep the three attributes in an Amazon DynamoDB table" introduces a new data store and a second copy to keep in step with the tags. "Store the three attributes as user-defined object metadata" fails because that metadata cannot be modified after upload; the only way to change it is to copy the object, which writes a new object version to the mirrored bucket each time a document is superseded. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-tagging.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMetadata.html

prompt: A company runs a public assistant on Amazon Bedrock with a versioned guardrail that has a denied topic for legal advice and a sensitive information filter. Model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs is the company's regulated response log. A safety audit sets two controls. First, the on-call engineer must be notified within minutes when the guardrail's refusals of legal-advice requests rise sharply, because this has previously signalled coordinated misuse. Second, several administrator roles legitimately replace the logging configuration during maintenance, so the API calls cannot be denied; if anyone removes the configuration, it must be put back automatically and the security team must be told. Which combination of actions implements both controls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an EventBridge rule for the DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration CloudTrail event that invokes a Lambda function to restore the configuration and notify.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationsIntervened metric in the AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails namespace for the SensitiveInformationPolicy policy type, with an SNS action.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationClientErrors metric in the AWS/Bedrock namespace for the model ID that the production assistant uses, with an SNS action.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationsIntervened metric in the AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails namespace for the TopicPolicy policy type, with an SNS action.
Attach an SCP to the account that denies DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration and PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration to every role except the logging role.

explanation: Guardrails publish `InvocationsIntervened` in the `AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails` namespace, and the `GuardrailPolicyType` dimension separates `TopicPolicy` from the other policy types. An alarm on the TopicPolicy series with an SNS action notifies within minutes when denied-topic refusals spike. The logging configuration is removed with `DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration`, a control plane call that CloudTrail records as a management event; an EventBridge rule can match it and invoke a Lambda function that calls `PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` again and publishes a notification. That is detection plus automatic restoration. The alarm for "the SensitiveInformationPolicy policy type" counts interventions by the personal-data filter, not refusals of legal-advice requests. "Attach an SCP" that denies the two logging APIs would block the administrator roles that have to replace the configuration during maintenance, which the audit rules out, and it restores nothing. "InvocationClientErrors" counts invocations that end in client-side errors; a guardrail refusal is a successful response, so that metric does not follow the misuse signal. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-guardrails-cw-metrics.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

prompt: A company runs a public assistant on Amazon Bedrock with a versioned guardrail that has a denied topic for legal advice and a sensitive information filter. The account is a member account of an organization in AWS Organizations, and model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs is the company's regulated response log. A safety audit sets two controls. First, the on-call engineer must be notified within minutes when the guardrail blocks or masks personal data far more often than usual, because this has previously signalled attempts to harvest customer records. Second, change control forbids automation that modifies production configuration, so the logging configuration must be impossible to remove or alter for every role in the account except the central logging role. Which combination of actions implements both controls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an EventBridge rule for the DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration CloudTrail event that invokes a Lambda function to restore the configuration and notify.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationsIntervened metric in the AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails namespace for the SensitiveInformationPolicy policy type, with an SNS action.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationClientErrors metric in the AWS/Bedrock namespace for the model ID that the production assistant uses, with an SNS action.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the InvocationsIntervened metric in the AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails namespace for the TopicPolicy policy type, with an SNS action.
Attach an SCP to the account that denies DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration and PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration to every role except the logging role.

explanation: Guardrails publish `InvocationsIntervened` in the `AWS/Bedrock/Guardrails` namespace, and the `GuardrailPolicyType` dimension has a `SensitiveInformationPolicy` value. An alarm on that series with an SNS action notifies within minutes when blocking or masking of personal data spikes. For the second control the audit wants prevention without automation: an SCP on the account that denies `DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` and `PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` to every role except the logging role means no other principal in the account can remove or change the configuration, whatever its IAM permissions. The alarm for "the TopicPolicy policy type" follows refusals under the legal-advice topic, not personal-data interventions. "Create an EventBridge rule ... that invokes a Lambda function to restore the configuration" is exactly the kind of automation that changes production configuration, which change control forbids, and it acts only after the log has already been switched off. "InvocationClientErrors" counts client-side errors of model invocations and says nothing about guardrail interventions, which are returned as successful responses. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-guardrails-cw-metrics.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A health insurer builds the corpus for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base from raw claims tables. The transformations are Apache Spark applications that the data team runs on its own Amazon EKS cluster, scheduled by a self-managed Apache Airflow deployment; the company runs no AWS Glue jobs. The jobs write curated tables that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and the team uses an Amazon DataZone domain as its business data catalog. Auditors ask the team to show, for any curated table, which upstream tables and which job runs produced it, and how that has changed over time. The record must be captured as the jobs run and must not be maintained by hand. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add an OpenLineage integration to the transformation jobs, and send their run events to the domain with the Amazon DataZone PostLineageEvent API.
Keep each change to a curated table as a new table version in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and compare the definitions returned by GetTableVersions.
Add the Glue databases to the domain as a data source with lineage enabled, and configure the Glue Spark jobs to send their lineage events to the domain.
Enable CloudTrail data events on the raw and curated S3 buckets, and query the object-level read and write events of each job role with Amazon Athena.

explanation: Data lineage in Amazon DataZone is OpenLineage-compatible: it captures lineage events from OpenLineage-enabled systems or through the API, and `PostLineageEvent` accepts OpenLineage run events. Spark jobs on the team's own cluster can emit those events on every run, so "Add an OpenLineage integration to the transformation jobs, and send their run events to the domain" produces a graph of datasets and job runs in the existing domain, and because DataZone versions lineage with each event, auditors can view it at an earlier point in time. "configure the Glue Spark jobs to send their lineage events" does not apply, because that setting belongs to Spark ETL job runs in AWS Glue and the company runs none; the transformations happen on Amazon EKS. "Enable CloudTrail data events" shows which role read or wrote which object, not which tables a job derived a table from, so the team would have to reconstruct lineage by hand. "compare the definitions returned by GetTableVersions" shows how a table's definition changed, but not its upstream tables or the job runs that produced it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datazone/latest/userguide/datazone-data-lineage.html

prompt: A health insurer builds the corpus for an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base from raw claims files in Amazon S3. AWS Glue Spark jobs read the raw bucket and write curated files that a final job exports to the S3 data source. After a privacy complaint, auditors do not ask how the tables were derived. They ask the team to prove, from now on, which IAM role read or wrote each individual object in the raw and curated buckets and at what time, including reads by people and tools outside the Glue jobs. The company has no Amazon DataZone domain and has decided not to adopt a data catalog product this year. The record must be captured automatically and be searchable with SQL. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add an OpenLineage integration to the transformation jobs, and send their run events to the domain with the Amazon DataZone PostLineageEvent API.
Keep each change to a curated table as a new table version in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and compare the definitions returned by GetTableVersions.
Add the Glue databases to the domain as a data source with lineage enabled, and configure the Glue Spark jobs to send their lineage events to the domain.
Enable CloudTrail data events on the raw and curated S3 buckets, and query the object-level read and write events of each job role with Amazon Athena.

explanation: The auditors want an access record at object level, for every principal. CloudTrail data events for Amazon S3 record object-level API activity such as GetObject and PutObject with the identity that made the call and the time; they are not logged by default, so they have to be enabled on the two buckets, and the delivered events can be queried with Amazon Athena. "Enable CloudTrail data events on the raw and curated S3 buckets" covers Glue job roles and any other reader. "Add the Glue databases to the domain as a data source with lineage enabled" needs an Amazon DataZone domain, which the company does not have and will not adopt, and lineage describes how datasets are derived, not who accessed an object. "send their run events to the domain with the Amazon DataZone PostLineageEvent API" has the same two problems, and it would see only the jobs that emit events, not people and tools outside them. "compare the definitions returned by GetTableVersions" shows changes to table definitions in the Data Catalog and contains no record of object reads or writes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/logging-data-events-with-cloudtrail.html

prompt: A law firm's research assistant calls RetrieveAndGenerate on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The firm's transparency policy requires every answer to rest on the firm's own precedents. To enforce a house writing style, a developer replaced the default knowledge base prompt template with a custom one; the request's retrieval configuration was not touched and contains no filter. Since that release, answers read well but consist of general statements of law: they no longer mention the firm-specific clauses and matter names that they used to quote. For the same queries, the Retrieve API still returns the expected passages from documents of every year, with the default number of results. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The number of results in the retrieval configuration is set too low, so the model receives just the first few of the passages that are relevant.
The custom template omits the $search_results$ placeholder, so the retrieved passages are no longer passed to the model that generates the answer.
The custom template omits the $output_format_instructions$ placeholder, so the model no longer receives the instructions for formatting citations.
A metadata filter in the retrieval configuration of the request excludes part of the corpus, so those documents cannot be retrieved or cited.

explanation: In a knowledge base prompt template, `$search_results$` is the placeholder that Amazon Bedrock replaces with the retrieved results for the user query. Retrieval still works, as the Retrieve API shows, but a custom template without that placeholder never hands the passages to the generating model, so it answers from general knowledge and the firm-specific content disappears. That matches "The custom template omits the $search_results$ placeholder". "The custom template omits the $output_format_instructions$ placeholder" does not fit: without that placeholder the response has no citations, but the answers would still be drawn from the retrieved passages, and here the content itself is no longer grounded. "The number of results in the retrieval configuration is set too low" does not fit because the retrieval configuration was not changed and the default number of results is in use; fewer passages would thin the answers, not remove all firm-specific content. "A metadata filter in the retrieval configuration" does not fit because the request has no filter and documents of every year are still retrieved. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A law firm's research assistant calls RetrieveAndGenerate on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. The firm's transparency policy requires every answer to show the passages it relies on, and the UI renders them from the citations in the response. In the last release a developer changed the request so that it builds its retrieval configuration from the signed-in lawyer's profile; the default prompt template is still in use. Since that release, answers are well grounded and cite several passages each, but lawyers in the Madrid office report that precedents from the Lisbon office are never cited, even for questions those precedents answer directly. A Retrieve call from the console test window, with no retrieval configuration, returns the Lisbon precedents for the same queries. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The number of results in the retrieval configuration is set too low, so the model receives just the first few of the passages that are relevant.
The custom template omits the $search_results$ placeholder, so the retrieved passages are no longer passed to the model that generates the answer.
The custom template omits the $output_format_instructions$ placeholder, so the model no longer receives the instructions for formatting citations.
A metadata filter in the retrieval configuration of the request excludes part of the corpus, so those documents cannot be retrieved or cited.

explanation: A Retrieve or RetrieveAndGenerate request can carry a `retrievalConfiguration` whose `vectorSearchConfiguration.filter` restricts results to documents whose metadata matches. The symptoms point there: answers are grounded and cited, the same query without a retrieval configuration returns the Lisbon precedents, and the only change is a configuration built from the lawyer's profile. "A metadata filter in the retrieval configuration of the request excludes part of the corpus" explains why a whole office's documents never appear for Madrid users. "The custom template omits the $search_results$ placeholder" does not fit because the default template is in use and the answers are grounded in retrieved passages. "The custom template omits the $output_format_instructions$ placeholder" does not fit for the same reason, and because responses do contain citations, which they would not without that placeholder. "The number of results ... is set too low" does not fit because answers cite several passages, and a low limit would drop the lowest-ranked passages from any office, not consistently every Lisbon document, including those that answer the question directly. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A public agency uses an Amazon Bedrock agent to pre-assess benefit applications. The agent calls two action groups and queries a knowledge base of eligibility rules. Under the agency's responsible AI policy, every applicant must receive, in the decision letter, a short explanation in everyday language of which eligibility rules were applied to the case. The letter service inserts the agent's response text into a fixed template and cannot be changed to call other APIs or to process structured data. Legal counsel has ruled that internal reasoning steps, tool names and raw tool inputs must not be disclosed to applicants. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Log InvokeAgent data events for the agent alias in CloudTrail, and keep the event record of every request in an S3 bucket with the retention that the policy requires.
Enable the trace on each InvokeAgent request, and render the rationale, invocation inputs and observations from the orchestration trace with the response.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, and run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query for the model requests and responses that belong to each session.
Add an instruction that tells the agent to end each answer with a short plain-language account of the rules it applied, and present that section with the response.

explanation: The requirement is a reader-friendly explanation that travels inside the response text, because the letter service can only insert that text into its template. An agent instruction that asks for a closing plain-language account of the rules applied puts the explanation where the letter service already looks, in everyday language and without internal detail, so "Add an instruction that tells the agent to end each answer with a short plain-language account" fits. "Enable the trace on each InvokeAgent request" returns the orchestration trace with the rationale, the invocation input sent to action groups or the knowledge base, and the observations; that is the faithful step record, but it is structured data that the letter service cannot process, and it exposes exactly the reasoning steps and raw tool inputs that counsel forbids disclosing. "Enable model invocation logging" stores raw model requests and responses in a log group, which is neither in the letter nor in everyday language. "Log InvokeAgent data events" records who called the agent and when, not which eligibility rules were applied. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/trace-events.html

prompt: A public agency uses an Amazon Bedrock agent to pre-assess benefit applications. The agent calls two action groups and queries a knowledge base of eligibility rules. Under the agency's responsible AI policy, the oversight board must be able to establish, for 7 years, which caseworker identity invoked the agent for which request and at what time, so that every automated pre-assessment can be attributed to an accountable person. Applications contain special-category personal data, and the data protection officer forbids storing prompts, agent reasoning or tool inputs in any audit store. Each caseworker signs in through the agency's identity provider, and the case-management application calls InvokeAgent with that caseworker's own federated IAM role session. The case-management UI must stay as it is. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Log InvokeAgent data events for the agent alias in CloudTrail, and keep the event record of every request in an S3 bucket with the retention that the policy requires.
Enable the trace on each InvokeAgent request, and render the rationale, invocation inputs and observations from the orchestration trace with the response.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs, and run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query for the model requests and responses that belong to each session.
Add an instruction that tells the agent to end each answer with a short plain-language account of the rules it applied, and present that section with the response.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock logs InvokeAgent as a CloudTrail data event, which is recorded when advanced event selectors are configured for the `AWS::Bedrock::AgentAlias` resource type. A CloudTrail event identifies who made the request and when in its userIdentity element, here the caseworker's own role session, and a trail delivers events to an S3 bucket where they can be retained for 7 years. "Log InvokeAgent data events for the agent alias in CloudTrail" therefore gives the attribution record without changing the UI. "Enable the trace on each InvokeAgent request" produces the rationale, invocation inputs and observations of each step; storing or rendering those would put agent reasoning and tool inputs into a record, which the data protection officer forbids, and the trace does not establish the caseworker identity. "Enable model invocation logging" captures the full request and response data of the model calls, so it stores the prompts that must not be kept. "Add an instruction that tells the agent to end each answer with a short plain-language account" changes the response text but records nothing about which caseworker invoked the agent. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

prompt: An HR software company uses an Amazon Bedrock model to draft interview feedback. Before each release, the responsible AI team must test whether drafts differ when only a candidate's name or gender changes. The team has 900 paired prompts. The works council has agreed a four-level rubric of its own that rates differences in warmth and seniority wording between the two drafts of a pair, and each rating must come with an explanation; generic definitions of bias are not accepted. As an independent second signal the council wants an algorithmic toxicity score that is not produced by a judge model. Because the drafts name real candidates, no employee may read them during testing. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run a model evaluation job that uses human workers, with the company's specialists as the work team, on selected pairs.
Run a programmatic model evaluation job with the toxicity metric on the paired prompts as a custom prompt dataset.
Run a model evaluation job that uses a judge model with the Builtin.ProfessionalStyleAndTone metric on the dataset.
Run a model evaluation job that uses a judge model with a custom metric that applies the company's own rating rubric.
Run a model evaluation job that uses a judge model with the Builtin.Stereotyping metric on the paired prompt dataset.

explanation: A judge-based model evaluation job can use custom metrics: you write the judge prompt, optionally with a rubric and rating scale, and the judge model returns a score and an explanation for each response. That is how the council's own four-level rubric is applied, so "a custom metric that applies the company's own rating rubric" is one action. Programmatic model evaluation jobs compute algorithmic metrics, including toxicity, and accept a custom prompt dataset, which gives the second signal without a judge model, so "a programmatic model evaluation job with the toxicity metric" is the other. "the Builtin.Stereotyping metric" scores stereotypes by its built-in definition, which the council does not accept in place of its rubric. "a model evaluation job that uses human workers" is ruled out because no employee may read the drafts. "the Builtin.ProfessionalStyleAndTone metric" judges whether writing style suits a professional setting; it applies neither the agreed rubric nor an algorithmic score, and it says nothing about differences within a pair. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-custom-metrics-prompt-formats.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-tasks.html

prompt: A recruitment platform uses an Amazon Bedrock model to draft interview feedback. Before each release, the responsible AI team must test whether drafts differ in stereotyped content when only a candidate's name or gender changes. The team has 900 paired prompts built from synthetic candidates, so staff may read every draft. The team has no rubric of its own and wants a standard, ready-made measure of stereotyped content, with a score and an explanation for every response so that the two drafts of a pair can be compared. It also needs the company's HR specialists to rate the lowest-scoring pairs themselves before sign-off. The process must be repeatable for every release. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run a model evaluation job that uses human workers, with the company's specialists as the work team, on selected pairs.
Run a programmatic model evaluation job with the toxicity metric on the paired prompts as a custom prompt dataset.
Run a model evaluation job that uses a judge model with the Builtin.ProfessionalStyleAndTone metric on the dataset.
Run a model evaluation job that uses a judge model with a custom metric that applies the company's own rating rubric.
Run a model evaluation job that uses a judge model with the Builtin.Stereotyping metric on the paired prompt dataset.

explanation: A judge-based model evaluation job scores every response on the selected metrics and returns an explanation with each score. `Builtin.Stereotyping` is the ready-made metric for stereotyped content, so running it over the pairs lets the team compare the two drafts of each pair, and 900 prompts fit within the 1,000-prompt limit of one job. For expert review, a model evaluation job that uses human workers sends responses to a work team that the company chooses, which can be its own employees, here the HR specialists. Both jobs can be rerun for each release. "a custom metric that applies the company's own rating rubric" needs a rubric and judge prompt that the team does not have and does not want to write; it asked for a standard measure. "a programmatic model evaluation job with the toxicity metric" measures toxic language, which is not the same as stereotyped content, and it is an algorithmic score, not a judge's score with an explanation. "the Builtin.ProfessionalStyleAndTone metric" rates professional writing style, not stereotypes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-evaluation-metrics.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/human-worker-evaluations.html

prompt: A bank's assistant uses a prompt stored in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Version 4 is in production. A fairness review found that answers to loan questions take a more cautious tone for some customer groups. An engineer has three candidate rewordings in mind and has not created a new version yet. Today she wants a first qualitative look at how each wording answers the same six example questions, so that she can discard the weak ones within the hour. There is no test dataset or reviewer team yet, no scores are required at this stage, and production traffic must stay on version 4. Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST effort?

options.text: Invoke each prompt version by its version ARN over the test prompts, then score both response sets in judge-based evaluation jobs with the same metrics.
Route a small share of production requests to the new version, tag each call with request metadata, and compare the versions from the invocation logs.
Invoke each prompt version by its version ARN over the test prompts, then have a work team of reviewers rate both response sets in a human evaluation job.
Open the prompt in Prompt builder, add the candidate wordings as variants with Compare variants, and review the outputs side by side for each test input.

explanation: Prompt builder lets an author add variants of a prompt, up to three, and compare their outputs side by side for the same test values. For three candidate wordings, six example inputs and a purely qualitative first look, "add the candidate wordings as variants with Compare variants" is the tool made for the job: no version, dataset or job is needed and production is untouched. "score both response sets in judge-based evaluation jobs" is the right gate before a release, but it presupposes prompt versions and a prompt dataset that do not exist yet, and it produces scores nobody has asked for at this stage. "have a work team of reviewers rate both response sets in a human evaluation job" fails for the same reasons and because there is no reviewer team. "Route a small share of production requests to the new version" fails because production traffic must stay on version 4, and there is no new version to route to. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-create.html

prompt: A bank's assistant uses a prompt stored in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Version 4 is in production. A fairness review found that answers to loan questions take a more cautious tone for some customer groups, and version 5 was created to correct this. Version 5 has already passed offline scoring on 600 counterfactual prompts and a review by the bank's own specialists. The risk committee now requires evidence from real customers before full release: over two weeks, version 5 may serve at most 5% of conversations, and the rate at which customers ask for a human agent must be compared between the versions, with every model call attributable to the prompt version that produced it. Model invocation logging is enabled. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Invoke each prompt version by its version ARN over the test prompts, then score both response sets in judge-based evaluation jobs with the same metrics.
Route a small share of production requests to the new version, tag each call with request metadata, and compare the versions from the invocation logs.
Invoke each prompt version by its version ARN over the test prompts, then have a work team of reviewers rate both response sets in a human evaluation job.
Open the prompt in Prompt builder, add the candidate wordings as variants with Compare variants, and review the outputs side by side for each test input.

explanation: The committee asks for a limited live exposure and a comparison of real customer behaviour per version. Sending a small share of conversations to version 5 does the first. For the second, per-request metadata can be set in the `requestMetadata` field of a Converse call and appears in the model invocation logs under the same field, so each logged call is attributable to its prompt version and can be joined with the escalation data. "Route a small share of production requests to the new version, tag each call with request metadata" is therefore the answer. "score both response sets in judge-based evaluation jobs" repeats the offline scoring that version 5 has already passed; a judge model's scores are not evidence from real customers. "have a work team of reviewers rate both response sets" repeats the specialist review and likewise involves no customers. "add the candidate wordings as variants with Compare variants" is an authoring aid for looking at outputs side by side; it serves no production traffic and measures no escalation rate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-mgmt-request-metadata.html

prompt: An insurer serves customers through two foundation models on Amazon Bedrock that come from different providers. The web client calls both through one service that uses the ConverseStream API and relays the stream to the browser; there is no post-processing step between the model and the customer. The company's AI policy forbids investment advice and requires personal data to be masked in every response, and prompts that ask for investment advice must be stopped before they reach a model. The compliance team wants one policy definition that it can version centrally and that is applied identically to both models, with the FEWEST changes to the existing system. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Send each response from a Lambda step to a small Amazon Bedrock model with a prompt that holds the policy, and release the responses that the reviewing model approves.
Call Amazon Comprehend PII detection from a Lambda step for both models, and match the responses against a list of investment terms that is held in AWS AppConfig.
Define one versioned guardrail with a denied topic and a sensitive information filter, and pass it in guardrailConfig on the Converse calls to both of the models.
Define one versioned guardrail with a denied topic and a sensitive information filter, and call ApplyGuardrail with source OUTPUT from a Lambda step for both models.

explanation: Both models are invoked through ConverseStream, and a guardrail named in `guardrailConfig` is evaluated on the prompt and on the model response as part of the call. One versioned guardrail with a denied topic for investment advice and a sensitive information filter is a single, centrally versioned definition, and passing it on the existing calls stops offending prompts before the model and screens the output, with one added request field and no new component. That is "pass it in guardrailConfig on the Converse calls to both of the models". "call ApplyGuardrail with source OUTPUT from a Lambda step" assesses output text only and needs a post-processing step that does not exist, so it screens no prompts and adds a component. "Call Amazon Comprehend PII detection from a Lambda step" also needs that missing step, splits the policy across two mechanisms, and a term list does not stop prompts before they reach the model. "Send each response ... to a small Amazon Bedrock model" likewise adds a step and a model call per response and does nothing about prompts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html

prompt: An insurer serves customers through two models: an Amazon Bedrock model called with the Converse API, and a fine-tuned model hosted on a SageMaker AI endpoint. An existing Lambda step post-processes every response before it is sent. The company's AI policy on financial statements is a 30-page document with many conditional clauses. Compliance requires that every withheld response is stored together with a written rationale of one or two sentences that cites the clause it breaches, so that customers can be told why. The same check must apply to the outputs of both models, and an additional model invocation per response has been accepted. Personal data is already removed upstream. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Send each response from a Lambda step to a small Amazon Bedrock model with a prompt that holds the policy, and release the responses that the reviewing model approves.
Call Amazon Comprehend PII detection from a Lambda step for both models, and match the responses against a list of investment terms that is held in AWS AppConfig.
Define one versioned guardrail with a denied topic and a sensitive information filter, and pass it in guardrailConfig on the Converse calls to both of the models.
Define one versioned guardrail with a denied topic and a sensitive information filter, and call ApplyGuardrail with source OUTPUT from a Lambda step for both models.

explanation: The check has to apply a long policy with conditional clauses and write a rationale that cites the clause, which is a generation task. A reviewing model that receives the policy and the response in its prompt can return a decision with a cited rationale, and because it runs in the existing Lambda step it treats output from the Amazon Bedrock model and from the SageMaker AI endpoint alike; the extra invocation has been accepted. That is "Send each response from a Lambda step to a small Amazon Bedrock model". "call ApplyGuardrail with source OUTPUT" can block text that matches a denied topic, but a denied topic is defined in a short description of at most 1,000 characters, not a 30-page policy, and the result reports which policy intervened, not a written rationale citing a clause. "pass it in guardrailConfig on the Converse calls" has the same limits and does not cover the model on the SageMaker AI endpoint, which is not invoked through Converse. "Call Amazon Comprehend PII detection" addresses personal data, which is already handled, and a term list cannot reason over conditional clauses or write a rationale. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-tiers.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-use-independent-api.html

prompt: A hospital network uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize clinical guidelines for nurses. Each request passes the guideline text as the grounding source, and a guardrail with a contextual grounding check blocks summaries that score below a grounding threshold of 0.75. The responsible AI committee asks for two additions and accepts changes to the application. Nurses must see the evidence behind each summary, and they must see a caution when a summary passed the check only narrowly; the committee does not want more summaries blocked. The committee also wants a weekly view of how grounding confidence is distributed across all summaries, not just how many were blocked. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a relevance threshold to the contextual grounding check in a new guardrail version, so that summaries that do not address the query are blocked.
Read the grounding score from the guardrail trace of each response, publish it as a custom CloudWatch metric, and show a caution banner for marginal scores.
Chart the InvocationsIntervened guardrail metric for the ContextualGroundingPolicy policy type in a CloudWatch dashboard that is reviewed every week.
Display the guideline passages that were supplied as the grounding source beside each summary, so that nurses can check every statement against them.
Raise the grounding threshold of the contextual grounding check from 0.75 to 0.9 in a new guardrail version, and point the application to that version.

explanation: A contextual grounding check produces a confidence score for every response it processes, and the guardrail assessment in the trace lists each contextual grounding filter with its `score`, `threshold` and action. The application can read that score, publish it as a custom CloudWatch metric to chart the weekly distribution across all summaries, and show a caution when a summary passed but sits close to 0.75. Showing the guideline passages that were passed as the grounding source next to the summary gives nurses the evidence. Those are "Read the grounding score from the guardrail trace" and "Display the guideline passages". "Chart the InvocationsIntervened guardrail metric" counts interventions, which is the blocked-only view the committee called insufficient. "Raise the grounding threshold ... from 0.75 to 0.9" blocks more summaries, which the committee does not want, and gives nurses neither evidence nor a caution. "Add a relevance threshold" checks whether a summary addresses the query, a different question from how well it is grounded, and it too would block more. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_GuardrailContextualGroundingFilter.html

prompt: A hospital network uses Amazon Bedrock to summarize clinical guidelines for nurses. Each request passes the guideline text as the grounding source, and a guardrail with a contextual grounding check blocks summaries that score below a grounding threshold of 0.75. After an incident with a weakly grounded summary, the responsible AI committee asks for two changes. Summaries with marginal grounding must no longer reach nurses at all; the committee rejects banners or extra reading on the ward as a safeguard. The committee also wants to see every week how many summaries the grounding check stopped. The application is supplied by a vendor: its guardrail identifier and version are configuration values, but its code and screens cannot be changed. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a relevance threshold to the contextual grounding check in a new guardrail version, so that summaries that do not address the query are blocked.
Read the grounding score from the guardrail trace of each response, publish it as a custom CloudWatch metric, and show a caution banner for marginal scores.
Chart the InvocationsIntervened guardrail metric for the ContextualGroundingPolicy policy type in a CloudWatch dashboard that is reviewed every week.
Display the guideline passages that were supplied as the grounding source beside each summary, so that nurses can check every statement against them.
Raise the grounding threshold of the contextual grounding check from 0.75 to 0.9 in a new guardrail version, and point the application to that version.

explanation: The grounding threshold can be set between 0 and 0.99, and responses that score below it are blocked. Raising it from 0.75 to 0.9 in a new guardrail version, and pointing the application's configuration to that version, keeps marginally grounded summaries from nurses without touching code. Guardrails publish `InvocationsIntervened` in CloudWatch with a `GuardrailPolicyType` dimension that has a `ContextualGroundingPolicy` value, so a dashboard on that series shows each week how many summaries the check stopped, again with no application change. Those are "Raise the grounding threshold" and "Chart the InvocationsIntervened guardrail metric". "Read the grounding score from the guardrail trace ... and show a caution banner" needs application code and a new screen element, and banners are rejected as a safeguard. "Display the guideline passages" also changes the vendor's screens and relies on extra reading on the ward. "Add a relevance threshold" blocks summaries that do not address the query; it does not tighten the grounding requirement that the incident was about. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-guardrails-cw-metrics.html

prompt: A team is about to change the retrieval configuration of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base: more results per query and a reranking model. The team has 300 test questions taken from search logs. No reference answers or other ground truth exist for them, and the subject-matter experts who could write some are unavailable until after the release date. Before release, a CI stage must show whether the passages retrieved with the new settings are relevant to each question and confirm that p95 retrieval latency stays under 800 ms. The results must not be influenced by the model that writes the final answer, which a different team is replacing in the same sprint. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with the citation precision and citation coverage metrics on the questions, and time the RetrieveAndGenerate calls in the test harness.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with the context relevance metric on the questions alone, and time the Retrieve calls made with the new settings in the test harness.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with the context relevance and context coverage metrics and ground truth in the dataset, and time the Retrieve calls in the test harness.
Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with the correctness and faithfulness metrics on the questions, and time the RetrieveAndGenerate calls in the test harness.

explanation: A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job scores what the knowledge base returns, with no response generator involved, so the answering model cannot influence the result. `Builtin.ContextRelevance` measures how relevant the retrieved texts are to the questions and needs only the questions. Latency is not an evaluation metric, so the harness times the `Retrieve` calls and computes p95. That is "a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with the context relevance metric on the questions alone". The option with "context coverage metrics and ground truth in the dataset" cannot run here: context coverage requires ground truth, supplied as `referenceResponses` in the prompt dataset, and none exists or can be written before release. "correctness and faithfulness" in a retrieve-and-generate job judge the generated answer, so the result depends on the answering model that is being replaced, and timing RetrieveAndGenerate includes generation time, not retrieval latency. "citation precision and citation coverage" also score the generated response and its citations, with the same dependence on the generator. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-evaluation-metrics.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-evaluation-prompt-retrieve.html

prompt: A team is about to change the generation side of an assistant built on an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base: a different response model and a rewritten prompt template. The retrieval configuration is unchanged and passed its own evaluation last month. The team has 300 test questions, each with a reference answer written by subject-matter experts. Before release, a CI stage must show whether the final answers are correct and whether they stay true to the retrieved passages, without statements the passages do not support, and it must confirm that p95 end-to-end response time stays under 6 seconds. The product shows answers without source links, so citations are not assessed. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with the citation precision and citation coverage metrics on the questions, and time the RetrieveAndGenerate calls in the test harness.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with the context relevance metric on the questions alone, and time the Retrieve calls made with the new settings in the test harness.
Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job with the context relevance and context coverage metrics and ground truth in the dataset, and time the Retrieve calls in the test harness.
Run a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with the correctness and faithfulness metrics on the questions, and time the RetrieveAndGenerate calls in the test harness.

explanation: The change is in the response generator, so the evaluation has to include generation. A retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job retrieves, generates and then scores the generated response; its metrics include correctness and faithfulness, which is the measure of whether the response stays true to the retrieved texts. End-to-end time is not an evaluation metric, so the harness times the `RetrieveAndGenerate` calls. That is "a retrieve-and-generate RAG evaluation job with the correctness and faithfulness metrics". The two retrieve-only options, with "context relevance and context coverage" or "the context relevance metric on the questions alone", score only what the knowledge base returns; retrieval has not changed and was already evaluated, and those jobs say nothing about the answers of the new model or about end-to-end time. "citation precision and citation coverage" do evaluate the generated response, but they measure how well its citations are supported, and the product shows no citations, so they do not tell the team whether answers are correct. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-base-evaluation-metrics.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt: A travel company runs a trip-planning agent built with Strands Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with observability enabled. For a planning request the agent must call search_flights, search_hotels and get_weather.
