The three calls are independent, and the agent is free to make them in whatever sequence the model chooses, which varies from session to session; additional read-only lookups are acceptable. A regression suite of recorded sessions must fail the build when any of the three required tools was not called, and this check must be deterministic and not scored by a judge model. The suite must also assess whether each session satisfied a list of natural-language success statements. Which AgentCore Evaluations configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: The tool selection accuracy and tool parameter accuracy evaluators on each tool call, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements as assertions.
Builtin.TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements supplied as assertions.
Builtin.TrajectoryExactOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements supplied as assertions.
Builtin.TrajectoryInOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements supplied as assertions.

explanation: AgentCore Evaluations accepts ground truth with a session: an `expectedTrajectory` of tool names and a list of `assertions`. The trajectory evaluators are scored programmatically, with no LLM call. `Builtin.TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch` passes when all expected tools are present in the actual sequence regardless of order, and extra tools are allowed, which is exactly a required set with a free sequence and optional lookups. `Builtin.GoalSuccessRate` validates whether the session satisfied the natural-language assertions. "Builtin.TrajectoryInOrderMatch" requires the expected tools to appear in the listed order, so valid sessions that searched hotels before flights would fail the build. "Builtin.TrajectoryExactOrderMatch" demands the same tools in the same order with no extras, so it would fail both for a different sequence and for an acceptable extra lookup. "The tool selection accuracy and tool parameter accuracy evaluators" are judged with prompt templates sent to a judge model for each tool call, so the check is not deterministic, and they do not compare the session with an expected set of tools. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/ground-truth-evaluations.html

prompt: A retailer runs a refund agent built with Strands Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with observability enabled. For a refund request the agent must call verify_identity, then lookup_order, then issue_refund, in that order. Every tool is a paid partner API, and the retailer's contract and its audit rules treat any further tool call in a refund session as a violation, including repeated or read-only calls. A regression suite of recorded sessions must fail the build when the session contains anything other than those three calls in that sequence, and this check must be deterministic and not scored by a judge model. The suite must also assess whether each session satisfied a list of natural-language success statements. Which AgentCore Evaluations configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: The tool selection accuracy and tool parameter accuracy evaluators on each tool call, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements as assertions.
Builtin.TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements supplied as assertions.
Builtin.TrajectoryExactOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements supplied as assertions.
Builtin.TrajectoryInOrderMatch with the expected trajectory, and Builtin.GoalSuccessRate with the success statements supplied as assertions.

explanation: AgentCore Evaluations accepts ground truth with a session: an `expectedTrajectory` of tool names and a list of `assertions`. The trajectory evaluators are scored programmatically, with no LLM call. `Builtin.TrajectoryExactOrderMatch` passes only when the actual sequence matches the expected one exactly: same tools, same order, no extras. That is the rule here, because any further call is a violation. `Builtin.GoalSuccessRate` validates whether the session satisfied the natural-language assertions. "Builtin.TrajectoryInOrderMatch" checks that the expected tools appear in order but allows extra tools between them, so a session with a forbidden additional call would pass the build. "Builtin.TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch" ignores order and allows extras, so issuing a refund before verifying identity would pass. "The tool selection accuracy and tool parameter accuracy evaluators" are judged with prompt templates sent to a judge model for each tool call, so the check is not deterministic, and they do not compare the whole session with an expected sequence. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/ground-truth-evaluations.html

prompt: A travel company's booking agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and emits OpenTelemetry traces through AgentCore Observability. The support team wants to score the specific sessions that are named in customer complaints, on the day each complaint arrives. The sessions must be rated against the company's compensation policy on a five-point scale that the support managers wrote themselves; the managers have reviewed the standard goal success and tool selection scores and found that they do not express that policy. Finance has not approved continuous scoring of production traffic, and the team wants to avoid building its own scoring pipeline. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a custom evaluator with the company's own evaluation instruction and scoring schema, and select that evaluator for the evaluation.
Run an Amazon Bedrock judge-based model evaluation job on a fixed prompt dataset every week, and chart the scores from the job's S3 output.
Create an online evaluation configuration that samples 10% of sessions, and build a dashboard and an alarm on the results that it writes to CloudWatch.
Select the built-in goal success rate and tool selection accuracy evaluators for the evaluation, and use their scores as they are returned.
Run an on-demand evaluation for each session in question, passing the span or trace IDs of that session to the evaluators that were chosen.

explanation: AgentCore Evaluations offers on-demand evaluation, in which you specify the exact spans or traces to evaluate by their IDs, which is the way to score the particular sessions named in complaints on the day they arrive. A custom evaluator lets you define your own evaluator model, evaluation instruction and scoring schema, and custom evaluators can be used with on-demand evaluations, so the managers' five-point compensation rubric is applied without a home-built pipeline. Those are "Run an on-demand evaluation for each session in question" and "Create a custom evaluator". "Create an online evaluation configuration that samples 10% of sessions" scores live traffic continuously, which finance has not approved, and a sample would rarely contain the session a complaint is about. "Select the built-in goal success rate and tool selection accuracy evaluators" fails because the managers found that those scores do not express the policy, and built-in evaluator prompt templates cannot be modified. "an Amazon Bedrock judge-based model evaluation job on a fixed prompt dataset" scores a model's responses to dataset prompts, not recorded agent sessions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/evaluations-types.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/custom-evaluators.html

prompt: A travel company's booking agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and emits OpenTelemetry traces through AgentCore Observability. Product leaders want a weekly quality report: goal success and tool selection scores trending over time on roughly 10% of production sessions, shown on a CloudWatch dashboard with an alarm when the scores fall. The leaders want the standard definitions of both scores so that the numbers can be compared with other teams, and nobody has written a rubric of the company's own. Scoring individual sessions on request is not needed, and the team wants to avoid building its own scoring pipeline. Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create a custom evaluator with the company's own evaluation instruction and scoring schema, and select that evaluator for the evaluation.
Run an Amazon Bedrock judge-based model evaluation job on a fixed prompt dataset every week, and chart the scores from the job's S3 output.
Create an online evaluation configuration that samples 10% of sessions, and build a dashboard and an alarm on the results that it writes to CloudWatch.
Select the built-in goal success rate and tool selection accuracy evaluators for the evaluation, and use their scores as they are returned.
Run an on-demand evaluation for each session in question, passing the span or trace IDs of that session to the evaluators that were chosen.

explanation: AgentCore Evaluations offers online evaluation, which scores live production traffic continuously. A configuration sets percentage-based sampling of sessions, for example 10%, and names the evaluators; results are saved to a CloudWatch log group and the scores are published as CloudWatch metrics, so a dashboard and an alarm need no custom pipeline. The built-in goal success rate and tool selection accuracy evaluators provide the standard definitions the leaders want. Those are "Create an online evaluation configuration" and "Select the built-in goal success rate and tool selection accuracy evaluators". "Run an on-demand evaluation for each session in question" scores sessions that someone picks by span or trace ID; it does not sample production traffic or produce a trend, and scoring on request is not needed. "Create a custom evaluator" needs an instruction and scoring schema of the company's own, which nobody has written, and its scores would not be comparable with other teams. "an Amazon Bedrock judge-based model evaluation job on a fixed prompt dataset" scores model responses to dataset prompts, not sampled production agent sessions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/evaluations-types.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/results-and-output.html

prompt: A company serves an onboarding workflow through an Amazon Bedrock flow. Client applications call InvokeFlow on the alias named prod, which points to version 7. Version 8, with a rewritten prompt node and a different model, has already passed the full suite of synthetic user journeys in the staging account. Release policy now requires a canary in production: for 24 hours, about 10% of real customer requests must be served by version 8 while the other requests stay on version 7, and completion rates are compared before the remaining traffic moves. The client teams have agreed to read routing settings from configuration, and going back to 100% on version 7 must not require a redeployment. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a second alias that points to the new version, and have the client applications choose between the two aliases by a traffic percentage held in AWS AppConfig.
Create a second alias that points to the new version and run the suite against it, then point prod to the new version, and point prod back to roll back.
Run the suite against the working draft through the test alias, and when it passes, create a version from the draft and point the prod alias to that version.
Point the prod alias to the new version and run the suite against prod, then point prod back to the old version if a check in the suite falls below its threshold.

explanation: A flow alias maps to exactly one version; its routing configuration holds a single entry, so one alias cannot split traffic between version 7 and version 8. A canary therefore needs two aliases and a decision on the caller's side. "Create a second alias that points to the new version, and have the client applications choose between the two aliases by a traffic percentage held in AWS AppConfig" serves about 10% of requests from version 8, and setting the percentage back to zero in configuration returns all traffic to version 7 without a redeployment. "Create a second alias ... then point prod to the new version" is a sound pre-release test, but version 8 has already passed the suite, and repointing prod moves all customers at once, not 10%. "Point the prod alias to the new version and run the suite against prod" also switches every customer at once. "Run the suite against the working draft" tests a mutable draft, not version 8, and ends with a full cutover of prod, so it provides no canary either. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows-deploy.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_agent_CreateFlowAlias.html

prompt: A company serves an onboarding workflow through an Amazon Bedrock flow. Client applications call InvokeFlow on the alias named prod, which points to version 7. Version 8 failed the suite of synthetic user journeys last week and was abandoned. A developer is now making several small edits per hour to one prompt node and must rerun the suite after every edit. The team does not want a flow version or an extra alias to be created for attempts that fail. Customers must stay on version 7 until an attempt passes; release policy accepts a version that the pipeline cuts from the draft in the same run in which the suite passed, and clients must not change the identifier they call. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a second alias that points to the new version, and have the client applications choose between the two aliases by a traffic percentage held in AWS AppConfig.
Create a second alias that points to the new version and run the suite against it, then point prod to the new version, and point prod back to roll back.
Run the suite against the working draft through the test alias, and when it passes, create a version from the draft and point the prod alias to that version.
Point the prod alias to the new version and run the suite against prod, then point prod back to the old version if a check in the suite falls below its threshold.

explanation: When a flow is created, it has a working draft and a test alias, `TSTALIASID`, that points to that draft. The suite can call InvokeFlow with the test alias after every edit, so failed attempts leave nothing behind, and customers stay on version 7 because prod is untouched. When a run passes, the same pipeline run creates a version, which is an immutable snapshot of the draft at that moment, and updates prod to point to it; clients keep calling prod. That is "Run the suite against the working draft through the test alias". "Create a second alias that points to the new version and run the suite against it" tests an immutable version, so every one of the hourly attempts would need a new version, and the team does not want versions or extra aliases for failed attempts. "Point the prod alias to the new version and run the suite against prod" would serve customers from an unvalidated version. "have the client applications choose between the two aliases" also needs a version per attempt, exposes customers to it, and changes the identifier that clients call. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/flows-deploy.html

prompt: A team re-created the data source of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base to move its documents to a new S3 prefix. The chunking strategy was kept: fixed-size chunking with 300-token chunks and 10% overlap. The old data source was deleted before the new one was synced. The application calls the Retrieve API with numberOfResults set to 20 and places all results in the prompt ahead of the task instructions. Since the change, input tokens per request are about the same as before, but the 20 results now often contain pairs of passages with identical text, one located under the old prefix and one under the new prefix, and answers cover noticeably fewer distinct facts. Relevance of the individual passages looks good. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The overlap percentage of the fixed-size chunking is set high, so consecutive chunks repeat a large part of the same text.
Retrieved child chunks are replaced by their parent chunks, so each of the results can carry up to 1,500 tokens into the prompt.
The deleted data source used the RETAIN data deletion policy, so the vector store still holds its chunks beside the new ones.
Query decomposition splits each question into sub-queries, so the results of several retrievals are combined into the prompt.

explanation: A data source has a data deletion policy. With `DELETE`, all data of the data source is deleted when the data source is deleted; with `RETAIN`, the data is retained, and in both cases the vector store itself stays. If the old data source was deleted under RETAIN, its chunks are still in the vector store, and the new sync added the same text again from the new prefix. Retrieval then returns both copies, so 20 results hold far fewer distinct passages, which matches identical pairs under the old and new prefix and thinner answers at an unchanged token count. That is "The deleted data source used the RETAIN data deletion policy". "Retrieved child chunks are replaced by their parent chunks" applies to hierarchical chunking, which is not in use, and it would raise the token count. "The overlap percentage ... is set high" does not fit a 10% overlap, and overlap repeats part of a neighbouring chunk, not a whole passage from another prefix. "Query decomposition" is a RetrieveAndGenerate setting; the application calls Retrieve, and the count is capped at 20. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-ds-delete.html

prompt: A team re-created the data source of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base to move from fixed-size chunking with 300-token chunks to hierarchical chunking with 1,500-token parent chunks and 300-token child chunks. The old data source was deleted with the DELETE data deletion policy before the new one was synced. The application calls the Retrieve API with numberOfResults set to 20 and places all results in the prompt ahead of the task instructions. Since the change, input tokens per request have risen severalfold, the model often ignores the formatting instructions at the end of the prompt, and requests with long questions fail because the input exceeds the context window. No two results contain the same text, and relevance looks good. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The overlap percentage of the fixed-size chunking is set high, so consecutive chunks repeat a large part of the same text.
Retrieved child chunks are replaced by their parent chunks, so each of the results can carry up to 1,500 tokens into the prompt.
The deleted data source used the RETAIN data deletion policy, so the vector store still holds its chunks beside the new ones.
Query decomposition splits each question into sub-queries, so the results of several retrievals are combined into the prompt.

explanation: With hierarchical chunking, the knowledge base searches over child chunks but replaces the retrieved children with their broader parent chunks before returning results, and `numberOfResults` counts the child chunks to retrieve. A setting that used to yield 20 passages of about 300 tokens can now yield many parents of up to 1,500 tokens each. That explains the severalfold rise in input tokens, the neglected instructions at the end of a very long prompt and the context window errors, while relevance stays good. That is "Retrieved child chunks are replaced by their parent chunks"; lowering `numberOfResults` or the parent size fixes it. "The deleted data source used the RETAIN data deletion policy" does not fit because the policy was DELETE and no two results share the same text. "The overlap percentage of the fixed-size chunking is set high" does not fit because fixed-size chunking is no longer used and results do not repeat text. "Query decomposition" is a RetrieveAndGenerate setting; the application calls Retrieve, which returns one result set for the query. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A support chatbot stores every turn of a conversation in Amazon DynamoDB and sends the full history on each Converse call. In sessions longer than about 60 turns, latency and cost climb steadily, and the longest sessions end with an error stating that the input is too long for the model. A form at the start of each session captures the order number, the product and the warranty status; analysis shows that these are the only early details customers refer back to, and otherwise they discuss the current step. The privacy office allows conversation text to be sent to a model only to answer the customer, so no additional model invocations over the transcript are permitted. Which combination of changes addresses the root cause? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store the fields captured at the start of the session as a structured record, and insert that record into the system prompt on every call.
Replace older turns with a model-written running summary that keeps the key facts, and send it together with the most recent turns.
Send the 10 most recent turns on each call, and leave all earlier turns out of the request so that the input keeps a bounded size.
Track the inputTokens value in the usage field of each response, and trigger the summarization step when it crosses a set token budget.
Enable prompt caching with a cache checkpoint after the conversation history, so that the repeated prefix is billed at the cache read rate.

explanation: The root cause is unbounded growth of the input: every call resends the whole history until it no longer fits the context window. Sending only the 10 most recent turns bounds the input, and the early details that matter are known in advance: they are the form fields, so storing them as a structured record and inserting it into the system prompt keeps them available on every call. Neither change needs another model invocation. Those are "Send the 10 most recent turns" and "Store the fields captured at the start of the session". "Replace older turns with a model-written running summary" needs a model call over the transcript to write the summary, which the privacy office does not permit, and "trigger the summarization step when it crosses a set token budget" depends on that same step. "Enable prompt caching" can make a repeated prefix cheaper, but the full history is still sent as input on every call, so the growth and the too-long error remain. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Converse.html

prompt: A support chatbot stores every turn of a conversation in Amazon DynamoDB and sends the full history on each Converse call. In sessions longer than about 60 turns, latency and cost climb steadily, and the longest sessions end with an error stating that the input is too long for the model. Customers in long sessions often refer back to things they said in their own words near the start, such as the symptoms they saw and the fixes they already tried; the session has no intake form, and these details differ from case to case. Additional model invocations are acceptable. Turns vary greatly in length, so the number of turns says little about the size of the input. Which combination of changes addresses the root cause? options.text: Store the fields captured at the start of the session as a structured record, and insert that record into the system prompt on every call.

explanation: The root cause is unbounded growth of the input: every call resends the whole history until it no longer fits the context window. The Converse response returns a `usage` object with `inputTokens`, so the application can measure how large the prompt has become, whatever the length of individual turns, and start compaction at a budget well below the limit. Compaction that replaces older turns with a running summary of the key facts, sent with the most recent turns, bounds the input while the customer's early free-form details stay available. Those are "Track the inputTokens value" and "Replace older turns with a model-written running summary". "Send the 10 most recent turns" drops the early details customers refer back to, and a fixed turn count does not bound tokens when turns vary in length. "Store the fields captured at the start of the session" does not apply because there is no intake form and the details are free text that differs per case. "Enable prompt caching" makes a repeated prefix cheaper, but the full history is still sent as input, so the too-long error remains. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Converse.html

prompt: A claims application in a member account calls Converse from a Lambda function. Its execution role allows bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the inference profile that it uses and on the foundation model in every destination Region, and the code passes no guardrailConfig. On Monday every call began to fail with AccessDeniedException, and the message refers to a guardrail ARN in the organization's management account. Nothing was deployed in the member account over the weekend. The security team confirms that on Sunday it attached an Amazon Bedrock policy in AWS Organizations to the application's OU. Calls from an administrator role in the same account, which allows all Amazon Bedrock actions on all resources, succeed. Which action resolves the error?

options.text: Add the member account to the resource-based policy on the guardrail in the management account so that it grants bedrock:ApplyGuardrail.
Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the foundation model ARN in each destination Region of the inference profile that the function uses.
Allow bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on the management account's guardrail ARN in the identity-based policy of the Lambda execution role.
Add guardrailConfig with the management account's guardrail ARN and its version to each Converse request that the function sends.

explanation: The symptoms point to organization-level guardrail enforcement. Once an Amazon Bedrock policy naming a guardrail is attached to the OU, the guardrail is applied automatically to Converse calls from the member accounts, and the setup guide requires that roles in member accounts have `bedrock:ApplyGuardrail` permission for the management account's guardrail. The administrator role, which allows all Amazon Bedrock actions, succeeds, so the cross-account sharing works for this account; the Lambda role allows only the invoke actions and is denied. "Allow bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on the management account's guardrail ARN in the identity-based policy of the Lambda execution role" fixes it. "Add the member account to the resource-based policy" does not fit because a role in the same account already uses the guardrail successfully. "Add guardrailConfig ... to each Converse request" names the guardrail but grants no permission, and the enforced guardrail is applied whether or not the request names one. "Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the foundation model ARN in each destination Region" is already in place, and the error refers to a guardrail, not a model. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-enforcements.html

prompt: A claims application in a member account calls Converse from a Lambda function. Its execution role allows bedrock:InvokeModel on the inference profile and foundation models that it uses and bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on all guardrail ARNs; the code passes no guardrailConfig. The account was created last week and was moved into the Workloads OU on Sunday. Since then every call fails with AccessDeniedException, and the message refers to a guardrail ARN in the organization's management account. Calls from an administrator role in the same account, which allows all Amazon Bedrock actions on all resources, fail in the same way. Applications in the older accounts of the OU are unaffected. The security team says the OU has had an Amazon Bedrock policy for months and that the guardrail's policy lists account IDs individually. Which action resolves the error?

options.text: Add the member account to the resource-based policy on the guardrail in the management account so that it grants bedrock:ApplyGuardrail.
Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the foundation model ARN in each destination Region of the inference profile that the function uses.
Allow bedrock:ApplyGuardrail on the management account's guardrail ARN in the identity-based policy of the Lambda execution role.
Add guardrailConfig with the management account's guardrail ARN and its version to each Converse request that the function sends.

explanation: Organization-level enforcement applies the management account's guardrail to every Converse call in the OU, and it has two permission sides. Roles in the member account need `bedrock:ApplyGuardrail` in their identity-based policies, and the guardrail needs a resource-based policy that grants `bedrock:ApplyGuardrail` to the member accounts. Here both the Lambda role and an administrator role already allow the action, yet both fail, while older accounts work. The new account is simply missing from a resource-based policy that lists account IDs one by one, so "Add the member account to the resource-based policy on the guardrail in the management account" resolves it. "Allow bedrock:ApplyGuardrail ... in the identity-based policy of the Lambda execution role" is already the case and did not help the administrator role either. "Add guardrailConfig ... to each Converse request" grants nothing; the enforced guardrail is applied regardless of what the request names. "Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the foundation model ARN in each destination Region" addresses model permissions, but the error names the guardrail and the administrator role fails too. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-enforcements.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-resource-based-policies.html

prompt: A nightly job classifies short support tickets with on-demand Converse calls to one model in one Region; the model has both a tokens-per-minute and a requests-per-minute quota. Many calls fail with ThrottlingException (HTTP 429) throughout the two-hour run, even though the SDK already retries with exponential backoff and jitter. CloudWatch shows that tokens per minute peak at about 15% of the token quota, while the number of requests per minute stays flat at the value of the request quota for the whole run. Each request sends roughly 400 input tokens and sets maxTokens to 50; the returned labels average 10 tokens. No ServiceUnavailableException errors are recorded. The job must finish inside its window, so it cannot be slowed down. Which change is MOST likely to stop the errors?

options.text: Call the model through a cross-Region inference profile, because the errors come from capacity in the Region and not from account quotas.
Set maxTokens close to the real output length, because input tokens plus maxTokens are deducted from the token quota when a request starts.
Raise the SDK retry count and widen the backoff with jitter, because the errors come from short bursts that pass within a few seconds.
Request an increase of the requests-per-minute quota for the model, because the job's request rate is what reaches the account's limit.

explanation: A 429 ThrottlingException means the request was denied for exceeding the account's quotas for Amazon Bedrock, and the evidence shows which quota: the request rate sits flat at the requests-per-minute quota for the whole run while tokens peak at 15%. The documented remedies for 429 include requesting a quota increase, so "Request an increase of the requests-per-minute quota for the model" addresses the limit that is actually reached. "Set maxTokens close to the real output length" matters when the token quota is exhausted by reservations, because input tokens plus `max_tokens` are deducted at the start of a request; here maxTokens is already 50 and token use is far below the quota. "Call the model through a cross-Region inference profile" is the advice for 503 capacity errors, which are unrelated to account quotas; none are recorded. "Raise the SDK retry count and widen the backoff" does not fit because the limit is hit continuously for two hours, not in short bursts, so more waiting only pushes the job past its window. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-api-error-codes.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html

prompt: A nightly job summarizes support tickets with on-demand Converse calls that name a model ID in one Region; the model has both a tokens-per-minute and a requests-per-minute quota. Many calls fail with ServiceUnavailableException (HTTP 503) in stretches of ten minutes or more, even though the SDK already retries with exponential backoff and jitter. CloudWatch shows that tokens per minute peak at about 30% of the token quota and requests per minute at about 20% of the request quota. Each request sends roughly 3,000 input tokens and sets maxTokens to 400; summaries average 300 tokens. No ThrottlingException errors are recorded. Policy allows the data to be processed in any Region of the same geography, and the job must finish inside its window. Which change is MOST likely to stop the errors?

options.text: Call the model through a cross-Region inference profile, because the errors come from capacity in the Region and not from account quotas.
Set maxTokens close to the real output length, because input tokens plus maxTokens are deducted from the token quota when a request starts.
Raise the SDK retry count and widen the backoff with jitter, because the errors come from short bursts that pass within a few seconds.
Request an increase of the requests-per-minute quota for the model, because the job's request rate is what reaches the account's limit.

explanation: The troubleshooting guide separates the two errors. A 503 ServiceUnavailableException indicates that the service is experiencing high demand or temporary capacity constraints, and it is not related to account-level quotas or rate limits, which return 429. Its documented remedies are retries with backoff and jitter, which the job already has, and cross-Region inference, which routes requests using compute across different AWS Regions. A geographic inference profile keeps processing inside the geography, which policy allows, so "Call the model through a cross-Region inference profile" is the change. "Set maxTokens close to the real output length" addresses token quota reservations; maxTokens is already near the summary length, usage is at 30%, and the error is not a quota error. "Request an increase of the requests-per-minute quota" does not fit because the request rate is at 20% of its quota and no 429 is returned. "Raise the SDK retry count and widen the backoff" does not fit because the errors last ten minutes or more, not a few seconds, and longer waits put the window at risk. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-api-error-codes.html

prompt: A contracts team extracts clause data with an Anthropic Claude model through InvokeModel on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. Requests include a JSON schema in output_config.format, and the downstream parser has received valid JSON for months. Yesterday a developer tightened the schema to catch bad values earlier: the liability_cap field received minimum and maximum keywords, and the clause_title field received maxLength. Since that deployment, every request returns HTTP 400 within milliseconds, on the first attempt and on every retry. Citations are not enabled on any content block, and the endpoint, model ID, inference profile and IAM policy are unchanged. Requests succeed again when the previous schema is restored. What is the cause, and what should the team do?

options.text: The grammar for the changed schema is still being compiled on the first requests; raise the client timeout and retry the requests that failed.
The schema uses constraints that structured outputs do not support; remove the numeric range and string length constraints from the schema.
The endpoint that now receives the requests does not support output_config.format; send these requests to the bedrock-runtime endpoint again.
Structured outputs cannot be combined with citations for these models; request the cited passages and the schema-constrained JSON in separate calls.

explanation: Structured outputs support a subset of JSON Schema. The documentation lists numerical constraints (`minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf`) and string constraints (`minLength`, `maxLength`) among the unsupported features, and states that a schema containing unsupported features is rejected with a 400 error immediately. The only change is the new keywords, the 400 is instant, and the old schema works, so "The schema uses constraints that structured outputs do not support" is the cause; the team removes those keywords and validates ranges and lengths in the parser. "Structured outputs cannot be combined with citations" describes a real incompatibility that also returns 400, but citations are not enabled here. "The endpoint that now receives the requests does not support output_config.format" does not fit because the requests still go to bedrock-runtime, which supports the parameter. "The grammar for the changed schema is still being compiled" does not fit because compilation of a new schema adds latency of up to a few minutes on first use; it does not produce an immediate 400 on every retry. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/structured-output.html

prompt: A team moved its hand-built prompt into Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. The managed prompt contains the system instructions and a user message with a {{ticket}} variable. prompt: A team added department and year attributes to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base so that queries can be filtered. For each document, such as claims-guide.pdf, it uploaded a sidecar file named claims-guide.metadata.json to the same S3 prefix as the document; every sidecar file is smaller than 1 KB. A sync that started after the upload completed without failed documents. The vector store is an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless index that the team created by hand two years ago and whose engine setting nobody remembers. Unfiltered Retrieve calls return good results, but any call with a filter such as department equals claims returns nothing, and the results of unfiltered calls show none of the custom attributes. Which causes should the team investigate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The sidecar files are stored in a different folder from their source documents, but a metadata file belongs in the same folder.
The vector index was created with the nmslib engine instead of the faiss engine, which causes the metadata files to be ignored.
The sidecar files are larger than 10 KB, which is the limit that the knowledge base documentation sets for a metadata file.
The sidecar files are not named after the full source file name, which for claims-guide.pdf is claims-guide.pdf.metadata.json.
The data source has not been synced since the sidecar files were uploaded, so the knowledge base has not ingested them yet.

explanation: The symptoms say the metadata never reached the index: unfiltered results carry no custom attributes, so a filter on them matches nothing. Two documented conditions are open here. A metadata file must use the same name as its source file, including the extension, with `.metadata.json` appended, so the sidecar for claims-guide.pdf has to be claims-guide.pdf.metadata.json, not claims-guide.metadata.json. And when the vector index is in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, the sync documentation says to check that it uses the `faiss` engine so that metadata files are not ignored; with `nmslib` a new index is needed, and nobody knows the engine of this hand-built index. Those are "The sidecar files are not named after the full source file name" and "The vector index was created with the nmslib engine". "The data source has not been synced" is excluded because a sync ran after the upload. "stored in a different folder" is excluded because the files share the documents' prefix. "larger than 10 KB" is excluded because every file is under 1 KB. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-data-source-sync-ingest.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/s3-data-source-connector.html

prompt: A team added department and year attributes to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base so that queries can be filtered. The documents, such as claims-guide.pdf, are in the docs/ prefix of the bucket. Yesterday the team uploaded one sidecar file per document, named like claims-guide.pdf.metadata.json and smaller than 1 KB each, to a separate metadata/ prefix to keep the bucket tidy. The last sync job finished two days ago. The vector store is an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless index that the console created last month with the faiss engine. Unfiltered Retrieve calls return good results, but any call with a filter such as department equals claims returns nothing, and the results of unfiltered calls show none of the custom attributes. Which causes should the team investigate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The sidecar files are stored in a different folder from their source documents, but a metadata file belongs in the same folder.
The vector index was created with the nmslib engine instead of the faiss engine, which causes the metadata files to be ignored.
The sidecar files are larger than 10 KB, which is the limit that the knowledge base documentation sets for a metadata file.
The sidecar files are not named after the full source file name, which for claims-guide.pdf is claims-guide.pdf.metadata.json.
The data source has not been synced since the sidecar files were uploaded, so the knowledge base has not ingested them yet.

explanation: The symptoms say the metadata never reached the index: unfiltered results carry no custom attributes, so a filter on them matches nothing. Two documented conditions are not met. Each time files are added, modified or removed in the data source, the data source must be synced so that the changes are indexed; the sidecar files arrived yesterday and the last sync ended two days ago. And a metadata file has to be in the same folder as its source document; here the documents are in docs/ and the sidecars in metadata/, so even a new sync would not attach them. Those are "The data source has not been synced since the sidecar files were uploaded" and "The sidecar files are stored in a different folder". "The sidecar files are not named after the full source file name" is excluded because the names already include the .pdf extension before .metadata.json. "The vector index was created with the nmslib engine" is excluded because the index uses faiss. "larger than 10 KB" is excluded because every file is under 1 KB. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/s3-data-source-connector.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-data-source-sync-ingest.html

prompt: A team traces its GenAI API, which runs on Amazon ECS, with the AWS X-Ray SDK. The service wraps each Amazon Bedrock Converse call in a subsegment and records the prompt template ID, the template version and a schema_valid flag from its JSON Schema check as annotations on that subsegment. After a template update, downstream parsing failures rose. In the trace console, a filter expression for template version 12 with schema_valid false works, but it returns only about one trace for every fifteen failed requests that the application log lists for the same hour. For the next week the team needs the trace of every failing request so that it can compare latency with version 11; a CloudWatch alarm on the failure count already exists. What should the team change?

options.text: Record the template ID, template version and schema_valid flag as X-Ray annotations and not as metadata, because annotations are indexed for filter expressions.
Add an X-Ray sampling rule that records 100 percent of the requests to the generation path, because the default rule records a small fraction of the requests.
Pass the template ID and template version in the requestMetadata field of each Converse call, because that field is written to the model invocation log records.
Publish the number of failed schema checks as a custom CloudWatch metric with the template version as a dimension, because alarms are evaluated on metrics.

explanation: By default the X-Ray SDK records the first request each second and five percent of any additional requests, so on a busy service most requests have no trace at all. That matches the evidence: the filter works, but only a small share of the failed requests appears. Sampling rules control how many requests are recorded for a set of criteria such as service name and URL path, and a rule can record all matching requests, which the documentation shows as a debugging rule for a problematic route. "Add an X-Ray sampling rule that records 100 percent of the requests to the generation path" gives the team every trace for the week. "Record the template ID, template version and schema_valid flag as X-Ray annotations" is already done, which is why the filter expression works. "Pass the template ID and template version in the requestMetadata field" tags model invocation log records; it creates no traces and no latency breakdown. "Publish the number of failed schema checks as a custom CloudWatch metric" yields a count, which the existing alarm already covers, not the traces of the failing requests. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-sampling.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts.html

prompt: A team traces its GenAI API, which runs on Amazon ECS, with the AWS X-Ray SDK. The service wraps each Amazon Bedrock Converse call in a subsegment and records the prompt template ID, the template version and a schema_valid flag as annotations; a sampling rule already records every request, and filter expressions on the annotations return all expected traces. After a template update, downstream parsing failures rose. To find out why, the team now wants to read the complete prompts and responses of the calls made with template version 12 and to compare input and output token counts per template version. Model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs is enabled, but nothing in a log record says which template produced it. A CloudWatch alarm on the failure count already exists. What should the team change?

options.text: Record the template ID, template version and schema_valid flag as X-Ray annotations and not as metadata, because annotations are indexed for filter expressions.
Add an X-Ray sampling rule that records 100 percent of the requests to the generation path, because the default rule records a small fraction of the requests.
Pass the template ID and template version in the requestMetadata field of each Converse call, because that field is written to the model invocation log records.
Publish the number of failed schema checks as a custom CloudWatch metric with the template version as a dimension, because alarms are evaluated on metrics.

explanation: The complete request and response bodies and the token counts of each call are in the model invocation log records, not in X-Ray traces. What is missing is a way to tell which template produced a record. Per-request metadata set in the `requestMetadata` field of a Converse call appears in the invocation log under a top-level `requestMetadata` field, so with "Pass the template ID and template version in the requestMetadata field of each Converse call" the team can filter and aggregate the log records by template version with CloudWatch Logs Insights. "Record the template ID, template version and schema_valid flag as X-Ray annotations" is already done, and annotations make traces searchable; they do not add prompts, responses or token counts to the log. "Add an X-Ray sampling rule that records 100 percent" changes nothing because every request is already recorded, and traces still lack the model bodies. "Publish the number of failed schema checks as a custom CloudWatch metric" gives a count per version, which the alarm already covers, but no prompt text and no token counts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-mgmt-request-metadata.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A payments company runs two workloads on one Amazon Bedrock model through the Converse API. A fraud-triage assistant used by analysts in three shifts sends a steady 400,000 input and 60,000 output tokens per minute around the clock. After on-demand throttling stopped triage during a traffic surge last quarter, the business requires capacity that is set aside for this assistant, with an uptime target, and finance has approved a three-month commitment at a fixed monthly price. A nightly regression harness replays multi-turn agent conversations in which the model calls tools; it has an eight-hour window, no latency target, and should cost as little as possible. Which design BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity on the Reserved tier for the interactive workload, and send the offline workload on the Flex tier.
Send the interactive workload on the Priority tier during its peaks and on the Standard tier otherwise, and send the offline workload on the Flex tier.
Keep the interactive workload on the Standard tier, and run the offline workload as a batch inference job with Amazon S3 input and output.
Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity on the Reserved tier for the interactive workload, and run the offline workload as a batch inference job.

explanation: The Reserved tier reserves prioritized capacity with separate input and output tokens-per-minute amounts, targets 99.5 percent uptime, runs for a 1-month or 3-month term at a fixed price, and is separate from the on-demand quota. The steady 400,000 and 60,000 tokens per minute are above the tier's minimums and the commitment is approved, so it matches the set-aside capacity requirement. The Flex tier gives a pricing discount for work that tolerates longer processing, and AWS names model evaluations and agentic workflows as examples; the harness keeps its synchronous tool loop. "Send the interactive workload on the Priority tier during its peaks" fails the set-aside requirement: Priority needs no reservation and draws on the on-demand quota that is shared across the priority, default and flex tiers, which is what was throttled. "Keep the interactive workload on the Standard tier" fails for the same reason. "run the offline workload as a batch inference job" fails because the harness calls tools over several turns, and batch inference does not support tool calling and processes each record independently. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html

prompt: A publisher runs two workloads on one Amazon Bedrock model. An internal editing assistant is used by 40 staff; its response times are acceptable today, and the budget owner will not pay a per-token premium or sign a capacity commitment for it. Each night a job must classify 2 million archived articles. Every article is one independent prompt with no tool use, the prompts are already exported as JSONL files to Amazon S3, and the results are needed in S3 by the next morning. The team does not want to write and operate a client that calls the inference API once per article and handles the retries. Which design BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity on the Reserved tier for the interactive workload, and send the offline workload on the Flex tier.
Send the interactive workload on the Priority tier during its peaks and on the Standard tier otherwise, and send the offline workload on the Flex tier.
Keep the interactive workload on the Standard tier, and run the offline workload as a batch inference job with Amazon S3 input and output.
Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity on the Reserved tier for the interactive workload, and run the offline workload as a batch inference job.

explanation: The editing assistant has no latency problem, so the default Standard tier fits and costs nothing extra. The nightly work is a set of independent single prompts that already sit in Amazon S3 as JSONL, with no tool use and a morning deadline: that is the shape of a batch inference job, which takes the input files from S3 in one `CreateModelInvocationJob` request and writes the responses to S3 asynchronously, so the team operates no per-article client. "Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity on the Reserved tier" fails in both options that contain it, because the budget owner will not sign a capacity commitment and the Reserved tier is a 1-month or 3-month reservation. "Send the interactive workload on the Priority tier during its peaks" fails because Priority carries a price premium that the budget owner refuses and the response times are already acceptable; its second half, "send the offline workload on the Flex tier", is a synchronous per-request tier, so it still needs the calling client with retry handling that the team wants to avoid. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/batch-inference.html

prompt: A SaaS company fronts Amazon Bedrock with an LLM gateway on Amazon ECS. The gateway calls the Converse API for 300 tenants through one shared role, so all spend appears under a single principal. Finance needs invoice-accurate dollars per tenant (the cost owner) in AWS Cost Explorer. The platform team will not create or manage a Bedrock resource or an AWS account for each tenant. Product managers need the token usage of each individual request, sliced by the feature that made the call; the feature changes from one call to the next, and they want to read it from the same record as the logged prompt and response. Model invocation logging is already delivered to CloudWatch Logs. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Have the gateway assume its Bedrock role once per cost owner with session tags, cache those credentials, and activate the tags as cost allocation tags.
Create one tagged application inference profile per cost owner, invoke the model through the profile ARN, and activate the tag as a cost allocation tag.
Pass a label in `requestMetadata` on every call, and aggregate the token counts in the model invocation logs by that label with CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Move each cost owner's traffic to its own member account in AWS Organizations, and group the Amazon Bedrock spend by linked account in AWS Cost Explorer.
Publish the token counts from each response as custom CloudWatch metrics with a label dimension, and build the alarms and dashboards on those metrics.

explanation: IAM principal attribution records the caller identity of every inference request and delivers billed dollars to Cost Explorer and CUR 2.0. Behind a gateway, AWS recommends assuming the Bedrock role per user or tenant with session tags (the trust policy must allow `sts:TagSession`), caching the credentials, and activating the tags as cost allocation tags; that gives per-tenant dollars without any per-tenant resource. Per-request metadata is the per-call mechanism: `requestMetadata` is written to the model invocation log record beside the request body, the response body and the token counts, and it can change on every call, so the already-enabled logs answer the product managers' question. "Create one tagged application inference profile per cost owner" would mean 300 profiles, which the team will not create or manage. "Move each cost owner's traffic to its own member account" breaks the same rule for accounts. "Publish the token counts from each response as custom CloudWatch metrics" fails the requirement to read usage from the same record as the prompt and response, because a metric carries numbers and no request content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-management.html

prompt: An insurer routes six business units through an LLM gateway on Amazon ECS that calls Amazon Bedrock with its task role. A security standard requires the gateway to keep using its task-role credentials directly: no additional role assumption is allowed, and the role's trust policy is frozen. All workloads must stay in the single existing account because of shared network controls. Finance needs billed dollars per business unit (the cost owner) in AWS Cost Explorer. Compliance forbids storing prompts, so model invocation logging stays disabled. Operations must be alerted within minutes when the tokens per minute used by any one feature exceed that feature's limit. Which combination of changes meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Have the gateway assume its Bedrock role once per cost owner with session tags, cache those credentials, and activate the tags as cost allocation tags.
Create one tagged application inference profile per cost owner, invoke the model through the profile ARN, and activate the tag as a cost allocation tag.
Pass a label in `requestMetadata` on every call, and aggregate the token counts in the model invocation logs by that label with CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Move each cost owner's traffic to its own member account in AWS Organizations, and group the Amazon Bedrock spend by linked account in AWS Cost Explorer.
Publish the token counts from each response as custom CloudWatch metrics with a label dimension, and build the alarms and dashboards on those metrics.

explanation: Application inference profiles attribute cost by the tags on the profile resource and deliver billed dollars to Cost Explorer and CUR 2.0 once the tag is activated as a cost allocation tag. Six profiles, one per business unit, are invoked by ARN with the gateway's unchanged task-role credentials, so no role assumption is involved. For the per-feature alert, the gateway already sees the token counts in each response; publishing them as custom CloudWatch metrics with a feature dimension supports an alarm within minutes and stores no prompt text. "Have the gateway assume its Bedrock role once per cost owner with session tags" is ruled out by the security standard, which forbids additional role assumption and freezes the trust policy that would need `sts:TagSession`. "Pass a label in `requestMetadata` on every call" fails because request metadata is recorded only when model invocation logging is enabled, and compliance keeps logging disabled. "Move each cost owner's traffic to its own member account" breaks the single-account rule. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cost-management.html

prompt: A legal-tech company is planning on-demand capacity for a contract-review assistant that calls an Anthropic Claude model on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. The model's documented output-token burndown rate is 5x, and the account's quota is 2,000,000 tokens per minute. At steady state the assistant sends 300 requests per minute. Each request reads a 10,000-token clause library from the prompt cache, adds 2,000 uncached input tokens, writes nothing new to the cache, and returns 800 output tokens; `max_tokens` is set to 1,000. Approximately how much of the tokens-per-minute quota does this workload consume once the responses complete?

options.text: About 840,000 tokens per minute, which is 42 percent of the quota.
About 1,800,000 tokens per minute, which is 90 percent of the quota.
About 3,840,000 tokens per minute, which is 192 percent of the quota.
About 4,800,000 tokens per minute, which is 240 percent of the quota.

explanation: For models on `bedrock-runtime`, the quota consumed by a completed request is InputTokenCount plus CacheWriteInputTokenCount plus OutputTokenCount multiplied by the burndown rate; CacheReadInputTokenCount is not counted. In this scenario the 10,000-token clause library is read from the cache and nothing is written, so each request consumes 2,000 + 0 + (800 x 5) = 6,000 quota tokens, and 300 requests per minute consume 1,800,000, which is 90 percent of the quota. "About 840,000 tokens per minute" is the uncached input plus the output counted once; it ignores the stated 5x burndown, which applies to quota even though billing counts actual tokens. "About 3,840,000 tokens per minute" adds the 10,000 tokens that the stem says are read from the cache and also ignores the burndown rate. "About 4,800,000 tokens per minute" applies the burndown rate but still counts the cache reads, which the documentation excludes from the quota. The start-of-request reservation of input plus `max_tokens` (3,000 here) is lower than the final figure, so it does not change the answer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html

prompt: A regulatory-filings company is planning on-demand capacity for an intake pipeline that calls an Anthropic Claude model on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. The model's documented output-token burndown rate is 5x, and the account's quota is 2,000,000 tokens per minute. At steady state the pipeline sends 300 requests per minute. Every request carries a different 10,000-token filing followed by a cache checkpoint, so the response metadata shows 10,000 tokens written to the prompt cache and none read from it. Each request also has 2,000 uncached input tokens and returns 800 output tokens; `max_tokens` is set to 1,000. Approximately how much of the tokens-per-minute quota does this workload consume once the responses complete?

options.text: About 840,000 tokens per minute, which is 42 percent of the quota.
About 1,800,000 tokens per minute, which is 90 percent of the quota.
About 3,840,000 tokens per minute, which is 192 percent of the quota.
About 4,800,000 tokens per minute, which is 240 percent of the quota.

explanation: For models on `bedrock-runtime`, the quota consumed by a completed request is InputTokenCount plus CacheWriteInputTokenCount plus OutputTokenCount multiplied by the burndown rate; only CacheReadInputTokenCount is left out. Here every filing is different, so the 10,000 tokens are written to the cache on each request and never read back. Each request therefore consumes 2,000 + 10,000 + (800 x 5) = 16,000 quota tokens, and 300 requests per minute consume 4,800,000, which is 240 percent of the quota: the workload will be throttled. "About 1,800,000 tokens per minute" treats the 10,000 tokens as cache reads, but the stem says they are cache writes, and cache writes count toward the quota. "About 840,000 tokens per minute" drops the cache writes and also ignores the stated 5x burndown on output. "About 3,840,000 tokens per minute" counts the cache writes but applies no burndown to the 800 output tokens. A checkpoint that is never reused adds cache-write cost and saves no quota, so the design should remove it or reuse the prefix. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html

prompt: A bank streams chat answers with `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` and applies an Amazon Bedrock guardrail whose sensitive information filters mask account numbers. Compliance requires that no unmasked text ever reaches a customer. Users complain that the first words take too long to appear. Profiling shows the same delay at quiet hours and at busy hours, and most of it passes while the model processes a 14,000-token system prompt and tool definitions that are identical on every request. The budget does not allow a higher per-token price, and the model was fixed by a validation sign-off that would take months to repeat. Which change MOST reduces the time until users see the first text?

options.text: Add a cache checkpoint after the static system prompt and tool definitions so that this prefix is read from the prompt cache.
Set `streamProcessingMode` to `ASYNCHRONOUS` in the guardrail configuration of the streaming request so that chunks are not held.
Send the requests on the Priority service tier so that they are processed ahead of the Standard and Flex traffic for the model.
Move the assistant to a smaller model in the same family that begins and completes its streamed responses more quickly.

explanation: Prompt caching reduces inference response latency and input token cost for long, repeated context: a cache checkpoint after the identical 14,000-token system prompt and tool definitions lets later requests read that prefix from the cache instead of reprocessing it, which attacks exactly the stage that profiling identified. It lowers the price, keeps the validated model, and leaves the guardrail in its default synchronous mode, so masking still happens before text is sent. "Set `streamProcessingMode` to `ASYNCHRONOUS`" is ruled out by the compliance rule: asynchronous mode releases chunks before the scan completes and does not support masking of sensitive information. "Send the requests on the Priority service tier" breaks the budget rule, because Priority is sold at a price premium, and the delay is the same at quiet hours, so contention is not the cause. "Move the assistant to a smaller model" conflicts with the validation sign-off that fixes the model. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: A travel company streams chat answers with `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` and applies an Amazon Bedrock guardrail whose sensitive information filters mask passport numbers. The privacy team requires that no unmasked text ever reaches a traveller. Prompts are short and differ on every request. The time until the first words appear is acceptable for most of the day but degrades sharply during two daily two-hour demand peaks, when on-demand traffic for the model is heavy. The business has approved a higher per-token price during those peaks for this customer-facing flow, and the model was fixed by an evaluation sign-off. Which change MOST reduces the time until users see the first text during the peaks?

options.text: Add a cache checkpoint after the static system prompt and tool definitions so that this prefix is read from the prompt cache.
Set `streamProcessingMode` to `ASYNCHRONOUS` in the guardrail configuration of the streaming request so that chunks are not held.
Send the requests on the Priority service tier so that they are processed ahead of the Standard and Flex traffic for the model.
Move the assistant to a smaller model in the same family that begins and completes its streamed responses more quickly.

explanation: The delay appears only in the two demand peaks, so the problem is how quickly the request is served when on-demand traffic is heavy. The Priority tier delivers the fastest response times for a price premium, needs no reservation, and prioritizes its requests over Standard and Flex requests; the business has approved the premium for the peaks, and the tier is chosen per request. "Set `streamProcessingMode` to `ASYNCHRONOUS`" is ruled out by the privacy requirement: asynchronous mode sends chunks before the guardrail scan completes and does not support masking of sensitive information, and the guardrail is not what changes at peak time. "Add a cache checkpoint after the static system prompt and tool definitions" does not apply, because the prompts are short and differ on every request, so there is no long repeated prefix to read from the cache. "Move the assistant to a smaller model" conflicts with the evaluation sign-off that fixes the model. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html

prompt: A brokerage shows each client a generated commentary on the client's positions. The commentary depends on intraday prices that change every minute, so it is generated when the client opens the page, with a non-streaming Converse call that takes 5 to 8 seconds. The product owner requires text to start appearing within one second of page load; the complete commentary may take longer. Each prompt is about 600 tokens, below the model's minimum for a cache checkpoint, and has no shared prefix of note. Traffic is spread through the trading day and is not throttled, and finance will not approve hourly capacity charges or a commitment. Which design BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: After the nightly data load, run a batch inference job for all accounts, store the results in Amazon DynamoDB, and read them when the page loads.
Call ConverseStream from the page's backend so that the first tokens of each response are rendered as soon as the model generates them.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput sized for the daily peak so that the page's requests have dedicated model capacity available to them.
Add a cache checkpoint with a one-hour TTL after the shared instructions so that each request processes only its own data as new input.

explanation: The requirement is about when text starts to appear, not when it finishes, and the input is only known at page load. ConverseStream returns the response as it is generated, so the first tokens can be rendered well before the 5 to 8 seconds that the whole commentary takes; it changes no price and needs no capacity purchase. "run a batch inference job for all accounts" fails because the commentary depends on intraday prices that change every minute, so results computed after a nightly load would be stale when the client opens the page. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput sized for the daily peak" fails because finance will not approve hourly capacity charges or a commitment, and the workload is not throttled, so capacity is not the cause of the wait. "Add a cache checkpoint with a one-hour TTL after the shared instructions" fails because the 600-token prompt is below the model's minimum for a checkpoint and has no shared prefix; the request would succeed, but nothing would be cached. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html

prompt: A tax-preparation service generates a filing summary when a taxpayer submits a form. Each request sends a 12,000-token rulebook that is identical for every taxpayer, followed by the figures the taxpayer typed moments earlier. The summary is rendered on the server into a PDF, so the taxpayer sees nothing until generation is complete. Requests arrive in bursts separated by quiet gaps of 20 to 40 minutes, and they are not throttled. The company wants the lowest inference cost and shorter processing per request, and finance will not approve hourly capacity charges or a commitment. Which design BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: After the nightly data load, run a batch inference job for all accounts, store the results in Amazon DynamoDB, and read them when the page loads.
Call ConverseStream from the page's backend so that the first tokens of each response are rendered as soon as the model generates them.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput sized for the daily peak so that the page's requests have dedicated model capacity available to them.
Add a cache checkpoint with a one-hour TTL after the shared instructions so that each request processes only its own data as new input.

explanation: The 12,000-token rulebook is identical on every request, which is the case prompt caching is built for: tokens read from the cache are billed at the lower cache-read rate and are not reprocessed, so both cost and processing time fall. The default cache lifetime is 5 minutes and resets on each hit; because the bursts are separated by gaps of 20 to 40 minutes, the one-hour TTL (`"ttl": "1h"` on the cache point, on models that support it) is what keeps the rulebook cached from one burst to the next. "run a batch inference job for all accounts" fails because the figures are typed moments before the request, so there is nothing to pre-compute after a nightly load, and prompt caching is not supported with batch inference. "Call ConverseStream from the page's backend" fails because the summary is rendered into a PDF on the server; streaming changes neither the cost nor the time to a complete document. "Purchase Provisioned Throughput sized for the daily peak" fails because finance will not approve hourly capacity charges and the requests are not throttled. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

prompt: An industrial distributor uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector index that includes a filterable text field. Technicians ask short, single-part questions that contain exact part numbers such as `XR-4471-B`. The Retrieve API returns chunks about similar parts, and the chunk that literally contains the part number is often missing from the five results. The documents were ingested without metadata files, and the application knows nothing about the user beyond the question. The latency budget has no room for another model invocation in the query path. Which change should the team make FIRST to improve retrieval relevance?

options.text: Add a reranker model to the Retrieve request, and raise `numberOfResults` so that more candidate chunks are retrieved and then scored.
Set `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` in the vector search configuration so that the raw text is searched along with the embeddings.
Enable query decomposition on RetrieveAndGenerate so that each question is broken into sub-queries before retrieval takes place.
Add a metadata `filter` to the vector search configuration, built from document attributes that the application already knows.

explanation: Semantic search compares embeddings, which place similar part numbers close together and do not reward a literal token match. Hybrid search combines the vector search with a search through the raw text, so a chunk that contains `XR-4471-B` verbatim is scored on that match. It is a request-level setting (`retrievalConfiguration.vectorSearchConfiguration.overrideSearchType`), it adds no model call, and it is available here because hybrid search is supported for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon RDS and MongoDB vector stores that contain a filterable text field. "Add a reranker model to the Retrieve request" inserts a model invocation into the query path, which the latency budget forbids. "Enable query decomposition on RetrieveAndGenerate" also adds model work and targets multifaceted questions, while these questions are short and single-part. "Add a metadata `filter`" has nothing to filter on: the documents were ingested without metadata files, and the application knows no attribute of the user or the part beyond the question text. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: An equipment maker uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base over the service manuals of 30 product lines, backed by an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector index with a filterable text field. Every manual was ingested with a metadata file that carries `product_line` and `model_year`, and a technician signs in to the application from a specific machine, so the application knows both values. Technicians ask short, single-part questions. The Retrieve API often returns passages from the manuals of other product lines, whose wording is almost identical to the correct passage. The latency budget has no room for another model invocation in the query path. Which change should the team make FIRST to improve retrieval relevance?

options.text: Add a reranker model to the Retrieve request, and raise `numberOfResults` so that more candidate chunks are retrieved and then scored.
Set `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID` in the vector search configuration so that the raw text is searched along with the embeddings.
Enable query decomposition on RetrieveAndGenerate so that each question is broken into sub-queries before retrieval takes place.
Add a metadata `filter` to the vector search configuration, built from document attributes that the application already knows.

explanation: The wrong passages come from other product lines, and the application already knows the technician's `product_line` and `model_year`, which are stored as metadata with every manual. A `filter` in `retrievalConfiguration.vectorSearchConfiguration` (for example `andAll` of two `equals` conditions) restricts the search to documents whose attributes match, so passages from other product lines cannot be returned. It is a request-level setting and adds no model call. "Set `overrideSearchType` to `HYBRID`" does not separate the candidates here: the stem says the competing passages are worded almost identically, so a raw-text match scores them alike. "Add a reranker model to the Retrieve request" inserts a model invocation into the query path, which the latency budget forbids, and a reranker that scores text would face the same near-identical wording. "Enable query decomposition on RetrieveAndGenerate" adds model work and targets multifaceted questions, while these questions are short and single-part. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt: A claims processor calls an Anthropic Claude model on demand through Converse on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. Every request repeats the same 9,000-token policy instructions, adds about 1,500 tokens of claim data, sets `maxTokens` to 16,000, and receives about 400 output tokens. At a sustained 80 requests per minute through the working day, the application receives `ThrottlingException` minute after minute, although the SDK already retries with backoff. The quota is 2,000,000 tokens per minute, and the tokens billed per minute are under half of it. Every request comes from an adjuster who is waiting on screen. Finance has not approved a capacity commitment, and a quota increase will take weeks. Which changes let more requests be admitted under the existing quota? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Lower `maxTokens` to a value just above the largest response that the application expects.
Add a cache checkpoint after the static instructions so that they are read from the prompt cache.
Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity for the workload on the Reserved service tier.
Configure the SDK client to retry throttled requests with exponential backoff and jitter.
Queue the deferrable requests in Amazon SQS, and release them at a steady rate below the quota.

explanation: At the start of each request Amazon Bedrock deducts the input tokens plus `max_tokens` from the tokens-per-minute quota and throttles if the quota is exceeded; the deduction is adjusted to the actual output during processing, and unused tokens are replenished when the request ends. Each request here reserves about 10,500 + 16,000 = 26,500 tokens, so 80 requests reserve about 2.1 million and breach the quota although real usage is far lower. Setting `maxTokens` close to the 400-token completions removes most of that reservation.
