Caching the 9,000-token instructions helps again, because tokens read from the prompt cache do not count toward the quota. "Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity" is ruled out because finance has not approved a commitment, and the Reserved tier is a 1-month or 3-month reservation. "Configure the SDK client to retry throttled requests" is already in place and cannot help when the over-reservation persists minute after minute. "Queue the deferrable requests in Amazon SQS" does not apply, because every request comes from an adjuster waiting on screen and none can be deferred. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html

prompt: A lender calls an Anthropic Claude model on demand through Converse on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. Each request is a unique 3,000-token application with no repeated prefix, `maxTokens` is already 600 for responses of about 450 tokens, and interactive traffic uses about 30 percent of the 2,000,000 tokens-per-minute quota on average. Two problems remain. Spikes of a few seconds when branches open cause `ThrottlingException` errors that users see, because the SDK client is configured with a single attempt. At 01:00 a job submits 200,000 re-scoring requests as fast as it can and exhausts the quota for an hour, although the results are not needed until 07:00 and would fit well within the quota if spread over that window. Finance has not approved a capacity commitment. Which changes resolve these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Lower `maxTokens` to a value just above the largest response that the application expects.
Add a cache checkpoint after the static instructions so that they are read from the prompt cache.
Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity for the workload on the Reserved service tier.
Configure the SDK client to retry throttled requests with exponential backoff and jitter.
Queue the deferrable requests in Amazon SQS, and release them at a steady rate below the quota.

explanation: Both problems are about timing, not about how many tokens each request reserves. The branch-opening spikes last a few seconds while average use is about 30 percent of the quota, so a retry with exponential backoff and jitter lands after the spike has passed; today the client makes a single attempt and passes the first `ThrottlingException` to the user. The re-scoring job has six hours of slack, so queueing its requests in Amazon SQS and releasing them at a steady rate keeps the job below the quota and leaves room for interactive traffic. "Lower `maxTokens`" does nothing more here: it is already 600 for 450-token responses, so the start-of-request reservation is close to actual use. "Add a cache checkpoint after the static instructions" does not apply, because each request is a unique application with no repeated prefix to read from the cache. "Reserve input and output tokens-per-minute capacity" is ruled out because finance has not approved a commitment, and the Reserved tier is a 1-month or 3-month reservation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html

prompt: A marketing team generates product descriptions with an Anthropic Claude model through the Converse API and wants to A/B test sampling settings on live traffic. Variant A uses temperature 0.7. Variant B uses temperature 0.4 and also sets the model's `top_k` parameter to 50. The application code already holds both sets of values and already splits the traffic, and developers are content to change the values in code. Model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs is enabled, and reviewers will score a sample of the outputs of each variant. The team wants to compare token usage and outputs per variant with the LEAST additional infrastructure and no new service. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Store each variant's parameters in AWS AppConfig, read them at run time, and tag every Converse call with a `requestMetadata` variant key.
Save each variant as a version of a Prompt management prompt with its own inference configuration, and invoke the version ARN through Converse.
Send each variant through InvokeModel with a native request body, and publish variant-labelled token counts as custom CloudWatch metrics.
Set each variant's `inferenceConfig` and `additionalModelRequestFields` in the application's Converse calls, and tag every call with `requestMetadata`.

explanation: Converse separates the parameters common to all models from the model-specific ones: `inferenceConfig` holds the base set such as `temperature`, and a parameter such as Claude's `top_k` is passed as JSON in `additionalModelRequestFields`. `requestMetadata` attaches key-value tags to a call, and they are written to the model invocation log record next to the request body, the response body and the token counts, so a CloudWatch Logs Insights query can group usage by variant and pull output samples for the reviewers. Nothing new is deployed, because the code already holds the values and logging is already on. "Store each variant's parameters in AWS AppConfig" adds a service, which the team ruled out, to solve a problem it does not have: developers are content to change values in code. "Save each variant as a version of a Prompt management prompt" also adds a resource to manage for the same non-problem. "publish variant-labelled token counts as custom CloudWatch metrics" adds a metrics pipeline and gives the reviewers no outputs to score, since metrics carry no response text. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html

prompt: A retailer generates product descriptions with an Anthropic Claude model through the Converse API. Prompt engineers who are not developers tune the prompt wording together with temperature and the model's `top_k` parameter, and they must be able to release a new combination without an application deployment. Governance requires that each released combination of wording and settings is kept as one snapshot inside Amazon Bedrock that is not edited afterwards, and that the application selects a combination by an identifier, so that a rollback is a change of identifier. The application will run two released combinations side by side as an A/B test. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Store each variant's parameters in AWS AppConfig, read them at run time, and tag every Converse call with a `requestMetadata` variant key.
Save each variant as a version of a Prompt management prompt with its own inference configuration, and invoke the version ARN through Converse.
Send each variant through InvokeModel with a native request body, and publish variant-labelled token counts as custom CloudWatch metrics.
Set each variant's `inferenceConfig` and `additionalModelRequestFields` in the application's Converse calls, and tag every call with `requestMetadata`.

explanation: Prompt management stores the prompt text together with its inference configuration: the base parameters such as `temperature`, plus model-specific parameters such as `top_k` as additional model request fields. Creating a version takes a snapshot of that configuration, and the application invokes a version by passing its ARN as the model ID in Converse, filling variables with `promptVariables`. Prompt engineers can therefore release a new combination in Amazon Bedrock without a deployment, and a rollback is a change of ARN. When a prompt is invoked this way, the request cannot include `inferenceConfig` or `additionalModelRequestFields`, which keeps the settings in the snapshot. "Store each variant's parameters in AWS AppConfig" allows changes without a deployment, but it keeps the settings apart from the prompt wording and outside Amazon Bedrock, so it does not give the single snapshot that governance requires. "Set each variant's `inferenceConfig` and `additionalModelRequestFields` in the application's Converse calls" and "Send each variant through InvokeModel with a native request body" both keep the values in application code, so every change needs a developer and a deployment. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management-create.html

prompt: A research institute hosts a fine-tuned open-weights LLM as an inference component on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. To stop paying for idle GPU instances, the team configured the endpoint to scale in to zero overnight and to scale out from zero when a request arrives, following the documented procedure, and both directions work. Usage begins at 08:00 sharp on every weekday and there is none at weekends. Each weekday the first requests fail for several minutes while an instance is provisioned. The client is a vendor application whose 30-second timeout and lack of retries cannot be changed. The team wants no failed requests at the start of the day and still wants to pay nothing overnight. Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: Create scheduled scaling actions that raise the inference component's minimum copy count shortly before the working day begins and lower it again in the evening.
Attach a step scaling policy to a CloudWatch alarm on `NoCapacityInvocationFailures` so that the first copy is added on demand.
Change the target tracking policy to the high-resolution `ConcurrentRequestsPerCopy` metric so that scale-out reacts sooner.
Raise the client timeout, and retry failed invocations with exponential backoff until the endpoint returns a response.

explanation: After an endpoint has scaled in to zero, it cannot respond until it provisions at least one instance; AWS states that provisioning takes several minutes and that invocations during that time produce an error. Because usage starts at a known time on weekdays, scheduled actions in Application Auto Scaling can raise the inference component's minimum capacity shortly before 08:00 on weekdays, so the copy is in service when the first request arrives, and return the minimum to zero in the evening so that nothing is paid overnight. "Attach a step scaling policy to a CloudWatch alarm on `NoCapacityInvocationFailures`" is already in place: the stem says scale-out from zero works, and that mechanism is triggered by a failed request, so it cannot prevent the first failures. "Change the target tracking policy to the high-resolution `ConcurrentRequestsPerCopy` metric" cannot help at zero copies, when no per-copy metric is emitted. "Raise the client timeout, and retry failed invocations" is excluded because the vendor application's timeout and retry behaviour cannot be changed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling-zero-instances.html

prompt: A news organization hosts an LLM as an inference component on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that serves readers around the clock, so the minimum copy count stays at two and the endpoint is never scaled to zero. A target tracking policy on invocations per copy adds copies. When a story breaks, the number of simultaneous requests triples within seconds; because each response streams for 20 to 40 seconds, the per-minute invocation count lags far behind the real load, scale-out starts minutes late, and requests queue until they time out. Breaking news cannot be predicted, and the clients already retry with backoff. Which change MOST improves how the endpoint handles these bursts?

options.text: Create scheduled scaling actions that raise the inference component's minimum copy count shortly before the working day begins and lower it again in the evening.
Attach a step scaling policy to a CloudWatch alarm on `NoCapacityInvocationFailures` so that the first copy is added on demand.
Change the target tracking policy to the high-resolution `ConcurrentRequestsPerCopy` metric so that scale-out reacts sooner.
Raise the client timeout, and retry failed invocations with exponential backoff until the endpoint returns a response.

explanation: `ConcurrentRequestsPerCopy` tracks the number of simultaneous requests an inference component is handling, including queued requests, and for streaming models it tracks each request until the last token. It is a high-resolution metric that emits data every 10 seconds, while standard metrics such as invocations per instance emit once a minute, so a target tracking policy on the predefined type `SageMakerInferenceComponentConcurrentRequestsPerCopyHighResolution` scales out much more quickly when concurrency rises. That fits long streamed responses, where load is concurrency and not invocations per minute. "Create scheduled scaling actions" needs a known time, and the stem says breaking news cannot be predicted. "Attach a step scaling policy to a CloudWatch alarm on `NoCapacityInvocationFailures`" addresses scale-out from zero instances; this endpoint keeps at least two copies, so that metric is not emitted. "Raise the client timeout, and retry failed invocations" is already done on the retry side and adds no capacity, so readers would only wait longer. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/endpoint-auto-scaling-add-code-define.html

prompt: A consultancy generates long reports with an Anthropic Claude 4 model on Amazon Bedrock. A browser application calls a Regional REST API in Amazon API Gateway that invokes a Python AWS Lambda function synchronously; the API uses the default integration timeout, and the browser code resubmits automatically on an HTTP 504. The function has a 15-minute timeout and calls `InvokeModel` with a boto3 client configured with `read_timeout` 900 and a single attempt. A report takes about three minutes. AWS X-Ray shows several separate Lambda invocations for one report, each with its own request ID and one Bedrock runtime subsegment that completes successfully after about three minutes. `InvocationThrottles` is zero. What is the MOST likely cause of the duplicate generations?

options.text: The API Gateway integration timeout ends the call before the function finishes, so the web client resubmits the request.
The SDK client's default read timeout expires before the response arrives, so the SDK resends the request to the model.
Lambda retries the function after each failed asynchronous invocation, so every retry issues a new model request.
The on-demand tokens-per-minute quota is exceeded, so the SDK retries each throttled request with backoff.

explanation: The default integration timeout of a Regional REST API is 29 seconds. A three-minute generation cannot return within it, so API Gateway answers the browser with a 504 while the Lambda function keeps running to completion; the browser code then resubmits, and each resubmission starts a new Lambda invocation with its own request ID and its own successful model call. That matches the traces exactly. The fix is to make the flow asynchronous, stream the response, or raise the integration timeout. "The SDK client's default read timeout expires" is excluded by the stem: the client is configured with `read_timeout` 900 and a single attempt, and each Bedrock subsegment completes successfully, where a read timeout would show failed subsegments repeated inside one invocation. "Lambda retries the function after each failed asynchronous invocation" does not fit, because API Gateway invokes the function synchronously and the invocations succeed. "The on-demand tokens-per-minute quota is exceeded" contradicts the zero `InvocationThrottles` value. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-execution-service-limits-table.html

prompt: A law firm generates long case summaries with an Anthropic Claude 4 model on Amazon Bedrock. An Amazon S3 event notification invokes a Python AWS Lambda function asynchronously when a brief is uploaded. The function has a 15-minute timeout and calls `InvokeModel` with a boto3 client configured with `read_timeout` 900 and a single attempt; a summary takes about three minutes. After the model returns, the function raises an AccessDenied error while writing the summary to an output bucket. The model invocation logs show three complete generations for every brief: the second starts about one minute after the first run fails, and the third about two minutes after the second fails. `InvocationThrottles` is zero. What is the MOST likely cause of the duplicate generations?

options.text: The API Gateway integration timeout ends the call before the function finishes, so the web client resubmits the request.
The SDK client's default read timeout expires before the response arrives, so the SDK resends the request to the model.
Lambda retries the function after each failed asynchronous invocation, so every retry issues a new model request.
The on-demand tokens-per-minute quota is exceeded, so the SDK retries each throttled request with backoff.

explanation: For asynchronous invocations, Lambda retries a function that returns an error: by default it runs the function two more times, waiting one minute between the first two attempts and two minutes between the second and third. S3 event notifications invoke the function asynchronously, and the function fails after the model call when the write to the output bucket is denied, so every brief is generated three times at exactly those intervals. Fixing the bucket permission removes the error; configuring fewer retry attempts or making the function idempotent limits the waste. "The SDK client's default read timeout expires" is excluded by the stem: the client uses `read_timeout` 900 with a single attempt and each generation completes. "The API Gateway integration timeout ends the call" does not apply, because the trigger is an S3 event notification and no API or web client is involved. "The on-demand tokens-per-minute quota is exceeded" contradicts the zero `InvocationThrottles` value and the fixed one-minute and two-minute spacing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-async-error-handling.html

prompt: A logistics company runs a Strands agent in containers on Amazon EKS; it does not use AgentCore Runtime or AgentCore Gateway. The agent calls Amazon Bedrock models and several internal tools that are HTTP services in the same cluster. The operations team wants each session's traces and spans, including the model and tool calls, to appear in the Amazon CloudWatch generative AI observability experience, with the least custom telemetry code. No requirement calls for a service-generated record of request and response bodies, and the privacy office has not approved Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging for this account. The AWS account has never used CloudWatch Application Signals or Transaction Search. Which steps are required? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable CloudWatch Transaction Search once for the account so that spans are ingested into CloudWatch Logs.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs so that each request and response body is recorded with the caller's identity.
Add the ADOT SDK to the agent image, start the agent with `opentelemetry-instrument`, and set the documented OTEL environment variables.
Enable tracing and `APPLICATION_LOGS` delivery for the AgentCore Gateway resource in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console.
Publish per-session token and tool-call counts from the agent code as custom CloudWatch metrics in embedded metric format.

explanation: AgentCore Observability supports agents hosted outside AgentCore Runtime. The documented setup is a one-time enablement of CloudWatch Transaction Search, which lets spans be ingested as structured logs, followed by adding the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK to the agent, running it under `opentelemetry-instrument`, creating an agent log group, and setting environment variables such as `AGENT_OBSERVABILITY_ENABLED=true`. Strands has built-in support for OTEL and the GenAI semantic conventions, so no custom tracing code is needed. The account has never used Transaction Search, so that step cannot be skipped. "Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs" is not needed for traces and has not been approved by the privacy office; it produces log records of model calls, not the spans of a session. "Enable tracing and `APPLICATION_LOGS` delivery for the AgentCore Gateway resource" has no resource to act on, because the tools are HTTP services in the cluster and no gateway is used. "Publish per-session token and tool-call counts" is custom telemetry code and yields metrics, not traces. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability-configure.html

prompt: A hospital network runs a LangChain agent in containers on Amazon ECS; it does not use AgentCore Runtime or AgentCore Gateway, and its tools are internal HTTP services. The account already has CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, with span ingestion, for another team's application. The agent emits no telemetry today. Operations wants each session's traces and spans to appear in the Amazon CloudWatch generative AI observability experience with the least custom telemetry code. The security team also requires a record that is produced by the Amazon Bedrock service, independently of the agent's code, of the full request and response of every model call together with the IAM principal that made it. Which steps are required? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable CloudWatch Transaction Search once for the account so that spans are ingested into CloudWatch Logs.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs so that each request and response body is recorded with the caller's identity.
Add the ADOT SDK to the agent image, start the agent with `opentelemetry-instrument`, and set the documented OTEL environment variables.
Enable tracing and `APPLICATION_LOGS` delivery for the AgentCore Gateway resource in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console.
Publish per-session token and tool-call counts from the agent code as custom CloudWatch metrics in embedded metric format.

explanation: Two different records are needed. For session traces, an agent hosted outside AgentCore Runtime adds the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK, runs under `opentelemetry-instrument`, and sets the documented OTEL environment variables; LangChain is one of the frameworks that work with the supported auto-instrumentation, so little code is needed. For the security requirement, model invocation logging is produced by Amazon Bedrock itself and records the request body, the response body, token counts and `identity.arn` for each call, whatever the agent's code does. "Enable CloudWatch Transaction Search once for the account" is a one-time, account-level step that the stem says is already done. "Enable tracing and `APPLICATION_LOGS` delivery for the AgentCore Gateway resource" has no resource to act on, because the tools are internal HTTP services and no gateway is used. "Publish per-session token and tool-call counts" is custom telemetry code that yields metrics, and metrics contain neither spans nor request and response content, so neither requirement is met. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability-configure.html

prompt: A telecom company serves a voice assistant through ConverseStream. Spoken replies are short and of nearly fixed length, about 60 tokens. A customer contract defines the service level as the caller hearing the first word within 1.5 seconds at the 90th percentile, whatever the cause: a release that lengthens the prompt and delays the first word counts as a breach in the same way as a slow service. The on-call team wants an alarm tied to that contractual number, not to a learned baseline. Throttling does not occur today and is covered by a separate alarm. Which alarm BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: A static alarm on p90 `TimeToFirstToken` that fires when the value exceeds a fixed number of milliseconds for several periods.
A metric math alarm on `OutputTokenCount` / (`InvocationLatency` - `TimeToFirstToken`) that fires when the value drops.
An anomaly detection alarm on p90 `InvocationLatency` that fires when the value rises above the band that CloudWatch expects.
A static alarm on the sum of `InvocationThrottles` that fires when the value stays above zero for several periods.

explanation: `TimeToFirstToken` is the time from when a request is sent to when the first token is received, published for the streaming operations ConverseStream and InvokeModelWithResponseStream, which this assistant uses. The contract is a fixed number on the first word at the 90th percentile, so a static threshold on p90 `TimeToFirstToken` measures the commitment directly, and it also rises when a longer prompt delays the first token, which the contract counts as a breach. "A metric math alarm on `OutputTokenCount` / (`InvocationLatency` - `TimeToFirstToken`)" computes output tokens per second; it subtracts the time to first token on purpose, so it stays quiet when the first word is late, which is the opposite of this contract. "An anomaly detection alarm on p90 `InvocationLatency`" measures time to the last token against a learned band, while the team wants the contractual number and the first word. "A static alarm on the sum of `InvocationThrottles`" detects quota pressure, which a separate alarm already covers and which says nothing about delay. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-metrics.html

prompt: A logistics company extracts data from shipping documents with non-streaming `Converse` calls to an Amazon Bedrock model. Traffic follows strong daily and weekly patterns, and latency is naturally higher in the daytime because daytime documents are longer. The team has no fixed latency target. It wants to be alerted when end-to-end latency is unusual for that time of the day and week, without maintaining thresholds as the document mix shifts. Three months of metric history exist in the `AWS/Bedrock` namespace, and throttling does not occur. Which alarm BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: A static alarm on p90 `TimeToFirstToken` that fires when the value exceeds a fixed number of milliseconds for several periods.
A metric math alarm on `OutputTokenCount` / (`InvocationLatency` - `TimeToFirstToken`) that fires when the value drops.
An anomaly detection alarm on p90 `InvocationLatency` that fires when the value rises above the band that CloudWatch expects.
A static alarm on the sum of `InvocationThrottles` that fires when the value stays above zero for several periods.

explanation: `InvocationLatency` is the time from when a request is sent to when the last token is received, and it is published for non-streaming `Converse` calls. A CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm learns the metric's daily and weekly pattern from history and fires when the value leaves the expected band, so it alerts on latency that is unusual for the time of day and needs no threshold maintenance; three months of history is ample. "A static alarm on p90 `TimeToFirstToken`" cannot work here for two reasons stated in the stem: the workload uses non-streaming `Converse`, and Amazon Bedrock publishes `TimeToFirstToken` only for the streaming operations; the team also has no fixed target. "A metric math alarm on `OutputTokenCount` / (`InvocationLatency` - `TimeToFirstToken`)" depends on the same streaming-only metric, so the expression has no data to evaluate. "A static alarm on the sum of `InvocationThrottles`" watches rejected requests, which do not occur here, and not end-to-end latency. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring-runtime-otps.html

prompt: A subsidiary's engineering team owns one member account in its parent company's AWS organization. The team has no access to the management account, and the parent's FinOps group will not make changes there this year. The account runs a single generative AI application that invokes Amazon Bedrock through an application inference profile tagged with an `app` key. Last month the account's Amazon Bedrock spend tripled for four days and nobody noticed. The team wants to be alerted when the spend on any service in its account, including Amazon Bedrock, departs from that service's own pattern, without setting thresholds. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: In the management account, create an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered to each `app` tag value, with alerts on actual and forecasted spend.
In the management account, create a customer managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on selected `app` tag values, with an alert subscription.
In the member account, create an AWS managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services, with an alert subscription for the team.
In the management account, create an AWS managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on the `app` tag key, with an alert subscription.

explanation: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection offers an AWS managed monitor for AWS services that automatically evaluates every service used by the account, learns each one's spending pattern without thresholds, and begins evaluating new services as they are used. That monitor type is available in both management and member accounts, so the team can create it and its alert subscription in the account it owns. Because the account runs a single application, an anomaly in the Amazon Bedrock service is an anomaly in that application. The other three options all begin "In the management account", which the stem rules out: the team has no access there and the FinOps group will not make changes. That is not a formality, because monitors for cost allocation tags can only be created in the management account, so the tag-based monitors cannot be moved into the member account. "an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered to each `app` tag value" would in addition rely on fixed thresholds, which the team does not want. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/getting-started-ad.html

prompt: A company that uses AWS Organizations runs 14 generative AI applications in one shared member account, and its FinOps team works in the management account. Each application invokes Amazon Bedrock through its own application inference profile tagged with an `app` key, and that key is activated as a cost allocation tag. Finance gives every application a fixed monthly allowance. Application owners must be warned when actual spend passes 80 percent of the allowance and when the month-end forecast exceeds it. A spike that stays within the allowance should not alert anyone, and a new application receives its allowance when it is approved. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: In the management account, create an AWS Budgets cost budget filtered to each `app` tag value, with alerts on actual and forecasted spend.
In the management account, create a customer managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on selected `app` tag values, with an alert subscription.
In the member account, create an AWS managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services, with an alert subscription for the team.
In the management account, create an AWS managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on the `app` tag key, with an alert subscription.

explanation: The requirement is a fixed allowance per application with warnings on actual and forecasted spend, which is what AWS Budgets provides: a cost budget can be scoped with a filter on an activated tag, the budgeted amount is the allowance, and alert thresholds can be set on Actual or Forecasted values as a percentage of the budgeted amount. A budget per `app` value therefore warns at 80 percent of actual spend and when the forecast exceeds the allowance, and a new application gets its budget when its allowance is approved. "an AWS managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on the `app` tag key" tracks every tag value independently against a learned pattern; it would alert on a spike that stays within the allowance, which the stem says should not alert anyone, and it has no notion of an allowance or a month-end forecast against one. "a customer managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on selected `app` tag values" has the same mismatch and aggregates the selected values. "an AWS managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for AWS services" evaluates Amazon Bedrock as one service, not each application. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/create-cost-budget.html

prompt: A bank runs Amazon Bedrock workloads in 20 accounts that call InvokeModel and Converse on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint; none of them uses agents or knowledge bases. The organization has no trail today. After an incident, auditors require an organization-wide record, protected against tampering, of which principal invoked which model and when, and the full prompt and response of any individual request. All evidence must be held as objects in an Amazon S3 bucket in a central audit account, where S3 Object Lock retains it for seven years. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an organization CloudTrail trail with log file validation, relying on management events to record the model invocation calls.
Add advanced event selectors to the organization trail for Amazon Bedrock data events on agent aliases and knowledge bases.
Enable model invocation logging to an S3 bucket in each workload account and Region, and replicate the objects to the audit account.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs in each workload account, and link the accounts to the audit account with cross-account observability.
Share the `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metrics with the audit account through cross-account observability, and create alarms on them there.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock logs InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, Converse and ConverseStream to CloudTrail as management events, which a trail records by default with the caller identity, time, source IP and model ID. An organization trail delivers them to a central bucket, and log file validation provides tamper evidence. CloudTrail does not contain prompts or responses; those come from model invocation logging, which records the request body, response body and `identity.arn` for each call. Its destinations must be in the same account and Region as the logging configuration, so each account logs to its own bucket and S3 replication places the objects in the audit account's locked bucket. "Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs" with cross-account observability lets the audit account query the logs, but the data stays in the workload accounts' log groups, which fails the requirement for objects in the audit account's S3 bucket. "Add advanced event selectors" for agent aliases and knowledge bases records nothing here, because the workloads use neither. "Share the `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metrics" gives counts and latency, with no principal and no content. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

prompt: An insurer runs Amazon Bedrock workloads in 12 accounts in one Region. An organization CloudTrail trail with log file validation already records management events. The applications call InvokeAgent and Retrieve as well as Converse. Auditors now require a record of which principal invoked which agent alias and queried which knowledge base. Investigators in the central audit account must also be able to run CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over the prompts and responses of the Converse calls, while a data-ownership policy requires that this payload stays stored in the workload account that produced it, with no copies elsewhere. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an organization CloudTrail trail with log file validation, relying on management events to record the model invocation calls.
Add advanced event selectors to the organization trail for Amazon Bedrock data events on agent aliases and knowledge bases.
Enable model invocation logging to an S3 bucket in each workload account and Region, and replicate the objects to the audit account.
Enable model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs in each workload account, and link the accounts to the audit account with cross-account observability.
Share the `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metrics with the audit account through cross-account observability, and create alarms on them there.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock logs the Agents runtime operations as CloudTrail data events, which a trail does not record by default: InvokeAgent needs an advanced event selector for the `AWS::Bedrock::AgentAlias` resource type, and Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate need one for `AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase`. Adding those selectors to the existing organization trail gives the record of who invoked which alias and queried which knowledge base. For the payload, model invocation logging to a CloudWatch Logs group in each workload account keeps the data where it was produced, and CloudWatch cross-account observability links those source accounts to the audit account as the monitoring account, so investigators can search and analyze the shared log groups without copying them. "Create an organization CloudTrail trail with log file validation, relying on management events" is already in place and does not cover the data events. "replicate the objects to the audit account" creates the copies that the data-ownership policy forbids. "Share the `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metrics" provides counts and latency, with no principal and no prompt or response. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

prompt: Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime call 14 tools through one AgentCore Gateway; some targets are AWS Lambda functions and others are OpenAPI endpoints that partners operate. Users report slow answers, and last week one agent looped on a single tool several thousand times before anyone noticed. The platform team needs to tell, for each tool, whether slow calls are caused by the target or by the gateway itself, and to be alerted when the call volume of any tool departs from its normal pattern. Normal volumes differ widely between tools and by time of day, so the team will not maintain static thresholds. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda targets, and instrument their downstream calls with the X-Ray SDK.
Compare `TargetExecutionTime` with `Duration` for each tool name in the `AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore` metric namespace.
Create CloudWatch alarms with a fixed threshold on the gateway `Invocations` metric for each tool name.
Create CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms on the gateway `Invocations` metric for each tool name.
Count the `toolUse` requests for each tool in the model invocation logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights.

explanation: AgentCore Gateway publishes invocation metrics in the `AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore` namespace with dimensions that include `Name`, the tool name. `Duration` is the total time from receiving the request to sending the final response, and `TargetExecutionTime` is the time taken to execute the target over Lambda, OpenAPI and so on, documented as the way to determine the target's contribution; the difference is the gateway's share, and it works for every target type. `Invocations` per tool is the call-volume signal, and a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm learns each tool's pattern and fires on a departure such as a loop. "Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda targets" covers only the Lambda targets; it shows nothing about the partner-operated OpenAPI endpoints or the gateway's own time. "alarms with a fixed threshold on the gateway `Invocations` metric" are the static thresholds that the team will not maintain, since normal volumes differ by tool and by time of day. "Count the `toolUse` requests" shows what the model asked for, carries no gateway timing, and a query alerts nobody. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability-gateway-metrics.html

prompt: Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime call nine tools through one AgentCore Gateway, and every target is an AWS Lambda function that the platform team owns. The gateway metrics already show that almost all of each slow call's `Duration` is `TargetExecutionTime`. Each function calls Amazon DynamoDB and two partner HTTP APIs, and the team needs to see which of those downstream calls consumes the time. Separately, a partner contract caps one tool at 600 calls per minute, with a financial penalty above the cap, and the team must be alerted when that tool reaches 500 calls per minute, a number that the contract fixes. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the Lambda targets, and instrument their downstream calls with the X-Ray SDK.
Compare `TargetExecutionTime` with `Duration` for each tool name in the `AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore` metric namespace.
Create CloudWatch alarms with a fixed threshold on the gateway `Invocations` metric for each tool name.
Create CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms on the gateway `Invocations` metric for each tool name.
Count the `toolUse` requests for each tool in the model invocation logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights.

explanation: The gateway metrics have already answered the first-level question: the time is in the targets. To see inside a Lambda function, active tracing records the function's segments in AWS X-Ray, and the X-Ray SDK adds subsegments for downstream calls, so the trace shows how long DynamoDB and each partner API take. All targets are Lambda functions that the team owns, so this covers every tool. For the contract, the limit is a fixed number, so a CloudWatch alarm with a static threshold of 500 on the gateway `Invocations` metric for that tool name is the direct fit. "Compare `TargetExecutionTime` with `Duration`" repeats what the stem says is already known and cannot look inside a target. "anomaly detection alarms on the gateway `Invocations` metric" fire on departures from a learned pattern, not at the contractual 500 calls per minute; steady growth toward the cap could stay inside the band. "Count the `toolUse` requests" shows what the model asked for, with no timing of downstream calls, and a query alerts nobody. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/observability-gateway-metrics.html

prompt: A company stores RAG embeddings in an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain that uses approximate k-NN indexes. A nightly ingestion job writes new documents with 32 parallel bulk workers. This week part of the bulk requests returned HTTP 429, while searches against existing data kept working. During the ingestion window CloudWatch shows `ThreadpoolWriteRejected` climbing and `CPUUtilization` near 95 percent on the data nodes. `KNNCircuitBreakerTriggered` is 0, `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage` is about 55, `JVMMemoryPressure` is about 60, and `FreeStorageSpace` is ample. The team wants earlier warning of this condition and a remediation that addresses its cause. Which approach should the team take?

options.text: Alarm on low `FreeStorageSpace`, and increase the EBS volume size of the data nodes or delete indexes that are no longer needed.
Alarm on high `JVMMemoryPressure`, and move the data nodes to instance types that provide a larger Java heap for the cluster.
Alarm on rising `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage`, and add data node memory or reduce the memory footprint of the vectors.
Alarm on `ThreadpoolWriteRejected`, and add data nodes or reduce the number of parallel bulk requests in the ingestion job.

explanation: `ThreadpoolWriteRejected` is the number of rejected tasks in the write thread pool. It is climbing during the ingestion window while CPU is near 95 percent and bulk requests return HTTP 429, so the data nodes cannot keep up with 32 parallel bulk workers. An alarm on that metric warns of the condition, and the cause is addressed either by adding data nodes or by reducing the bulk concurrency of the job. "Alarm on rising `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage`" targets the k-NN circuit breaker, which rejects new `knn_vector` indexing when the value reaches 100; the stem shows the metric at about 55 and `KNNCircuitBreakerTriggered` at 0, so that limit was not hit. "Alarm on high `JVMMemoryPressure`" watches the Java heap, which is at about 60 percent, well below the level at which OpenSearch Service blocks writes. "Alarm on low `FreeStorageSpace`" targets disk, which the stem says is ample; a storage shortage produces a `ClusterBlockException` on writes, not 429 rejections from a busy write pool. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/managedomains-cloudwatchmetrics.html

prompt: A company stores RAG embeddings in an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain that uses approximate k-NN indexes. This week every write failed with `ClusterBlockException`, including writes to an index that holds only text, while searches kept working. CloudWatch shows `ClusterIndexWritesBlocked` at 1 and `JVMMemoryPressure` above 92 percent for the last 40 minutes, since new dashboards began to run heavy aggregations on text fields. `FreeStorageSpace` shows 60 percent of the volume free, `KNNCircuitBreakerTriggered` is 0, `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage` is about 48, and `ThreadpoolWriteRejected` is flat. The team wants earlier warning of this condition and a remediation that addresses its cause. Which approach should the team take?

options.text: Alarm on low `FreeStorageSpace`, and increase the EBS volume size of the data nodes or delete indexes that are no longer needed.
Alarm on high `JVMMemoryPressure`, and move the data nodes to instance types that provide a larger Java heap for the cluster.
Alarm on rising `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage`, and add data node memory or reduce the memory footprint of the vectors.
Alarm on `ThreadpoolWriteRejected`, and add data nodes or reduce the number of parallel bulk requests in the ingestion job.

explanation: When `JVMMemoryPressure` exceeds 92 percent for 30 minutes, OpenSearch Service triggers a protection mechanism and blocks all write operations; writes then fail with `ClusterBlockException` until the metric returns to 88 percent or lower for five minutes. That is the condition in the stem: the heap has been above 92 percent for 40 minutes, `ClusterIndexWritesBlocked` is 1, and even a text-only index is blocked. An alarm on the Maximum of `JVMMemoryPressure` at a lower level warns earlier, and scaling the data nodes to a larger heap addresses the cause, together with fixing the aggregations on text fields. "Alarm on rising `KNNGraphMemoryUsagePercentage`" targets native memory for k-NN graphs; it stands at about 48, the circuit breaker is 0, and that breaker rejects only new `knn_vector` indexing, not writes to a text index. "Alarm on low `FreeStorageSpace`" addresses the other documented cause of `ClusterBlockException`, but 60 percent of the volume is free. "Alarm on `ThreadpoolWriteRejected`" watches a metric that the stem says is flat. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opensearch-service/latest/developerguide/handling-errors.html

prompt: A support organization syncs an Amazon S3 data source into an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base every hour. Ingestion jobs finish with status COMPLETE, but agents keep finding recently uploaded manuals that the assistant cannot cite. The job statistics show nonzero counts of failed and skipped documents and nothing more. For every future sync the team wants a queryable record that names each document that was ignored or that failed during embedding or indexing, together with the reason, and an alarm when that happens, with the LEAST custom code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable model invocation logging with the embedding modality, and analyze the embedding model's records in CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase` resource type, and deliver them through a trail to Amazon S3.
Run a scheduled Lambda function that calls `GetIngestionJob` after each sync and publishes the statistics as custom CloudWatch metrics.
Configure delivery of the knowledge base's `APPLICATION_LOGS` to CloudWatch Logs, and add a metric filter on the failure statuses.

explanation: Knowledge base logging is a vended log delivery (log type `APPLICATION_LOGS`) to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3 or Amazon Data Firehose that tracks the status of each file during an ingestion job. Resource-level records carry the document location, a `status` such as `RESOURCE_IGNORED`, `EMBEDDING_FAILED` or `INDEXING_FAILED`, and the `status_reasons`, so CloudWatch Logs Insights can list the affected manuals and a metric filter with an alarm covers every future sync without code. "calls `GetIngestionJob` after each sync and publishes the statistics" needs custom code and still yields only counters such as `numberOfDocumentsFailed` and `numberOfDocumentsSkipped`, which the team already has; it cannot name a document or a reason. "Enable model invocation logging with the embedding modality" records model calls, not per-document ingestion outcomes: a document that is ignored before embedding produces no model call, and no record states why indexing failed. "Enable CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase` resource type" captures Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate calls, which are query-time operations, not ingestion. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/knowledge-bases-logging.html

prompt: A support organization runs an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that several applications query. Ingestion is healthy: the hourly sync reports no failed or skipped documents. After a data-handling incident, the team must keep, for every future query, a record of which IAM principal called Retrieve or RetrieveAndGenerate on which knowledge base and when. The records must land in the central log-archive bucket that already holds the company's other audit trails. The audit does not need the content of the queries or the retrieved passages, and the team wants the LEAST custom code. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable model invocation logging with the embedding modality, and analyze the embedding model's records in CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the `AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase` resource type, and deliver them through a trail to Amazon S3.
Run a scheduled Lambda function that calls `GetIngestionJob` after each sync and publishes the statistics as custom CloudWatch metrics.
Configure delivery of the knowledge base's `APPLICATION_LOGS` to CloudWatch Logs, and add a metric filter on the failure statuses.

explanation: Amazon Bedrock logs Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate to CloudTrail as data events, which are not recorded by default: an advanced event selector for the `AWS::Bedrock::KnowledgeBase` resource type turns them on. Each event carries the caller identity, the time and the resource, and a trail delivers the events as log files to the S3 bucket you specify, here the central log-archive bucket, with no code. "Configure delivery of the knowledge base's `APPLICATION_LOGS`" tracks the status of files during ingestion jobs; ingestion is healthy, and those logs contain nothing about who queried the knowledge base. "Enable model invocation logging with the embedding modality" records the embedding model's request and response data, which is query content the audit does not need; it does not name the knowledge base that was queried, and the option leaves the records in CloudWatch Logs instead of the log-archive bucket. "calls `GetIngestionJob` after each sync and publishes the statistics" needs custom code and reports ingestion counters, which say nothing about query-time callers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

prompt: An insurer uses Amazon Bedrock Agents with multi-agent collaboration: a supervisor agent routes work to a policy-lookup collaborator that queries a knowledge base and to a claims collaborator that calls an action group. A nightly regression suite replays a golden dataset of 200 questions with known answers through `InvokeAgent` and stores only the final text. Six answers are now wrong, and the final text does not show whether the supervisor misrouted the request, the knowledge base returned the wrong passage, or the claims collaborator passed wrong parameters to its action group. Which approach identifies where each error entered with the LEAST additional instrumentation?

options.text: Enable model invocation logging, and reconstruct each agent's steps by correlating the logged prompts and completions of the sessions.
Set `enableTrace` on the `InvokeAgent` calls, store the trace, and inspect each step's rationale, invocation input and observation.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the agent aliases, and review the `InvokeAgent` events that were recorded for the sessions.
Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the action group's Lambda function, and instrument its downstream calls with the X-Ray SDK.

explanation: When trace is enabled, each chunk of the `InvokeAgent` response is accompanied by a trace part that records the agent's step-by-step reasoning. The orchestration trace holds the rationale, the invocation input (which collaborator, action group and parameters, or which knowledge base query, was chosen) and the observation (what the collaborator, action group or knowledge base returned). With multi-agent collaboration the trace part also names the collaborator and the caller chain, and a routing classifier trace covers the supervisor's routing step. Storing these lets the suite compare a failing run with a passing one and pin the faulty step, with only a request flag. "Enable model invocation logging" yields raw prompts and completions that must be stitched together by hand, without the structured step and collaborator attribution, so it is more work for less. "Enable CloudTrail data events for the agent aliases" records that `InvokeAgent` was called and by whom, not the reasoning or the retrieved passages. "Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the action group's Lambda function" shows timing inside one tool and misses routing and retrieval, two of the three suspected causes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/trace-events.html

prompt: An insurer uses Amazon Bedrock Agents with multi-agent collaboration: a supervisor agent routes work to a policy-lookup collaborator that queries a knowledge base and to a claims collaborator that calls an action group. A nightly regression suite replays 200 questions through `InvokeAgent` with trace enabled and stores the trace. All answers are correct, but 12 runs exceed the 20-second budget. In those runs the stored trace shows correct routing and correct parameters, and the time passes between the action group's invocation input and its observation. The action group's Lambda function calls a policy database, a pricing API and a document store in sequence. Which approach identifies the cause of the slow runs with the LEAST additional instrumentation?

options.text: Enable model invocation logging, and reconstruct each agent's steps by correlating the logged prompts and completions of the sessions.
Set `enableTrace` on the `InvokeAgent` calls, store the trace, and inspect each step's rationale, invocation input and observation.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the agent aliases, and review the `InvokeAgent` events that were recorded for the sessions.
Enable AWS X-Ray active tracing on the action group's Lambda function, and instrument its downstream calls with the X-Ray SDK.

explanation: The stored trace has already localized the problem: routing and parameters are correct, and the time is spent between the action group's invocation input and its observation, that is, inside the Lambda function. The agent trace stops at that boundary. Active tracing makes Lambda send the function's segments to AWS X-Ray, and the X-Ray SDK adds subsegments for the function's downstream calls, so each slow run shows how long the policy database, the pricing API and the document store took. "Set `enableTrace` on the `InvokeAgent` calls" is already done, and the stem shows what it can and cannot see: it records what went into the action group and what came back, not the three calls in between. "Enable model invocation logging" records model prompts and completions, and the slow interval contains no model call. "Enable CloudTrail data events for the agent aliases" records that `InvokeAgent` was called and by whom, with nothing about the time spent inside the function. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-xray.html
